text.0_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Proverbs. In everything there are matter, form, agent, and purpose. Accordingly, he says that the matter of the book is proverbs: a collection of parables. For in order to understand obscure and profound matters that are unknown, one devises a parable for them from things that are known, so that through the familiar garment of the parable, one may perceive what is clothed within it—namely, the unknown meaning of the parable. The agent is Solomon, son of David, and three titles are given to him, because truths become known in three ways: 1) Through wisdom or prophecy; concerning this it says Solomon, for he was wise and the spirit of God rested upon him. 2) Through tradition; concerning this it says son of David, for he possessed a tradition received from his forefathers. 3) Through examination and experience, which are perfected through the gathering of many wise men; concerning this it says king of Israel, for because he was king over this wise and discerning people, all the wise men gathered around him, and he was thereby able to examine every matter, as he said, “All this I tested through wisdom.”
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: “To know wisdom”—the purpose of the book is to know wisdom, etc.
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: The definition of wisdom is to know, regarding all traits, ways, and modes of conduct, that each of them has two paths opposed to one another, such as cruelty and compassion, pride and humility, boldness and shame, eating and fasting, holiness and impurity. Conduct in accordance with one path is wisdom, while its opposite is folly. For example, to conduct oneself with humility is wisdom, whereas to conduct oneself with pride is folly. At times, however, pride is wisdom and humility is folly, as when dealing with the wicked and the insolent. Likewise, regarding everything to which the terms good and evil, proper and improper, may be applied, wisdom teaches which path one should follow, and how, when, and to what extent one should employ each trait.
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 2_Comment: The general principle is that a person cannot understand the ways of wisdom on his own, nor can they be established by demonstration. They are received from God alone, Who ordained the laws of wisdom and taught them to mankind through the two Torahs—the Written Torah and the Oral Torah—in which He prescribed for man all the specific actions determined according to the ways of wisdom. Accordingly, however, it is impossible “to know wisdom,” for knowledge applies only to something that a person knows with certainty, namely, something known through the senses or through self-evident principles. This is impossible with wisdom, which is apprehended neither through the senses nor through rational demonstration, but only through tradition.
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 3_Comment: However, through his proverbs, Solomon taught man to know wisdom, for he explained things that are unknown by means of things that are known, so that through the proverbs a person may apprehend the principles of wisdom with clear knowledge.
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 4_Comment: He accomplished this by teaching through his proverbs to know wisdom and discipline. That is, since the laws of wisdom are opposed to the natural inclination of the human heart—for the heart naturally conceives images contrary to those of wisdom, as it is said (Genesis 8:21), for the inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth—the heart conceives thoughts of pride, jealousy, vengeance, cruelty, and the like. These evil thoughts arise in the heart on their own, and through them the appetitive and emotional faculties wage war against wisdom, while man naturally inclines after them. Since the laws of wisdom cannot be established by rational demonstrations, a person cannot withstand these forces through the power of reason. Nor will the nature of his soul contend against them; on the contrary, the laws of wisdom conflict with the soul’s natural inclinations. He therefore requires discipline: he must chastise and restrain the powers of his soul so that they do not deviate from the laws of wisdom—neither by choosing the path of folly nor by allowing those powers of his soul that incline toward the good to extend and spread beyond the limits that wisdom has prescribed for them.
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 5_Comment: And what is this discipline? This will be explained below (Proverbs 15:33): The fear of the Lord is the discipline of wisdom. From the faculty of fear implanted in the soul there emerges a particular branch—fear of the Lord—which binds the powers of his soul with cords so that they do not transgress the law. For since he believes in God and knows that the laws of wisdom were given by God, he fears God because of His glory and greatness, His judgment and punishment, and he is afraid to depart from the laws of wisdom commanded and enjoined by the supreme King, exalted and sublime. We have already said that knowledge applies only to something known with certainty through sensory perception, a self-evident principle, or demonstration. Nevertheless, a person may also attain certain knowledge of something that he has not learned through the senses or through demonstration, but has received from a trustworthy person in whom he firmly believes, so that the matter becomes engraved in his mind without any doubt, as though he had seen it with his own eyes or apprehended it with his intellect. Thus, through discipline—that is, fear of God, Who made known and taught the laws of wisdom—when his heart believes in Him and in His words and he observes them resolutely out of fear of Him, wisdom becomes established in people’s hearts as something certain. Through discipline, therefore, they come to know wisdom and discipline with clear and certain knowledge.
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 6_Comment: To understand—Understanding differs from wisdom, for it is the ability by which a person understands one thing from another. It also applies to matters that may be described as true or false, as well as to understanding the difficult expressions and obscure riddles spoken by men of understanding.
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 7_Comment: Whereas wisdom is gathered into the soul from without, understanding proceeds outward from the human soul, passing among matters and investigating them, penetrating to know their depths, and uncovering hidden things through the deductions of understanding. This, too, will be taught in this book: to understand words of understanding—to comprehend the obscure sayings of understanding and to understand one thing from another.
text.0_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: To receive the discipline of enlightenment. There is discipline, and there is the discipline of enlightenment. The intellect differs from understanding, for it is a penetrating faculty within man that enters into matters beyond the reach of understanding, such as comprehending matters of wisdom that cannot be clarified through rational demonstrations, and likewise comprehending the truth of the sublime Being and the mysteries of the Account of Creation and the Account of the Chariot, in order to apprehend the greatness of the Creator of the universe. All these are functions of the intellect. The discipline arising from fear of the Lord because one fears His punishment is called simply “discipline.” But the discipline arising from awe of His exaltedness—when one apprehends the greatness of the Holy One, blessed be He, and, in awe of His exaltedness, fears to act contrary to the laws of wisdom that he comprehends through sound intellect—is called “the discipline of enlightenment,” for it is attained through the faculty of the intellect. At times, the Holy Spirit accompanies it, and it is then called “sound intellect.” All this one will receive from the proverbs and figurative expressions of this book. Through these proverbs, he will likewise acquire righteousness and justice, meaning how he should conduct himself in matters between man and his fellow and in civil governance. Justice is what one does according to the law, whereas righteousness goes beyond the letter of the law, taking into consideration the place, time, and circumstances, in accordance with which one will sometimes deviate from the strict line of the law and act according to righteousness. Likewise, he will practice equity. This term applies both to uprightness in one’s opinions regarding theoretical matters and to uprightness in one’s actions regarding practical matters—whether in matters belonging to the category of wisdom or to that of understanding—when one’s thought and actions follow the laws of uprightness. All this will be learned from these proverbs.
text.0_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: To give. He now explains for which classes of people he composed this book, saying that it will benefit every class. To give prudence to the simple—prudence is the opposite of simplicity, for the simple person believes everything, whereas the prudent person understands a matter properly. Through prudence, his heart will not be enticed by everything, and he will examine each matter with his intellect. Therefore, “the prudent” is always presented as the opposite of “the simple.” He thus says that these proverbs will help instill prudence in the heart of the simple person, so that he will examine his ways and conduct and not be like a gullible dove. He adds that the youth, though he is not simple and possesses prudence, nevertheless, because he is young in years, lacks knowledge and discretion. Knowledge is acquired through extensive examination by means of the senses or through the application of intellectual principles; but one who is young in years has not yet examined matters and has not acquired clear knowledge. Likewise, he lacks discretion, which is defined as profound thoughts, for these are not yet present in the heart of a youth. These proverbs will give him both knowledge, enabling him to examine and know each matter, and discretion.
text.0_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Let the wise man hear. These proverbs will also benefit the wise and the understanding. The wise man—defined as one who has received the laws of wisdom from his teachers or through the study of the Torah—will increase his learning, for wisdom is exceedingly broad and has no end. Through these proverbs, he will increase his learning, and his ear will receive many details that were not explained in the Torah or in the tradition of the Sages. And the understanding man—one who understands one thing from another and derives one intellectual conclusion from another by means of deductions—will acquire strategies. The term “strategies” denotes deriving intellectual conclusions through numerous deductions linked together in a chain. Through this book, he will acquire many premises and learn to construct and derive numerous deductions by means of his understanding, one from another and the next from that one, thereby expanding the scope of his understanding.
text.0_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: To understand a parable and its meaning. He now explains the form of the book, which contains both parable and figurative meaning. The figurative meaning is the intended lesson of the parable. From it, they will also learn to understand the parables of the Written Torah and their figurative meaning—that is, the inner intellectual concept beneath the outer garment, which is the parable. Thus, in accounts such as those of the Tree of Knowledge and the serpent, and the like, one will understand both the parable and its intended meaning. Likewise, in the Oral Torah, one will understand the words of the Sages and their riddles: the teachings through which the Sages explained the commandments of the Torah, the ethical instructions they gave, and the like, as well as the aggadic and esoteric teachings that they expressed in the form of riddles. Only the wise of heart can understand these, and they will find their interpretation through the proverbs of this book.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge. Every branch of wisdom has a starting point through which that wisdom becomes known, and these are its foundations. Thus, geometry builds its foundations upon sensory perception and self-evident principles, while natural science is founded upon observation and experience.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: However, the wisdom of the Torah and the wisdom of moral conduct—referred to in this book simply as “wisdom”—have foundations that cannot be known through rational demonstration, as explained above. Rather, this wisdom is received from God, Who established it and also investigated it. Therefore, one cannot attain the status of knowledge regarding it—that is, know it with certainty—except through discipline and fear of the Lord. As stated in verse 1, through the faculty of fear implanted within the soul, a person fears the Lord and is afraid to transgress His will. He prepares his heart to observe the laws of wisdom given by God, and they become established in his heart as trustworthy and true. In this way, he attains knowledge of them, for through his faith in God, the Lawgiver of the laws of wisdom, they become as certain to him as something apprehended through the senses or through self-evident principles. This applies only to one who believes in God and His commandments without doubt.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 2_Comment: However, the fools—the definition of a fool being one who doubts and does not believe—raise doubts both about wisdom and about the fear of the Lord, which is the discipline that constitutes the beginning and foundation of the knowledge of wisdom. They therefore despise both wisdom and discipline.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 3_Comment: This is what he meant by saying that fools despise wisdom and discipline: because the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge. That is, wisdom has no other starting point through which it can be known and apprehended with certainty except the fear of the Lord, which is founded upon faith in God and in the laws of wisdom that came from Him. Fools doubt all these things and therefore despise discipline and the fear of the Lord, together with the wisdom that rests upon them.
text.0_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear. To this he responds to them and demonstrates that the laws of wisdom do have foundations and self-evident principles that every human intellect must necessarily accept. He says: My son, hear the discipline of your father, which he proceeds to explain. The first moral instruction with which a man disciplines his son is something about which no doubt whatsoever can be raised; it is as certain as something apprehended by the senses. From this he establishes that discipline in general is something founded upon and apprehended by the human intellect, and constitutes clear knowledge in which there is no doubt. Therefore, do not forsake the teaching that your mother teaches you. Alternatively, “your mother” refers to the teaching of the community as a whole, which is the universal mother. Do not forsake it, for it has a foundation in discipline and knowledge.
text.0_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: For they are a graceful wreath upon your head—like an ornament of grace fastened upon your head—and necklaces for your throat, ornaments worn around your neck. The head signifies thought and intellect, whose dwelling place is in the head, while the throat, from which speech emerges, signifies the adornment of speech. This means that these moral teachings will impart grace to your thoughts and your speech. The term “wreath” denotes something attached to a person externally, for wisdom does not arise from within the soul, as understanding does, but is received from an external source.
text.0_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: “My son, if sinners entice you”—this is the moral instruction that the father gives his son.
text.0_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: For when he wishes to instruct him in wise conduct, he begins with a simple matter whose reason is evident, clear, and apprehensible with certainty even to a young child: that he should not join a band of murderers to kill people and commit robbery. This is known to everyone, both because of the gravity of murder, which is contrary to human nature, and because of the danger involved, since he places his own life at risk.
text.0_Chapter, 9_Verse, 2_Comment: Therefore, a father begins with this when teaching discipline to his young son, explaining to him the nature of the path of folly and its wickedness. For a teacher begins with something simple and clear, and from this gradually elevates him in his instruction, teaching him not to heed the enticement of sinners in any matter.
text.0_Chapter, 9_Verse, 3_Comment: Therefore, he first states, If sinners entice you, do not consent, a general warning not to listen to them, for their enticements are contrary to the laws of wisdom. He then illustrates this for him with an example drawn from enticement to murder:
text.0_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: If they say, “Come with us; let us lie in wait for blood.” This refers to a band of murderers enticing him. Such a situation may occur in two ways. Sometimes the intended victims resist them and fight for their lives. The murderers then proceed by ambush, plotting through strategies of warfare how to overpower and capture them, and bloodshed ensues between them. Concerning this, it says, Let us lie in wait for blood. At other times, the intended victims are weak or fainthearted people who will not fight against them. Concerning this, it says, Let us secretly ambush the innocent without cause. In that case, the victims are innocent and do not deserve death even according to the murderers’ own judgment, for they did not fight against them. Any harm inflicted upon them is entirely without cause, since the murderers cannot claim that the victims fought against them and killed some of their men. Therefore, the verse uses the expression “let us secretly ambush,” for they do not approach by means of ambush and open combat, but conceal themselves along the road in order to fall upon the victims as they pass and rob them.
text.0_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Let us swallow them. Regarding the case described as Let us secretly ambush the innocent without cause, they will not kill the victims, since they did not fight against them. Rather, Let us swallow them alive, like Sheol—that is, we will swallow them and their property, while they remain alive as perpetual slaves, just as the earth opens its mouth and a person descends alive into Sheol together with all that belongs to him, as occurred with Korah. Regarding the case in which they lie in wait for blood and kill their victims, Let us swallow them whole, like those who descend into the pit, for one who descends into the pit is dead. Nevertheless, although they are no longer alive, they are “whole”; that is, we will take all their wealth and possessions, like one who descends into the pit and leaves everything he owns to his heirs.
text.0_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: All. First, we shall find all kinds of precious wealth, such as silver and gold. Second, we shall fill our houses with spoil: the objects they find and take as spoil will be divided so that each person may bring his share home for use among his household possessions. The gold and wealth, however, they will not take to their individual homes, but will place in the band’s common treasury, as he proceeds to explain:
text.0_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Your lot. As for the spoils consisting of objects and utensils, they will divide these among themselves by lot, with each person taking his portion home. Cast your lot among us—take your share by lot as one of us. But the wealth and money will be placed in the common purse of the band’s treasury: we shall all have one purse, and you will have a share in it.
text.0_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, do not walk on the road with them. A “road” is a broad route established for the public, whereas “paths” are used by individuals. He adds that not only should you refrain from walking with them on their broad road, which is established for them all, but do not walk in their path—the path taken by even one of them. He further adds that not only should you refrain from walking together with them, but even when they are not present there, withhold your foot from walking on a path taken by one of them, for they will murder you as well.
text.0_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: For their feet run toward evil. The father informs his young son that everything toward which they run is evil, for robbery is an evil thing. In this way, the father begins teaching his son with something that his intellect can easily understand. He then adds that, beyond its being evil, they will also murder you, for they hasten to shed blood. Nor should you think that you will meanwhile escape from their hands, for they will act swiftly.
text.0_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: For the net is spread freely in the sight of every winged creature. When a bird sees a net with various kinds of food scattered upon it, it imagines that the food is being given to it freely and that nothing will be demanded from it in return.
text.0_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: But they—the hunters—lie in wait for their blood; that is, either they lie in wait to kill them, or they secretly ambush their lives, intending to capture them alive.
text.0_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: So are the ways of everyone who pursues unjust gain. Every person who pursues unjust gain follows this path: he spreads a net to catch the unsuspecting person, who, like a gullible dove, is enticed into his net. It appears to him that he is being given money and precious wealth for nothing, but in truth, the unjust gain takes the life of its owner. When they see that you possess wealth, they will take your life and rob it from you, as it says, “They hasten to shed blood.” In this way, the father also makes clear to his son the danger involved. From what is known, he thus teaches him what is unknown: to guard himself against the enticement of sinners in every form.
text.0_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Wisdoms. After mentioning how a father begins teaching the laws of wisdom to his young son, he says that wisdom reveals herself gradually, becoming increasingly manifest from one level to the next. He enumerates four ascending stages. At first, she sings aloud outside. “Outside” is the place behind the houses, where only the small children and the residents of the courtyard are found. Afterward, in the streets she raises her voice. The street is the broad area before the houses, where the adults who live in that alley are found. Raising one’s voice is more than singing aloud, for one who sings does so to himself, whereas one who raises his voice intends another person to hear him. Thus, wisdom first begins to reveal herself privately to the youths behind the houses. Afterward, she becomes more manifest, until the preacher stands and raises his voice in the street before the adults. And afterward—
text.0_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: At the head of the bustling places she calls out. She reveals herself in the marketplace, where all the inhabitants of the city gather for commerce. There she “calls out,” for calling out is more than raising one’s voice: one who calls directs his call toward particular people, whereas one who merely raises his voice addresses everyone generally. That is, the prophet or preacher will then stand before great multitudes. Afterward, at the entrances of the gates in the city, she speaks her words. The judges and elders sit there, and there she speaks her words and reveals her wisdom to the elders of the gate, until the light of wisdom breaks forth like a radiant light that grows increasingly bright until the day is fully established. And she says:
text.0_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: How long, simple ones, will you love simplicity? The simple person is enticed toward the path of folly without knowledge. Therefore, it says: How long will you love being enticed without knowledge? For wisdom gives prudence to the simple. And how long will scorners desire scorning for themselves? The scorner mocks wisdom because it has no rational demonstrations. He does not hate wisdom because it cannot be known with certainty; rather, scorners refuse to accept it through tradition, by means of discipline and fear of the Lord, because they delight in mocking matters of faith for which there is no demonstration. The fool, however, knows the laws of wisdom but turns away from them because of his desire, since the laws of wisdom oppose the inclinations of his evil heart. In this respect, he is worse than the scorner, for the scorner does not hate knowledge and mocks only something that he cannot know with certainty. But the fool, although he knows the laws of wisdom with certainty, turns away from them because fools hate knowledge, since the knowledge of wisdom places a bridle upon the desires of the heart.
text.0_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: Return at my rebuke. Wisdom tells them to turn back from their evil way: 1) because of the rebuke through which she reasons with them and teaches them the ways of wisdom and its truth; 2) I shall pour forth my spirit to you—the spirit of wisdom will be like a flowing spring within their hearts and will teach them its laws and truths; 3) I shall make my words known to you—this refers to the punishment destined for one who abandons wisdom, as he proceeds to explain.
text.0_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: Because. Corresponding to what was stated, “Return at my rebuke,” it says, because I called and you refused. Wisdom calls to people and reasons with them. She also calls within their hearts and pours her spirit upon them, as stated, “I shall pour forth my spirit to you,” for the faculties of the human soul were prepared to receive the laws of wisdom, and the heart senses the spirit of wisdom filling all the chambers of the soul and whispering to it to heed her voice. Nevertheless, you refused to heed this call. Corresponding to I shall make my words known to you—the words concerning the punishment destined for one who transgresses the laws of wisdom—it says, I extended my hand. Extending the hand signifies striking, as in, “I shall stretch out My hand against you and destroy you.” I wanted you to return to the ways of wisdom out of fear of punishment, but no one listened.
text.0_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: And you rejected. Corresponding to the statement “Because I called,” which refers to the counsel that wisdom places within a person’s heart, as though advising him concerning the good path on which he should walk, it says, you rejected all my counsel. Corresponding to “I extended my hand,” which refers to her rebuking him through fear of punishment, it says, you did not desire my rebuke—you did not desire to heed the rebuke, as stated, “but no one listened.”
text.0_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: I, too, shall laugh at your calamity. Calamity is the trouble itself, whereas fear precedes the trouble, for fear is defined as apprehension of something when one does not know what one fears. It adds, I shall mock when your fear comes, which occurs before the trouble, and then explains:
text.0_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: When your fear comes like devastation. Fear will come like devastation and darkness, for fear intensifies in the gloom, when one cannot see the nature of the thing one fears.
text.0_Chapter, 26_Verse, 1_Comment: And your calamity shall arrive swiftly like a whirlwind. Immediately after the devastation and fear, calamity will follow. There is a distinction between “coming” and “arriving”: “arriving” denotes a definite and complete arrival. He therefore adds that it has already begun to arrive, and its coming is recognizable by its signs.
text.0_Chapter, 26_Verse, 2_Comment: When distress and anguish come upon you. “Distress” is the external trouble, whereas “anguish” is the soul’s inner torment (Verzweiflung, despair). When inner anguish accompanies external trouble, it is exceedingly bitter and painful, for then all hope is lost, and a person trembles and falls into utter despair.
text.0_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: Then they will call me, but I shall not answer. He depicts wisdom as initially still close to them, so that they can call her, but she will not answer them. Afterward, she will distance herself from them until they seek me early but will not find me. The first situation applies to fools who know the laws of wisdom but do not observe them because of their desires. Afterward, they descend to the condition of those who doubt the laws of wisdom, or to the level of the simple, who do not know the laws of wisdom at all.
text.0_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: Because they hated knowledge. This is the level of fools, as it is written, “Fools hate knowledge,” for because of their desires, they do not desire knowledge at all. We have already explained (in verse 2) that although the laws of wisdom cannot be established through rational demonstration, one can nevertheless attain knowledge of them through discipline and fear of the Lord. Through fear of the Lord, the laws of wisdom become firmly established in one’s heart and become as clear to him as something he has perceived through the senses or apprehended through self-evident principles. But they did not choose the fear of the Lord, for because they follow their desires, they do not desire the fear of the Lord that would bring them to knowledge. As it is written, “Desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but departing from evil is an abomination to fools.” Consequently—
text.0_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: They did not desire my counsel. They did not wish to accept the laws of wisdom, whether through the counsel that wisdom gives them by means of reason or through fear of punishment, for they despised all my rebuke, as it says, “You rejected all my counsel and did not desire my rebuke.”
text.0_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: And they shall eat. Therefore, they will receive punishment both for the fruit of their way—their actions in following their corrupt paths—and for their counsel, through which they denied the laws of wisdom and faith. Concerning this, it says, they shall be sated with their own counsels. Satiety is greater than eating; because they committed evil deliberately, their punishment will be correspondingly greater.
text.0_Chapter, 31_Verse, 0_Comment: For the waywardness of the simple will kill them. The simple do not know the laws of wisdom at all. They possess waywardness, for their intellect is wayward, and this will kill them. Fools, however, know the laws of wisdom and are not wayward in intellect; they merely turn away from the ways of wisdom because of their desires. Since they seek tranquility and the pleasures of this world, the tranquility of fools will destroy them. This tranquility will destroy them both in this world and in the World to Come. Destruction is worse than being killed, which affects only this world, for the simple sin unintentionally and have a share in the World to Come, unlike fools, who act willfully.
text.0_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: But one who listens to me will dwell securely, for his heart trusts in his wisdom, and will be tranquil, without fear of evil, for wisdom will protect him from every external danger, so that no evil will befall him.
text.1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, if you receive my sayings. There is a distinction between a saying and a commandment. One who commands obligates the person commanded to observe his instruction, as a father commands his son and a master his servant. Wisdom contains commandments, such as the commandments of the Torah, which one is obligated to fulfill. Concerning these, it says, and treasure my commandments with you, for treasuring them means preserving them continually within one’s heart and not forgetting them, as it says, “So that you may remember and perform all My commandments.” Wisdom also contains sayings, such as the moral teachings of the Torah and its teachings concerning beliefs and doctrines, which one must receive and accept.
text.1_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: To incline your ear to wisdom. I have already explained that wisdom teaches concerning all actions and modes of conduct to which the terms good and evil apply, whereas understanding concerns matters of beliefs and doctrines to which the terms true and false apply. We have also explained that a person cannot derive the laws of wisdom from his own mind, but must receive them from the Sages, who received them from the prophets, or through the study of the Torah. Concerning this, it says, “Incline your ear to wisdom.” Understanding, however, a person attains by means of his own faculty of understanding. Concerning this, it says, incline your heart to understanding, for this does not require hearing with the ear, but understanding with the heart.
text.1_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: For if you call out to understanding. Understanding is the process by which one reflects little by little and increases knowledge, deriving one thing from another. You must call understanding and summon it to yourself—that is, apply your heart to every matter of wisdom and understanding, diligently striving to understand its reason. Discernment, however, is the conception of universal understanding that encompasses all things. A person cannot summon it to himself, for it is beyond man to comprehend every mystery and discover every desirable matter. Rather, he raises his voice to discernment, like one calling from afar, seeking to attain whatever he is capable of attaining from universal understanding.
text.1_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: If you seek her like silver and search for her like hidden treasures. Seeking silver is accomplished through commerce, by profiting from one’s business or the work of one’s hands, whereas searching for hidden treasures requires digging into the depths of the earth or the depths of the sea. The analogue of seeking silver is that a person exchanges and surrenders all the desires of this world for the sake of wisdom. The analogue of searching for hidden treasures is the effort one exerts to delve deeply into the profound teachings of wisdom and bring forth the pearls concealed in its depths—the mysteries of the Torah and sound wisdom.
text.1_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Then you will understand the fear of the Lord. It has already been explained that the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Since the laws of wisdom cannot be established by demonstration and are opposed to the inclination of the heart, they cannot become firmly engraved upon the heart except through fear of the Lord. As our Sages said, “If there is no fear, there is no wisdom.” Through fear of the Lord, the laws of wisdom that the Lord commanded and gave to mankind become firmly established within the heart. However, they also said, “If there is no wisdom, there is no fear,” for a person cannot understand the greatness and exaltedness of the Lord so as to fear Him except through wisdom, which teaches him to walk in the ways of the Lord. Through it, he understands the greatness of the Creator of the universe, until he comes to understand the fear of the Lord. We have already explained that through fear one attains knowledge of wisdom. Although wisdom is not known through sensory perception or demonstration, through fear a steadfast belief in the laws of wisdom given by the God of the universe—Whose greatness he fears—becomes established in his heart. He becomes accustomed to them until they are as certain to him as things known through sensory perception or self-evident principles. If, however, he intensifies his pursuit of wisdom, seeking it like silver and searching for it like hidden treasures, he will then attain the level of finding the knowledge of God: the sublime knowledge concerning Divine matters, such as the Account of Creation and the Account of the Chariot, which may be transmitted only to one who is wise and capable of understanding through his own knowledge.
text.1_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: For the Lord gives wisdom. It has already been explained that a person cannot attain the laws of wisdom on his own, but must receive them through the Torah of the Lord and through the teachings of the Sages, who received them from the prophets. However, through the intensity of his pursuit—seeking wisdom like silver and searching for it like hidden treasures—he may merit to apprehend the laws of wisdom through the Holy Spirit, like our father Abraham, of blessed memory, whose two kidneys flowed with wisdom and who observed the Torah even before it was given. Wisdom is then bestowed upon him as a gift from the Lord, so that he apprehends its laws on his own. Furthermore, from His mouth come knowledge and understanding. Although a person can attain knowledge and understanding on his own—knowledge through examining what he perceives with his senses or through a self-evident principle, and understanding by applying his faculty of understanding to the knowledge he has acquired and deriving one thing from another—the knowledge and understanding he attains remain exceedingly deficient. He acquires them with great effort, reasoning backward from effects to causes and relying upon numerous experiments and premises, and he will often err in his conclusions. With the Lord’s assistance, however, he receives from His mouth knowledge and understanding through an immediate and truthful apprehension, entirely free of error or doubt.
text.1_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: (7–8) He stores up sound wisdom for the upright. In addition to the universal works that the Lord created during the six days of Creation, He prepared works to be performed in every generation in accordance with the laws of wisdom, for the needs of the providential governance that is renewed in each generation according to the deeds of that generation. These works are called sound wisdom, because they are determined according to His wisdom for the purposes of Providence, reward, and punishment. These works are brought into actuality through the upright people who arise in that generation [the upright being defined as those who follow a straight path in their understanding and actions, and who are greater than the righteous]. Thus, the Midrash states: “Joseph was destined to provide sustenance; Moses was destined to bring redemption.” Accordingly, it says that the Lord stores up sound wisdom for the upright who are destined to arise in the world: He prepared for them the works that they would perform in their days according to the laws of His wisdom. The clauses correspond: He stores up sound wisdom for the upright, to preserve the paths of justice. The upright preserve the paths of the Lord’s governance of His world, which proceeds according to justice. Thus, the deeds performed in Egypt—to strike the Egyptians and bring Israel out—accorded with the Lord’s judgments and His principles of reward and punishment. He assigned these deeds to the upright men who arose in that generation, Moses and Aaron, who were the agents of His Providence charged with preserving the paths of His justice. He is a shield to those who walk with integrity, and He guards the way of His faithful ones. One who walks with integrity is a person whose righteous conduct remains continually fixed upon one path, without ulterior motives or change. Although such people will never depart from their righteousness of their own accord—for this defines a person of integrity—they may nevertheless encounter an obstacle arising from the path itself: they may not know the way, or stumbling blocks may lie upon it. For a person of integrity is not necessarily upright and may stumble because of those who mislead him, the misfortunes of the time, or error and mistake. The Lord therefore shields them from every external cause and guards their way from stumbling.
text.1_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Then you will understand righteousness. In addition to the wisdom, understanding, and knowledge of God that He will bestow upon him, he will also understand righteousness and justice, which govern conduct between one person and another. Justice is what is required by the strict letter of the law, whereas righteousness is what one does beyond the letter of the law. Likewise, regarding character traits and the qualities of the soul, he will understand equity—that which uprightness requires. This includes two matters: 1) the straight middle path, which is always good; and 2) the circuitous path, for at times one must depart from the straight path and take a circuitous route, such as by acting cruelly or proudly toward the wicked. Such conduct is not always good, for cruelty and pride are intrinsically evil traits; it is good only when it ultimately leads one back to the straight path. Concerning this, it says, every good circuitous path.
text.1_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: When wisdom enters your heart. Through Divine assistance, he will attain the level of one called “wise of heart”—a person in whose heart the laws of wisdom have become so firmly established that the inclination of the heart no longer opposes them, for they have become like a second nature within him. The heart always symbolizes the governing faculty within man. When a person’s heart is filled with wisdom and its laws are so deeply implanted within him that the impulses of desire and the evil traits that oppose wisdom no longer rule over him, wisdom has already entered his heart and taken root there like a flourishing native tree, and the heart’s struggle against wisdom has ceased. Likewise, knowledge will be pleasant to your soul. Another person attains knowledge only through great bitterness, strenuous effort, and numerous doubts; but you will attain knowledge—namely, the knowledge of God mentioned above—with pleasantness, for you will attain it easily through the Holy Spirit and Divine illumination.
text.1_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Discretion will watch over you. Discretion consists of the counsels and profound thoughts of wisdom. It will protect you from stumbling in regard to the laws of wisdom, which guide you in matters containing two possible paths—good and evil. Understanding, which distinguishes between truth and falsehood in matters concerning truths, will also guard you. He now explains how discretion will watch over you.
text.1_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: To save you from the way of evil. This means that you will not stray from the ways of wisdom toward evil and desire. Through profound thoughts of wisdom, one will be saved from the enticements of desire, for the evil inclination is found only in a heart empty of wisdom. And understanding will guard you from a man who speaks perversities concerning matters of faith—that is, from those who deny the foundations of faith through false investigations and misleading deductions that are contrary to the truth. Understanding will protect you from this by enabling you to know how to answer a heretic.
text.1_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Those who forsake. Corresponding to “to save you from the way of evil,” it says, those who forsake the paths of uprightness to walk in the ways of darkness. A “way” is the broad road established for the public, from which smaller paths branch off toward villages and small towns. He depicts the Torah as possessing not only a straight broad road, but also many branching paths that are all straight. For numerous paths branch from each commandment: from the trait of compassion, for example, branch the giving of charity, granting a benevolent loan, returning a pledged article, and the like. These are “paths of uprightness.” With wickedness, however, not only is gloom spread over its individual paths, but even its broad road is darkness rather than light, for it is the opposite of wisdom, which is the light of the heart.
text.1_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Those who rejoice. Corresponding to “a man who speaks perversities”—one who denies the foundations of faith—it says that he rejoices in doing evil. Those who sin because of desire are filled with remorse, for after satisfying their desire, they grieve over the evil they have committed. But those who speak perversities and deny the principles of faith—those who sin because of unbelief—rejoice in doing evil. They also exult when an evil reversal occurs—when evil befalls the righteous and the wicked prosper, which is among the reversals of this world. The righteous grieve over this, but these people exult over such evil reversals, for they thereby reinforce their belief that Providence may be denied and that they may fulfill every desire of their hearts. The verse therefore says they exult, for exultation denotes a response to something new: they exult when the evil reversals of the times newly occur.
text.1_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Whose paths. A “path” is a straight route leading directly from a city to a village, whereas a “circuitous path” is a route that curves around. The way of wisdom contains both straight and circuitous paths, for at times one must depart from the straight path to one side—such as employing boldness against those who mock him for serving God, or pride and cruelty against the wicked and those who revile the Lord. Although he thereby departs from the straight path, through this circuitous route he ultimately returns to it. He resembles a person traveling from one place to another who encounters robbers along the road and takes a circuitous route so that he may safely reach an inhabited city. The sinners and deniers, however, have crooked paths, for they do not travel upon the straight path but only upon a circuitous one. Nor can it be said that this circuitous route will return them to the straight path leading to an inhabited city, for they are perverse in their paths, turning away from the desired destination to wander in emptiness where there is no road.
text.1_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: To guard you from a strange woman. There is a distinction between “strange” and “foreign.” Something “strange” is alien to the particular matter in question, whereas something “foreign” merely comes from another land. Here he speaks both of the inclination toward sexual immorality and of the inclination toward idolatry, for idolatry is likewise compared throughout Scripture to harlotry, since one who commits harlotry strays from his God and from His covenant. Wisdom will save you from a strange woman, so that you do not stumble into sin, and from a foreign woman who has abandoned the faith of Israel and worships foreign gods, and whose words are seductive, enticing you toward idolatry, unbelief, and heresy. He now explains the reference to the strange woman.
text.1_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Who forsakes the companion of her youth. She is unfaithful to her husband. Corresponding to the foreign woman, it says, and forgets the covenant of her God, straying after the Baals and embracing heretical beliefs.
text.1_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: For she sinks. Concerning the adulterous woman, it says, for her house sinks toward death, for she brings about the body’s death before its appointed time. Concerning the foreign woman, it says, her circuitous paths lead to the shades, for she leads to the destruction of the soul, which will come to rest among the assembly of the dead. It says “her circuitous paths” because even the methods of reasoning and investigation by which she circles toward her house, seeking to establish her heretical and denialist doctrine through circuitous arguments that deviate from uprightness and truth, descend toward the shades; for they, too, lead to the soul’s excision and destruction.
text.1_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: All. Corresponding to the statement, “For her house sinks toward death,” it says, none who enter her will return, for one who enters her house will never return from there, but will die. Corresponding to the statement, “Her circuitous paths lead to the shades,” it says, nor will they attain the paths of life. One should not imagine that this resembles another circuitous route through which a person ultimately returns to the straight path, for from this circuitous route they will not attain the paths of life. Alternatively, it means that none who enter her will ever return in repentance; and even if they do repent, they will no longer attain the paths of life, for heretical belief will cling to them and ferment their intellect like leaven in dough, so that they will never again return to the paths of religion and faith. Thus, our Sages said that one who separates himself from heresy dies immediately, for if he were to remain alive, he would return to his folly.
text.1_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: So that you may walk in the way of the good. A “way” is the broad road, whereas “paths” are the smaller routes leading from a city to a village. This means that through diligent study of wisdom, you will walk upon the established way particular to good people, who do good to their fellows. It adds, and observe the paths of the righteous—the individual paths followed by righteous people who act beyond the letter of the law in particular circumstances, according to what each situation requires. Our Sages likewise interpreted it this way (Bava Metzia 83a): Rabbah bar bar Ḥana hired certain porters to carry a barrel of wine for him, and they broke it. He took their cloaks, and they came before Rav. Rav said to him, “Return their cloaks.” He asked, “Is this the law?” Rav replied, “So that you may walk in the way of the good.” The porters then said, “We are poor, we have labored all day, and we have nothing to eat.” Rav said to him, “Go and pay them their wages.” He asked, “Is this the law?” Rav replied, “And observe the paths of the righteous.” This second matter was an individual path of righteousness required by the circumstances, because they were poor.
text.1_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: For the upright. There is a distinction between the upright and those of integrity. The upright are naturally straight, both in the ways of understanding and in matters of character: their intellect, nature, and traits proceed of themselves along the straight path. Those of integrity are defined as people whose conduct remains fixed and unchanging at all times, whether in prosperity or adversity, because they do everything for the sake of the Lord, without any ulterior motive. The upright will dwell in the land, but it is conceivable that their conduct may sometimes change for the worse, in which case they will not remain in it forever. Because they are also people of integrity, they will remain in it, for they will never waver from their righteousness.
text.1_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And the wicked. But the wicked will be cut off from the land. “The wicked” includes those who persist in their wickedness, both in matters between man and God and in matters between one person and another—the opposite of people of integrity, who persist in their righteousness. They will be cut off forever, in contrast to people of integrity, who will remain in the land forever. The treacherous in their dealings with others, although they will not be cut off forever, will be uprooted from it temporarily, in contrast to the upright.
text.2_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, do not forget my Torah. The Torah encompasses all the subjects taught within it, such as the laws and rulings that a person must study even when he does not personally perform them, including the commandments concerning the priests, the sacrifices, and the like. It also includes the narratives of the Torah, from which we derive the principles of faith concerning Providence, prophecy, reward, and punishment. He warns him not to forget the Torah, but to meditate upon it day and night until he remembers all of it. And let your heart preserve my commandments. The commandments must be actively performed or, in the case of negative commandments, carefully avoided. Since most of them oppose the inclination of the heart, it says, “Let your heart preserve them,” for the heart is the governing faculty of the soul, which must rule over the soul’s other faculties and direct their actions in accordance with the commandments of the Lord.
text.2_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: For length of days and years of life. When these expressions appear together, “length of days” denotes days of prosperity, for then one’s days seem long and are filled with goodness, whereas “years of life” denotes an increase in the number of one’s years. This means that through the merit of Torah study and observance of the commandments, years will be added to his life, and he will enjoy length of days—that is, days of prosperity—as well as years of peace, meaning peace in his body, his possessions, his household, and everything belonging to him.
text.2_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Let kindness and truth not forsake you. Most of the teachings of the Torah are included within kindness and truth. The commandments, for the most part, concern kindness between one person and another, whereas beliefs and doctrines are included within the attribute of truth, for one must believe the truths made known through the Torah. Let neither of these forsake you: attain true beliefs and doctrines through the Torah, and practice kindness through the commandments. There is also a “Torah of truth” and a “Torah of kindness.” The commandments and forms of conduct performed out of obligation, as well as the straightforward intellectual teachings accessible to everyone, are called the Torah of truth. The extraordinary deeds performed by the devout and spiritually elevated out of piety, as well as the extraordinary apprehensions attained by those possessing the Holy Spirit concerning Divine matters, the Account of Creation, and the Account of the Chariot, are called the Torah of kindness. Let neither of these forsake you. In accordance with a person’s conduct in kindness and truth, the Holy One, blessed be He, will deal with him through these same attributes, measure for measure. Bind them around your throat—the throat represents the speech that emerges from it. Speak of them continually until they become habitual upon your tongue. Also, write them upon the tablet of your heart. The heart is the governing faculty within man, and it is continually surrounded by traps and snares spread against it by the impulses of desire and the evil images that arise within his spirit. These oppose the laws of wisdom, causing wisdom to be forgotten. One must therefore engrave the laws of wisdom upon the tablet of the heart as though they were permanently inscribed, never to be erased. He should read this inscription throughout his life, so that he will learn to banish evil thoughts and the impulses that lead to sinful deeds.
text.2_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And find favor and sound understanding in the eyes of God and man. This means that although a person may also find favor and understanding through human wisdom and understanding—for people say of those possessing understanding that they have attained insight, and through their wisdom they likewise find favor in the eyes of others—through the Torah and Divine wisdom, they will find favor in the eyes of God as well. They will also attain “sound understanding,” meaning that the Spirit of God will be poured upon them, enabling them to understand through sound intellect. This refers to apprehension through the Holy Spirit, by which they grasp truths with Divine assistance. This results from finding favor in the eyes of the Lord, Who enables them to apprehend His truth.
text.2_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Trust in the Lord with all your heart. Since the laws of wisdom transcend human understanding and a person cannot apprehend them through his own faculty of understanding, if he relies upon his understanding, it will lead him astray toward the opposite of the ways of wisdom. Therefore, it says, do not rely upon your understanding, for a person does not attain wisdom through his own understanding; rather, it is given by God. He must therefore trust in the Lord with all his heart, follow the commandments of the Lord concerning the laws and commandments of the Torah and wisdom, and not rely upon his own understanding at all.
text.2_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Know Him in all your ways. “Ways” are the broad roads, whereas “paths” are the smaller routes that branch from them. Since the paths of wisdom are innumerable—for wisdom extends to an exceedingly great number of particular cases—a person cannot know how to conduct himself according to the Torah and wisdom in every particular situation that arises. The answer is that you should know the Lord in all your general ways. In such ways as compassion, generosity, and humility, conduct yourself according to the Lord’s command. All this rests upon the commandment, “You shall walk in His ways”: just as He is compassionate, and so forth, so must you be. And He will make your paths straight. Through Divine assistance, even your particular paths will be straight—for example, regarding the individual acts belonging to the way of generosity, you will know how much to give, to whom, when, how, and the like.
text.2_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not be wise in your own eyes. Some people consider themselves wise. Since the laws of wisdom cannot be established through demonstration and oppose the natural inclination of the heart, such a person imagines that the path he chooses for himself is the path of wisdom and that everything he does is wise. This defines one who is wise in his own eyes: he disputes the true laws of wisdom received from the Lord because they oppose the desires of his heart, his opinions, and the impulses behind his actions. Rather, fear the Lord, Who established the laws of wisdom according to His supreme wisdom, and turn away from evil. Through fear of the Lord, you will turn away from evil and walk in the ways of wisdom, as it says, “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.” As explained there, through fear of the Lord, a person submits to the laws of wisdom commanded by the Lord and does not rely upon his own judgment and wisdom.
text.2_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Healing. Although the laws of wisdom oppose your natural inclinations, do not think that walking in the ways of wisdom will make your body ill. The laws and commandments of wisdom prohibit many foods and command a person to sanctify himself and abstain from excessive consumption. The verse therefore says that, on the contrary, it will be healing to your navel. The navel, which receives drink and nourishment, will not only remain free of illness; rather, the Torah’s prohibitions and abstention from forbidden foods will provide healing for its ailments. Likewise, do not think that the forms of abstinence from pleasure and desire prescribed by the Torah will dry out the marrow of your bones. On the contrary, they will be moisture for your bones, for the laws of wisdom strengthen the body’s health and invigorate your bones—both naturally, since excessive indulgence weakens the body, and through the Lord’s Providence.
text.2_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Honor. After teaching him to know the Lord in all his ways and to trust in Him, because the laws of wisdom ordained by Him will bring him healing and recovery, he adds that the same principle applies to all his affairs, including the acquisition of possessions. Their first portion must be attributed to the Lord, for He gives everything and everything comes from His hand. Therefore, you must honor Him with your wealth and with the first of all your produce, for the first portion belongs to Him. Through this—
text.2_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Then your storehouses will be filled with abundance, and your winepresses will burst forth with new wine. If you believe that the beginning of all things comes from Him, then blessing will be sent by Him upon all the work of your hands. From this, he derives an analogy concerning wisdom, which is the absolute beginning of all things, as the Targum renders “In the beginning” as “With wisdom.” You must therefore return wisdom to the Lord and recognize that all its laws and limitations come from Him. Do not be wise in your own eyes by attributing wisdom to your own understanding. Rather, fear the Lord and turn away from evil, acting according to His commands, and through this all your conduct will be blessed.
text.2_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, do not despise the discipline of the Lord. Whenever “discipline” and “rebuke” are used regarding human beings, discipline is administered through compulsion or suffering, whereas rebuke consists of clarifying a matter through rational demonstrations and proofs. Therefore, regarding discipline, it uses the expression “do not despise,” for a person naturally despises suffering. Regarding rebuke, however, it says, do not become weary of His rebuke. Rebuke is not despised in itself, since it is presented through words of reason and knowledge, but the listener may sometimes become weary of it. Regarding the Lord, however, we sometimes find that rebuke is also administered through suffering. In such cases, “discipline” refers to the suffering that the Lord brings upon a person to correct a past sin and chastise him for his previous transgressions, whereas “rebuke” refers to the suffering that the Lord brings upon him to return him to the good path in the future. This resembles the “sufferings of love” mentioned by our Sages, who taught that whoever the Holy One, blessed be He, desires, He crushes through suffering. The condition of such suffering is that a person accept it with love and take it to heart so that he may improve his ways. Concerning this, it says:
text.2_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: For the Lord rebukes the one whom He loves. Rebuke is a sign of love, for out of His love, the Lord watches over a person to improve his conduct and elevate him from one level to an ever-higher level. And like a father, He favors his son. Just as a father desires to elevate his son from one level to the next, withholding luxuries and indulgences from him and inclining his shoulder to bear the yoke of Torah and persistent study, and the like, so does the Lord act—and all this proceeds from His great love for him.
text.2_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Happy is the man who finds wisdom. Wisdom is not acquired through contemplation, as understanding is, which a person derives from his own knowledge through reflection. Rather, he receives wisdom from the Lord, as explained above. Happy is the person who finds all the laws of wisdom and acquires them as his possession, like one who finds a valuable object: although he found it outside himself, it nevertheless becomes his possession and belongs to him. And happy is the man who brings forth discernment, for he produces and derives understanding from his own knowledge by understanding one thing from another. There is a distinction between understanding and discernment: discernment is attained when a person has reflected upon all the general paths and comprehends every matter of understanding in all its details.
text.2_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: For it is better. This is explained in accordance with what is stated below (Proverbs 16:16): How much better it is to acquire wisdom than fine gold, and acquiring understanding is preferable to silver. We explained that:
text.2_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: * Wisdom, since a person does not attain it through his own understanding and contemplation but receives it from the Lord, is compared to fine gold, which is found deep within the mountains like a discovered treasure. Wisdom is similarly found as a discovery received from the Master of wisdom, as it says, Happy is the man who finds wisdom.
text.2_Chapter, 13_Verse, 2_Comment: * Discernment, however, is attained through a process resembling commerce, as a person understands and derives one thing from another, as it says, and the man who brings forth discernment. It is therefore comparable to acquiring silver, with which people buy and sell through commerce and exchange.
text.2_Chapter, 13_Verse, 4_Comment: * Corresponding to the statement and the man who brings forth discernment, it explains: for trading in it is better than trading in silver.
text.2_Chapter, 13_Verse, 5_Comment: * Corresponding to the statement happy is the man who finds wisdom, it explains: and its yield is better than fine gold.
text.2_Chapter, 13_Verse, 6_Comment: For these are perishable possessions that do not become integrated into the soul, whereas wisdom and discernment are enduring and eternal possessions that become an integral part of the human soul.
text.2_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: She is more precious than pearls. Pearls are precious because they are not found upon the earth, the element upon which man lives, but within another element—the element of water—for they originate in the depths of the sea. Likewise, the laws of wisdom do not originate in the human intellect, an intellect dwelling within matter; rather, their source is in Heaven and in the Divine intellect, which is even more remote than the depths of the seas—profound and exalted, exceedingly distant; who can find it? Although a person must surrender his bodily desires, pleasures, and appetites as the price of wisdom, none of the things you desire and surrender for her sake can equal her, for she is more precious than all of them, since through her you will attain things of still greater value. For—
text.2_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: Length of days is in her right hand; in her left hand are wealth and honor. Silver, fine gold, and pearls hold wealth and honor in their right hand, for their principal purpose is to obtain wealth and honor. Wisdom, however, holds wealth and honor in her left hand, like something secondary that one holds with the left hand. In her right hand, she holds something more precious: length of days, which includes both the goodness of life in this world and eternal life in the world that is entirely long.
text.2_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Her ways. A “way” is a broad road established for the public, whereas “paths” are routes traveled by individuals. Accordingly, it says, her ways are ways of pleasantness. The general ways of wisdom are the roads that lead to pleasantness—the spiritual delight of the soul attained upon reaching its ultimate purpose—for the soul of one who occupies himself with wisdom will thereby be satisfied with spiritual radiance.
text.2_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: And all her paths are peace. The smaller paths branching from the broad road, upon which each individual walks in governing himself and his household, lead to peace. For the well-being of one’s body, household, society, and possessions—all of which are included within the term “peace”—depends upon the conduct each person follows in the particular paths of wisdom, all of which branch from her broad and universal ways.
text.2_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: She is a tree of life to those who hold fast to her. There is a righteous person, and there is one who subdues his inclination. The righteous person is one whose heart naturally inclines toward wisdom and whose inclination does not entice him to transgress its laws. One who subdues his inclination is a person whose nature inclines toward evil, but who conquers his inclination. Accordingly, it says that wisdom is a tree of life to those who hold fast to her—that is, to one who subdues his inclination, who holds fast to wisdom as though against her will. It is as though wisdom seeks to separate from him because his nature opposes her, but he holds her with all his strength and does not allow her to depart, for he conquers his inclination. And those who support her are happy refers to one whose natural disposition does not oppose wisdom. He does not need to hold her against her will, but merely to support her, and he is happy. The verse teaches a novel point regarding each. It need not inform us that one who conquers his inclination attains spiritual happiness, for we already understand that the greater his struggle to conquer his inclination, the greater his happiness and reward—“according to the effort is the reward.” We might, however, have imagined that this inner battle against his inclination shortens his life. It therefore says that wisdom is a tree of life for him, prolonging his life as though he had eaten from the Tree of Life and would live forever. Regarding one who supports wisdom—one in whom wisdom dwells naturally and who experiences no inner struggle—we might have thought that his reward would not be as great. The verse therefore teaches that those who support her are also happy.
text.2_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: (19–20) The Lord founded the earth through wisdom. This metaphor corresponds to what is stated (below, chapter 24): “Through wisdom a house is built, through understanding it is established, and through knowledge its chambers are filled with every precious and pleasant treasure.” There, the construction of the house is attributed to wisdom; the completion of the building, which is its establishment—for “establishing” denotes completing the construction—is attributed to understanding; and the filling of the house’s chambers with precious vessels is attributed to knowledge. In the same way, he depicts the universal structure—the world. Its foundation was laid through wisdom; its establishment, meaning the completion of its construction, was accomplished through understanding; and the filling of its chambers—the filling of the world with the Lord’s blessing through the waters of the depths and the dew of Heaven—is attributed to knowledge. In this image, the earth is the building’s foundation and the heavens are its ceiling, for setting the ceiling in place completes the building, as it says, “Who builds His upper chambers in the heavens.” The depths, the dew, and the rains of blessing fill the world with every form of goodness and blessing. The foundation of the world’s structure was created something from nothing, and this is attributed to wisdom, as it says, “In the beginning God created,” which the Targum renders, “With wisdom.” The completion of the structure during the six days of Creation proceeded by bringing forth one existing thing from another, and this is attributed to understanding. That is, wisdom derives its materials from “nothing”—from the Lord Himself, Who is Infinite—whereas understanding derives one thing from another and one intellectual concept from another. This corresponds to the completion of the building, which involved bringing forth one existing thing from another. The governance of the world after the six days of Creation is compared to filling the world’s chambers with every precious vessel: from that time onward, the depths below are opened and the skies above pour down dew throughout all the days of the world. This is attributed to knowledge. It has already been explained that everything described as wisdom admits two opposite possible paths of existence. Thus, when the Creator brought the world from nothing into existence, His thought encompassed many possibilities for bringing the world into existence in other ways, but He chose to create it in this way according to supreme wisdom. As the Sages said, the Holy One, blessed be He, created worlds and destroyed them until He said, “This one pleases Me; those did not please Me.” This is the defining characteristic of wisdom. Once He had brought the primary materials into existence from nothing, however, there was no longer another possible way to derive one existing thing from another, but only the single way determined by the preparation of the original material. As the Midrash illustrates through the parable of one who sows six seeds simultaneously, each of which emerges at its appointed time. This exemplifies understanding, in which there are not two opposite possible paths of existence, but only one path. Thus, He brought forth one thing from another according to the laws of understanding. His orderly governance throughout all the days of the world—opening the depths and pouring down dew in accordance with the Providence through which He attends to the needs of His world—depends upon knowledge. The creatures produced by the earth also possess free choice to do good or evil, and their conduct therefore admits two possible paths. This belongs to the governance of wisdom, and through this He founded the earth; for the foundation of the world’s creation was that beings possessing free choice should be created and conduct themselves according to wisdom. In the heavens, however, there is neither free choice nor conduct classified as good or evil. Rather, the heavenly beings apprehend their Creator and distinguish between truth and falsehood, which is the defining characteristic of understanding. The world’s constant governance—whether according to the order of nature and the celestial system or according to Providence and miracles—depends upon the knowledge of God: He knows the order of governance, the needs of the world, the ways of those below, and what is required for their perfection and continued life, with penetrating knowledge extending to the end of all generations. This is the meaning of knowledge.
text.2_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, let them not depart from your eyes. Therefore, let the ways of wisdom not depart from your eyes—that is, from your inner eyes, the eyes of the heart. Preserve sound wisdom and discretion. Discretion consists of profound thoughts concerning wisdom, whereas sound wisdom consists of the deeds performed according to wisdom. This means that you must ensure that your actions, contemplation, and thoughts all conform to the ways of wisdom. Although you preserve sound wisdom, which is action, you must also preserve discretion, which is profound contemplation of wisdom, for study leads to action. An unlearned person cannot be pious, and an ignorant person cannot be God-fearing.
text.2_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And they will be life to your soul. Through this, you will attain the life of the soul, for the soul is called living only when it exercises its spiritual faculties to understand and act according to wisdom. Otherwise, although the body is alive and capable of sensation, the spiritual soul is dead and regarded as though it does not exist. And they will be grace around your throat. When you speak with your throat and teach the ways of wisdom to others, you will find favor in the eyes of God and man, as explained above in verse 4.
text.2_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: Then you will walk. This means that Divine Providence will accompany you and protect you from every mishap. He enumerates three situations: 1) while a person is traveling on the road, when he is especially vulnerable to robbers, ambushers, and murderers; 2) while he is lying down and sleeping at home, when he is in greater danger than while awake; and 3) while he is awake at home, when protection may also be required in a time of fear and calamity. These situations are similarly ordered in the verse, “You shall speak of them when you sit in your house, when you walk upon the road, and when you lie down.” Here, however, they are arranged to teach that Providence will accompany him while he travels upon the road, and even while he lies down at home, where he is not as greatly endangered, and even while he sits awake in his house, where there is ordinarily no danger. Nevertheless, the Lord will protect him. In each case, the verse mentions two things: first, that he will feel secure in his heart and will not be afraid because he trusts in the Lord; and second, that the Lord will actually save him from every mishap. Regarding traveling on the road, it says, you will walk securely on your way, which refers to his sense of security, and your foot will not stumble, which refers to the protection with which the Lord will guard him, as it says, “For He will command His angels concerning you,” and, “lest you strike your foot against a stone.” Regarding the time of sleep, it says:
text.2_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: When you lie down, you will not be afraid. This refers to his sense of security.
text.2_Chapter, 23_Verse, 1_Comment: And you will lie down, and your sleep will be sweet. This refers to the protection that will guard you from being terrified by bad dreams and from other harms that may occur during sleep. Regarding the state of wakefulness, it says:
text.2_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not fear sudden terror. This refers to his sense of security. Regarding protection, it says that you should not fear the devastation of the wicked when it comes. Even when the devastation destined to destroy the wicked arrives, do not fear, for you will be saved through the Lord’s Providence.
text.2_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: For the Lord will be your confidence. “Confidence” is defined as security from evil in which a person takes no action to save himself from it, because his heart is steadfast and he does not fear. Although in a time of trouble, one who is confident and gives no thought to saving himself may easily be caught in a snare, with you it will be different: the Lord will be your confidence. Your confidence and hope will rest upon the Lord’s Providence, and He will guard your foot from being caught in a snare.
text.2_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not withhold good. I have already explained that these verses contain both a parable and its figurative meaning. Just as, according to the parable, it is self-evident that one should not withhold good from its rightful recipient—that is, from one who deserves it—when it is within the power of your hand to do it, so one must not withhold good from the spiritual soul, whose welfare consists in walking in the ways of the Lord, when it is within one’s power to bestow goodness and kindness upon it.
text.2_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not say to your fellow, “Go and return, and tomorrow I will give.” This means that not only should you refrain from withholding good altogether, but you should not postpone doing good until tomorrow when you have it with you and can do the good today. Likewise, one should not postpone the good of the soul or defer it until tomorrow, as it is said, “Do not say, ‘When I have free time, I will study.’” Rather, you should do good while you are still in your vigor, during the days of your youth.
text.2_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not devise. This, too, is both a parable and its figurative meaning. Just as it is improper to devise evil against your fellow when he dwells securely beside you and is not at war with you, so it is improper for the faculties of the body to devise evil against the faculties of the soul and cast them into the pit of destruction while the soul dwells securely with the body. For God sent the soul into the body to preserve it and bring it goodness in its ultimate end.
text.2_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not contend. Just as it is improper even to quarrel with a person without cause, unless he has repaid you with evil out of hostility—for “requital” denotes an emotional response of the soul that produces hatred—and if he harmed you without acting from such hostility and hatred, you are obligated to forgive him, how much more improper is it for the faculties of the body to wage war and contend with the faculties of the soul. Although a person may imagine that the faculties of his soul cause him harm by preventing him from pursuing worldly desires and pleasures, they do not do so out of hatred.
