On the contrary, they restrain him because of the soul’s love and compassion for him.
text.2_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not envy. He commands him not to follow the way of a violent man, a term that includes anyone who wrongs his own soul and turns away from the good path. He warns him not to follow such a person either because he envies his success, concerning which it says, do not envy a violent man, or because he deliberately chooses his ways, regarding them as good, concerning which it says, and do not choose any of his ways. He proceeds to explain that a person may wrong his soul in four ways and warns against them all. First, one may deviate from uprightness through his understanding, for uprightness belongs to understanding. Concerning this, it says:
text.2_Chapter, 31_Verse, 0_Comment: For one who deviates is an abomination to the Lord, but His secret is with the upright. The upright are those whose hearts are straight and who proceed uprightly in their understanding. They are beloved by the Lord, so that He reveals His secrets to them—the mysteries of the Account of Creation and the Account of the Chariot. Conversely, one who deviates from uprightness and whose understanding follows crooked paths is an abomination to the Lord, for he will descend into heresy and unbelief. Second, one may do evil because of wickedness. A wicked person is defined as one who acts evilly toward God and other people and whose nature inclines him toward wickedness. Concerning this, it says:
text.2_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: The curse of the Lord is in the house of the wicked. Even if you see that the wicked person possesses an established house, know that the curse of the Lord will rest upon it, diminishing it, depriving it, and ultimately destroying it. But He will bless the dwelling of the righteous. Although the righteous do not possess an established house but only a dwelling—a term that can denote a sheepfold or temporary tent—the Lord will nevertheless bless even their dwelling. Third, one may wrong his soul through the trait of mockery. The mocker habitually ridicules the laws of wisdom because he does not understand their reasons, arrogantly imagining that anything whose reason he cannot comprehend has no substance. Concerning this, it says:
text.2_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: If He encounters mockers, He will mock. The Lord will cause them to become objects of mockery and conversation in the mouths of all people, measure for measure. But to the humble, who do not arrogantly dispute the laws of wisdom, since in their humility they know that their intellect is too limited to grasp its mysteries, the Lord will grant that they find favor in the eyes of others. Fourth, one may wrong his own soul by belonging to the class of fools. A fool is defined as one who disputes the laws of wisdom because he chooses to follow his desires, even though he knows those laws. Concerning this, it says:
text.2_Chapter, 34_Verse, 0_Comment: The wise will inherit honor. The wise, who conduct themselves according to the laws of wisdom, will inherit honor, for the honor of the soul shines within them and raises them above disgrace—namely desire, which is the soul’s degradation and humiliation. This honor will be their eternal inheritance, just as the soul is eternal. But fools are raised up by disgrace: desire, which is the soul’s disgrace and humiliation, lifts them up to dispute the soul’s honor and to subject it to something base and contemptible—the desires of matter and the animal soul. Through this they dispute the laws of wisdom, for images of disgrace and desire rise from the depths of the soul to the surface of the heart and overpower the images of honor and wisdom. Their end is continual shame and disgrace.
text.3_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear, children, the discipline of a father. That is, I shall relate to you a father’s discipline—the discipline I received from my father, as he explains in verse 3. And attend, so as to know understanding. Besides relating the discipline my father gave me, listen also to what I discerned about it through my own understanding, so that through this you will know these matters with clear knowledge. This is the meaning of “so as to know understanding.”
text.3_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: For. Regarding the tradition of discipline that he received from his father, he says, For I have given you a good teaching: what I received through tradition is intrinsically good, and I have given and transmitted it to you. Regarding what he discerned through his own understanding, which is attributed to him, he says, Do not forsake my Torah either.
text.3_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: For I was a son. He explains that the discipline he received from his father was exceptionally choice and precious. A father bequeaths good discipline to all his sons, and certainly to the son chosen above all his other sons, to whom he transmits special and exalted matters. I was chosen above all his sons for two reasons. First, I was a son to my father: although I was not my father’s only son, I was his principal son, who would build his father’s house and sit upon his throne after him. Second, I was tender and an only child when I was before my mother. To her I was an only son, and because of her, and his love for her, I was regarded in his eyes as an only son as well.
text.3_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: He instructed me and said to me. Instruction means showing someone the path through action. Thus, he showed me the ways of wisdom by my seeing his deeds and conduct in practice, as our Sages said: serving Torah scholars is greater than studying Torah. And he said to me refers to what he told me orally: Let your heart uphold my words. The heart—the governing power of the soul—is restless and does not remain in one state for even a moment, because desire and the inclination of the heart constantly entice it to depart from the laws of wisdom. Therefore, my words will support your heart so that it remains in the state of wisdom and does not move from its place. Furthermore, keep my commandments and live: keep them because they are God’s command, even when no reason for them is apparent, and through this you will live.
text.3_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Acquire wisdom; acquire understanding. He cautioned him that both wisdom and understanding should become possessions attached to his soul. I have already explained the distinction between wisdom and understanding. He told him that in his words he would find both wisdom, which teaches the proper modes of conduct in matters described as good or evil, and understanding, which distinguishes truth from falsehood in beliefs and opinions. Do not forget, and do not turn away from the sayings of my mouth: do not depart from my sayings either through forgetfulness or through being turned away from the proper path by the inclination of desire.
text.3_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not forsake her, and she will guard you; love her, and she will preserve you. Love is a higher level than merely not forsaking her, for a person may refrain from abandoning something he does not love when he derives benefit from it. He therefore adds that you should love her and cleave to her with your soul, because of the goodness within her, which is greater than what is merely pleasant or useful. Through this, she will preserve you. Preservation is greater than guarding: as you increase your love, she will increasingly preserve you with extraordinary care.
text.3_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: The beginning of wisdom is: acquire wisdom. It has already been explained that wisdom has no prior principles or foundations upon which it is based. It is unlike understanding, which has a beginning and starting point: a person contemplates words of wisdom or knowledge that he has already acquired, derives one thing from another, and compares one thing with another. Thus the beginning and starting point of understanding lies outside understanding itself. Wisdom, however, has no separate beginning, for the beginning and foundations of wisdom are wisdom itself—that is, the laws of wisdom received from God are wisdom’s foundation, not anything else. This is the meaning of “The beginning of wisdom is: acquire wisdom.” But the beginning of understanding is not understanding itself; rather, it consists of other acquisitions that one has gathered in the soul from wisdom or every kind of knowledge. Through these acquisitions within the soul, one understands, derives one thing from another, and acquires understanding. Thus, with all your acquisitions, acquire understanding. For example, one who possesses the elementary foundations of geometry or natural science contemplates them and derives matters of understanding; likewise, with every acquisition from any field of knowledge gathered in his soul, he will understand and acquire understanding.
text.3_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Exalt her, and she will elevate you. First, one forms in his heart an appreciation of wisdom’s importance and exaltedness; correspondingly, wisdom will elevate him. Then, she will honor you when you embrace her: if you join yourself to her lovingly, cleave to her, and embrace her as your intimate wife, always enraptured by love of her, she will additionally bequeath to you the spiritual honor of the soul.
text.3_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: She will give. She will then increase love and kindness toward you until she places a wreath of grace upon your head, so that you find favor in the eyes of God and man. The head signifies the faculties of intellect, so that you will find favor and sound understanding. Then she will bestow upon you a crown of glory. A crown is worn by a person of distinction as a sign of his rank; you will wear a crown of glory that will remain your glory for generations. This is greater than honor and favor.
text.3_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear, my son, and also take and accept my sayings; then the years of your life will be increased, as stated above in 3:2.
text.3_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: I have instructed you in the way of wisdom. A “way” is a straight road, while a “course” is a circuitous road. A person must ordinarily follow the intermediate path, the established straight road, which is the way of wisdom—for example, the way of compassion, modesty, humility, and the like. Therefore he says, “I have instructed you in the way of wisdom.” Sometimes, however, one must turn from the straight road and travel a circuitous course if the desired destination cannot be reached directly—for example, when the direct road is obstructed by mountains and ridges. Similarly, one whose nature inclines toward miserliness cannot immediately follow the intermediate path of generosity; he must first incline toward the opposite extreme, prodigality, which is the circuitous course, through which he will become accustomed to reaching the straight, intermediate path of generosity. In this situation one must know how the circuitous course will bring him around to the straight road. Thus, I have guided you in courses of uprightness: he must know the upright measure of the circuitous course so that he does not deviate to the other side, like those described as perverse in their courses (above, 2:15). Here mere instruction—simply showing him the road, as in “I have instructed you in the way of wisdom”—is insufficient. He needs guidance, to be led by the hand through the circuitous course so that he does not err. Therefore he says, “I have guided you.”
text.3_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: When you walk, your step will not be constrained. Sometimes a person proceeds on the way of the Torah at an ordinary walking pace, fulfilling the commandments according to law and obligation. This is “when you walk.” Then his steps must not be constrained—that is, he must not be sluggish in performing the commandments, but must fulfill them properly and follow the regular road. At other times a person proceeds on the way of the Torah at a run: he acts with piety and runs with great fervor to add safeguards, boundaries, holiness, and abstinence. He must then beware of stumbling, like the four who entered the Pardes, of whom Aḥer cut down the shoots. Thus, if you run, you will not stumble.
text.3_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Hold fast to discipline; do not let go. Since the inclinations of the heart oppose the laws of wisdom—because the heart’s images incline toward evil and are contrary to the way of wisdom—a person needs discipline, by which he binds the powers of his soul so that they do not depart from wisdom’s ways. I explained at the beginning of the book that this discipline is fear of the Lord, as it says, “Fear of the Lord is the discipline of wisdom.” Through fear of the Lord, one fears violating the laws of wisdom that He gave. Yet even this discipline and fear of the Lord do not awaken spontaneously in the human soul; one must grasp them with all his strength so that fear of the Lord does not leave his memory for even a moment. He therefore says, Hold fast to discipline—like one forcibly holding something—and do not let go, for if you release it for a moment, it will leave your memory. Through this, guard her—you will preserve wisdom, because holding fast to discipline keeps wisdom’s laws within the heart—for she is your life. Wisdom is the life of the soul, as stated above (3:22), “They will be life to your soul.” Without wisdom, one does not live a spiritual life, but only an animal life, which is not “your life,” that is, the life proper to a human being.
text.3_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not enter the path of the wicked, and do not advance on the way of evil men. There is a distinction between a “way” and a “path”: a way is the great road leading from city to city, whereas a path is one of the many smaller roads branching from the great road toward small towns and villages. There is also a distinction between the wicked and evil men. The wicked are so called because of their deeds, for they commit wicked acts; “evil” includes one whose very character is evil even if he does not act wickedly, such as a sectarian or heretic whose evil lies in thoughts of heresy and denial. Every wicked person has a particular path along which he practices his wickedness: one follows a path of murder, another of adultery or theft, and so forth. Thus, Do not enter the path of the wicked. Evil men, however, have a general way—the general way of denying Providence, reward, and punishment. Thus, Do not advance on the way of evil men. The verb translated “advance” is always associated with spiritual happiness. That is, do not imagine that their philosophy contains a path to happiness, or that their syllogisms and investigations will lead you to the way of faith. Do not attempt to learn their general method of inquiry and employ their premises in studying Torah and faith in the hope of thereby reaching spiritual happiness. Do not expect to find any happiness there.
text.3_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Disrupt it. You must spoil this way and know what to answer a heretic. If you cannot disrupt it, at least do not pass through it. If you have already encountered this way—that is, if you have studied their investigations and opinions—turn away from it and pass on along the way of Torah and faith.
text.3_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: For they cannot sleep unless they do evil. If they have not themselves done evil, they cannot sleep at all. Their sleep is robbed unless they cause someone to stumble. If they do not cause others to stumble, then although they sleep after having done evil themselves, it seems to them that their sleep has been stolen, for they think they should not have slept before causing others to stumble as well. Here he describes the evil men—the sectarians and heretics. He will now explain the wicked mentioned in “Do not enter the path of the wicked.”
text.3_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: For they eat the bread of wickedness: the bread they eat was obtained through wickedness, and the wine they drink was obtained through violence.
text.3_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: But the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn. There is a distinction between a “way” and a “path”: a way is the broad road, while a path is smaller and branches from the broad road toward villages and side destinations. Although it may appear to you that the righteous do not walk upon a broad road, because the beginning of their path is thorny and difficult to traverse, nevertheless, though its beginning is thorny, its end is level. The narrow path upon which they walk initially resembles the light of dawn—the light that first begins to break at sunrise. It is not direct light from the sun, but reflected light produced as the sun’s rays penetrate the vapors. Afterward, however, it shines increasingly: it becomes direct light and continually grows brighter, until the day is established at noon. So too the soul’s light, although at first covered by the clouds and vapors of the body, and although the sunlight is concealed, penetrates the body’s mists and matter’s darkness until it becomes brilliant light in the soul’s radiance. But—
text.3_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: The way of the wicked, although it may appear that the wicked walk upon a broad road whose beginning is level, is nevertheless like deep darkness, which is darker than ordinary darkness, so that they do not know what makes them stumble. He also adds a greater point: even the path of the righteous—their particular deeds—is filled with light and radiance, whereas even the broad way of the wicked—their general conduct—is filled with gloom, and all the more so their particular deeds.
text.3_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, attend to my words. “Words” refers to extended discourse, in the manner of one who expounds at length and explains the reasons for matters, while “sayings” refers to the precise language in which those words are clothed. That is, attend to the reasoning of the extended discourse, and also incline your ear to the exact form of the sayings, preserving their wording. For example, the language in which the Written Torah was given constitutes the “sayings,” while the laws transmitted orally at length constitute the “words.” You must pay attention to both.
text.3_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: Let them not depart from your eyes. In every action you perform, keep the words of the Torah before your eyes so that you act according to its commandments. Also, keep them within your heart, so that the meditation of your heart always follows the ways of wisdom. This is the same as what was stated in 3:21: “Let them not depart from your eyes; preserve sound wisdom and discretion.”
text.3_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: For they are life to those who find them. To the person who finds them—that is, the person for whom the words of Torah and wisdom have become a personal possession—they are life, namely the life of the soul. They are also healing to all his flesh, namely the body. Thus they are life to both soul and body; and even for one whose bodily order has been impaired and who becomes ill, they provide healing. They are unlike medicinal drugs, for which each organ requires a distinct remedy; the medicine of Torah benefits every organ and every type of illness.
text.3_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: Above every object of guarding, guard your heart. This follows what is stated: “Do good, Lord, to the good and to those upright in their hearts; but as for those who turn aside to crooked ways, the Lord will lead them away with the workers of iniquity.” I explained there that the essential thing is for a person to be upright in his heart and conscience, even when his outward deeds sometimes appear not to be upright. This is the definition of something curved: it is straight on the inside but appears bent externally. The Lord will deal well with all who are upright and good in their hearts; He will even punish one who judges them unfavorably because of an outward irregularity, for the Merciful One desires the heart. Thus, of everything from which one must guard and protect himself, the principal matter is to guard the heart so that it is protected from evil, for from it are the sources of life. The heart is the principal source from which life proceeds; the body is secondary to it, and an outward act is not evil when the conscience is upright, as the Sages said, “Great is a transgression performed for the sake of Heaven.” Nevertheless, I caution you—
text.3_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: Remove from yourself crookedness of mouth. Ensure that your outward conduct also gives people no opportunity to malign you and causes no desecration of God’s Name, even when your intention is pure and acceptable. The lips are more external than the mouth, and speech of the mouth is more substantial than speech of the lips. He warns you not to perform an act that would create grave suspicion, to the point that the mouth would distort your actions and say that you followed a crooked way and departed from uprightness. He adds, distance perversity of lips from yourself: even if the act would not generate such “crookedness of mouth” as to distort your conduct, but could produce only slight criticism upon external lips, you must avoid even that. “Perversity” is lighter than “crookedness,” for perversity is only a slight deviation. Do not merely remove perversity of lips from yourself; distance it, so that there is a great distance between you and even such speech. Correct your outward conduct so thoroughly that no one can speak even a slight word against you, even remotely.
text.3_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: Let your eyes look directly ahead. The eyes signify the open eyes, while the eyelids signify closing the eyes by means of the lids that cover them. A person must open his eyes in matters of the soul, looking toward God and His works, seeing His deeds and mighty acts, and walking in His ways. Thus, Let your eyes look directly ahead. “Directly ahead” indicates straight alignment with a particular point, and it is often used of alignment toward God; from this comes the expression “uprightness cannot enter” (Isaiah 59:14–15). Your eyes must look directly toward the ways of the Lord, as it says, “My eyes are always toward the Lord,” as I explained there. And let your eyelids direct themselves before you. In matters of the body and its desires, however, one must close his eyes and not stray after what his eyes see, so that through your eyelids your path will be made straight before you in matters concerning yourself—your body and its desires. This also means that in doing so they will go against what is “before you”: against the inclination of the heart, its desires, and the wishes of the body and matter.
text.3_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: Weigh the course of your foot. There is a distinction between a “way” and a “course”: a course is circuitous. When one must turn from the direct road and travel a circuitous route until it returns him to the road leading to the desired destination, the measure by which that circuitous route is calculated so as to reach the straight road is called a “balance.” A person should always follow the intermediate path, the good path in every trait. If at times he must turn from the intermediate path and follow a circuitous route—as when he has departed from the mean toward one extreme and must grasp the opposite extreme in order to return to the straight line—this requires a measured balance. For example, one who has adopted excessive pride must grasp the opposite extreme, extreme lowliness, and accustom himself to it until he returns to the midpoint, humility. This measure is called the balance. Thus, Weigh the course of your foot, and through this all your ways will be established: you will return to the straight road, which is the intermediate line. Yet with all this, I command you:
text.3_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not turn to the right or to the left. Initially, one must take care not to depart from the intermediate line, neither to the right nor to the left, neither toward excess nor toward deficiency. In this way, remove your foot from evil.
text.4_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, attend to my wisdom. These are the laws of wisdom. It has already been explained that the laws of wisdom cannot be demonstrated by proof; they are received through tradition, and you must listen to and accept them. Incline your ear to my understanding. Understanding is what a person comprehends through his own reason, deriving one thing from another by means of his understanding. Incline your ear to weigh these matters upon the scales of your understanding.
text.4_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: To preserve discretion. Corresponding to “attend to my wisdom,” he explains that you should preserve discretion—the profound counsels of wisdom. Corresponding to “incline your ear to my understanding,” he says, and your lips shall guard knowledge. As I have explained, “knowledge” applies to matters apprehended with certainty, either by the senses or through demonstrations of understanding. I have also explained that knowledge is associated with the lips. Through understanding, contemplate until you attain knowledge and clear certainty, so that your lips, which express words of knowledge, will preserve that knowledge.
text.4_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: For the lips of a strange woman drip honey. This contains both a parable and its meaning. The parable concerns a strange woman and the inclination of desire. The enticements of her lips resemble honeycomb, because she sweetens his desire for him, and her palate is smoother than oil: the taste of the transgression seems smooth as oil, and he senses no defect in it. In the allegorical meaning, it speaks of the inclination toward idolatry, through which the heart strays after alien opinions. The lips always allude to knowledge: the opinions upon which they build their proofs seem as sweet as honeycomb. Likewise, the flavor of her wisdom—the palate always alluding to wisdom—seems as smooth as oil, without defect.
text.4_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: But her end is bitter as wormwood. This is the opposite of “her lips drip honey.” Sharp as a double-edged sword is the opposite of “her palate is smoother than oil.” The soul tastes bitterness even in the premises they established, and through the conclusions they derive from them to deny the foundations of faith, it is cut down by the double-edged sword—the sword of punishment.
text.4_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Her feet descend to death. One who follows her and obeys her—as in “the people at your feet” (Exodus 11)—will be led by her to death. Her steps support the grave. Sheol is the deep pit into which a person may sometimes fall while still alive. Even the steps of one merely going toward her, though he has not yet lain with her, support the pit into which he will fall, and he will no longer be able to escape. Allegorically, one already captured by heresy will suffer the death of the soul; even one who merely follows its way, employing its deceptive syllogisms and philosophical premises, may no longer be able to escape.
text.4_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Lest you weigh the path of life. We have explained the distinction between a path and a course: a course is a circuitous road, and the measure used to calculate a circuitous course so that it reaches the straight road is called a balance. Do not attempt to travel a circuitous route through the harlot’s house in order to reach the path of life, calculating how you will return from that course to the straight path—as in the proposal, “Let us pass the entrance of the harlots, subdue our inclination, and receive a reward.” Her courses wander: her courses move and deviate from the straight path, and you will not know how to return to the path of life. Allegorically, do not say that through investigation and philosophy you will return to faith and establish everything by proof; afterward your soul will wander in circuits of doubt, and you will no longer find the true way to the light of faith.
text.4_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And now, children, listen to me. Listen to the laws of wisdom received from the Lord, and do not depart from the sayings of my mouth. The mouth alludes to wisdom; do not depart from it toward philosophical inquiry and the opinions of heretics.
text.4_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Distance your way from her. Do not let your road pass by her, and do not approach the entrance of her house even when the harlot is not there. Allegorically, distance yourself from the ways of idolatry and heresy. Do not even approach the premises and syllogisms through which one enters the gates of denial. Do not say that you will use those syllogisms to build a faithful house for Torah and testimony.
text.4_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Lest you give your splendor to others. Splendor is the soul’s inner beauty. Through immorality the light of the intellect and the soul’s splendor are dimmed, and your years are given to a cruel one, as a cruel disease that rules over adulterers dominates your body. Allegorically, through heresy you surrender your splendor—your soul and intellectual powers—to “others,” to matters that do not promote the soul’s happiness but lead it to destruction. You give your years to a cruel one, for the years of the wicked are shortened.
text.4_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Lest strangers be sated with your strength. The body’s generative power will satiate strangers—that is, a strange woman. And your labors—your wealth and possessions acquired through toil, as in “through toil shall you eat of it”—will be in the house of a foreigner. The children of the foreign woman, who are not regarded as related to you, will inherit you, for the child of a gentile woman has her status.
text.4_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And you will groan at your end, when your flesh and body are consumed. At the end, when your flesh is exhausted through the wearing away caused by desire, you will groan and regret the past. Allegorically, when one approaches his end and his flesh and desires—which led him to depart from the foundations of faith in order to satisfy bodily desire—are consumed, he will groan and regret. He will then contemplate the eternal world that he lost through the strange woman, meaning heresy. One whose loins are girded with faith does not grieve over the consumption of the flesh, because he hopes for the life of the soul.
text.4_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And you will say: How I hated discipline. Discipline comes through chastisement or fear of punishment; this you hated completely. Reproof consists of reasoning with a person and returning him to the good way through intellectual arguments. I did not hate this outright, but my heart despised it; I regarded it with contempt.
text.4_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: I did not listen to the voice of my teachers, nor incline my ear to those who instructed me. One who instructs is greater than one who merely directs. A director shows a person once how something should be done; an instructor teaches him repeatedly, through rational study, and explains the matter. He adds that he did not even incline his ear to hear such instruction.
text.4_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: I was almost—because of something slight, namely the desires of this world, which are worth nothing and endure only briefly. How could I sell my birthright for this little pleasure, until I was amid every evil, with every calamity coming upon me and the loss exceeding the gain? Moreover, my evils came upon me publicly, amid the congregation and assembly, bringing humiliation and wrath.
text.4_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Drink water from your own cistern. Instead of the inclination’s enticement to hew broken cisterns that cannot hold water, drink from your own cistern—the waters of wisdom and knowledge. A cistern differs from a well: the water of a cistern is collected rainwater, while the water of a well springs forth. He compares the beginning of wisdom-study to collected cistern water, because at first one receives the laws of wisdom solely through tradition. Afterward they become flowing water from within your well: they resemble well water and an ever-strengthening spring, as one develops new insights through his own reason. The waters of knowledge also become so strong within his heart that they flow outward from the well to teach Torah and wisdom to others, until—
text.4_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: Your springs disperse outside. His teachings spread to his children and students, and afterward streams of water flow in the streets. There is a distinction between “outside” and “the street”: outside means behind the houses, where only members of the household are found, while the street is the broad public area before the houses. Eventually all Israel will draw and drink from the waters of his wisdom, which will become streams spreading in every direction, as the Sages said: he becomes like an ever-strengthening spring and a river that never ceases.
text.4_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Let them be yours alone. Although the springs of your wisdom spread outward, the teachings will be stated in your name, and the reward for the wisdom will be yours alone. And not for strangers with you. Although your students who disseminate your wisdom will also share the reward with you, they are not strangers, for they are regarded as your children.
text.4_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Let your source be blessed. The source is the place from which the spring that spreads through the depths of the earth begins to flow. Allegorically, it means that your intellect will be blessed, for you will find sound understanding from the Lord. And rejoice in the wife of your youth, namely the Torah that you received in your youth.
text.4_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: A loving doe and a graceful ibex. Both the doe and the ibex dwell upon divided mountains and rocks, and their womb is narrow, as it says, “Do you know the time when the ibexes of the rock give birth; do you observe the calving of the does?” The doe awakens love and the ibex awakens grace. He compares the higher wisdom to a doe and ibex in their swift course over divided mountains. Wisdom likewise comes from above, from a lofty place; it moves swiftly through its intellectual apprehensions and arouses love and grace. Corresponding to the graceful ibex he says, Let her breasts satisfy you at all times: the breasts are associated with union, when grace is aroused. Corresponding to the loving doe he says, Be enraptured always with her love, even when not engaged in union. Allegorically, when you unite with wisdom to produce conclusions and new insights, her breasts will satisfy you by enabling you to discover new things; even when you produce no new insights, be enraptured with love of her by reviewing the earlier truths you have already attained.
text.4_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Why, my son, should you be enraptured with a strange woman? You would then go still further astray and embrace the bosom of a foreign woman, who is worse than the strange woman, being the daughter of a foreign god. Allegorically, the strange women are deceptive branches of wisdom. Why should you become enraptured with them when wisdom and knowledge are available in the Lord’s Torah? The foreign woman represents the teachings of heresy and denial, which you will later embrace.
text.4_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: For a man’s ways are directly before the eyes of the Lord. A way is the straight road, while a course is circuitous; measuring a course so that it reaches the straight road is called weighing it. A person’s straight spiritual ways stand directly before the Lord, Who prepared the straight way for him through the Torah, as it says, “You shall make known to them the way in which they shall walk.” And He weighs all his courses. If at times he must travel a course that deviates from the straight way—for example, through exceptional piety beyond the letter of the law, or by temporarily overriding a Torah law for the needs of the hour, as Elijah did on Mount Carmel—the Lord weighs and directs that course too, so that through it he reaches the straight way.
text.4_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: His iniquities will capture the wicked man. In contrast to the good ways of a person, which are before the Lord’s eyes and in which the Lord assists him to purify himself and walk rightly, the wicked man’s ways do not come from the Lord; his own iniquities capture him. As the Sages said, one who comes to purify himself is assisted, while one who comes to defile himself is merely given an opening. There is a distinction between iniquity and sin. Iniquity denotes distortion of the intellect, while sin denotes the actual deed; iniquity is distorted thought, while sin is a defect in action. When desire entices and compels the wicked man to transgress, while he fears the Lord’s punishments and the Torah’s command, he summons iniquity—intellectual distortion—to assist him. He distorts his thought to deny the commandment and its Commander, His knowledge and Providence, reward and punishment, and similar matters. His iniquities thereby capture him into violating the command. Nevertheless, his principal support is not intellectual distortion. Had there been no sin—his desire for the transgression—he would not have relied upon iniquity and denial. Rather, he is supported by the cords of his sin: the cords of his desire support him, and through them he employs iniquity and denies the commandment to satisfy his inclination. By becoming habituated to sin, however, he is drawn into heresy and grasps iniquity—intellectual distortion and denial—until eventually—
text.4_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: He will die without discipline. He will no longer accept discipline, meaning warnings about the Lord’s punishments. Even when the Lord punishes him, he will not receive discipline, and in the abundance of his foolishness he will go astray. He will cling to folly, for the fool casts doubt upon everything. He will not believe that the punishment came through Providence, but will doubt and attribute it to chance. Therefore he will not accept discipline, because he explains everything as happenstance.
text.5_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, if you have guaranteed for your fellow that you will do something for him, and afterward have struck your palm for a stranger concerning something contrary to your guarantee to your fellow—for example, you guaranteed that you would sell your fellow a house or field and afterward struck your palm with a stranger to sell him that same property. There is an ordinary guarantor and a guarantor who assumes primary liability; he adds that to the stranger you gave a handshake, which is stronger than an ordinary guarantee.
text.5_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: You have been ensnared by the sayings of your mouth. First you were ensnared by guaranteeing for your fellow, and you are obligated to fulfill your word both because his guarantee came first and because he is your fellow. Afterward, you were captured by the sayings of your mouth, for by giving your handshake you were caught in a trap.
text.5_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Do this, therefore. This is the counsel you should follow in order to be saved. Since you have come into your fellow’s palm and his guarantee came first, go, humble yourself before the stranger so that he releases you from the handshake; and press your fellow, or magnify and appease your fellow by fulfilling his desire until he releases you from the obligation you assumed.
text.5_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Give no sleep to your eyes—no settled sleep—and not even a momentary slumber.
text.5_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: “Save yourself like a gazelle from the hand.” A captured gazelle escapes by the strength of its body and its horns.
text.5_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And like a bird from the hand of the trapper. A trapper places adhesive, and the bird is ensnared when its feathers stick to it. It escapes by plucking out the feathers adhering to the snare.
text.5_Chapter, 4_Verse, 2_Comment: So too you should escape: either through your bodily strength, or by leaving your money and clothing in the hands of the person for whom you guaranteed.
text.5_Chapter, 4_Verse, 3_Comment: All this is a parable. Its meaning concerns the guarantee that every person has given the Lord to observe His Torah and commandments, as the Sages said, “Everything is held as collateral”; or the guarantee to preserve his soul in purity. Afterward he strikes his palm for the stranger—the evil inclination or the desiring material body that he follows to act contrary to his guarantee. Through this, “you are ensnared by the sayings of your mouth.” Throughout this book the mouth alludes to wisdom: first he is ensnared by the sayings of his mouth to act according to the laws of wisdom, and afterward he is captured into acting contrary to those laws.
text.5_Chapter, 4_Verse, 4_Comment: The counsel is this: since you have come into the palm of your Fellow—having promised and sworn to the Lord to observe His commandments, and having obligated yourself to protect your soul from the traps of the evil inclination—you must subdue your material nature. This is the meaning of “go, humble yourself.” You must also exalt and magnify your Fellow, meaning the Holy One, blessed be He, or the soul. Give no sleep to your eyes, but serve the Lord continually and escape from the evil inclination. “Like a gazelle from the hand”: run like a gazelle to do the will of your Creator, and when the evil inclination has seized you in its hand, wrench yourself free through your strength for Torah and testimony. If it has drawn you into its net through enticement, escape like a bird from the trapper’s snare by abandoning your feathers—your external garments: distribute your imaginary possessions to the poor, shave your hair for Heaven like the Nazirite who came before Simeon the Righteous, and afflict your body through suffering.
text.5_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: “Go to the ant, sluggard.” All the powers of creation are implanted in the human soul. Every power and trait found in any species of animal is therefore also found in the human soul. Animals possess many traits unnecessary for their own survival; the Lord implanted those traits so that people would learn from them, as our Sages said: had the Torah not been given, we would have learned modesty from the cat, and so forth. The Lord implanted in the ant the trait of diligence in gathering and storing, so that a person would learn from it to apply himself and greatly increase his gathering of wisdom. Thus: you, sluggard, who think that diligence is absent from your soul, or that it is neither good nor useful, go to the ant. You will find this trait implanted in it not merely for its survival, but so that you may observe its ways and become wise—learning from it to gather the laws of wisdom with diligence and great effort.
text.5_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Which has no chief, officer, or ruler. Among people, individuals sometimes adopt a particular trait even when it is not good because a chief—the distinguished person standing at their head—conducts himself that way and all imitate his deeds, or because an officer and ruler compels uniform conduct through officials and taskmasters. The ant does not act for either of these reasons, and nevertheless—
text.5_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: It prepares its bread in summer, after gathering its food at harvest. Harvest precedes summer. Throughout the harvest it gathers kernels of grain for food; afterward, when harvest has ended and summer begins, with no more kernels in the field, it prepares its bread by placing it in a protected location and cutting off the tips of the kernels so they will not sprout. Learn from this to gather abundantly the laws of wisdom and words of Torah in your heart throughout your youth; do not say that you have enough. After gathering them all, understand them through your intellect, as the Sages said: first a person should learn, and afterward reason. Prepare provisions for the appointed day, just as the ant prepares for winter, for only one who labored on the eve of the Sabbath will eat on the Sabbath. After gathering the laws of wisdom, prepare them through understanding and intellect to become the soul’s bread, for wisdom and Torah are the radiant nourishment of the soul for the appointed day.
text.5_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: How long, sluggard, will you lie down? Harvest has passed and summer has ended, yet you still lie idle and have done nothing. A sluggard habitually sleeps for hours into the day; after awakening, he spends the rest of the day lying upon his bed. Thus, “How long will you lie down?” More than this: When will you arise and awaken from your sleep? Allegorically, in youth he sleeps and discerns nothing because of foolishness. Even after awakening and understanding the purpose of man and that he should engage in the Lord’s Torah, he afterward lies down and does nothing because of laziness. Therefore: how long will you be lazy, and more seriously, how long will you remain immersed in foolishness?
text.5_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: A little sleep. First he sleeps a settled sleep; afterward, a little slumber, neither fully asleep nor fully awake. Even after awakening from slumber, there is a little folding of the hands to lie down upon the bed and do nothing.
text.5_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And your poverty will come like a traveler. As his property is depleted, poverty arrives like an ordinary traveler proceeding unobstructed, because at first he does nothing against the poverty approaching him. And your want like an armed man. Afterward want comes upon him, lacking bread and all his needs. Then he rises and fights against want, wishing to drive it from his house; but want stands against him like a man bearing shield and buckler, and he cannot drive it from his house or do anything against it.
text.5_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: A man. One who is a worthless man casts off the yoke of Heaven in commandments between man and God, and in commandments between man and his fellow he is a man of iniquity. His sin is recognizable in seven things. First, in the organ of speech: he walks with a crooked mouth, speaking perversely against the laws of wisdom, for the mouth alludes to wisdom. Second, regarding the instruments of action and the eyes, it says—
text.5_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: He winks with his eyes, contrary to “Do not stray after your eyes.” Third, with the organs of movement, he signals with his feet, hinting evil messages with them. Fourth, with his hands, he points with his fingers. Fifth, regarding thought—
text.5_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Perversities are in his heart. In matters of faith he thinks ideas contrary to faith; in human affairs he devises evil against his fellow. Seventh, he sends forth quarrels between one person and another.
text.5_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore his calamity will come suddenly. His calamity will arrive quickly in time, and the execution of his punishment will also be swift: he will suddenly be broken, without remedy, because he will not repent.
text.5_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: These six—the first six matters he listed—the Lord hates; and the seventh, sending forth quarrels, is an abomination to His soul. It is worse than all the others because it destroys society as a whole.
text.5_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Haughty eyes. He lists them again in detail with more severe forms. Corresponding to “he winks with his eyes,” he adds haughty eyes—pride that arrogantly opposes faith. Corresponding to “he walks with a crooked mouth,” he adds a lying tongue. The tongue always signifies understanding, which is set against wisdom by means of arguments of understanding and deceptive syllogisms. Corresponding to “he points with his fingers,” he says, hands that shed innocent blood.
text.5_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: A heart. Corresponding to “he devises evil,” he says, a heart that devises thoughts of iniquity. Corresponding to “he signals with his feet,” he says, feet that hurry to run toward evil. Corresponding to “perversities are in his heart,” he adds—
text.5_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: He breathes lies as a false witness. He speaks falsehood and bears false testimony regarding matters of faith. Corresponding to the seventh, which is the Lord’s abomination, he again says, and one who sends forth quarrels among brothers.
text.5_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, preserve your father’s commandment. A commandment is something by which the commander compels the commanded person to carry out his instruction, like a father’s command to his son or a master’s to his servants. Torah consists of teachings, such as beliefs, opinions, and ethical instruction. He therefore attributes commandments to the father who compels obedience, and directs that they be preserved even when contrary to the heart’s nature. Do not forsake your mother’s Torah. He attributes Torah to the mother. Once a person preserves his father’s commandments, he will naturally not forsake the mother’s Torah, because the human soul is naturally drawn after Torah. Only when a person rejects a commandment does he abandon Torah and deny foundations of faith so that he can cast off the commandments’ yoke. One who preserves the commandment will not forsake Torah.
text.5_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: Bind them continually upon your heart. Although the commandments are remote from the heart’s nature, bind them with cords so that they remain continually attached to your heart, and incline your heart—the governing power within the body—to observe them. Tie them around your throat as well: speak of them continually, for through repetition they will also be preserved in your heart. All this concerns the commandments. Regarding your mother’s Torah, he says—
text.5_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: When you walk about. He speaks of the three situations mentioned above (3:23–25): walking on the road, lying down, and arising at home. When you walk about on the road, where dangers are present, she will guide you along the straight way. When you lie down, when danger exists because you are not employing your senses or intellect, she will guard you. When you awaken from sleep, she will be your conversation.
text.5_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: For a commandment is a lamp, and Torah is light. An individual commandment is compared to an individual lamp; the comprehensive Torah is compared to the universal light. A lamp burns only while oil and wick are present. So too a commandment applies while a person is confined within the body. Light shines by its own nature; similarly, the light of Torah cleaves to the soul because it is a Divine soul, and after separation God’s light still shines above them and their crowns are upon their heads. Just as light enables a lamp to shine, so engagement in Torah enables a person to observe commandments, for an ignorant person cannot be pious. Light comes from above and a lamp from below; likewise, Torah’s light is from above, while the lamp of the commandment operates below in bodily matters and is joined to the soul, resembling oil and wick in which light catches and shines. And the reproofs of discipline are the way of life. Even one possessing light and a lamp must walk upon the way of life; otherwise the light and lamp will not help him. What leads him on that way? The reproofs of discipline. By accepting rational reproof through discipline and fear of the Lord, he walks on the way of life. The lamp of commandment and light of Torah then protect him from pits, thorns, and briars, as it says, “Fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge.”
text.5_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: To guard you from an evil woman—an Israelite harlot—from the smooth tongue of a foreign woman—a gentile harlot—even though she entices you with smooth speech. Allegorically, the evil woman signifies branches of wisdom leading to denial of God, and the foreign woman’s smooth tongue signifies the ways of idolatry, although they proceed through seemingly rational syllogisms. The tongue always alludes to understanding.
text.5_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not desire her beauty in your heart. Guard yourself from being captured by her beauty and from being enticed when she signals with her eyelids. Allegorically, do not desire their methods of speculation and inquiry, and do not be drawn after their proofs, which may appear substantial to you and seem to perceive the very eyelids of dawn.
text.5_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: For on account of a harlot who is unmarried, a person may be reduced to a loaf of bread, losing his wealth and livelihood. But another man’s wife hunts a precious soul: she hunts the soul itself, even if it is precious and exalted, like that of a prophet or prince.
text.5_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: Can one scoop up fire? He gives two parables. The first is of scooping fire into one’s bosom—actual fire placed in his bosom, which will completely burn his garments. The second is—
text.5_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: Can a man walk upon coals? They are not flames but coals, and he does not scoop them into his bosom but merely walks upon them; nevertheless, his feet will be burned.
text.5_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: So is one who comes to his fellow’s wife. He resembles one who scoops fire into his bosom. Moreover, whoever touches her—even if he does not lie with her but merely touches her, like the second parable of walking upon coals—will not go unpunished; his feet will be burned.
text.5_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: People do not despise a thief. A thief is superior to an adulterer. First, necessity compelled him, for he steals to fill his soul when he is hungry. Second, if—
text.5_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: He is found, his punishment has a limit: he shall pay sevenfold. If he stole an ox or sheep, he pays four additional oxen or three additional sheep, besides returning the stolen animal itself. Through this, he may give all the wealth of his house and discharge his punishment through money.
text.5_Chapter, 31_Verse, 0_Comment: One who commits adultery with a woman, however, lacks a heart. He is unlike the thief who stole to fill his hungry soul. He does it because he destroys his own soul, for adultery will not satisfy his hunger; there is one organ in man such that feeding it only makes it hungrier.
text.5_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: A wound. The thief pays only money, while the adulterer finds a wound. The thief is not despised, but the adulterer finds disgrace. The thief’s shame is erased through the fourfold or fivefold payment, but his disgrace will not be erased.
text.5_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: For jealousy is a man’s fury. The fury of the woman’s husband burns because of jealousy: he is jealous for his honor and because the honor of his household was profaned. Therefore, he will not show compassion on the day of vengeance, for vengeance caused by jealousy knows no compassion.
text.5_Chapter, 34_Verse, 0_Comment: He will accept no ransom. If the adulterer wishes to give him monetary compensation, he will not accept it, because his wife has become forbidden to him and his children’s status has been profaned; money cannot atone for this. He will not consent even if you increase the bribe. Even if you offer the judges a great bribe so that they declare his wife permitted and thereby remove the cause of jealousy, he will not consent, because vengeance will still burn within his heart.
text.6_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, keep my words. Likewise, it says above (2:1), “If you receive my words and treasure my commandments with you,” as explained there.
text.6_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Keep my commandments and live. A person performs the commandments and lives through them, while the Torah is the light of the eyes that shows him the way in which to walk. Therefore, keep my Torah like the pupil of your eye: just as a person guards the pupil of his eye from blindness, so must he guard the Torah, the intellectual eye through which he sees light.
text.6_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Bind them upon your fingers, so that every deed you perform with your fingers accords with the Torah. Write them upon the tablet of your heart, so that every thought of the heart accords with the ways of wisdom. The heart is the ruling power of the soul, and the concepts of wisdom must be inscribed upon it as God’s writing engraved upon the tablets, to still the tumult of the images of desire that rise against the heart. That is, both your thoughts and the actions of your fingers should all follow the Torah’s counsel.
text.6_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Say to wisdom, ‘You are my sister.’ Closeness to a sister comes through birth, whereas closeness to an intimate acquaintance comes through choice. As explained, a person does not discover the laws of wisdom on his own; they are given to him by God, just as love for a sister is given by God. The human soul is constituted with all the faculties that bear wisdom, and wisdom’s laws are implanted in the soul from its creation, like a sister whose kinship is by birth. Understanding, however, is generated by a person from his own knowledge, as he understands one thing from another. Therefore, it says, and call understanding your intimate, for this resembles an acquaintance whom he has drawn close by his own choice.
text.6_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: To guard you from a strange woman. A “strange” woman may even be an Israelite if she is not his wife, whereas a “foreign” woman is specifically from another nation. Ordinarily he will not love a foreign woman unless she entices him with smooth speech; therefore it says, from the foreign woman who makes her words smooth. Allegorically, studies foreign to the wisdom of Torah are called a strange woman. Nevertheless, what was foreign may conceivably become his wife through marriage, and these disciplines may likewise be used for Torah purposes. The foreign woman represents doctrines of heresy and idolatry, which are wholly alien to Torah, though they make their claims attractive through philosophical arguments that lead to heresy. The Torah will save him from both.
text.6_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: For at the window of my house, through my lattice, I looked out. Through a window one sees revealed things, while through a lattice one observes hidden matters. That is, I saw both in an open vision and in a concealed vision.
text.6_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: I saw among the simple. Through the window I saw the simple, who lack the sense to conceal their deeds; through the lattice, I discerned among the youths—those who are not simple and conceal their actions. By looking through the lattice I understood how he was a youth lacking a heart, meaning that he lacked the ruling power needed to restrain his desire.
text.6_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Passing through the marketplace. I saw that at first he merely passed through the marketplace, but then inclined near her corner, the corner where she sat. Afterward, he strode on the way to her house, as the text explains.
text.6_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: At twilight. At first he passes through the marketplace at twilight, meaning at the beginning of night. Since dawn is also called twilight, it specifies in the evening of the day, meaning the twilight at day’s end. Afterward, he strides toward her house in the pupil of night and darkness.
text.6_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And behold, a woman came to meet him. Just as he intended to take the road to her house, so she came out to meet him, dressed as a harlot: her nakedness and sexuality were naturally inclined toward promiscuity. She was guarded of heart, lacking the ruling power to master her desire, for her heart—the ruling faculty—was besieged, with thoughts of desire constantly surrounding it with images of sin, as in “her heart is snares and nets”; her heart was confined and guarded by them.
text.6_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: She is clamorous. Her entire nature and disposition depart from equilibrium. In her traits she is noisy and constantly angry. Do not suppose that she rages at rebellious maidservants; on the contrary, she herself is rebellious and provokes her husband and household. She also abandons modesty, for her feet do not remain in her house, but rather—
text.6_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Sometimes outside, behind the house, and sometimes in the streets, in the public domain crowded with people; moreover, she lurks at every corner to hunt those walking off to the side.
text.6_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: She seized him. She advances in brazenness from one degree to the next: first she takes hold of him; then she grows still bolder—she kisses him, hardens her face even more, and says to him.
text.6_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Peace-offerings were incumbent upon me. She tells him that she is inviting him to a mitzvah feast to eat the meat of peace-offerings, and that for her it is the joy of a mitzvah, for today I fulfilled my vows. The evil inclination begins with a mitzvah.
text.6_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore I came out. At first she says that because she saw him walking, she came out to meet him. She grows bolder and says that she went out to seek his face and look for him—that when she set out she did not know he would chance to meet her, but intended from the outset to seek him.
text.6_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: With spreads. She grows bolder, proposing that he lodge there in her house, and that her couch is spread with costly coverings upon which he may lie.
text.6_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: I have perfumed my bed. She grows bolder still, saying that he will lie upon her own bed. When she said, “I have spread my couch,” she had not specified that he would lie on her bed; he could lie on her couch while she slept elsewhere. But my bed means the place where she herself will lie.
text.6_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Come, let us sate ourselves with love, and she adds, let us delight ourselves with lovemaking, for the term “lovemaking” explicitly denotes intercourse and union.
text.6_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: For he is not— so that he will not fear her husband, she says that the man is not in his house; and so that he will not fear that he may return, she says, he has gone on a distant journey. Lest he say that her husband may need money for commerce and return home, she says—
text.6_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: He took the money-bag in his hand. And lest he fear that the business will be completed quickly and her husband will return, she says, he will come home at the appointed day: he has a fixed time for returning and will not come before then.
text.6_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: She inclined him. Observe that at first he did not listen to her; only with her abundant persuasion did she incline him to turn toward her. Afterward, with the smoothness of her lips and flattering words, she drives him away from his place, so that he begins moving after her.
text.6_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: He suddenly follows her. Once displaced from his position, he suddenly begins to walk, for had he delayed and consulted his reason, he would have restrained himself. It therefore happens suddenly. Even so, at first his heart reproaches him and he goes under compulsion, like an ox led to slaughter, which does not go willingly but by force. Later he will go willingly; nevertheless, he goes like a jingling serpent to discipline a fool. Though the hissing serpent goes willingly to punish the fool, it still makes a sound warning the fool—who doubts everything—to beware its venom. So too, even as he goes willingly, his heart sounds a warning about the venom hidden there.
text.6_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: Until an arrow pierces his liver. The arrow of desire pierces his liver and makes his blood, whose source is in the liver, boil like a pot. Then he no longer goes unwillingly but willingly, as a bird hastens into a snare, moving swiftly, not knowing that it is at the cost of its life. So too, he now goes willingly, and his heart no longer reproaches him.
text.6_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: And now, sons, listen to me. First listen and understand why my words are correct; afterward, attend even to the words of my mouth without demanding any reason at all.
text.6_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: Let your heart not turn aside to her ways. A “way” is a public road, while a “path” is for an individual. Not only must your heart not turn toward her ways—that is, to commit adultery with her—but do not stray into her paths: do not err by entering even her small paths, such as speaking with her or looking at her. A person might tell himself that he is certain he will not sin and will earn a reward, as in, “Let us go past the door of the harlots, subdue our inclination, and receive a reward.” That too is a small path branching from her ways.
text.6_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: For— it explains that one must not turn to her broad ways, for she has felled many wounded. Nor should one trust his righteousness, supposing that he will not sin, and stray into her smaller paths, for mighty are all those she has slain: the people she killed were mighty and strong in Torah and fear of Heaven, yet they did not withstand the trial. Therefore, do not approach her at all, as stated above: “Do not draw near the entrance of her house.”
text.6_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: For her house is the ways to Sheol. Sheol is the deep pit, and one may fall into it even before dying. Thus, even one who merely walks by the way of her house is already walking on the ways to Sheol and will fall into a deep pit. It pictures death dwelling in Sheol’s deepest chambers; whoever enters Sheol descends from there to the chambers of death—meaning that he will come to commit the sin.
text.7_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Does not wisdom call? In contrast to the harlot, who comes in darkness and gloom, wisdom calls publicly.
text.7_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: It has already been explained that giving voice is less forceful than calling, for:
text.7_Chapter, 0_Verse, 2_Comment: * Wisdom comes from above and is received from Hashem, the Giver of wisdom. It calls to a person to heed wisdom’s laws and accept them.
text.7_Chapter, 0_Verse, 3_Comment: * Understanding gives forth its voice, because it emerges from the human intellect and announces that a person possesses the power to contemplate and to understand one thing from another. A person senses this voice in the depths of his soul; he calls to understanding and draws it out of his own intellect.
text.7_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: At the head of the heights. In contrast to the harlot, who leaves her house for the outside and the streets, wisdom is pictured as descending from on high. First it stands at the head of the heights, upon the great way, the public road. Afterward, at the house of paths it stations itself, by the smaller paths along which individuals travel alone to the city. From there it takes its stand.
text.7_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Beside the gates, at the mouth of the city. It stands at the city gate through which people enter the city; afterward, at the entrance of the doorways it sings, at the entrances used by individuals.
text.7_Chapter, 2_Verse, 2_Comment: * Wisdom first comes through simple matters and laws entrusted to the entire populace. It is pictured as standing on the public road traveled by everyone. These are the plain meaning of the Torah’s words, its straightforward narratives, and the commandments according to their plain sense, which are given equally to the whole populace.
text.7_Chapter, 2_Verse, 3_Comment: * Afterward, it stands at the house of paths, traveled only by particular individuals. These are teachings of Torah not entrusted to the entire populace but only to sages, who walk on paths of their own: the homiletical and intellectual approaches to Torah, the ways of piety in the commandments, and the reasons for the commandments.
text.7_Chapter, 2_Verse, 4_Comment: * Afterward, it stands beside the gates where the Sanhedrin and judges sit. These are the Torah’s laws entrusted to the Sanhedrin and the great sages of heart, who received the entire Oral Torah and from whom instruction issues to all Israel.
text.7_Chapter, 2_Verse, 5_Comment: * Afterward, it sings at the entrance of the doorways, where individuals sit secretly in their chambers of instruction. These are the Torah’s mysteries, such as the Account of Creation and the Account of the Chariot, which are not expounded publicly but only to an individual—and only to exceptional individuals.
text.7_Chapter, 2_Verse, 6_Comment: These four correspond to “amon as a pedagogue,” “amon as great,” “amon as concealed,” and “amon as hidden”—the four levels of PaRDeS, as is known.
text.7_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: To you, men, I call. “Men” are the great; wisdom’s call comes particularly to you.
text.7_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: And my voice is to the sons of man. Other, lesser people hear my voice, although the call is not directed specifically to them.
text.7_Chapter, 3_Verse, 2_Comment: For wisdom comes only into the hearts of those who have sanctified their heart to be its sanctuary and removed every abomination and evil image from its chamber, until they are called “wise of heart,” because their heart rules through wisdom. Nevertheless, it gives its voice to the entire mass of humanity, and each person merits receiving from it according to his understanding. It gives its voice even to those who deviate from it through simplicity or foolishness. Concerning this it says—
text.7_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Understand cunning, you simple ones. Cunning is the opposite of simplicity. The simple person deviates from wisdom’s laws because his heart is enticed by everything, and he lacks the shrewdness to examine and consider his ways. Wisdom puts shrewdness into his heart, as stated (1:4), “to give cunning to the simple,” and as explained there. And fools, understand the heart. Fools differ from the simple: they do not lack wisdom—a fool may at times possess great knowledge—but deviate from wisdom’s laws because images of desire and evil traits rule them. Their heart, the ruling power of the soul, cannot overcome their inclination; therefore they dispute wisdom’s laws, which stand as an adversary before their desires. Wisdom consequently tells them to understand the heart: learn to rule your spirit and enable your heart to overcome your desires. You will thereby clear a way for wisdom to dwell gloriously in your sanctuary.
text.7_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Listen, for I speak noble things. It now sets forth how Hashem revealed wisdom and gave it to humanity through the Torah He gave His people. It considers four aspects. Every commandment has “speech” and “saying”: the saying is the wording in which the commandment was stated in the Written Torah, while the speech is the commandment’s explanation transmitted orally, in which its details were fully explained. Wherever Scripture says, “Hashem spoke to Moses, saying,” “spoke” means that He addressed him at length and taught him orally the commandment’s details and laws; “saying” means, “thus He said,” the wording of the Written Torah. There are two further aspects: first, the reasons and mysteries of the commandments; second, received teachings that are hidden secrets, such as the secrets of Torah, the Account of Creation, and the Account of the Chariot. In each there are two levels, as in “To you, men, I call, and my voice is to the sons of man”: exalted subjects stated for the great men and sages of the nation, and simple matters stated for the populace. Regarding the Oral Torah, which constitutes most of Torah, it says, Listen, for I speak noble things. The Oral Torah, in which I spoke at length about all the laws, particulars, and interpretations of the commandments—as denoted by “spoke”—consists of noble things. A nagid commands the people, and these teachings likewise come as officers and commands to be performed. And just as a nagid is great and honored among the people, these are all great, established laws entrusted to the leaders and teachers of the nation. This corresponds to “To you, men, I call.” Yet the opening of my lips is also uprightness. The lips signify plain, revealed speech; the opening of the lips is the beginning of simple discourse, intended for the populace who do not understand noble and elevated matters. It too is upright: words of integrity acceptable to reason, which every person can perceive as straight and understand with an upright heart.
text.7_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: For my palate utters truth. The palate tastes food and here alludes to the reasons for the commandments, which likewise were not written but were transmitted for reflection, thought, and study. They too are divided between the great and the general populace. Great people attain through the reasons for the commandments truths concerning the soul and its bond with God, divine attachment, and the resting of His spirit upon those who observe His commandments. In their secret dimension, all the commandments contain received truths about the order and repair of the worlds, their interconnections, the mystery of the soul and its bond with existence as a whole, and the drawing down of divinity, emanation, and influence, and the joining, ascent, and descent of the lights through the commandments. These are all truths contemplated by wisdom through intellectual reflection, secretly and inwardly. This is hinted by the palate, the innermost organ of speech, beyond the tongue, mouth, and lips. Nevertheless, each commandment also has reasons that may be explained to the populace: all serve to distance wickedness, injustice, evil traits, and alien beliefs, as in the reasons given by the Guide in the third part of his work. These too have a place in wisdom’s voice to ordinary people. Therefore it says, wickedness is an abomination to my lips: the lips indicate revealed speech, and the revealed reasons make wickedness abhorrent and distance it.
text.7_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: All the sayings of my mouth are in righteousness. It now speaks of the Written Torah, denoted by “saying,” the wording in which each commandment was stated. All were spoken through the power of supreme wisdom; therefore they are called the sayings of my mouth, for the lips allude to wisdom. In their plain sense they were stated in righteousness, and from all of them the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness. This is equal for all people. They also contain teachings unique to exceptional individuals, in that there is nothing twisted or crooked in them. Human statements contain irregular expressions that depart from linguistic rules, superfluous phrases, and defective formulations. In the Written Torah, however, there is nothing twisted or even crooked, for every unusual wording, apparent redundancy, and transposition in the Torah contains lofty wisdom, interpretations, secrets, and wonders of wisdom for those of sound understanding upon whom the spirit of Hashem rests.
text.7_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: They are all— Regarding the fourth aspect, the Torah’s hidden mysteries, some attain them through the power of understanding, contemplating Hashem’s greatness, His deeds and wonders in the Account of Creation, and His hosts and camps in the Account of the Chariot. Others attain them through knowledge: lucid perceptions in the souls of holy people who are pure of heart concerning divine matters. I have explained that knowledge must be straight. A straight line is the shortest line between two given points. Knowledge applies to anything known through sensory perception or first principles, and one must direct the object of knowledge along the shortest path to its attainment. This is exceedingly difficult in human knowledge, for ordinarily a person travels in circles, testing and examining until he reaches clear knowledge. But the lucid perceptions of the Torah’s secrets are straight to those who find knowledge: those who find knowledge of God within their souls attain it through Torah and divine assistance by a straight and short path. Understanding is characterized as “directly opposite”: one point corresponding to another. The discerning person moves from premise to conclusion through reasoning and inferences, yet often his understanding does not face the object directly, for his inferences lead him astray in many directions. The Torah’s secrets attained by one wise and discerning from his own knowledge are all direct to one who understands: he apprehends the presence of Hashem, His glory, greatness, and deeds without any deviation from the point of truth.
text.7_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Take my discipline and not silver. Silver is spent to purchase whatever is needed, whereas fine gold is not spent but stored among treasures. Accordingly, it compares the discipline of wisdom to silver. As explained, “fear of Hashem is the discipline of wisdom.” Since wisdom’s laws cannot be demonstrated by proofs of knowledge and the impulses of the human heart oppose wisdom, a person must bind the powers of his soul through discipline—fear of Hashem. Through it he accepts wisdom’s laws and observes them out of fear of Hashem, Who commanded them. Thus, wisdom’s discipline is something expended: through it one acquires wisdom’s laws and stores them in the heart’s treasury, as in “fear of Hashem is his treasure.” It therefore commands people to take wisdom’s discipline rather than strive to acquire silver. With silver they purchase vanities and temporal things without substance, but with wisdom’s discipline they purchase precious treasures—the words of wisdom, more valuable than any desire. And knowledge is preferable to fine gold. Fine gold is not spent but stored because it is precious; better still is to store words of knowledge—knowledge of God, the secret of His governance and providence, and every precious perception. These become part of the soul and fill it with a treasury of every desirable vessel. They are more precious than fine gold, whose owner gains nothing from it beyond the sight of his eyes.
text.7_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: For wisdom is better than pearls. This explains “Take my discipline and not silver.” Even if what silver buys is pearls, precious objects, what wisdom’s discipline purchases is better, for through it one acquires wisdom as a possession of the soul, and it is better than pearls. Above (3:15) it said, “She is more precious than pearls,” speaking of value, as explained there. Here it speaks of goodness. The advantage of pearls is their property of lending grace to their wearer, but this grace exists only in human eyes. Through wisdom, however, one finds favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man, as stated above (3:4) and explained there. This exceeds the grace of pearls. Although silver buys things desired by the body—pleasant foods and human pleasures—while acquiring wisdom requires a person to surrender all bodily desires and restrain every craving, nevertheless all desires cannot compare to it. Wisdom is more precious than all of them; by exchanging bodily desires for wisdom, he receives something more precious and exalted in their place.
text.7_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: I, wisdom, dwell with cunning. Cunning is the soul’s power to weigh each matter before acting, as in “Every cunning person acts with knowledge”; its opposite is simplicity.
