A person may sometimes use cunning for evil, but one who has gathered wisdom’s laws into his soul uses his cunning to consider his course according to those laws, consult himself in every matter, and devise how his deeds may accord with wisdom’s laws. Thus it says, “to give cunning to the simple”: wisdom teaches them to devise and reflect upon their deeds. Hence, “I, wisdom, dwell with cunning,” for cunning without wisdom will generally be used for evil.
text.7_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: And I find knowledge of profound designs. “Designs” are deep thoughts in wisdom. By deepening his thought in wisdom, a person finds knowledge and attains a clear understanding of it. Through profound study, its laws become fixed in his heart as a reliable foundation, until they resemble first principles or sensory perceptions. Thus cunning precedes wisdom; profound designs follow it; and knowledge follows them.
text.7_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: The fear of Hashem. It was already explained that “the fear of Hashem is the beginning of knowledge” (above 1:7). Since wisdom’s first principles cannot be known by proof, one cannot reach knowledge of them with certainty except through discipline and fear of Hashem. Through fear, it becomes fixed in his heart to believe and act according to wisdom’s laws established by Hashem. Profound plans and deep reflections upon wisdom cannot bring him to knowledge unless fear of Hashem precedes them. It was likewise explained (there, verse 2), regarding “to know wisdom and discipline,” that one cannot reach knowledge of wisdom except through discipline, which is fear of Hashem. Wisdom’s laws contradict the natural tendency of the human heart, which raises evil images opposed to wisdom and battles its laws. When images of pride rule his soul, he becomes wise in his own eyes and imagines in his arrogance that the impulses of his heart are themselves wisdom’s laws and should be followed, while in fact he follows their opposite. He therefore cannot attain knowledge of wisdom except through fear of Hashem. There is a remedy to quiet the tumultuous waves of the soul and its evil images: “fear of Hashem is the discipline of wisdom,” for fear of Hashem is hatred of evil, pride, and arrogance. When fear rules his heart, he clothes himself in humility, submits to the laws of wisdom given by Hashem, and fear erases evil images such as jealousy and desire from his heart. Yet the Sages said: “If there is no fear, there is no wisdom; if there is no wisdom, there is no fear.” Fear alone accomplishes nothing if he does not know wisdom’s laws. Even with fear in his heart, he will not walk by wisdom’s laws because of an evil way and a mouth of perversity. That is, he has already trained his soul in practices opposite to wisdom. In youth, evil images rule his heart, become citizens of his soul, and form a paved road along which all his thoughts and deeds travel. Even the powers of intellect and understanding speak perversity—that is, they legislate rules conforming to the images of desire that rule his soul, the opposite of wisdom. This is called “a mouth of perversity,” for the mouth alludes to wisdom. But when wisdom accompanies fear, he is saved from all this, for I hate an evil way and a mouth of perversity. Wisdom hates them, leads him on a good way, and speaks with a mouth of wisdom. When fear accompanies it, humbling the soul’s pride, arrogance, and evil images, he attains knowledge of wisdom, and its laws become fixed in his heart with clear certainty.
text.7_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Counsel and sound action are mine. Counsel is the decision a person reaches about how to act when several courses are possible: he deliberates which way to choose, and the conclusion settled in his heart is counsel. Since wisdom concerns a matter with two opposite possible courses and teaches the chosen path, wisdom’s laws are counsels directing a person which way to walk. As explained, sound action is the deed performed according to wisdom, as in “He stores sound action for the upright”: Hashem prepared wondrous deeds to be performed in every generation according to wisdom through the upright who would arise in that generation. Thus, both counsel and the wondrous deed performed according to wisdom are attributed to wisdom. It explains, I am understanding; strength is mine. Counsel requires understanding, for the counselor must consider every possible side and select the good one upon which to decide, as the Sages said, “One who increases counsel increases understanding.” Because I am understanding, counsel is mine. Sound action—wondrous deeds performed according to wisdom—requires strength to bring them about. Therefore, corresponding to “sound action is mine,” it explains, “I am strength”: I give the upright strength to perform the sound action I stored for them.
text.7_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: (15–16) Through me kings reign. Wisdom’s laws include both the wisdom of royal government and the wisdom of judicial government. These are distinct, as in “Behold, a king shall reign for righteousness, and officers shall rule for judgment.” There is governance according to fixed law, entrusted to judges and officers. It follows Torah law, called judgment: judges clarify the judgment, and officers use their authority to compel the people to fulfill the ruling. There is also governance not according to fixed law, entrusted to the king under the laws of kingship, which differ from ordinary Torah law. He judges according to the time, circumstances, and persons involved; this is called righteousness. As Maimonides writes in the Laws of Kings, a king may execute many people in one day and judge according to his discretion for the needs of the hour. This too is governed by laws of supreme wisdom. The king is accompanied by counselors, the ministers of advice. Therefore it says, Through me kings reign, and counselors legislate righteousness: the king together with the counselors establishes righteousness, for “a king shall reign for righteousness.” The counselors legislate the laws of righteousness, and the king compels and judges the people according to them. Regarding the fixed judgments of Torah, it says, Through me officers rule, and nobles—all the judges of the earth. All receive their laws from Torah, supreme wisdom, which transmitted laws and principles for royal and judicial government, upon which the survival of civil society and the ordering of the world depend.
text.7_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: I love those who love me. One who has already cleaved to wisdom in love is loved by wisdom in return; it reveals its secrets to him as a lover reveals secrets to the beloved, and guards him from every sin, as in “love her and she will guard you,” just as one lover protects another. Those who seek me at dawn will find me. One who has not yet acquired wisdom but strives after it, seeks it every morning, and searches for it will find it with Hashem’s assistance.
text.7_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Wealth and honor are with me. Above (chapter 3) it said, “In her left hand are wealth and honor,” but here it explains: enduring wealth and righteousness. Corresponding to wealth, it says enduring fortune, for human wealth does not remain long in one’s possession and does not accompany the fruit of his labor into the future. Wisdom’s fortune, however, is ancient wealth that endures for many days, and he carries it with him into the eternal world. Corresponding to honor, it says righteousness, for human honor is often not justly deserved, but the honor of wisdom comes through righteousness and righteous deeds. It is true honor, as in “Your righteousness shall go before you; the glory of Hashem shall gather you in.”
text.7_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: My fruit is better than fine gold and pure gold. “Fruit” includes every kind of produce, even what is not fully ripened; “crop,” in its precise sense, refers to grain and only when fully mature. Finished crops are traded to other lands, while fruit is stored within the country. Fine and pure gold are stored in treasuries; correspondingly, wisdom’s fruit is better than fine and pure gold. Silver is used in trade, and understanding—deriving one thing from another—is compared to silver (as stated above in chapter 3), because it too is traded. When wisdom’s fruit has fully matured in a person’s knowledge and become a crop, he then contemplates it through understanding and derives one thing from another. This is represented by silver, which is traded to acquire other things. Then my crop is preferable to silver, for through it one acquires precious, eternal things.
text.7_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: I walk in the path of righteousness. Hashem conducts Himself toward those who keep His Torah through two attributes: judgment and righteousness. As I have explained, Hashem’s treatment of the righteous according to their merit and righteousness is called judgment, because it follows strict law. The additional good He bestows beyond their merit from supreme benevolence, without regard to entitlement, is called righteousness. There is a difference between a path and a trail: many travel a path, while an individual travels a trail. The attribute of judgment follows each individual’s trail, weighing his reward particularly according to the trail he personally walked and according to his deeds. The attribute of righteousness follows a general path, because it does not consider each person’s individual deeds. Accordingly, supreme wisdom says that in governing the righteous, I walk in the path of righteousness, granting them goodness from supreme benevolence through a miraculous, wondrous path, and also amid the trails of judgment, weighing each person’s reward according to the trail on which he walked, acted, and accomplished. Through this—
text.7_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: To bequeath. I am prepared to bequeath to those who love me something of substance—that is, the fruit of their righteousness, for merit truly exists and itself prepares the reward for their righteousness: they eat the fruit of their deeds. This reward is substantial and enduring, possessing true existence, unlike the vanities of this world, which are nothing. Beyond this, I will fill their treasuries—in addition to the substance prepared for them by judgment—with precious gifts through supreme benevolence.
text.7_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: Hashem acquired me at the beginning of His way. Wisdom is the form of all the worlds. All were made and established, measured and prepared, according to wisdom’s laws; through it, by it, according to its measure and pattern, every world from beginning to end was formed and perfected. When Hashem first began His way of bringing creation out of nothingness—which is called a “way,” because the first revelation of the primordial will was the emanation of a holy and awesome realm in which He revealed the ways by which He would govern the world through kindness, might, and His holy attributes of mercy, graciousness, patience, and splendor—wisdom was the beginning of His way. The modes of His governance emanated in that first hidden emanation were all founded according to wisdom’s laws, and wisdom preceded them, as the Targum renders “In the beginning” as “with wisdom.” After revealing His ways and attributes, He began to perform His works. Then His firstborn son, the world of the Throne and governance, came into being, in which He founded in holiness how He would govern the worlds, and God sat upon His holy throne. These works too were made according to wisdom’s laws; universal governance follows wisdom’s measure. Wisdom was therefore before His works, from then—from the beginning of work and action.
text.7_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: From eternity I was installed. Afterward came into being the pure lights—the world of angels—prepared to carry out the missions of governance and move the celestial system, “mighty in strength, performing His word.” At that point it is called a “world.” This was the first light created before heaven and earth, the light of the separate intellects. They too were formed according to wisdom’s laws, which spread through each world in accordance with that world’s governance. Therefore it says, from eternity I was installed, from the beginning, before the earth: in the world formed before the world of action, of which the earth is one component, I was installed there as ruler, directing it according to wisdom’s ways.
text.7_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: When there were no— Afterward the earth emerged from the womb of chaos. At that time the four elements were mingled together in prime matter, and the depths had not yet separated independently. Thus, when there were no depths, I was brought forth: wisdom had already been formed there and hovered upon the face of chaos with its wings and with the spirit of God. Even after the depths were clarified, when there were no springs heavy with water—for at first the depths were mixed with the element of air, as I explained in the commentary on the Account of Creation—wisdom stretched over them a measuring line and plummet.
text.7_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: (25–27) Before the mountains were embedded. Mountains and hills did not yet exist, for the element of earth was covered by the element of water. Before He made land and open spaces, dry land had not yet appeared, nor was the first dust of the inhabited world visible and fit for habitation. Then God said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters.” I explained in the commentary on the Account of Creation that through the firmament, where Hashem placed into nature the property that vapors rise to the cloudy region—the firmament dividing water from water—the vaporous waters mixed with the element of air rose to the firmament. There they were separated from the air by the natural laws governing rainfall, as explained in the commentary to Job, chapter 26, on “He binds up water in His clouds, yet the cloud beneath them is not torn; He inscribed a circle upon the face of the waters.” This law that Hashem inscribed upon the waters—that they should stand in the firmament, formed like a circle over the deep to receive the waters of the deep in clouds—revealed the face of dry land, and through it the waters of the depths gathered into the sea. Thus it says, when He prepared the heavens, I was there: His preparing of the firmament called heaven, as in “God called the firmament heaven,” occurred through wisdom’s laws, as it says (Job 28:26), “When He made a law for the rain and a path for the lightning of thunder, then He saw it and declared it; He prepared it and also investigated it,” as I explained there. When He inscribed a circle upon the face of the deep refers to the circle of the firmament that surrounded, as though drawn by a compass, the deep that then covered the globe of the earth.
text.7_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: When He strengthened the skies above. “The skies” always signify miraculous governance above the nature of the celestial system that follows our heavens. The revelation of dry land was contrary to the original natural state, in which earth was covered by water. Hashem therefore strengthened the skies, from which miraculous governance proceeds, and through them the springs of the deep became mighty, while the air was separated from the elemental waters.
text.7_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: When He set— Therefore, He set the sea its law, so that the waters would not transgress His command, and the waters gathered to one place, as in “You covered it with the deep as with a garment … You set a boundary,” as explained there; and similarly (Job 38:8), “He enclosed the sea with doors,” and said, “Until here shall you come and no farther.” When He inscribed the foundations of the earth, the earth’s foundations were engraved and fixed so that it would be fit for habitation. All this was done according to the laws of supreme wisdom.
text.7_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: I was beside Him as a nursling. It pictures wisdom as always nurtured in His embrace. At first it was beside Him like a delightful child; He carried it as a nurse carries an infant and continually delighted in it. It had not yet performed deeds or actions to play before Him through its works, but was simply His delight. After He created time, I was playing before Him at every moment: through wisdom He then brought forth the works of Creation at every successive moment of the days of creation. Each day is pictured as another time because new creatures were born in it, and the times and orders changed as creation rose and emerged into actuality. This was play and joy before Him, because everything followed wisdom.
text.7_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: Playing. Afterward, I was playing in the inhabited world of His earth, once the world was prepared for habitation and the creatures of water and dry land were created. From then on, my delights were with the children of man. Once creation was complete, the “play”—a metaphor for the new actions produced through wisdom during the days of Creation—ceased, and wisdom again became a delight as before. Yet it was no longer nurtured only in the Creator’s embrace, for He gave it to humanity. People would delight in it, occupy themselves with wisdom, and conduct themselves by it. It is Hashem’s delight that they resemble Him by walking in His ways, meditating upon His Torah, and delighting in it.
text.7_Chapter, 31_Verse, 0_Comment: And now, sons, listen to me; happy are those who keep my ways. Wisdom’s ways are the ways of God, the mechanisms upon which the foundations of all the worlds were established and by which they all endure. “Listen to me” means to accept the teachings, after which comes guarding them in the heart.
text.7_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: Listen to discipline. Although it is difficult to accept wisdom’s laws, which have no demonstrative proof, and difficult to keep them because the inclination of the heart opposes them, this is corrected by listening to discipline—fear of Hashem, which is the discipline of wisdom. Through fear, a person binds the powers of his soul to accept wisdom’s laws (as explained above, 1:2), and thereby become wise—that is, accept those laws. This corresponds to “And now, sons, listen to me.” And do not neglect it or nullify them; this corresponds to “happy are those who keep my ways.”
text.7_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: Happy is the person who listens to me, diligently attending at my doors day by day. It pictures wisdom seated within its closed sanctuary, “all glorious within, the king’s daughter.” It does not reveal itself to anyone, and the doors are shut. One who seeks it must diligently attend at the closed doors, guarding the doorposts of my entrances, watching for the moment when the entrance opens. Then he will find wisdom when it appears through the doorway.
text.7_Chapter, 34_Verse, 0_Comment: For one who finds me— whoever finds me when the entrance opens finds life, the life of both soul and body, and also obtains favor from Hashem.
text.7_Chapter, 35_Verse, 0_Comment: But one who sins against me, transgressing wisdom’s laws, wrongs his soul: he commits violence against his spiritual part, whose entire life comes from wisdom’s bread and drink. And all who hate me—those who hate wisdom and cause it to be hated—love death. Since wisdom is life, as it says, “One who finds me finds life,” one who hates it hates life and loves death.
text.8_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Wisdom has built her house. This returns to the earlier teaching that the world was built through wisdom, as stated, “Hashem acquired me at the beginning of His way.” It compares the world’s construction to a house, as in “Through wisdom a house is built,” which, as explained there, refers to the construction of the world; likewise, “Hashem founded the earth through wisdom.” It pictures wisdom as building her house on the first day of Creation, when the universal structure emerged from nothingness into existence. The Sages compared this to one who sows six seeds. Afterward, she hewed out her pillars: the individual components of the world emerged, each on its own day, as the pillars of the house. The house built by the first utterance initially hung loosely in the air upon prime matter, existing only potentially and not actually. Its pillars were seven, the seven days of Creation, each producing its offspring at its appointed time. The world-house was then perfected upon strong pillars. Even on the Sabbath the principal pillar supporting the great house was created: miraculous governance, through which Hashem acts when necessary and overrides the laws of nature, as explained in its place. This too is among wisdom’s pillars upon which He placed the inhabited world. In contrast to the woman of folly described below, wisdom is characterized by three things: first, she built herself a house and established its pillars; second—
text.8_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: She slaughtered her meat. The feast prepared for her guests is filled with every good thing and prepared openly before everyone: she slaughtered and prepared meat, and mixed her wine. Allegorically, wisdom is the soul’s nourishment and is compared to one preparing every kind of food to sustain the heart. Wisdom’s teachings steady the heart so that it will not be shaken by the winds and storms—the images of the inclination that terrify it. Mixing wine alludes to teachings of understanding: wine gladdens and elevates the heart, while understanding enables a person to understand one thing from another and broaden his discernment. She also set her table with sweets and all other provisions, alluding to knowledge, which encompasses every kind of knowledge in the world.
text.8_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: She sent. Third, wisdom does not personally summon the guests, but sends her maidens. Wisdom does not come to a person by itself; he must receive it from sages, prophets, and teachers. They are the maidens whom she sends in every generation, and through them she calls upon the wings of the city’s heights to invite people to the feast.
text.8_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Whoever is simple— They invite both the simple and the one lacking a heart. The simple person is enticed because he lacks knowledge and has not grasped wisdom’s laws; he is like a gullible dove. One lacking a heart may know wisdom’s laws but lacks the ruling power to subdue his inclination and overcome his desires and evil images, which oppose wisdom’s laws. She says to him: to the simple person she says—
text.8_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Come, eat of my bread, meaning: accept wisdom’s laws and thereby abandon simplicity, for wisdom places shrewdness in his heart, as in “to give shrewdness to the simple,” explained there. To the one lacking a heart she says, drink of the wine I have mixed: he must understand the depth of wisdom’s teachings through the power of understanding, which is compared to wine. It explains that she says to the simple, “Come, eat of my bread,” and thereby—
text.8_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Forsake simplicity and live. Through wisdom’s bread he will abandon simplicity. To the one lacking a heart she says, “Drink of the wine I have mixed,” meaning, advance on the way of understanding. The wine is understanding: contemplate the depth of wisdom’s teachings, and you will find the soul’s happiness on this way of understanding. You will thereby turn from the inclination of desire toward happiness and goodness.
text.8_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: One who disciplines— It explains that wisdom’s maidens summon only the simple and those lacking a heart, not scoffers and wicked people, who will not heed wisdom’s call. One who disciplines a scoffer brings disgrace upon himself. Discipline differs from rebuke: discipline operates through fear of punishment, while rebuke uses rational argument and evidence. The scoffer does not mock rational proofs; he mocks wisdom’s laws because they lack demonstrative proof and rest principally upon fear of Hashem, which is wisdom’s discipline. They must be accepted because they were given by Hashem, Whom one must fear, along with His punishment, as in “fear of Hashem is the beginning of knowledge.” The scoffer will not accept this because it lacks rational proof. Thus, if one disciplines a scoffer without establishing the matter through rational rebuke and evidence, he brings disgrace upon himself, for the scoffer will mock and despise him. One who rebukes a wicked man receives his blemish. The deliberately wicked man will not even heed rational rebuke. Though one proves the matter rationally, he receives the wicked man’s blemish: the wicked man insults him by calling him wicked, which is a blemish.
text.8_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not— Although the scoffer disgraces only one who disciplines him, not one who rebukes him with rational proof, since he cannot mock something demonstrated by reason, nevertheless he does not love rational rebuke either, as stated below (15:12): “A scoffer does not love one who rebukes him; he will not go to the wise.” He avoids sages lest they argue with him rationally. Therefore, do not rebuke a scoffer, even through rational argument. Although he may not disgrace you, lest he hate you, for because he dislikes rebuke he will hate you for it. But rebuke a wise man; reason and argue with him, and he will love you, because he loves rebuke. Accordingly, wisdom’s maidens, sent to invite the simple and those lacking a heart to wisdom’s feast, also call the wise to be among its guests. Although the wise have already received and know wisdom’s laws, nevertheless—
text.8_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Give to a wise man, and he will become wiser still. Since wisdom is exceedingly broad and its commandments have no end, even a wise man will continually receive wisdom’s laws and add to his wisdom. Make known to a righteous man, and he will increase his learning. The righteous man differs from the wise man. The wise man received all wisdom’s laws by tradition; the righteous man conducts himself righteously even without knowing every law as the sage does, having become accustomed to them through repeated practice. Thus the Sages said that serving Torah scholars is greater than studying Torah. Wisdom’s laws must be made known to him because he did not learn them all through systematic study. Hence, “make known to a righteous man”—making known applies to what he does not yet know—and he will add this teaching to what he has already acquired through habitual observance of wisdom’s laws.
text.8_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: The beginning of wisdom is fear of Hashem. It now explains why wisdom sends her maidens to summon people rather than calling them herself. Wisdom cannot be attained independently through demonstrative proofs, and its laws oppose the heart’s nature. Wisdom’s beginning and foundation is fear of Hashem: people receive it by tradition from the sages and prophets of the generation, who teach it in Hashem’s name; through fear of Hashem they accept the wisdom He gave. And the beginning of the knowledge of holy matters is understanding. A person reaches the knowledge of the holy—clear knowledge of wisdom’s subjects like the holy people on earth—through understanding. After accepting wisdom’s laws through fear of Hashem, firmly believing they were given by Him, and deeply contemplating wisdom, people attain knowledge of it, as in “to know wisdom and discipline,” explained there. At the beginning of the book it says, “The first part of wisdom is fear of Hashem,” whereas here it says “the beginning.” “First part” participates in the substance itself, as in “the first of your grain” and “the first of your dough.” One kind of fear of Hashem is itself among wisdom’s laws: reverence for Hashem Himself, which wisdom requires and which is its choicest first part. Another fear is not among wisdom’s laws: fear of punishment, lest Hashem punish him or withhold good if he departs from wisdom’s laws. This is fear for oneself, not wisdom’s proper awe of Hashem’s exaltedness. Nevertheless, although it is not the first part of wisdom, it is the beginning of wisdom, because it helps a person submit to and obey wisdom’s laws from fear of punishment. Wisdom’s maidens proclaim this fear upon the heights of the city through the Torah and the prophets, warning people not to rebel against Hashem’s commandments because of punishment and loss of good. So too, wisdom’s messengers tell people to keep her laws because—
text.8_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: For through me your days will be multiplied. This is motivated by love of reward: through wisdom, his days of goodness will be multiplied and years of life added to him, as explained above at 3:2.
text.8_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: If— That is: if you have become wise, it is for your own benefit; you have become wise for yourself, for you receive good through wisdom. Conversely, if you have scoffed at wisdom’s teachings, you alone will bear the punishment. This is the warning not to depart from wisdom’s laws because of fear of punishment and loss of good.
text.8_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: The woman of folly. After describing wisdom’s words and the pleasantness of her teaching, it says that opposite her the woman of folly is clamorous, enticing people toward folly. Folly differs from simplicity. Simplicity results from lacking knowledge and shrewdness, like a gullible dove; folly is departing from wisdom because desire roars within. A fool knows wisdom’s laws and may even be a great sage, but his inclination and desire lead him astray. Thus the woman of folly is clamorous: she knows and understands, but clamors because of desire and the evil inclination. The woman of simplicity, however, clamors and knows nothing, because the simple person knows nothing.
text.8_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: She sits. Folly and simplicity did not build a sound house upon pillars; their house hangs in the air. They destroy the great house—the world established upon wisdom’s pillars. She prepared neither meat, mixed wine, nor a table, for she lacks every goodness and happiness and is empty of all the soul’s delights. She does not send her maidens; she herself sits at the entrance of her house, because folly and its evil images come to a person on their own. She sits on a throne upon the city’s heights, for she reigns over the kingdom of the body, and all bodily powers follow her as servants. She does not call the city’s settled inhabitants—an allegory for those who dwell tranquilly and whose evil inclination does not disturb them from serving Hashem—but rather—
text.8_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: To call to those passing on the road, those who have not yet reached the city but are still traveling—that is, who have not yet corrected their traits or settled their judgment. They pass along the soul’s ways, straightening their paths, wishing to direct their paths toward uprightness and balance. Every person desires to straighten his course, and the human soul is naturally upright unless folly, evil images, and desires lead it astray. A “way” is the great road and “paths” branch from it, for error and doubt occur in the individual paths, where ambushers ensnare and distort him.
text.8_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: Whoever is simple— She calls only to the simple and to one lacking a heart: the woman of simplicity calls the simple, while the woman of folly calls the one lacking a heart, who lacks the ruling power to restrain his desires. She says to him—
text.8_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Stolen waters are sweet. Although she offers neither sweet wine nor meat pleasant to the palate, giving him water and bread instead, because they are stolen waters obtained through prohibition and effort, they taste as sweet as wine. A person finds sweet what is not his and has been forbidden to him. She similarly makes sin, performed secretly, illicitly, and by stealth, taste sweet.
text.8_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: He does not know that the shades are there. It is deadly poison to the soul, and the place to which she summons her guests lies in the depths of Sheol, for through sin the soul is cut off and goes to destruction.
text.9_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: A wise son, who has gathered wisdom’s laws into his soul and conducts himself by them, gladdens his father, for this indicates that his father taught him the way of wisdom and discipline. A foolish son, who departs from wisdom’s way because of desire—which defines a fool—causes his mother’s sorrow. A mother draws him especially close. Therefore Scripture regularly attributes good to the father and evil to the mother: the father teaches discipline, while the mother yearns for her son and prevents the father from disciplining him with the rod.
text.9_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: They do not benefit. Something may be good or useful. Treasuries of money and grain, though not intrinsically good, can be useful in distress. But treasures of wickedness—accumulated through wickedness and violence—are not even useful. Below (11:4) it says, “Wealth does not benefit on the day of wrath”; wicked wealth is useless even in peace. But righteousness—good deeds between man and God—saves from death.
text.9_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: He will not let go hungry. During famine, when treasuries are useless because no grain can be purchased, nevertheless Hashem will not let the soul of the righteous go hungry, as in “in days of famine they shall be satisfied.” It adds “the soul of the righteous,” because Hashem grants every desire of his soul. But He thrusts away the calamity of the wicked: Hashem drives the wicked man’s ruin onward, so that once he begins to fall he will fall completely and not arise.
text.9_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: A deceitful palm makes one poor. “Palm” denotes only the hand’s palm, whereas “hand” denotes the entire hand. The deceitful palm—the swindler’s palm—will not make him rich but poor. One who is neither industrious nor quick to earn a livelihood through the work of his hands, but seeks support through deceit rather than labor, using only the palm with which he cheats, will be made poor by that palm. But the hand of the diligent makes rich. The diligent person is energetic in his work and labors with his whole hand and strength; his hand will enrich him.
text.9_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: One who gathers in summer is a discerning son. Summer follows harvest, and one who “gathers” collects the remaining kernels one by one. A son discerning in his work remains occupied even in summer, when nothing remains in the field to harvest or bring in, gathering the leftover kernels. One who sleeps during harvest is a shameful son. The sluggish, lazy son not only sleeps in summer; even during harvest, when all the grain is in the field and it is the season for fieldwork, he sleeps and does nothing. Allegorically, the discerning son studies even in old age. Though he can then originate little and only gather bit by bit—as the Sages describe one who studies when old—nevertheless, “in the evening do not rest your hand.” The shameful son sleeps even in youth, the time of harvest and gathering.
text.9_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Blessings are upon the head of the righteous. Everyone blesses one who acts righteously because of the good he bestows upon all. It pictures the whole world placing its hands upon his head and blessing him. But the mouth of the wicked conceals violence. By committing violence, the opposite of righteousness, the wicked man is not only left unblessed by others; he himself strives to conceal deeds that contain a curse rather than a blessing.
text.9_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: The remembrance of the righteous. “Name” differs from “remembrance”: name is the person’s designation, while remembrance is what people recall of him through his deeds. Even the righteous man’s remembrance remains for a blessing, for his deeds are recalled and blessed in every generation. But even the name of the wicked will rot: not only are their deeds not remembered, but their very name and essence decay and disappear, for they possess neither spiritual nor hereditary continuity.
text.9_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: The wise of heart takes commandments. A sage conducts himself according to wisdom’s laws. Yet, as explained, the heart’s inclination naturally opposes wisdom, and every person continually battles his heart’s inclination and desires, which move him opposite wisdom’s way. One who has become so accustomed to wisdom’s way that it is second nature, and whose heart—the ruling power—no longer awakens toward evil at all, is called “wise of heart.” An ordinary sage hears or observes a commandment, conducting himself according to Hashem’s command, but does not “take” it. Nowhere else is taking used of a commandment. A command compels its subject to obey; he acts because of the commander, not from himself, since without the command his inclination would do the opposite. “Taking,” however, denotes willingly seizing and pursuing the commandment. Only the wise of heart, who no longer suffers inner conflict and in whose heart wisdom naturally rests, takes the commandment naturally and willingly. But one foolish of lips will struggle. The fool doubts wisdom’s laws and truths, unlike the simpleton and the fool driven by desire. “Foolish of lips” describes one who inwardly believes wisdom but voices doubts externally. Although he generally acts wisely because his heart inclines toward belief, his lips speak folly and doubt, for he has not resolved that wisdom’s laws admit no doubt. Opposite the wise of heart, for whom wisdom is second nature, he struggles and toils; or, as explained, the word means wavering between two sides, at times departing from wisdom, as follows.
text.9_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: One who walks in integrity. It illustrates this through wisdom’s way versus folly’s way. One who walks innocently on wisdom’s way resembles a traveler at a crossroads who has been shown the straight road, believes the guide, and follows it. He walks securely, gaining two benefits: he does not stumble, and he travels confidently without fear. Conversely, one who rejects the good road shown to him and makes his ways crooked onto a winding road will be made known through suffering; alternatively, he will become visible to highway robbers and wild animals found on crooked roads. Having described these opposites, it describes two intermediate cases. Opposite the person who actively makes his ways crooked and is exposed, one who winks his eye travels on the straight road but gestures toward the second road and searches to determine which is correct. Although unharmed because he remains on the straight road, he nevertheless causes sorrow in his heart through doubt, as in Isaiah 50, “You shall lie down in sorrow.” Likewise, one merely foolish of lips, who does not even look for the crooked road because inwardly he trusts the report identifying the good road and follows wisdom’s way, yet externally voices foolish doubts, will also struggle.
text.9_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life. Wisdom’s way is the way of life because it leads to true life; its opposite is the way of death. Whoever draws and drinks wisdom’s water lives forever. The fountain from which this life flows has three forms: intellect may grasp the good way, as below (16:22), “The understanding of its possessor is a fountain of life”; or it may come through a life-giving Torah received from sages who learned wisdom’s ways in Torah books, as below (13:14), “The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life.” Trusting received tradition requires fear of Hashem, wisdom’s discipline, as explained above (1:7); hence “fear of Hashem is a fountain of life” (14:27). One may also learn wisdom’s particular ways by observing a righteous person and imitating him, learning from his mouth how to act in each case; hence, “the mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life.” The righteous differs from the sage. The righteous need not be a sage who has systematically studied wisdom’s laws and can formulate “the teaching of the wise,” an ordered doctrine covering life and death, good and evil. Through practical reason and habitual righteousness in particulars, he can decide only the individual cases that arise. The fountain of life is therefore in his mouth, not in his systematic teaching. The sage, however, can formulate general laws embracing all wise conduct—called “the teaching of the wise”—and laws for escaping the way of death and its snares through fear of Hashem. Therefore “escaping the snares of death” is stated of the teaching of the wise and fear of Hashem. But the mouth of the wicked not only cannot teach through their conduct; on the contrary, conceals violence, as explained above at verse 6.
text.9_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Hatred arouses disputes. Quarrel differs from dispute. Quarrel is the act of contending and may occur over nothing; the matter over which people quarrel is called strife. If its cause is money or wrongdoing that generates a legal claim before a judge, it is called a dispute—the issue being adjudicated—and it remains unclear who is right. An obvious offense receives a more specific name such as trespass, betrayal, or judgment. The wise man says: the true cause of these disputes is not the issue itself but the emotional state of the parties. Friends, or people without mutual hatred, do not insist upon small matters such as neighbor damages. Hatred in the soul arouses disputes: mutual hostility and resentment awaken controversies that would otherwise sleep. But the soul’s attribute of love covers all offenses, even serious ones; certainly it prevents disputes from arising over minor matters.
text.9_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Wisdom is found on the lips of one who understands. The sage differs from the discerning person. The sage receives wisdom’s laws from his teachers and follows them without investigating their reasons; the discerning person investigates, understands, and derives one thing from another. The sage keeps wisdom confined in his heart and must consult it whenever a case arises to determine whether his act accords with the laws received from his teachers. The discerning person understands each matter’s reason and has built further conclusions upon it, so wisdom’s laws are habitual on his lips. “Lips” differ from mouth and tongue: lips signify external speech without thought. Thus wisdom is pictured as lying ready on the discerning person’s lips, so that he need not think about it, for it is always prepared before him. But a rod is for the back of one lacking a heart. The heart is the ruling power of the soul, directing its faculties according to wisdom’s laws. One consistently following an alternative opposed to wisdom is called crooked of heart. But one with no governance at all, acting moment by moment according to whatever enters his mind, now one way and now another, so that the ruling power never guides him toward wisdom or folly, is called lacking a heart. Such a person needs a rod to direct him. A human being with free choice is guided by his heart; a horse or donkey, lacking a heart that governs its traits, requires an external force—as in “a whip for the horse and a bridle for the donkey.” One lacking a heart resembles an animal and needs a rod to compel him not to twist his paths and cause harm.
text.9_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: The wise store away knowledge. It was explained regarding “to know wisdom” (1:2) that wisdom is received by tradition and cannot be known through proofs of understanding or sensory perception. Nevertheless, one may attain knowledge of it by accepting its laws as clearly true in his heart, observing them, and contemplating them with understanding until they become clear knowledge. The wise store knowledge away from harmful people lest they turn it toward evil. This also includes divine knowledge attained by sages, which must be hidden and guarded, since such secrets are not transmitted to everyone. Below (12:23) it says, “A shrewd man conceals knowledge.” Concealing differs from storing: one who stores something does not hide it completely, but places it where not everyone sees it, though it remains revealed. Concealing knowledge is an act of shrewdness, not wisdom. The wise do not hide it from worthy people, as in “the tongue of the wise improves knowledge” (15:2) and “the lips of the wise scatter knowledge” (15:7). Storing also implies guarding knowledge from the unworthy. But the mouth of a fool stores imminent ruin. The fool doubts everything and therefore can possess no knowledge—clear certainty—about anything. He even stores away and does not reveal an imminent, visible ruin because he doubts it. Thus the wise refrain from revealing good lest it be harmed, while fools guard visible harm from being revealed.
text.9_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: The rich man’s wealth is his fortified city. Wealth is an accumulation of money and many valuable things; a city here is a fortified city. The rich man needs no fortified city in which to escape adversaries, because his wealth is his strong city, sheltering him from the reversals of time—human adversaries—and from hunger, cold, and every deprivation. Accordingly, the ruin of the poor is their poverty. A poor man is one who once possessed wealth and lost it; his diminished wealth resembles enemies conquering his fortified stronghold. This is his ruin, for he lacks shelter from time’s reversals. Allegorically, the soul’s inner wealth is the wisdom gathered in the heart. It is the soul’s strong city against its internal enemies—desires and the evil inclination. But when people lack the wealth of wisdom, folly attacks and conquers the city.
text.9_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: The labor of the righteous leads to life; the crop of the wicked leads to sin.
text.9_Chapter, 15_Verse, 1_Comment: There is a difference between labor and a completed deed:
text.9_Chapter, 15_Verse, 2_Comment: * Activity devoted to something and preparing its means is called labor.
text.9_Chapter, 15_Verse, 3_Comment: * Completing the thing is called a deed.
text.9_Chapter, 15_Verse, 4_Comment: For example, sowing, plowing, and all preceding activities are called labor relative to the crop; when the crop is finished, the deed is complete.
text.9_Chapter, 15_Verse, 6_Comment: * Even the righteous person’s labors lead to life: the intermediate means through which he prepares the goal are themselves directed toward life, and all the more so the goal—the righteous deed itself.
text.9_Chapter, 15_Verse, 7_Comment: * For the wicked, even the crop of wickedness leads to sin: even the finished crop, the goal of his deed, produces sin and deficiency; it is a false end.
text.9_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: One who keeps discipline is on the path of life. Discipline differs from rebuke. Discipline operates through compulsion, binding the soul so that fear of punishment keeps it within its boundary. Rebuke uses rational argument and evidence to demonstrate the benefit of the good way. Ordinarily, discipline prevents a person from taking the evil way through fear of punishment, while rebuke leads him along the good way because he understands its benefit. It therefore teaches something greater: one who keeps discipline is not only prevented from the way of death, but is also led onto the path of life, because turning from evil begins the performance of good. But one who abandons rebuke leads astray. Not only does he fail to walk the path of life; he also strays onto the way of death. The two ways stand opposite one another, and abandoning the way of life means straying onto its opposite.
text.9_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: (18–19) One who conceals hatred, etc.; in an abundance of words. Maimonides, commenting upon “All my days I grew among the sages and found nothing better for the body than silence,” divides speech into four types: forbidden speech, discretionary speech, commanded speech, and permissible speech. The discerning person speaks only one-quarter of what might be spoken. The evil form of speech—spreading slander about another—contains several evils. One conceals hatred with lying lips: he necessarily hides his hatred and falsely claims to love the other; consequently, he spreads slander, and because his hatred is concealed, people believe it. Several evils are therefore included, and he is a fool, acting contrary to wisdom through the evil of his heart. Even one who does not engage in forbidden speech nevertheless finds that in an abundance of words, transgression does not cease, because most kinds of speech, even discretionary conversation, lead to sin. Therefore, one who restrains his lips is discerning: he restrains them completely and speaks only words of wisdom.
text.9_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: The tongue of the righteous is choice silver. As explained consistently, the tongue signifies inward speech and reasoned matters contemplated through understanding, whereas the lips denote outward speech. Linguists associate the tongue with understanding, the mouth with wisdom, and the lips with knowledge, agreeing with our explanation. The tongue signifies matters of understanding. The lips, entirely external, indicate speaking matters that have become habitual and issue automatically; this occurs only with knowledge, known as clearly as sensory facts and therefore spoken without reflection. The mouth is intermediate, indicating wisdom received from teachers—neither internally understood like matters of understanding nor externally habitual like matters of knowledge. The tongue of the righteous is his contemplation of righteousness through understanding. It resembles choice silver without dross. Every human understanding ordinarily contains dross, since one must examine every opposing possibility before finding the proper conclusion, and the discarded alternatives are the dross. The righteous person, however, is habituated to righteousness and contemplates it through practical reason trained by action. Whenever a particular case arises, experience immediately teaches him how to act without doubt; he instantly strikes the proper target, producing pure silver without dross. But the heart of the wicked is of little worth. The wicked are distant from righteousness, and their heart—the ruling power—never maintains one course but continually skips to another evil trait. Their heart is almost as though nonexistent, without settled rule; certainly it cannot decisively understand the good way, for it possesses no definite way at all.
text.9_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: The lips of the righteous shepherd many. As explained, the lips signify outward speech. Through the righteous person’s tongue, he contemplates the course he should choose for himself, as in the preceding verse; his mouth, in matters of wisdom, is a fountain of life, as in verse 11. His lips represent the habitual teachings he voices; they shepherd many by teaching them his ways and paths. But fools die for lack of a heart. A fool doubts wisdom’s ways, the opposite of the knowledge symbolized by the righteous person’s lips, which express clearly known matters. Not only does the fool lack clear knowledge with which to teach wisdom’s ways openly to the many; he cannot even shepherd himself. He dies for lack of a heart, lacking the ruling faculty that would guide his desires according to wisdom’s ways and laws, because he doubts them.
text.9_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: Hashem’s blessing makes rich. Wealth obtained through human striving is not true wealth, and its owner eats the bread of sorrows: while eating, he grieves, remembering the toil and labor through which he obtained it and worrying that it may diminish. He therefore restricts his food as though doing so would increase his wealth. Since it is not true wealth, he remains poor in his own mind. Hashem’s blessing, however, produces true wealth, and sorrow adds nothing with it. He need not grieve in order to add to his wealth through anxious restraint; he eats joyfully and generously because blessing is present in all he possesses.
text.9_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: It is like sport to a fool to perform depravity. The fool departs from wisdom’s ways because of his heart’s inclination and desires.
text.9_Chapter, 22_Verse, 1_Comment: It explains that according to whether the rule of his heart follows wisdom or folly, his nature changes until his deeds are no longer attributed to conscious choice, but to habit and a second nature implanted within him:
text.9_Chapter, 22_Verse, 2_Comment: * The fool commits depravity without thought, knowledge, or preparation, just as a person necessarily laughs when something amusing appears, rather than through deliberation and choice.
text.9_Chapter, 22_Verse, 3_Comment: * Likewise, wisdom is natural to a man of understanding. One who has gathered every matter of understanding into his soul—which defines comprehensive understanding and distinguishes it from an individual act of understanding—has wisdom ready upon his lips, as explained above on (Proverbs 10:13), Wisdom is found on the lips of one who understands. Consequently, wisdom and conduct according to its ways arise automatically through habit, like laughter that comes naturally by itself.
text.9_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: What the wicked man dreads will come upon him. Dread is something he fears, hides from, and devises strategies to escape; this distinguishes it from other expressions of fear. Even what the wicked man dreads and uses every strategy to escape will nevertheless come upon him, for his strategies will not help. But He grants the desire of the righteous. Hashem grants even what they merely desire in their hearts, without their needing to do anything to attain it. Thus the wicked man suffers the evil he strove to escape, while the righteous man not only escapes evil but receives goodness for which he did not strive at all, because Hashem grants it providentially, as explained below (11:23; 13:21).
text.9_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: When the storm passes, the wicked man is gone. The wicked man has no firm root in existence, only accidental endurance, like something weakly rooted that wind carries away when a storm passes. While years proceed normally, he endures by nature; during upheaval, the storm carries him away and sweeps him from his place. But the righteous is the foundation of the world. He endures in existence through the perfection of his soul and Hashem’s providence. During a storm, the wind and events of time not only fail to move him; he serves as a firm foundation not merely for himself but for the entire world, as Noah did. Thus Bereishit Rabbah (section Noah) interprets “When the storm passes” as the generation of the Flood, and “the righteous is the foundation of the world” as Noah; related verses below (12:7; 14:1) are interpreted there similarly.
text.9_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: Like vinegar to the teeth. It disparages the lazy messenger. He resembles something sour eaten to stimulate appetite, but which instead dulls the teeth; although appetite is awakened, the person cannot chew. Likewise, like smoke to the eyes: sparks may be kindled to illuminate a house, but though light is produced, the smoke dims the eyes so one cannot see. So is the lazy person to those who send him: not only do they fail to obtain the purpose of his mission; he also ruins the objective. Everything said about laziness also allegorically applies to one who neglects the universal mission for which he was sent into this world—the perfection of his soul.
text.9_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: Fear of Hashem adds days. Although fear ordinarily shortens life, fear of Hashem adds to a person’s days. But the years of the wicked are shortened through Hashem’s punishments. On the first side it says “days,” which also implies days of goodness and tranquility; “years” often denotes years of distress. The wicked do not spend their days in goodness, and their years are also shortened.
text.9_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: The assured expectation of the righteous is joy. Assured expectation differs from hope. One expects something certain to come, or something promised for a known time; one hopes for something uncertain and unpromised. The righteous possess assured expectation because their reward is undoubtedly promised, and therefore they rejoice. This differs from prolonged expectation that makes the heart sick, because expectation of Hashem’s kindness is continually fulfilled and does not disappoint. But the hope of the wicked will perish. The wicked have no assured expectation, only a hope that they may become wealthy or the like, which is uncertain; in truth, their hope perishes.
text.9_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: Hashem’s way is a stronghold for the innocent. Ruin is the opposite of strength: strength is the soul’s courage and firmness, while ruin is inner collapse. Hashem’s way and governance are a stronghold for the innocent, for in His ways they see how He supports the fallen, watches over the oppressed, and conducts all His paths with kindness, truth, righteousness, mercy, and grace. The innocent person who practices these traits finds strength by observing that Hashem governs existence in the same manner. But it is ruin to workers of iniquity, because their ways of wrongdoing oppose God’s ways and the world’s continued existence.
text.9_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: The righteous will never be moved. Being moved results from a cause, such as weak legs or sloping ground. Even when the righteous man slips because he did not stand in a good position, he will not remain moved forever, for “seven times the righteous falls and rises.” But the wicked will not dwell in the land. Even while dwelling upon level ground rather than a slope, with an apparently fixed residence, they will not remain there, for the wicked will be shaken out of it.
text.9_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: The mouth of the righteous yields wisdom. It was explained (verse 11), regarding “the mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life,” that the righteous person did not gather wisdom’s laws through systematic received study like the sage; rather, through his righteousness he became habituated to following them. He can therefore teach how to act wisely in each particular case, although he lacks the sage’s general doctrine and system. Wisdom’s source is consequently in his mouth, where it produces fruit. When asked how to conduct a particular matter, wisdom sprouts and yields in his mouth the correct answer. He also possesses an advantage over the sage, in that the tongue of perversity will be cut off. The tongue signifies the ways of understanding. If someone brings a perverse tongue—rational demonstrations in the way of investigation that contradict wisdom—the sage cannot withstand him, because the sage is not necessarily discerning: wisdom is received by tradition, and he cannot establish it with evidence and proofs against an investigator who denies its principles. The righteous person, however, counters him with proofs from experience and observation. He has tested each particular matter until attaining clear knowledge like sensory demonstration. The tongue of perversity is thereby cut off, and the arms of its reasoning cannot stand before him.
text.9_Chapter, 31_Verse, 0_Comment: The lips of the righteous know favor. I explained at verse 21, “the lips of the righteous shepherd many,” that the righteous person has attained knowledge of the particulars of wisdom’s ways and knows them clearly. This is denoted by “lips,” which utter them outwardly as evident matters. “Favor” means both what is pleasing to Hashem and the appeasement of anger. The righteous person knows how to state what is pleasing to Hashem and to people—whatever brings honor to its doer and honor from other people. He knows this clearly; therefore it says “know” and refers to the “lips.” But the mouth of the wicked speaks perversity. Their mouth, through which they speak of conduct contrary to wisdom—the mouth alluding to wisdom—is perversity, as though they had received laws opposite to wisdom’s ways.
text.10_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Deceitful scales are an abomination to Hashem. It teaches that turning from evil is itself an active good. Although deceitful scales are an abomination, do not think that by using a perfect weight one has merely avoided an abomination and only turned from evil. He has thereby fulfilled Hashem’s will, and it is reckoned to him as performing a commandment, as the Sages said: one who sits and does not transgress receives a reward like one who performs a commandment.
text.10_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: When presumption comes. The presumptuous person disputes wisdom’s ways and the truth with arguments and deductions, and deliberately transgresses them brazenly. He is the opposite of the modest person, who hides his face from aspiring to lofty levels and recognizes his lowly worth, as in “Moses hid his face.” Wisdom comes with the modest, for wisdom’s ways become established only in the heart of one who believes, accepts, and listens to his teachers rather than presuming to dispute them. But when presumption comes, disgrace comes with it—the opposite of honor—for the paths he chooses are contemptible and contrary to wisdom’s honorable ways.
text.10_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: The integrity of the upright guides them. The upright differ from the righteous. The upright person’s heart naturally follows a straight course in beliefs, opinions, and matters of understanding—as “upright” commonly describes understanding—and in traits and deeds rooted in wisdom. In wisdom’s ways, he differs from the righteous because his nature inclines toward good through the uprightness implanted within him, while the righteous person acts thus because he learned righteousness and became accustomed to it, subduing his inclination and training himself against his nature. The upright person also looks beyond the strict laws of righteousness to his heart’s uprightness and acts beyond the letter of the law, as the Sages explained concerning “you shall do what is upright and good.” Walking on the good way requires both that the road be straight and that it guide him, as in, “Hashem, lead me in Your righteousness; make Your way straight before me.” One who is not upright needs help from above to straighten his road. Even one whose road is naturally straight still needs it to guide him, because bodily needs and circumstances may obstruct him. Integrity means remaining fixed in perfection without deviation and without any ulterior motive. When this integrity is found in the hearts of the upright, it guides them, because distracting impediments will not restrain them. But the perversity of traitors devastates them. Traitors are the opposite of the upright in heart and act contrary to uprightness. Perversity corrupts uprightness and righteousness and devastates them like robbers on a crooked road, plundering the soul’s wealth and casting it into the pit of destruction.
text.10_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Wealth does not benefit on the day of wrath. Although wealth is useful in peaceful times, as in “the rich man’s wealth is his fortified city,” it is useless on a day of universal wrath, such as plague or war. On the contrary, wealth may then be preserved for its owner’s harm. But righteousness saves from death even on the day of wrath. This does not repeat the statement above (10:2), which concerns natural death.
text.10_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: The righteousness of the innocent straightens his way. We explained (verse 3) the differences among the upright, innocent, and righteous. The upright person’s way is naturally straight, unlike the innocent person. Innocence means that one’s deeds remain constantly in one condition without wavering; if he is naturally upright, he never departs from his uprightness, but so long as he is not naturally upright, he is not assured of walking straight. The wise man explains that through the righteousness of the innocent—his habitual practice of righteousness—it becomes natural to him, and this habit straightens his way toward uprightness. But the wicked falls through his wickedness. The wicked person, the opposite of the innocent, persistently practices wickedness until it becomes acquired in his soul and fills his road with pits into which his soul falls, descending to destruction.
text.10_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: The righteousness of the upright saves them. The upright do not need righteousness to straighten their way, as does the innocent person, because their road is naturally straight, as explained at verse 3. Their righteous deeds instead save them from snares and the evils of the time, when traitors are trapped by calamities and ruin; the upright are saved through the merit of their righteous deeds.
text.10_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: When a wicked man dies, hope perishes. Hope differs from assured expectation. One expects something certain to come, like daylight or a promise, while hope concerns something uncertain. The wicked have no assured expectation, only hope, as explained concerning “the hope of the wicked perishes,” for they do not expect the reward stored for the righteous but merely hope for uncertain temporal success. At death this hope vanishes. The assured expectation of the bereaved also perishes. His children mourning him had confidently expected to inherit their father’s estate, but this too disappears, for strangers inherit his labor and his wealth is lost through an evil circumstance.
text.10_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: (8–9) The righteous— If the wicked prepares evil against the righteous, the outcome is that the righteous is rescued from distress and the wicked takes his place, as with Haman and Mordecai. It explains: if the wicked destroys his neighbor with a hypocritical mouth, enticing the righteous through flattery in order to destroy him, the righteous are rescued through knowledge, and the evil returns upon the informer and the one who dug the pit. It may also mean that one who flatters and fails to rebuke seeks to destroy his neighbor, as in “a man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net before his steps.”
text.10_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: (10–11) Through the goodness of the righteous; through the blessing of the upright. The righteous actively perform justice, while the upright possess understanding, naturally incline toward good, and go beyond the letter of the law, as explained at verse 3. The upright bestow blessing upon the city, and through their blessing the city is elevated in rank and dignity, because blessing proceeds from an additional sacred abundance within the soul of the one who blesses. The righteous bestow their material goodness through righteous deeds; through their goodness the city rejoices, because people receive good from them. With the wicked, both are reversed. Regarding the city’s joy, when the wicked perish there is song, because they actively harm others; spiritually, through the mouth of the wicked it is demolished, whether by their curse, slander, or evil speech.
text.10_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: One who despises his neighbor lacks a heart. Below (14:21) it says, “One who despises his neighbor sins”; each follows its context. There it concerns despising him without cause, which violates wisdom’s laws. Here it concerns responding after his neighbor first despised him. Though not a sin, it opposes understanding’s laws, as in (14:29), “One slow to anger possesses great understanding, while one short-tempered exalts folly.” Fools lack a heart, as in “fools die for lack of a heart”: they lack the ruling power over their spirit and do not use understanding to examine matters properly, doubting even matters of understanding, which requires patience and forbids immediate contempt. Therefore, a man of understanding remains silent, even when entitled to answer an insult—this being the special meaning of remaining silent.
text.10_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: One who goes about as a talebearer reveals a secret. A talebearer’s nature is to reveal his companion’s secret. A secret is a deposit entrusted to his spirit; just as one does not deposit property with an unreliable person, one must not entrust a secret to an untrustworthy spirit. When someone is a talebearer, know that his spirit is untrustworthy. Elsewhere it says, “One who reveals a secret goes about as a talebearer,” teaching the converse: if someone reveals secrets, we know his nature is to bear tales. But one faithful in spirit conceals a matter. Not only does he refrain from revealing a secret; he actively covers and hides the matter, and certainly does not spread his companion’s affairs through tale-bearing.
text.10_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Without strategies a people falls. Below (20:18) it says, “Thoughts are established through counsel, and wage war through strategies.” Thought differs from counsel. Counsel is the decision reached through understanding concerning which course to choose. Thought considers all possibilities and is manifold; after choosing one, the settled conclusion is counsel, as in “Many thoughts are in a man’s heart, but Hashem’s counsel shall stand.” Thus, thoughts are established through counsel: until a firm counsel is adopted, a person moves like foam upon waves of thought; when he selects a definite counsel, he finds a base. This suffices for ordinary worldly matters, such as choosing a business. War, however, requires more than counsel, because the enemy also has counsel, and one’s plan may fail against his—as Hushai the Archite answered Ahithophel’s counsel. A strategy is a chain of numerous counsels, joining causes and consequences so that whichever way the enemy turns, a prepared response confronts him. Thus, “wage war through strategies,” and here, without strategies a people falls, also concerns war. War therefore requires many counselors, each proposing another plan, because every plan may have a place: if one fails against the enemy, another is used. Hence, deliverance comes through many counselors. This is also an allegory for the inner war against the internal enemy; it appears again in Chapter 24, where that inner war is explained.
text.10_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: (Proverbs 11:15) One who guarantees a stranger will surely suffer harm. As explained below (17:17), although a friend must help his friend in every way he can, including serving as guarantor, he should not enter a hand-clasping surety of immediate liability, through which payment may be collected directly from the guarantor.
text.10_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: Thus it says that one who guarantees a stranger, even through ordinary surety, will suffer harm. Even for a friend whom he is compelled to guarantee, one who hates hand-clasping is secure: he will not undertake immediate surety, through which he cannot rely even upon his friend because creditors may first collect from him.
text.10_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: A gracious woman. When wealth and honor are gifts of God they commonly appear together: if one uses wealth to perform kindness, charity, and good, he also inherits honor. When separated, honor remains a virtue when deserved through one’s traits and qualities, whereas wealth becomes a defect when acquired through robbery and violence or used for evil. The verse pictures these two qualities standing separately and needing someone to support them—that is, an owner who maintains them. A gracious woman supports honor: mighty men are unnecessary, for honor is not gained through tyranny, but through a good woman who finds favor by her good deeds—or allegorically, through the precious, good, wise soul, the figurative woman of this book. But tyrants, who misuse force to oppress the poor, support wealth.
text.10_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: A man of kindness benefits his own soul. A man of kindness habitually does good to everyone without expecting repayment and without requiring an emotional impulse such as pity or compassion. His opposite is the cruel person, who not only withholds kindness but, even when moved by the suffering of the oppressed, hardens himself and does not help. A person has two parts: his soul, the spiritual soul, and his flesh, the body. Although a man of kindness appears to harm his body by distributing his money to others, he benefits his spiritual soul, which inherits the stored good. The verb “repay” denotes an act joined with an emotion of love or hate: he repays his soul because he loves the spiritual part that is the person’s essence. But a cruel person troubles his own flesh. The cruel person not only damages his spiritual soul; do not imagine that he thereby benefits his body. He troubles his flesh as well, because others will treat him cruelly, and “one who troubles his house inherits wind.” The intermediate person, who is neither kind nor cruel, may not benefit his soul, but does not trouble his flesh.
text.10_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: (18–19) The wicked performs a false labor. A deed differs from labor: labor is activity directed toward something, while a deed is its completion. The wicked appears to complete his deed—for example, accumulating wealth, building a house, or planting a vineyard through oppression and violence. In truth, imagined possessions are not ends in themselves but merely activities and means toward an end. If their purpose is a successful life, what is life’s purpose? Temporal life is likewise not an end in itself. Judged by their purpose, these are false labors: in what he performs, he accomplishes nothing; he does not attain the sought end. He resembles one who sows seed and grows plants but produces no flour. But one who sows righteousness—doing what is good before God—appears to sow rather than complete a deed, because righteousness’s end is not visible at the time; like one sowing in the ground, he will reap after many days at harvest. He will reap a true reward. Thus, righteousness truly leads to life: one who sows righteousness with joy reaps a true reward, because his upright deeds lead both to life in this world—as above, “righteousness saves from death”—and to true life in the World to Come. But the wicked person’s deed is a false labor, because one who pursues evil pursues it toward his own death. Pursuit means striving to obtain something quickly. Evil that would naturally remain distant from the wicked is hurried toward him before its time. He thus pursues his bodily death through premature punishment and his soul’s death in the World to Come, as above: “The labor of the righteous leads to life; the crop of the wicked leads to sin.”
text.10_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Those crooked of heart are an abomination to Hashem, but those innocent in their way are His delight.
text.10_Chapter, 19_Verse, 1_Comment: Abomination and delight are two extremes. Between them is a middle state that is neither delight—something He desires—nor abomination, as explained at 1:1, 12:22, and 15:8.
text.10_Chapter, 19_Verse, 2_Comment: The heart represents the ruling power in a person, directing all his faculties according to wisdom’s and righteousness’s laws.
text.10_Chapter, 19_Verse, 3_Comment: One who always governs himself through wisdom is called wise of heart and is innocent in his way: the conduct and course he follows remain continually whole, never collapsing or departing through desires and the heart’s inclinations, because his heart rules through fear of Hashem. Such a person is pleasing in Hashem’s eyes and obtains His favor.
text.10_Chapter, 19_Verse, 4_Comment: One crooked of heart is the opposite of one wise of heart: he disputes wisdom’s laws and directs his powers contrary to them. This is an abomination in Hashem’s eyes.
text.10_Chapter, 19_Verse, 5_Comment: Between these extremes is one who is not crooked of heart and does not dispute wisdom’s laws, but is also not innocent in his way. Although inwardly he does not dispute wisdom, he sometimes departs from the good road when the spirit of inclination rises against him. He is neither a delight nor an abomination, for he still stands within the bonds of battle and may ultimately conquer or be conquered.
text.10_Chapter, 20_Verse, 1_Comment: Hand to hand, the evil person will not go unpunished. Hashem’s punishments reach the evil person through direct providence, without an intermediary; He Himself punishes him by His hand. The punishment passes hand to hand, like something given directly from the giver’s hand into the recipient’s, rather than through nature’s agents. When punishment operates through intermediaries, it may fail to reach the evil person himself because his hour is favorable and his fortune supports him; it may also strike righteous descendants who did not sin, as with Achan: “Did not Achan trespass concerning the devoted thing, and wrath came upon the entire congregation of Israel? He was not the only man who perished for his sin,” because the punishment came through concealment of the Divine countenance. But when it comes directly from Hashem’s hand to the evil person, the evil will not go unpunished, while the offspring of the righteous escape. When punishment is entrusted to a destroyer, once permission is granted it does not distinguish good from evil. Not only the righteous person but even his offspring escape providential evil, as in, “God remembered Abraham and sent Lot from the upheaval.”
text.10_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout. An ornament adds grace and beauty only to one already suited to beauty. A ring placed in a pig’s snout does not beautify its face, because the whole animal is filthy; not only does it add no grace, but the pig soils the ring. So too, a beautiful woman who departs from good sense: the beauty adorning her face does not beautify her when she is inwardly ugly. “Taste” denotes the soul’s character and traits as revealed outwardly, as in “he changed his behavior before them” and “blessed is your good sense, and blessed are you.” The term is borrowed from food, whose bitter or sweet, good or bad quality the palate senses; similarly, a person’s impressions, traits, and speech reveal whether his nature is good or evil, wise or foolish. When her speech and conduct reveal evil and inner ugliness, outward beauty is useless; her corrupt character instead soils and disgraces it. Allegorically, a person may have a beautiful form, a soul prepared for intellectual attainment, learning, and understanding, yet possess evil traits and corrupt deeds. His Torah and knowledge disgrace him like a pig wearing a gold ring, as the Sages said of one who studies but does not speak gently: people say, “Woe to the teacher who taught him Torah.”
text.10_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: The desire of the righteous. Desire differs from hope. One who desires has no expectation of attaining the object but merely longs for it; one who hopes already has some expectation of attainment. The wicked person’s desire is evil, both because he desires evil—others’ possessions, violence, robbery, and forbidden things, as in “the soul of the wicked desires evil”—and because he will not attain it, as in “the desire of the wicked perishes.” But the desire of the righteous is only good: he desires only good, as in “for Your name and remembrance is the desire of the soul,” and Hashem grants his desire, as in “He grants the desire of the righteous” and “Hashem, You hear the desire of the humble.” It is also good because its fulfillment is pleasant to the soul. But the hope of the wicked is wrath.
