Even what they hope for and consider ready to attain becomes wrath in two ways: they fail to attain it and become enraged, as in “their hope is the expiration of the soul” (Job 11:20); and their very hope is evil, as in “the wicked wait for me to destroy me.” They hope for universal wrath and distress upon others, through envy or love of honor, so that only they remain tranquil; in the end the wrath falls upon them. As explained above in Chapter 10, the righteous possess assured expectation, while the wicked possess only uncertain hope. Wrath means anger passing beyond its proper boundary.
text.10_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: There is one who scatters and yet gains more, and one who withholds what is upright only to suffer want. The sages taught that a person should choose the middle way. Generosity lies between wastefulness and miserliness, both of which are wrong, as they said: one who distributes his wealth should not distribute more than one-fifth. Common opinion holds that, if one inclines toward an extreme, miserliness is preferable to wastefulness: the latter loses wealth, while the former at least preserves it. The wise man says the opposite. One who distributes does not always lose wealth; at times his generosity increases it, because his reputation grows among the wealthy, who lend to him and trust him, increasing the honor of his wealth. Thus, there is sometimes one who scatters and yet gains more. But one who withholds what is upright through miserliness only diminishes, for his stinginess and narrow eye drive people away, and his wealth disappears because no one conducts business with him. This may also come through Divine punishment, as Ecclesiastes describes a man to whom God gives wealth but does not empower him to enjoy it.
text.10_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: (25–26) A soul of blessing will be made prosperous; one who withholds grain will be cursed by the nation. The second verse explains the first. Whoever withholds grain from sale will be cursed by the nation, because by hoarding produce to raise prices he causes people to die of hunger, bringing the nation’s curse upon himself. But upon one who supplies grain and feeds people in famine, blessing comes upon his head. This blessing is so great that the soul receiving it will be made prosperous: by supplying food, his own soul is enriched. One who gives others drink will also be watered and fully satisfied. Scripture uses “made fat” of the soul, as in “I will satiate the soul of the priests with abundance” and “your soul will delight in richness,” referring to the essential moisture that increases bodily strength; watering denotes complete satisfaction through drink. All this is an allegory for one who withholds wisdom and Torah instruction from students—he withholds grain. It therefore says that the “nation,” meaning the community of the faith, will curse him. One who supplies and teaches Torah receives blessing; his spiritual soul is enriched with spiritual abundance. One who waters students by teaching Hashem’s way is himself watered: Hashem teaches him knowledge and makes known the way of understanding. The metaphor of bread and water for Torah study was explained in Isaiah 55, “All who thirst, go to water; go, buy and eat.”
text.10_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: One who earnestly seeks good. It teaches that human nature inclines more readily toward evil than good, because evil images are planted in the soul from childhood and material powers respond more strongly to senses and desires. Therefore it says, one who earnestly seeks good, and one who searches for evil. Good must be sought at dawn—an especially intense seeking renewed each morning—whereas evil requires only ordinary searching. One who earnestly seeks good must first seek favor, causing his powers to desire good, because desire for good is not naturally implanted in the soul’s faculties; he must excavate the soul’s depths until he draws out this desire. But one who searches for evil—it comes to him by itself; he need not seek a willing impulse, because matter and desire are already prepared for evil. “Seek” also denotes prayer: he must request Hashem’s assistance, for one who comes to purify himself is helped and must seek favor from Hashem. Evil comes by itself to one who seeks it, for one who comes to defile himself is given an opening.
text.10_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: One who trusts in his wealth will fall. It portrays human affairs through the metaphor of a fruit tree. Its fruit is the soul’s fruit for Torah and testimony. If one engages in Torah and serves Hashem, “the righteous flourishes like a palm” and gives fruit in season. External possessions—wealth—resemble leaves that protect and shelter the fruit, freeing him from material needs that would distract him from Torah and Divine service. But one who trusts only in his wealth and considers it primary will fall like a leaf falling from a vine, for leaves without fruit are nothing. But the righteous flourish like foliage: they blossom and produce flower and bud, the beginning of fruit—that is, holy fruit of praise for wisdom and knowledge. Wealth is then like the leaf surrounding and protecting the blossom so that the fruit endures.
text.10_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: One who troubles his house inherits wind. He destroys his household’s order, damages its vessels, and spends beyond his means, leaving nothing to inherit or bequeath, though “a house and wealth are an inheritance from fathers”; he inherits wind. This is an allegory for the figurative house, the soul’s dwelling, of which it says (24:3), “Through wisdom a house is built, through understanding it is established, and through knowledge its rooms are filled with every precious and pleasant treasure.” Collecting wisdom’s laws within the soul—how to conduct all traits and movements toward good and away from evil—constructs the house, as a builder gathers and arranges wood and stone. Understanding wisdom’s laws and deriving one thing from another completes the building. When all is known clearly, both traits and divine conceptions fill the soul’s house with precious, beautiful vessels, as in “lips of knowledge are a precious vessel.” Properly ordered, “the house of the righteous is a mighty fortress.” But the wicked man, who doubts and disputes wisdom’s laws and certainly lacks understanding and knowledge, troubles his house; then he inherits wind. The soul’s precious wealth and vessels disappear, leaving vanity and striving after wind—the stormy wind that raises images of desire against the heart, strikes the house’s four corners, and carries it away. Hence the conclusion: a fool is servant to one wise of heart. One wise of heart has the soul’s ruling power—the heart—govern according to wisdom’s images and laws without deviation, filling his house with precious treasures. The fool is his opposite, doubting and disputing wisdom’s laws, poor in knowledge, and fit to serve the wise of heart as the poor man serves the rich.
text.10_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and the wise man acquires souls. The righteous person uses wisdom’s laws to practice righteousness, while the sage gathered wisdom’s laws from teachers through study. “Say of the righteous that it is good, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds” compares righteousness to a fruit-bearing tree whose fruit the righteous and their companions eat. The fruit is their deeds—actions flowing from qualities of the soul. Whoever eats this fruit eats from the tree of life and lives forever in the soul’s life; that is, one learns from his deeds and acts likewise. The sage acquires souls through words—for acquiring people is through words—drawing souls through teachings that convey wisdom’s laws. The righteous gives them life by feeding them his fruit, meaning that they imitate his deeds.
text.10_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: (Proverbs 11:31) Behold, the righteous is repaid on earth; how much more the wicked and the sinner. After saying (11:30), the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, referring to the soul’s life, it follows that if the righteous commits some sin, evil reaches him in this world, for (Ecclesiastes 7:20), there is no righteous man on earth who does not sin. He is therefore repaid on earth so that his reward is preserved for the world of souls, where he lives forever. All the more so will the wicked sinner be repaid for his sin; but his repayment occurs in the World to Come, for he did not eat from the tree of life and his soul dies in the world of souls.
text.10_Chapter, 30_Verse, 1_Comment: The verse’s sense is: behold, the righteous person who sins is repaid; how much more the wicked person who sins.
text.10_Chapter, 30_Verse, 2_Comment: We also learn that the wicked person is punished even for a minor sin, all the more so than the righteous.
text.11_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: One who loves discipline loves knowledge. Discipline differs from rebuke. Rebuke reasons with a person through rational proofs and shows him good and evil; discipline compels acceptance through punishment—whether he fears the disciplinarian’s punishment, anger, and command like a child before an adult, or is told of Hashem’s punishments for disobedience. One who loves rebuke certainly loves knowledge because rebuke rests upon reason and knowledge. Here it adds that one who loves discipline loves knowledge, because discipline’s foundations likewise rest upon fear of Hashem and knowledge of His providence, reward, and punishment, which are clarified through knowledge. Knowledge is largely founded upon sensory attainment and matters made clear by sensory evidence, both famous and received: what occurred to the Flood generation, the generation of dispersion, Sodom, Egypt, and Korah’s assembly. Thus he loves knowledge. One who hates discipline is certainly brutish—unprepared to receive knowledge—for even children fear punishment and accept discipline. One might think that one who hates rebuke, which is founded on rational argument, is not brutish. It teaches that he too is brutish and considered an animal, for anyone worthy of being called a rational human being is naturally prepared to receive rebuke, or at least not to hate rebuke that opens his intellectual eyes.
text.11_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: A good man obtains favor from Hashem, but He condemns a man of schemes. The verb “scheme” denotes deep thought concerning how to accomplish something. In wisdom it means profound reflections upon wisdom; when directed against another, it generally means evil, as in, “one who plans to do evil is called a master of schemes,” for he deeply considers how to harm and ensnare his neighbor. When “condemn” is causative and intransitive, it indicates that his wickedness has grown so great that it goes outward to harm others. Wickedness includes offenses both against God and man; one who condemns acts wickedly toward another. The good man does not devise deep schemes but obtains favor from Hashem, striving that Hashem desire his deed, as in “commit your way to Hashem and your thoughts will be established.” Hashem then directs his simple thoughts toward an end pleasing to Him. Desire differs from favor: favor means wanting something because it is proper, upright, and good. The favor obtained from Hashem is His approval of the person as worthy. The good man arranges his thoughts so that Hashem finds favor in him; he neither devises schemes nor acts wickedly. But a man of schemes, who does not rely on Hashem but devises profound plots, performs deeds that condemn him.
text.11_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: A person is not established through wickedness, but the root of the righteous will not be moved. A base differs from a root. A base supports a detached object, as “a copper laver and its copper base,” while a root belongs to something growing and is united with its branches. The wicked have no root. A person’s root is above, in purity: man resembles an inverted tree whose root is above—the mind, planted in the intellectual world from which he receives influence. The righteous cleaves to this upper root. The wicked, cut off from it, stands only through his body upon the material world, like a detached object upon a base. Even that base will collapse, because his wealth was gathered through wickedness. The righteous possess a root: man resembles a tree whose root stands in purity while its branches incline toward impurity. Though a branch sometimes bends aside, the root does not move; it remains in purity and in the enduring spiritual world, and eventually the branch follows the root.
text.11_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: A woman of valor is her husband’s crown, but one who brings shame is like rot in his bones. A crown is clothing external to the body, placed upon the head as a sign of distinction and honor. A woman of valor not only strengthens his bones but crowns his head; through her he is praised before many peoples, as in “her husband is known at the gates.” A shameful woman is lazy in her deeds. Not only does she bring him no honor; he hides her, and she is like rot in his bones. A wife is bone of his bones, so it is as though part of him has decayed: the other half of his body, his wife, develops rot and causes his own portion to decay.
text.11_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: The thoughts of the righteous are judgment; the strategies of the wicked are deceit. Thought, counsel, and strategy differ. One who thinks has not yet formed counsel, but raises possibilities in his mind—whether and how to act. Once he reaches a clear conclusion, it is called counsel. One who devises multiple counsels, as in war, preparing different plans against an enemy’s unknown plans, forms a strategy—a linked set of counsels. Even the righteous person’s simple thought is judgment: he follows justice and righteousness without deviation. Even the wicked person’s strategies—the whole chain of plans—serve deceit, enabling him to defraud, oppress, and rob his neighbors. The righteous therefore need no strategies; the simple thought of performing justice suffices, because the straight road requires no plotting. The wicked, who must depart from justice and ensnare others through deceit, require intricate strategies joining many evil plans to trap the oppressed.
text.11_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: The words of the wicked are an ambush for blood. “Words” denotes extended, arranged speech. The wicked prolong their speech to carry out plans that lie in wait for blood, speaking slander and tale-bearing to destroy their neighbors. The upright have the laws of uprightness naturally implanted in their hearts and go beyond the letter of the law, the opposite of an ambush for blood; their mouth saves them. Above (11:6) it says, “the righteousness of the upright saves them, while traitors are trapped by calamities.” There their righteousness saves them from natural and providential evils. Here it concerns chosen human evils: their mouth, speaking according to wisdom’s laws and uprightness, saves them by teaching how to escape the wicked person’s ambush.
text.11_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Overturn the wicked, and they are no more. Although the wicked appear firmly rooted, when the time for punishment arrives and their measure is full, the Holy One overturns them. Overturning reverses something in quality, quantity, or position: a tree’s roots are placed above and branches below, or a person’s head below and feet above, as in “He overturns cities from their root.” Then they cease to exist, as in, “I saw a powerful wicked man spreading like a luxuriant native tree; he passed away, and behold, he was gone.” This is measure for measure. The wicked person lives inverted: man resembles a tree whose root—his head—is above and whose branches cling to earth, but the wicked man’s head, mind, and thoughts cling to earth. Hashem’s punishment is to overturn him completely, annihilating him. But the house of the righteous stands. When the righteous sins, he is punished promptly; “seven times the righteous falls and rises.” His root is not uprooted, only his property or body is afflicted. Not only he, but even his house stands. Above (10:25) it says, “When the storm passes, the wicked is gone, but the righteous is the foundation of the world,” concerning natural evils; here it concerns providential punishments. Midrash Noah applies both verses to the Flood generation and Noah.
text.11_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: A man is praised according to his intelligence. Intelligence is a special human faculty governing matters beyond understanding’s reach, such as grasping wisdom’s laws in their truth. Linguists note that expressions of understanding are not joined directly to wisdom—Scripture says “intelligent in every wisdom,” not “understand wisdom”—because this exceeds ordinary human understanding. Intelligence likewise grasps exalted conceptions such as Hashem’s glory, which cannot be reached through deductions beginning with sensory facts or first principles. Intelligence mentioned in Scripture is ordinarily good, but the inclination of the heart and immersion in desire can mislead it. The heart is the soul’s ruling power and needs the counsel of understanding and intelligence; when evil images and desires dominate it, it draws even these counselors into serving the inclination. Then intelligence assists evil. If his heart, the ruling power, is perverse and departs from uprightness and wisdom, his intelligence is despised, serving desire and inclination like a slave. Thus, a man is praised according to his intelligence: with great intelligence he grasps wisdom’s laws and the truth of Hashem’s ways and earns praise and glory—but only when his heart is upright and rules according to wisdom and understanding rather than listening to wandering inclinations. When he is perverse of heart, intelligence becomes contemptible; the greater it is, the more it assists him in evil.
text.11_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Better one lightly esteemed who serves himself than one who honors himself and lacks bread. Conventional signs of honor include not performing manual labor oneself, because such labor is considered disgraceful. Yet choosing this supposed honor and refusing work may leave one without bread. The verse teaches that this is not wisdom. He merely “honors himself”—appears honored without truly being so—and lacks bread, a real disgrace, since he has no servant to work for him. One who appears lightly esteemed because he works for himself actually possesses honor: he has a servant, namely himself, and is satisfied with bread. Allegorically, one who honors himself and is ashamed to study lacks the bread of Torah, while the humble person serves himself—that is, his soul.
text.11_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: The righteous knows the soul of his animal, but the mercies of the wicked are cruel. The righteous follows justice’s laws not only toward people but even toward his animal. He understands its nature, feeds it at the right time and measure, and does not burden it beyond its capacity. This too belongs to wisdom and justice, as in “I will give grass in your field for your animal,” followed by “you shall eat and be satisfied,” and the Torah’s prohibition against animal suffering. He learns this from the supreme Righteous One, Hashem. The Sages said that the Holy One knew the dog’s food is scarce and therefore kept its food in its intestines for three days—part of universal justice. The wicked person rejects justice’s laws; even apparent mercy from him springs from concealed cruelty. He may spare a captive not to kill him, but to enslave him; he may feed his animal more only to impose heavier labor. His mercy is rooted in self-interest. Allegorically, man has two parts: the body is his animal and the soul is the human being. The righteous gives each its proper portion. When desire entices him for his animal’s sake, he knows the soul of his animal—the spiritual soul animating the body. That soul desires the opposite of the animal’s desire, so he kills the animal’s desire to preserve its soul. The wicked mercifully indulge their animal with every desire but destroy its soul—great cruelty toward their own being and spiritual soul.
text.11_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: (11–12) One who works his land will be satisfied with bread; the wicked desires the snare of evil men. Although human nature inclines toward rest while soil requires labor—the worker being subjected to hard service day and night—a person must consider the result: through work he will be satisfied with bread. Better to bear labor’s yoke than hunger’s pain. This judgment comes from the soul’s ruling power called the heart. But one who pursues empty things, seeking livelihood through idleness without working his land, lacks a heart; he lacks the ruling power that rebukes laziness by anticipating its consequence.
text.11_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: This teaching is repeated below (28:19): One who works his land will be satisfied with bread, but one who pursues empty things will be satisfied with poverty; a faithful man has abundant blessings, but one who hastens to become rich will not be innocent. There it concerns another matter, for pursuing empty things takes two forms:
text.11_Chapter, 10_Verse, 2_Comment: * One may seek livelihood without ordinary labor through commerce, voyages across seas and deserts, finding treasures, and the like. These are empty pursuits because profit is uncertain. This is the subject there, as indicated by “a faithful man has abundant blessings”: one who trusts Hashem and sows his land—faith being associated with the Order of Seeds because he trusts Hashem and sows—receives abundant blessings from heaven’s dew and the deep below. Through faith and trust, one who works his land will be satisfied with bread. But one who pursues empty things, hastening to become rich and seeking schemes for instant wealth because he lacks faith and trust, will instead be satisfied with poverty.
text.11_Chapter, 10_Verse, 3_Comment: * Here it concerns pursuing empty things to become rich through robbery and violence, as the conclusion proves: the wicked desires the snare of evil men. The wicked person refuses labor and seeks to live by hunting others, trapping people and taking their money through deceit and wicked schemes. He lacks a heart, for his heart does not rule him according to wisdom’s laws. But one who works his land and conducts himself justly, neither oppressing nor trapping others but sowing grain rooted in the earth—the root of the righteous, which they planted in their soil, provides bread to the eater.
text.11_Chapter, 10_Verse, 4_Comment: These two ideas also possess metaphor and allegory, for the cultivated soil has a metaphor within a metaphor. Here the soul is compared by the sages to a field potentially prepared to produce fruit. Just as land requires labor to remove thorns, plant seed, water, and cultivate it, so evil images must be removed from the soul, wisdom and discipline sown within it, and it watered with intelligence and knowledge until it produces holy fruit of praise. One who cultivates his soil is ultimately satisfied with bread—the nourishment of wisdom and discipline, the soul’s bread. One who pursues empty things is the wicked person who did not cultivate his soil and desires the snare of evil men: images of desire that cast great nets around the small city and trap its spiritual powers. He lacks a heart and does not govern the soul according to wisdom’s laws. But one who cultivates his soil, clears its thorns, and plants divine seeds—the root of the righteous—produces wisdom.
text.11_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: In the transgression of the lips is an evil snare. The lips signify outward speech. Sometimes one speaks only with the lips, not with mouth and tongue—that is, without first considering what to say. His lips move without understanding or intelligence and may transgress against him and prepare a snare. For example, before a king he may carelessly utter something improper and be trapped by his words; in court one careless statement may ensnare him. The righteous person, who conducts everything justly, has trained his lips not to utter anything improper, as in “the lips of the righteous shepherd many” and “the lips of the righteous know favor.” Even after entering distress, he escapes it through lips trained to speak according to practical knowledge, as explained in those passages.
text.11_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: From the fruit of a man’s mouth he is satisfied with good. It pictures man as a tree of the field, whether barren or fruit-bearing. A fruit tree’s essence is the fruit by which it is valued; man’s fruit is in his mouth. Just as a tree’s finest power is its fruit, which reveals its nature and goodness, so speech and intellect revealed through a person’s mouth are the fruit of this human tree. In this book, “mouth” generally signifies wisdom. When he speaks wisdom, he produces fruit and its clusters ripen; he is not a barren tree like one who lacks wisdom and does not open his mouth at the gate. Unlike an ordinary tree, however, whose owner is not necessarily satisfied by its fruit while others eat it, a person himself is satisfied by his fruit: wisdom’s fruit satisfies its owner’s soul with brightness and brings his powers to perfection. A person ascends toward perfection by two ladders, contemplation and action. Wisdom satisfies him personally; charitable and kind deeds performed by his hands are fruit that satisfies others who receive his good, while Hashem returns his recompense. Thus, the recompense of a man’s hands He returns to him. Reward differs from recompense: recompense follows the emotion aroused in the soul during the deed by its implanted traits—for example, charity arising from compassion or from love of one’s neighbor. According to this human emotional quality, Hashem repays him in accordance with his soul’s character. “Returning” differs from reward and recompense: one returns the thing itself, while reward gives something else in exchange. Hashem returns to him the very righteousness he gave others, so his soul loses nothing. In sum, he directly eats wisdom’s fruit, while the fruit of good deeds returns from Hashem as reward and recompense.
text.11_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: The fool’s way is upright in his eyes, but one who heeds counsel is wise. It says elsewhere that a way may appear upright to a man while its end is the ways of death. One path looks straight at first but leads to death and destruction; another initially seems full of thorns and pits but leads to paradise. Drawing one’s flesh with wine and pursuing bodily pleasures initially seems good and straight, but ends in death because the body decays and the self-indulgent person dies prematurely. The spiritual way—rejecting pleasures, withdrawing from this world, and following the soul—begins with thorns but leads to eternal paradise. The fool doubts and disbelieves wisdom’s laws; he will not heed counsel warning that the road appearing straight is the way of death. Only what seems temporarily good is upright in his eyes. He therefore strays from intelligence’s path and rests among the shades (21:16). But one who heeds counsel is wise. The sage, who has gathered wisdom’s laws into his soul and follows them, does not choose the way upright in his own eyes; he heeds wisdom’s counsel, which reveals its thorn-filled end, and chooses the path that seems initially difficult but leads to life and happiness.
text.11_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: A fool’s anger is known that very day, but a shrewd man conceals disgrace. Wisdom, understanding, and intelligence require patience and not displaying anger immediately. Even when anger exists within, it should not be revealed outwardly, for anger itself is an ugly trait and should be hidden as a disgrace demonstrating a corrupt disposition, as in “a man’s intelligence makes him slow to anger” and “one slow to anger possesses great understanding.” The fool, who has not implanted wisdom’s laws in his soul, is unaccustomed to restraining his spirit and delaying anger, as in “one short-tempered performs folly.” Therefore, on the very day he becomes angry it is known to everyone, because he expresses it in action. Wisdom and understanding command patience and prohibit vengeance: taking revenge or harming one who sinned against him violates wisdom’s laws. Even one who has not learned wisdom may act this way from shrewdness, knowing that if he rages his companion will insult him and observers will despise him. Thus the shrewd man conceals disgrace: to avoid humiliation he cunningly hides anger in his heart until he can take revenge without disgrace. This comes from shrewdness, not wisdom; wisdom commands him to conceal and eliminate the anger itself, preventing it from secretly ruling his spirit. The fool not only fails to suppress anger within his soul but announces it to others, bringing disgrace upon himself.
text.11_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: (17–19) One who breathes truth, etc.; there is one who speaks rashly, etc.; the lip of truth, etc. It pictures a man appearing before a judge against his companion and making a truthful claim, while the other brings a false witness. A wise judge distinguishes truth from falsehood through examination. The first sign is that one speaking truth speaks calmly and quietly because truth is with him; the liar speaks noisily, formally testifies, swears, and makes declarations to strengthen his words, multiplying deceit and schemes. Thus, one who breathes truth—even if he merely exhales it with the lightest movement of his lips—declares righteousness; this slight statement suffices to explain and establish justice, because his trustworthy report deserves belief. But a false witness, although formally testifying, declares deceit; deceit is readily recognizable in his words. Even if one speaks rashly through vows and oaths to strengthen his claim, like sword-thrusts that stab the litigant by condemning him unjustly, the tongue of the wise brings healing. “Tongue” denotes analytical speech: sages following wisdom’s laws investigate through understanding and its proofs, derive one matter from another, recognize the deceit, and heal the wounded party. It then explains the lip of truth. Lips are light, external speech; the tongue is elevated, logical, reflective discourse. Truth needs neither rhetoric nor clever deductions, for it stands eternally by itself without proofs. Thus even the lip of truth is established forever. But a tongue of falsehood, although presenting lies through logical arguments and evidence, lasts only for a moment, because the forgery and deceit are quickly recognized; a little truth dispels much falsehood.
text.11_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Deceit is in the heart of those who devise evil, but counselors of peace have joy. It contrasts devisers of evil with counselors of peace, as in “He makes peace and creates evil.” Peace sustains existence, while evil destroys it. Counselors of peace desire existence’s preservation; peace includes every good—domestic and civic peace. They seek the public’s welfare and counsel the preservation of goodness, uprightness, and justice. They are called counselors because they deliberate according to wisdom and truth; counsel normally aims at good and is given openly. Those who devise evil seek to destroy existence, demolish the world’s pillars, end civilization, and destroy truth and justice—false witnesses, evildoers, and destroyers of the public and individual. They plot secretly so no one knows; therefore their hearts are filled with deceit, for they must conceal their evil lest the community recognize and guard against them. They are always sad and anxious lest their evil and deceit become known. But counselors of peace are filled with joy: good rejoices in its deeds, while evil is continually saddened; deceit cannot dwell with joy because it is full of fear and trembling.
text.11_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: No iniquity will be caused to the righteous. The verb denotes preparing a cause for an outcome, as in “God caused it to come to his hand.” One transgression causes another: the Sages said that one who killed is providentially given an opportunity to kill again so that he will be exiled. But the righteous person who holds to justice’s ways has no cause that will bring him to perform any unjust iniquity; he will not commit it even unintentionally. On the contrary, one commandment draws another. For the wicked, one sin draws another until they are filled with evil, as one evil produces another until their measure is full.
text.11_Chapter, 21_Verse, 1_Comment: Lying lips are an abomination to Hashem, but those who practice faithfulness are His delight. Abomination and delight are opposites, as are lying lips and practitioners of faithfulness. One who promises to perform something—whether a commandment, kindness, or good for another—speaks faithfully and proves trustworthy if he fulfills it; if he does not, he spoke falsely. One habitually promising without performing has lying lips and is an abomination to Hashem, because speech and action do not agree. Even if his words were only external lip-service, it is an abomination. One who practices faithfulness makes deed agree with word—speaking faithfully and performing—and is Hashem’s delight.
text.11_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: A shrewd man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaims folly. The fool driven by desire is not the doubting fool. The latter doubts everything, including wisdom’s laws, because he does not understand them. The former knows wisdom’s laws, but desire overpowers and defeats him, so he does not follow them; as in “fulfilled desire is sweet to the soul, but turning from evil is an abomination to fools.” Though he knows it is evil, desire makes departure from evil abhorrent. He therefore seeks excuses and casts doubt upon wisdom’s laws. Knowledge is clear certainty; folly is doubt, its opposite. The fool does not desire knowledge and prefers doubt as a mask for following his heart’s desire, as in “depart from a foolish man, for you will not know lips of knowledge”; “the tongue of the wise improves knowledge, but the mouth of fools pours out folly”; “the lips of the wise scatter knowledge, but the heart of fools is not so”; and “the heart of the discerning seeks knowledge, but the mouth of fools feeds upon folly.” Because his heart—the ruling power—drives him toward desire while he fears punishment, he calls upon folly and doubt for security, questioning Hashem’s punishments and wisdom’s laws governing the world; thus “one who trusts his own heart is a fool.” The shrewd man is not necessarily a sage who received all wisdom’s detailed laws, yet shrewdness prevents him from acting where doubt exists. He continually weighs his path and does not enter a doubtful road in darkness before understanding it, as in “the shrewd man’s wisdom is to understand his way, but the folly of fools is deceit.” Their folly and doubts deceive their own souls, for they truly know their folly is baseless. Therefore, “the simple inherit folly, but the shrewd crown themselves with knowledge,” and “every shrewd man acts with knowledge, but a fool spreads folly.”
text.11_Chapter, 22_Verse, 1_Comment: Here it further explains the difference in their conduct:
text.11_Chapter, 22_Verse, 2_Comment: * The shrewd man conceals knowledge. Even what he knows, he hides and reveals to no one. This distinguishes the shrewd from the wise, for (Proverbs 10:14), the wise store away knowledge but do not conceal it completely. They know through received wisdom’s laws and teach it to the many, whereas the shrewd man knows through his own investigation and guards it for himself rather than others.
text.11_Chapter, 22_Verse, 3_Comment: * But the heart of fools, because their ruling power has been defeated by desire, necessarily calls upon folly for protection. They claim to depart from wisdom’s laws because they doubt them; they proclaim and publicize folly as a mask.
text.11_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: The hand of the diligent will rule. The diligent person is the opposite of both the lazy and the deceitful. He works without laziness, diligently and honestly rather than through deceit, and does not hasten to become rich without labor, as in “the thoughts of the diligent lead only to abundance … one who hastens leads only to want” (21:5). Through diligence he becomes rich; the lazy and deceitful become poor and downtrodden. It pictures the diligent as the wealthy people of the country, whose power grows until they rule the land, while deceit, impoverished and humbled, becomes tributary like slaves paying tribute to their masters.
text.11_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs it down. Every trait lies hidden in the human soul until the spirit raises an image of it upon the heart. A person can raise or lower this image. He may awaken a good or evil image from his traits, and the spirit reveals and raises it to the heart to rule there—pride or humility, jealousy, desire, and the like. Anxiety, concern for the future, is also among the soul’s powers. When its image rules the heart, it consumes soul and flesh. Even a wealthy, tranquil person may continually grieve that his house will be destroyed, his wealth vanish, his children die, or enemies rule him. When anxiety rises upon the heart, the wise man gives two remedies: first, lower the image into the soul’s depths, where darkness covers it, by diverting attention from such thoughts; second, raise good images opposed to anxiety—picture a good future, a stable house filled with Hashem’s blessing, and hope for the end. Thus, when anxiety is in a man’s heart and rules it, either let him lower it, or a good word will gladden it, for a good image opposing the saddening evil image brings joy. The Sages likewise offered both interpretations: one said, “remove it from his mind,” and another, “discuss it with others.” Both are true and rest on the verse’s two parts. “Lower it” means remove it from thought; “a good word will gladden it” means divert it to other, good and joyful thoughts.
text.11_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: The righteous searches out his companion. The righteous person does not rely upon his own way, fearing that he may err. He is not necessarily a sage who learned wisdom’s laws from teachers; rather, through practical experience, observing righteous people and their conduct, he habitually acts wisely. He therefore examines and studies his companion—or adds to and improves his own deeds through his righteous companion. The wicked, however, trusts the road upright in his own eyes and learns from no one; the way of the wicked leads them astray.
text.11_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: (Proverbs 12:27) The deceitful man will not roast his game. The deceitful man is the opposite of the diligent. He gains profit through fraud, like a hunter who catches birds by deceit, as in (Jeremiah 5:27), like a cage full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit. He does not labor diligently to acquire wealth, but gains it through robbery and deceit. He must hide his game so that no one sees it and cannot display it to anyone. But a person’s precious wealth is the wealth of diligence: wealth gathered through diligent effort is precious wealth. “Diligent” describes the wealth, as above (Proverbs 12:24), the hand of the diligent will rule.
text.11_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: On the path of righteousness is life, and the way of its trail is toward no death. Way, path, and trail differ. A way is the great public road from city to city; a path branches from it toward villages; a trail is for individuals. Righteousness—the commandments between man and God—travels on a path, not a universal way but one particular to the people of the faith whom He sanctified. On this path is life, both in this world and the World to Come, as in “which a person shall perform and live through them.” Righteousness also has a trail followed by individuals such as Moses and Elijah, who sanctified themselves like ministering angels and performed Hashem’s righteousness. Their righteousness resembled that of the heavenly beings who are not mortal and over whom death held no power: Elijah entered alive among the heavenly beings, and Moses died by the Divine kiss. Although after shedding physicality and walking among the heavenly beings they entered the public way fixed for the heavenly world, while still clothed in matter their course was called a trail, because such exalted individuals are few. One who travels from that individual trail onto the way, gaining passage among the eternal beings, reaches no death; death is not found there at all.
text.12_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: A wise son is one who practices according to the laws of wisdom. And the laws of wisdom are difficult for the nature of the heart to accept and practice, because the images of desires will rise on the soil of the soul like a cloud. The soul must be cleansed by the moralizer who disciplines his son and informs him of the punishments of Hashem and the evil that leads to deviating from the laws of wisdom. While he is a youth, he should be disciplined in the tribe until he is convinced to accept the laws of wisdom, because fear is what disciplines the soul until the images of wisdom rule in its heart. When he is a wise son, it is a sign that the moralizer of his father has acted in him. And the son who has not heard rebuke from his father from his days is not only an unwise son, but he is a scoundrel who mocks the laws of wisdom.
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: (Proverbs 13:2): A man who keeps his mouth shut will eat well -
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: It was already said above (Proverbs 12:14): A man who keeps his mouth shut will be satisfied with good, and there he comes to a different consideration.
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 2_Comment: And here it comes to say that his mouth is the tree of knowledge of good and evil. We have already explained that the mouth alludes to wisdom, the tongue alludes to understanding, and the tongue alludes to understanding (and they all come to the same conclusion (Proverbs 18:20): A man's mouth... and the fruit of his lips... is in the hand of the tongue..., see there).
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 3_Comment: And he wants to say that the fruit of the mouth is the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, because in wisdom there are two paths, for example pride and humility, mercy and cruelty, and the like, and they must be guided by wisdom, and the man who uses wisdom for good will eat the good from the tree;
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 4_Comment: But the traitor, who uses his qualities contrary to the path of wisdom, will eat poison from the fruit of his mouth, and will use all his qualities for evil by the serpent that tempts him to evil, and this is what is called a traitor, for the traitor does not keep the words of his mouth and his promise, and in a parable, he does not use the path of wisdom as it was imprinted upon him.
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 5_Comment: And we have already explained that giving is a comprehensive matter in all that is appropriate, whether in terms of money or in terms of measure.
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 6_Comment: And Lakman (ibid.) already explained the difference between wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, which are implied by the mouth, lips, and tongue, in what he said:
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 7_Comment: * Whoever breaks a man's mouth will satisfy his stomach,
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 8_Comment: * And "the fruit of his lips shall be satisfied,"
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 9_Comment: * Life and death are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit,
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 11_Comment: * Wisdom is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and from it our stomachs will be filled, whether good or evil, according to the preparation;
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 12_Comment: * And knowledge is the grain that is finished, because it is the clear knowledge, and from it one will be satisfied with bread for the full;
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 13_Comment: * But the tongue, which she understood, in which she would distinguish between truth and falsehood, does not depend on good and evil (for good and evil are only in the public eye), only on which life and death depend, and it is the tree of life, and those who love it will eat of its fruit and live forever.
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 14_Comment: And in the way of the simple, first (Proverbs 12:14) he spoke with the fruit of his mouth, speaking in Torah and prayer, and then he spoke with the speech of one who speaks in the way of the earth:
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 15_Comment: * One must guard his speech and not profane the words of his lips, and then he will eat well, because he will be faithful and will eat from his labor. Above all, he said he will be satisfied, and here he said he will eat, because satisfaction indicates the reward of the soul, as in (Isaiah 11:11): And he will be satisfied with the purity of your soul, and eating indicates that he will eat well;
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 16_Comment: * And the traitor, who does not guard his faith, which is the traitor's fence, his soul will eat poison.
text.12_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: He who guards his mouth, opens his lips, there is a difference between a mouth and a tongue, because the tongue is the external speech, and the mouth is the internal speech in wisdom, and there is a difference between a creator and a guard, because the creator is more than the one who guards what he created with constant guarding, and illustrates that the mouth and lips are like a wall in form around the soul, and they close it off so that its enemies and enemies may not come near it, and it is not only the lips that need to be guarded, which are the external walls that the enemy stands around, but the external accent that speaks without the mind must be guarded, because one must also guard his mouth, and even the speech in wisdom must be under extra guard, as it is written that Hashem is in heaven and you are on earth, therefore your words will be few, and in this one guards his soul, because it has a wall in form around it, but he who opens his lips, which are the external wall, is a threat to him, and as explained in my book, its joy is against the strength and the fortress, and R"l also in Torah and wisdom must guard the openings His mouth, and by it he will preserve his soul, but he who opens his lips to speak evil and gossip, it is a curse to his body as well:
text.12_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: From desire and not his soul is lazy, the lazy person is the opposite of the diligent person who does work with agility and diligence, and here is the lazy person who does not want to toil in work. Do not say that he does not have desire, because in truth his soul desires more than any other person, because desire will be stronger in someone who has no way to fulfill his desire, only that his hands, feet, and limbs do not obey his soul to fulfill its will, in such a way that his limbs do not agree with his lustful soul, because they desire in idleness, he will kill his soul, as it is written: The desire of the lazy person will kill him because his hands will not do it, and he wanted to say: The lazy person's soul is from desire, and there is none, but the diligent, although they tire their bodies with work, their souls will be satisfied, because they have all their desires, and the lazy person is likened to engaging in wisdom, his spiritual soul is from desire and there is none, and it will die an eternal death at his hands, unserved. For his spiritual soul. And the diligent, although his body is weary, his spiritual soul will be nourished with the fat of the house of the Lord and will drink of the eternal stream:
text.12_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: A righteous man will hate a false word. The foundation of justice is built on the love of truth. If his heart inclines to falsehood, he will not do justice, but will pervert justice, hear slander and gossip, and condemn his fellow man to his duty, all of which is against justice. Therefore, the righteous man who does justice will hate a false word. And the evil man who does the opposite of justice, will love lying, shame his fellow man's odor in his absence, and slander him to his face by gossiping and slandering him and slandering him with false words. It should be interpreted that the righteous man will shame and slander the wicked man because he hates a false thing, and therefore he will hate the wicked man who lies:
text.12_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Righteousness will make a perfect path, and wickedness will pervert sin. Here, the distinction is between a pure path and sin, and wickedness and righteousness, and a perversion and a perversion. A pure path is one whose path is pure in nature and does not incline to lust and deficiency, and there is no deficiency in his path that deficiency and sin are the opposite of innocence. And here, a pure path will not be perverted by wickedness, because his path is pure in nature and he corrects his path according to intellectual manners to do justice and justice as reason requires and to abstain from evil. However, as long as he does not walk in righteousness, that is, the commandments between a person and a place that are not required by reason, he will already depart from innocence by not knowing the right path, because the intellect cannot judge about everything what is good and what is bad. Only righteousness will create a pure path, and if he walks in righteousness, it will create innocence, and he will be a righteous and pure person. Likewise, righteousness without innocence is not safe from an obstacle, because then he will do righteousness for the sake of external appeals, and when he finds comfort and benefit in the opposite, he will deviate from it. And there must be a path to completion, and then righteousness will create it.
text.12_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: And condemnation will distort sin. Whoever has sin in him, meaning a deficiency that inclines to his desires, which is the boundary of sin that is from the side of desire, then condemnation will rule to distort and distort his path:
text.12_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: (7-8) Some become rich, etc. A sinner, etc. There are those who, to the eye, appear to be getting rich, but after intellectual examination, in reality, he has nothing. Likewise, sometimes it appears to the eye that someone is becoming poor and has exhausted his wealth, and in reality he has great wealth. This is because the possession of wealth is not a real possession, but an imaginary possession, just as a madman would say, "This is my house and this is my possession," as Maimonides says in "Teaching the Confused," to the point that what we call rich is someone who has many possessions, but an imaginary vanity, because there is no real connection between the possessions and the one who buys them. Sometimes the wealth is lost in a bad matter during his life, and in any case, they leave it to others to dream of when they die, until he only becomes rich according to appearances, and in reality he has nothing, because it is not a possession that is attached to his soul. But whoever scatters his wealth for charity and kindness and buys with it The integrity of his soul, which is the root of the eternally living man, is true wealth, and this impoverished man has great wealth reserved for eternity in the world of souls, and it is true wealth and great and very great eternal wealth. He explains that the ransom of a man's soul is his wealth, the root of wealth is if he ransoms his spiritual soul, if he gives the poor the condition to redeem his soul from corruption, and in this the ruler did not hear a rebuke, he will not be angry with the ruler who comes to take the ransom of his soul from him to revive him in eternal life, because he will give it to him with great joy:
text.12_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: (Proverbs 13:9): The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked is snuffed out - The light is the very light, like the light of the sun that always shines and does not need oil or a wick; and the candle is what is made into a lamp by oil and a wick.
text.12_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: * The righteous, their souls will shine with "an everlasting, eternal light, and (Psalms 77:11): Light is spread out for the righteous, and they do not need a lamp, which is the body, because the spiritual soul will forever rejoice in the spiritual light, and this will always rejoice, as it is said (Psalms 77:11): And the upright in heart will rejoice, (Psalms 22:11): Rejoice in the Lord.
text.12_Chapter, 8_Verse, 2_Comment: * But the wicked, the light of their material success is only in this world, as long as the candle and wick exist, meaning, the entire life of the body, and after the oil and wick are consumed - the candle will burn out, and their success will be lost.
text.12_Chapter, 8_Verse, 3_Comment: And this is also attributed to what is said (Proverbs 13:8): A man's wealth is the ransom of his soul, for it is necessary to revive the soul, which is a perpetual light, not the body and the lamp of its success which will fade away; and this rich man, the physical one, has nothing.
text.12_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Only with malice will one give a matzah. I have already explained that there malice comes to the one who deliberately disagrees with the laws of wisdom and truth in public and does not submit to the words of the sages, as it is written, "And the soul that does it with malice will not listen to the priest." There is a difference between a matzah and a quarrel, which matzah is the great quarrel that is close to beating and war. Now, when a quarrel arises and differences of opinion arise among the people, they will not come to the matzah if they consult, that is, they will gather and consult on a path of advice as to which path is best, and each one will express his opinion, and the decision between the opinions will be according to the laws of wisdom that they received from their rabbis. After the advice, they will see whose words are founded on wisdom and accept that advice. And it is written, "And those who consult wisdom," if they consult, they will follow the laws of wisdom and so they will do. And the matter will not come to the matzah only if there is malice that vehemently disagrees with the laws of wisdom and truth, for then there is no decision and advice will not be of any use, and then it comes to the matzah. Matzah, like the ice that melted and divided the laws of wisdom and poured out on Hashem in the assembly of Korah:
text.12_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Fat wealth will diminish, also says someone who has great wealth, if he follows vanity, his wealth will diminish, because wealth requires effort and care to add to it, and if its owners follow vanity, their wealth will be scattered and not added to, and it will diminish each time until it is exhausted. However, even someone who does not have wealth, but he strives and gathers it by hand, who does not scatter, but gathers it and adds little by little, and gathers it with his hands and with his labor, it will increase and he will come to possess great wealth. And this is a parable about the business of Torah: Even the great sage who has accumulated much wisdom, if he follows vanity, his wealth will decrease and he will forget his Torah, but he who studies and strives to add to his wisdom every day will increase and become wiser in his later years:
text.12_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Long-awaited expectation sickens the heart and the tree of life is the coming of desire. There is a difference between expectation and hope and desire. The one who hopes hopes for something and has no promise that his desire will certainly come, but the one who hopes has a promise and is certain that the thing he hopes for will come, and the one who desires does not have any hope either. He only desires the thing and has no hope that it will be obtained. He also said that if expectation lasts and does not come in the near future, but only in the distant future, it has already sickened his heart. Although it is certain that the thing will come, his heart is sick because it did not come sooner. When the stage of the one who desires is sick, and he is sick for which he has no cure since there is no hope at all, as the saying goes, lazy desire is a dead end. And so when the desire comes, which is something he did not hope for, it is like a tree of life that revives the soul of the one who desires:
text.12_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: He who despises a word will be punished, and he who fears a mitzvah will be punished, the ancients already differed, whether a person needs to fulfill all 313 mitzvot or is it enough to fulfill one mitzvah, and as in the verse "And she opened her mouth without a law," one said to one who did not learn even one mitzvah, and another said to one who did not fulfill even one mitzvah, and both are true, he must believe and be ready to fulfill all of Hashem's mitzvahs, and if he despises even one mitzvah, it is said of him that Hashem spoke in this, because in this he disbelieves in the entire Torah, and Azza He who despises a word will be punished, if he despises even the first word, punishments and punishments will come to him, indeed, someone who believes in the entire Torah and all of its mitzvahs, but has not come to him with only one mitzvah to fulfill, will already receive a reward as if he had fulfilled the entire Torah, because we know that if other mitzvahs come to him, he will fulfill them, and Z"s And he fears a mitzvah if he fears a mitzvah even though he has fulfilled only one mitzvah, He will be paid and receive a reward for all the Torah:
text.12_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: The Torah of a wise man is a source of life to avoid the pitfalls of death, as I have already explained above (10:11) that the path of wisdom is called the path of life and the opposite path of foolishness is the path of spiritual death, and whoever draws the water of wisdom and drinks from it will live forever, and the source from which the water flows is either by seeing the deeds of the righteous and his conduct, for the mouth of the righteous is a source of life, or by fearing Hashem, as the word of the Lord says (14:27), but there is a path of death opposite to it, the two pitfalls surrounding the soul to trap it in their net, and they are desires and evil traits, and to be saved from the pitfalls of death one must draw the water of life from the Torah of a wise man, that the wise man who has received all the laws of wisdom will study them in a thorough study and will make known all the rules and details of what the path of wisdom is and what the path of foolishness is. And the Torah of a wise man is that Torah is the study that is thorough in everything, and it is A source of life, from which those who draw know how to avoid the mines of death:
text.12_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Good sense will grant grace, there is sense and good sense, sense is the power that an educated person has to penetrate everything with sudden knowledge and to judge things that are hidden from the power of wisdom and understanding, and also about things that have no sense of entry into them, such as the knowledge of Hashem and the spiritual and the like from scholars who are after nature, and that good sense is one who attains the Spirit of Hashem, which is above the human mind, which sometimes goes in a crooked way, but if he is accompanied by help from on high, he will truly understand and know everything by the Spirit of Hashem upon him, and that this sense comes mostly through grace to one who finds favor in the eyes of Hashem and Azzah and finds favor, and good sense in the eyes of Hashem and man, it is called a gift because it comes from above to one who finds favor, who then finds a good sense to be wise in the Spirit of Hashem, but one who precedes him good sense and anticipates the Spirit of Hashem according to His preparation, then will grant grace, does not find favor, only receives it in the way of giving, By good understanding, the Lord will bless him, as it says, "I know you by name, and you have also found favor in my sight." And he said, "Please show me your glory." And behold, whoever has good understanding and attains to the Spirit of Hashem will also drink from the fountain of life, and the Lord will grant him grace to know how to turn away from the pits of death by the help of Hashem from on high with His Holy Spirit. And the lesson of the scripture The law of the wise is a fountain of life, and also Good understanding will grant grace to turn away from the pits of death, but the path of steadfast traitors, those who betray the Lord and walk the path of death with their steadfast path. The steadfast is the hard place in which one will not work or sow, whether in a stream, or in the solid mountains, rocks and crags on which no soil suitable for sowing has come, and they will not drink from the water of life because they are not worthy to receive dew and rain, and likewise the path of traitors is not worthy to receive from the source of life:
text.12_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: Every naked man acts with knowledge, and a fool spreads a veil, I have already explained above (12:23) that the naked man has a veil of knowledge, that it is the nature of the naked man to cover his knowledge and not reveal to others what he knows, and yet every naked man acts with knowledge, he will not do anything out of doubt until he knows with clear knowledge whether his action is right and whether it is directed towards the goal, because this is the nature of cunning, so that he will not walk in darkness and in confusion, as the saying goes: The wisdom of the naked man understands his path, and as I explained there, and the fool is one who deviates from the laws of wisdom for the sake of his desires, even if he attains the laws of wisdom, he will cast doubts in them so that he can do as he desires, and he said there that the heart of fools is called a veil, which besides not covering it, he will call and publish it, and here he said that he will spread a veil like one who spreads a garment, that he will spread all the sides of his vision and do his action in darkness because of the veil spread over his ignorance:
text.12_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: A wicked angel will fall into evil. There is a difference between an angel and a messenger, in that the messenger is the one who goes and turns back to bring repentance. The wicked angel who does not fulfill his mission in the place he was sent, only spoils there and does not bring repentance as he was sent, like the spies who spoiled, fell into evil and were punished and died in a plague. And a faithful messenger who walks in faith and brings repentance in faith, heals the plague of the wicked angel, like Caleb and Joshua, and through the recommendation of the Supreme Soul, sent by Hashem from the upper world to walk here in the land of defilement and return what it sends. And the wicked angel who does not fulfill his mission and spoils here and is not willing to return what it sends, will fall into evil and the punishments of hell. And a faithful messenger who straightens his path and walks in truth and faith and will be like a messenger who returns to his master to say, "I have done everything you commanded me," brings healing, and the sun of righteousness and healing has risen for him in its wings:
text.12_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: The shame and disgrace of a moral violator. There is a difference between morality and rebuke. Rebuke is the argument in words and evidence of reason, and morality is the chastisement of the soul's strength through the terror of punishments and disorder, and disgrace is the reversal of honor. Here, the one who observes rebuke and is satisfied with the teaching that is taught to him according to reason will be honored, for he is the one who deserves honor, and the one who does not observe rebuke will not be honored. However, the one who violates morality, who also does not fear the punishments of Hashem and completely breaks the yoke, will not only not be honored, but will find shame and disgrace, so that he will lose his wealth and become a disgrace to his honor:
text.12_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: Desire becomes, informs that the fool is not gullible because he knows the laws of wisdom, and if it were not for the desire that compelled him, he would turn away from evil according to the laws of wisdom, but because delight becomes a guarantee for the soul, although there is no good or beneficial in desire, there is a guarantee for the animal soul, and he cannot overcome his desire because of the guarantee, because he chooses the guarantee over the good and beneficial, and therefore it is abominable that fools turn away from evil, because they want the guarantee:
text.12_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: He who walks with the wise will become wise. He who walks with the wise will learn from their deeds and their wisdom and will act according to the laws of wisdom, and he who associates with the foolish will break, because he will learn from them to pursue lust, and they will teach him folly and he will not know the laws of wisdom at all. And he said, "He who walks with the wise will be like a shepherd like a fool, for with the wise he will not have a companion, he will only follow them, and with the fools he will have a companion, for wisdom is difficult to learn, not so with fools. Also, a shepherd is like a fool in the matter of shepherding and leading them, although he may imagine that he is a shepherd and leading them in the end, according to Be the tail to the lions and do not be the head to the foxes:
text.12_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: Sinners will be pursued by evil, says the punishment for sins does not come from Hashem, because evil does not come from Him, only the evil they have done will pursue them relentlessly until it overtakes them, in such a way that the punishment is continuous with the nature of evil itself, he is Satan, the angel of death, and it is not the serpent that kills, but sin that kills. However, the reward of the commandments will come from Hashem in particular and the righteous will be rewarded with good, through their reward even when the reward is not found in the nature of the commandment, Hashem will reward them with good in particular, apart from the good that is continuous with the nature of the commandments, and it is like the parable of a king who commanded his servants not to eat a certain type of fruit because it is the poison of death, and that they should eat a certain type of fruit because it is good for the health of the body. Those who eat the poison of death will receive their punishment from the deadly poison itself, and those who eat the good fruit, in addition to what they ate is good and beneficial, will receive a reward for having heard the king's commandments:
text.12_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: Good will bequeath to children of children, after saying that evil will pursue the sinner, and that Hashem will reward the righteous with good, he responds in contrast to what we sometimes see that the righteous have torment and the wicked are in peace, Azzah. If you see that the righteous has not received his reward, it is because Good will bequeath to children of children, and that Hashem will reward his reward to his sons and to his generations after him, (and so it is said in the Midrash that Hashem answered Moses, "If I had given the fathers their wages in their lifetime, what would they have bequeathed to their sons?"), and if you see the wicked standing in his wealth, know that the wicked will be strong against the righteous, and he only guards it, until the righteous comes and inherits it, and as the saying goes, "The wicked will prepare and the righteous will wear it."
text.12_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: A great man eats the head of a lion, and there is one who perishes without justice, referring to the previous one, he says, and if you ask, why doesn't Hashem pay the reward for justifying himself? And why did we see that the righteous man, whose world is nourished by his merit, and whose own merit is not nourished, as Rabbi Ben Dosa said about him, "The whole world is nourished because of my son Hanina, and my son Hanina, and a thornbush is enough for him, from the Lord's side, to the Lord's side?" He replies that we have seen in reality that abundance of food comes through the plowshares, that the people of the land are plowed up to remove the thorns and briers from there, that this is hard work that the landowners will do, and through them comes abundant food, and in 27 there are among the landowners who perish without justice, who die of hunger and have no food for them, even though all the food comes through their work, and likewise, even though abundant food comes through the righteous and their merit that remove the thorns that hinder abundance, in 27 he will be found among them who perish of hunger, and a thornbush is enough for him, and this is because Hashem knows that if he has wealth, his merit will not be enough to reduce abundance so much, just as if the landowners had bread, they would not have They will hire themselves to plow and to light the fire, and this is one of the wonders of leadership, and in the 27th century the stone was blameless in its actions and all its ways were just:
text.12_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: The darkness of his tribe hates his son. Whoever is the darkness of his tribe in his longing for his son, he hates him, because then he will not learn wisdom, because a wise son disciplines a father, and this is a sign that his death for his son, who cannot see in his grief, is more to him than the benefit of his son, and thus he loves A'A more than his son and hates his son, but he who loves his son and disciplines him, disciplines him every morning for his good in the end, and this is also an answer to the question of why Hashem brings torment upon the righteous and there is one who perishes without justice, because it is from His love for him, as it says, "For as a man disciplines his son, the Lord your Hashem disciplines you, and therefore he disciplines him in torment to be his discipline and to be his good in the end:
text.12_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: A righteous man eats to his heart's content. The righteous man does not eat to fill his stomach, only to satisfy his soul to the point of satisfaction is not permissible. It would also imply that he eats to satisfy his spiritual soul, as he only needs to revive his soul. However, wicked men who eat to fill their stomachs, their stomachs will always be lacking, because everything he has makes him crave more and there is no end to his cravings. This is also a response to the above, because Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa was truly satisfied with a basket of carob and did not want more, because he did not want only to satisfy his soul and the pleasures of this world were nothing in his eyes, because the main pleasure is the pleasure of the soul in the world to come:
text.13_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Women's Wisdom, the wise man will depict wisdom and cunning as two women, likening wisdom to a woman, because the soul that receives wisdom receives it from the higher, influential intellect, and the learned and educated souls are the good women, women of might, who listen to their higher husband, and he overflows upon them with his spirit to enlighten them with his truth, and the foolish and foolish women are the harlots under their husbands, walking in darkness without light into stubborn paths, the paths of death. And behold, the parts of wisdom are very many and have no end, and wisdom in its entirety, which gathers all the details of wisdom, is likened in a parable to a house built from many trees and stones and sand and lime and beams, and when they are joined together, a king's temple will be built, and he depicts that Women's wisdom built her house, wisdom in its entirety that built the sublime house, all the wise women, all the educated souls in the fear of Hashem, the prophets and the wise men, the educated men with good intellect, joined this building and built the house, and a scythe in her hands Destroy us, but the ulata that imposes limitations on all the laws of wisdom, this woman does not build, only destroys and annihilates, for the entire power of the ulata is only to destroy the laws of wisdom, which with wisdom will build a house, and she is engaged in destroying and not building, destroying and not establishing:
text.13_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: He who walks uprightly, I have already explained that the upright is one whose mind walks straight from his nature, and the boundary of the upright is the shortest line between two fixed points, and the upright is one who walks with his mind on the shortest and straightest path, and in particular falls on matters of understanding, because the human mind is made in such a way that if it does not incline to the side, it will always observe the truth, as the saying goes: "For Hashem made man upright, and they sought many accounts," that Hashem made every person who always attains the truth also through the paths of understanding who observes to know the truth and the false, and when he observes the Hashemhead, he will understand that there is a Hashem who creates and oversees, rewards and punishes, and so on. Likewise, one who inclines from uprightness and seeks many accounts and misleading philosophical strictures, departs from the short, straight line and goes astray from his path, and then he will come to heresy in all these corners, and this is why He who walks uprightly He who fears the Lord, for he will attain through common sense and through miracles the understanding that there is a Hashem. Judge and overseer, and fear Him because of His greatness and exaltation, His punishment and reward. Only those who have strayed from their ways and seek many and difficult accounts, straying from the straight line planted in the mind, and come to deny Hashem and despise Him, because they will deny the aspects of providence and the like:
text.13_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: In the mouth of the fool, the fool is the one who is satisfied with the laws of wisdom, and behold, the laws of wisdom have no miracles about them, and they do not know that by the whole human mind they are only from Hashem. And whoever is not proud and does not dare to exceed the limit of his mind to say that with his mind he can achieve everything, he will submit to the laws of wisdom given by Hashem and believe in them and will not dispute them. Only the fool is proud in his mouth. His mouth that speaks perverse things has turned the way of wisdom, as if his wisdom is wisdom. He is the cause of his pride, and his pride stands out from his mouth like a bud emerging from a tree. But the lips of the wise, the lips depict the external speech, and they will come to the wise when they speak words of wisdom with lips that hint at the knowledge of the Lord, who returned to them to know, that by believing in the laws of wisdom, they are to them as things known in knowledge, this will protect them from pride, because they will submit to the supreme wisdom and believe in it, because Hashem will give wisdom:
text.13_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: If there are no thousands of wild animals, the thousands are the oxen that are taught to plow and work the land, and when the ox is taught to plow, then it is called a master (from the word "learned" and "trained"), and it is placed in a manger to fatten it, because it will graze in the beauty of the grass and it gives grain with its strength, because abundant crops are produced by the strength of an ox, but if there are no thousands, if the oxen have not learned to work the land, then they are placed in a manger to fatten them and fatten them. Not only do they not produce more crops, they are lacking because they will eat the wild animals in a manger, and it is a parable and admonition on the above that a person should be like an ox to the yoke and like a donkey to the burden, and should be a master and learned to plow on the plot of wisdom and in the field of reason and knowledge, and then he will produce abundant crops, which are the crops of the soul and the fruit of the mind, because souls are not subject to labor, only the bodies are the animals that will teach them to work in the service of Hashem and in the upper garden of heaven and to produce abundant crops. The harvest is in the strength of a learned and patient ox, as the saying goes, "Our champions are suffered." But he who is not a champion and a scholar, who is the wretch who disputes wisdom and has not learned its ways, does not cultivate his land, but merely wastes the fruit of wisdom by standing at the manger to fatten and fatten up with the pleasures of the present, and besides being of no use, he also harms and destroys the sacred harvest.
text.13_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: A faithful witness will not lie and utter lies until he is a liar. There is a difference between a lie and a falsehood. A lie is a lie that is immediately obvious, and a lie seems true at first, and in the end it is revealed that it is a lie. A lie is a matter of judgment and does not exist. And here a false witness must utter lies, because he will not say anything that is a lie that is obvious to everyone, and he must lie, meaning he must say something that will not be recognized as false, and later it will be recognized that it was a lie, and this is called a lie. But a faithful witness will not lie, because he will speak the truth that remains true forever, as the saying goes: The tongue of truth will be established forever, and he will utter lies, because the blow comes upon the incomplete speech because he will not be able to complete his speech, and then it will be recognized that it was a lie, only to utter incomplete speech by deceit, and there is a saying for this, which testifies to the laws of wisdom and faith. He will not lie because his words will be established forever, because The laws of faith are the eternally existing truth, and the fool who testifies lies to dispute the laws of wisdom through his own efforts will produce falsehoods and misleading assertions that, after combination and examination, will not hold true and will be like a disappointment:
text.13_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: A fool seeks wisdom, but there is none, and knowledge is easy for a wise man. The fool is one who jokes about the laws of wisdom, because there are no examples for the laws of wisdom, only that they are accepted, and they must be accepted with humility and faith. However, the fool whose way of joking is to joke about wisdom, but will not joke about knowledge, which is about things known by example or through the senses. And here it is difficult for a wise man to come to the full knowledge, that is, to know the ways of wisdom with clear knowledge as he knows tangible things, because the ways of wisdom are only accepted. However, the wise man who, after researching the laws of wisdom, attains their meaning and derives something from something, if knowledge were easy, he will attain the laws of wisdom with clear knowledge and easily.
