He did not act proud and arrogant when he was in the king's court, but he went out to his brothers and became like one of them, and he saw and participated in their suffering, which was the teacher of his suffering and mercy. And his goodness, and it was known that the judgment he rendered against the Egyptian was from the side of righteousness and love of justice, and so was Joseph, who brought the burden of his brothers, before recounting his qualities, that he was a shepherd with them in the flock and was a servant of the sons of Bilhah, submitting to them, serving them, not boasting, not hating them, and that the burden of the burden was brought out of their love so that their father might rebuke them, And by his deeds it was known that his actions were pure and upright:
text.19_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: A hearing ear and a seeing eye, Hashem made both of them. These two senses, which are sight and hearing, are the most helpful in understanding, and the ear precedes the eye, so that first it receives through reception and hearing, and then it sees with its eyes and it becomes clear to it that it is true, because if it does not hear first, it will not understand what it has seen, and after hearing and seeing it will understand to know, as it says: "Hear and hear, but do not understand; and see and see, but do not know." And for this reason it is said that Hashem made these two senses, and so He made both of them because they are strange to one another, and man needs to use these two senses in honor of the Lord, so that he may hear the words of the Torah and wisdom from the mouths of the wise, and see and discern the works of Hashem from the perspective of observing creation, as it says: "For I will see your heavens, etc."
text.19_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not love a year, lest he who opens his eyes inherits seven loaves, simply put, in a parable, that the accumulation of wealth requires diligence and diligence, and the lover of sleep inherits, and the one who closes his eyes in sleep will not be satisfied with bread, and it was borrowed from the proverb that the word "suba" is not satisfied, but from the verse "open your eyes" it is clear that there is a proverb in it, because the act of opening the eyes of sight is not said about opening the eyes of sight, only about opening the eyes of the mind, and the sleep of the mind is found even when a person is awake and his physical eyes are open, if his spiritual soul sleeps and the slumber of matter has fallen upon it and his eyes of mind are closed from looking at Hashem, and it is drawn to the verse "hearing ear and seeing eye, Hashem made both of them", which in the verse "both of them" implies that the ear and the eye are twofold, as there is also a spiritual ear and an intellectual eye, about which the language of hearing came about understanding the mind, and hearing the voice of Hashem, and the language of seeing about seeing the mind, and my heart saw much Wisdom and knowledge, and Hashem made both, so that by seeing and hearing with the external sense, he would hear and see with the internal, intellectual sense. Just as it is not good if a person sleeps all the time and does not engage with the physical ear and eye, for then he will inherit and his body will not be satisfied with the bread of his bosom, so one must open his eyes, for the wakefulness is rooted in the spiritual eyes, for if he loves the sleep of the intellect, he will inherit and lose the property of the soul, which is the Torah and wisdom, but if he opens the eyes of his mind, then his soul will be satisfied with the bread of the law, according to which he will live eternal and spiritual life:
text.19_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: <b>The buyer will say, "It is bad," says the way of the world that a buyer who comes to buy something will say about the thing that it is bad, and after he is jealous and it is gone from the seller's possession, then he will boast about the object he bought. And this is because he first considered the price that is being asked for the object that he is so angry about, saying that it is bad in comparison to its price, but after he has already paid its price, then he will exalt himself in his eyes because he was jealous at a great price. And this is a parable, in contrast to the one who said, "Do not love sleep, because the Torah is purchased for a little sleep and a little pleasure." And although he initially said, when buying wisdom, he would say, "It is bad," because he would consider its value to be the price he would pay for it, which is the exertion of the body and the abandonment of sleep and pleasure. Later, when wisdom is purchased, he will boast, and explain his words.
text.19_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: There is gold, because this property that he acquired through his labor, which is the language of knowledge (the boundary of knowledge is that he will have clear knowledge from wisdom, as something he has achieved in tangible things, which was alluded to above in the phrase "a seeing eye and a hearing ear, Hashem made," as above, and by opening his eyes, he will attain the language of knowledge, meaning clear knowledge that this is knowledge, and that it will be familiar to him from the language and outward, as it is always explained that the language alludes to knowledge). Here, the language of knowledge is a very precious instrument that has no equal in the world, because if he bought and gave it for the price of gold and pearls, it would not be so precious, because there is a lot of gold in reality and there are many pearls, and they are many in the world, but the language of knowledge is a precious instrument that is not found at all:
text.19_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: "He took his garment because he was a foreigner - there is a difference between a foreigner and a foreigner:
text.19_Chapter, 15_Verse, 1_Comment: * The stranger will also be from this land when he is not from his family or his city,
text.19_Chapter, 15_Verse, 2_Comment: * And the foreigner is from another country.
text.19_Chapter, 15_Verse, 4_Comment: * If he is surety for a stranger, you shall take his garment, and shall not touch his body if he has none;
text.19_Chapter, 15_Verse, 5_Comment: * But if he is surety for a foreigner, let him be punished himself, for he is a greater sin,
text.19_Chapter, 15_Verse, 6_Comment: And he has a parable, which he alludes to in the word "foreigner," which according to the parable is a foreign prostitute, like "to keep from a foreign woman from her deceitful words," and according to the parable, he speaks here and there about false opinions and the opinions of the worshipers of the Almighty, that one who perceives false wisdom under the wisdom of the Torah and morality is a prostitute with a foreign people, and here he alludes to it in the name of "guarantee," because the guarantor accepts the responsibility of the borrower, and likewise he accepts the responsibility of the external opinion with which he prostitutes himself, to drive away any creditor from her in difficulties and difficulties:
text.19_Chapter, 15_Verse, 7_Comment: * And if a surety is for a stranger, meaning knowledge that is outside the wisdom of the Torah and its roots (but in 27 it is not foreign because it contains knowledge of a foreigner and the worship of a foreigner), he shall take from him his garment and the splendid garment and the golden earrings that Israel wore on Mount Horeb,
text.19_Chapter, 15_Verse, 8_Comment: * But the surety for a foreigner, who is a worshiper of a foreign god and a foreigner, shall be cut off from the assembly of the Lord and from his portion with the foreigner who sold himself as a surety for a pledge, and therefore this verse comes again to remind us <small>(27:13)</small>:
text.19_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: A man is a false bread. According to the parable, whoever eats false bread, meaning bread that comes through theft, deceit, fraud, and the like, at first it seems to him that he is a false bread, because it came to him without effort, but later his mouth will be filled with gravel and arrows, because he will be punished by the judges or by Heaven, and according to the parable, continuing upwards, the one who holds onto external opinions, heresy, and idolatry will desire to have food for his soul's desires. Here is this bread that feeds his spiritual soul, which is false bread from false opinions. At first it seems to him that he is a false bread, as the saying goes, "For the sifter is filled with the lips of a stranger," but later his mouth will be filled with gravel and arrows, thorns, and the death of the soul, and his mouth alludes to the wisdom of the Lord, which is full of false wisdom, which are arrows for the spiritual soul:
text.19_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Thoughts in counsel are prepared and in stratagems make war, we have already explained this above (12:14) that all the many thoughts that a person thinks about the possible sides are called thoughts, and they are like a flowing stream of water, and when he chooses one of the possible parts to do according to the purpose, it is called counsel, and then there is a foundation and basis for the thoughts and they no longer float on the wings of the wind, and alas Thoughts in counsel are prepared, and one counsel is needed, indeed in war, stratagems are needed, which is the combination of many counsels, because even the fighter against him has thirteen counsels, and there we explained that therefore in war it is good to have many counsellors so that they can advise on several counsels on all the sides that the enemy will turn, and we have already explained above (15:22) that without a secret and with many counsellors, thoughts will arise, because if they do not keep counsel secret, it will not come to the purpose, and then there is also a need for many counsellors so that they can also advise on the manner That the advice would be spoiled by revealing the secret, and therefore he said here:
text.19_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: A secret exile goes astray and his lips entice you, do not interfere, because after the advice is barren and he will be spoiled by revealing the secret, you must be very careful of those who are accustomed to revealing the secret, and they are three, a] someone who is by nature a secret exile and is not a faithful spirit, b] someone who is a gossip-walker, whose way is to reveal a secret through his gossip, c] <his lips entice you, who speaks deceitful words with his lips and out of his habit of talking a lot will not keep his secrets from his enticement, With all these you must not interfere, because your advice will be spoiled by them:
text.19_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Cursing his father and mother, you will be a light in the dark. The one who curses his father and mother who gave birth to him will be depicted in two ways, a] A person whose life is a burden on him and thinks in his heart that the evils in the world outweigh the good (as the teacher who was a true scholar of some sects brought) and therefore the reality is bad, and his absence is better for him, Cursing his father and mother who were his grandfather to his reality in this bad life, and about him it was said That his light was dimmed in the dark, for a person's light is his fortune and success that shines on his head, and even those whose light is dim or extinguished still have some light, like someone whose light was dimmed at night and sees by the light of the moon, and he is the hope that is in the heart of every person, but this person dimmed his light and remains in the dark without the light of hope and hope at all, as the saying goes: The lamp of the wicked is dimmed, and the wicked in darkness will die, and there is another way that he curses his father and mother for the inheritance he desires They will die first so that he can inherit their inheritance quickly, and therefore the lives of his children will be difficult for him, and Hashem forbid.
text.19_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: An inheritance that is initially and subsequently seized will not be blessed, because there is no blessing in both inheritance and discovery, as the Sages say, because only property that comes through effort, not by chance, will not be blessed, and when the inheritance comes before the time, which is like a discovery, it will not be blessed on two counts, a) because it is an inheritance, b) because it is initially and subsequently seized, and therefore its later will not be blessed, and in this case he will not have success in his inheritance:
text.19_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: (22-23) Do not say, "I paid you a bad price," etc. A stone and a stone are an abomination to the Lord, etc. If a person has done you wrong in trade, who has deceived you and sold you counterfeit goods, Do not say, "Pay him with counterfeit money as he did, for in this your loss will be repaid." And "I paid him a bad price," do not say so, but Hope in the Lord and he will save you and fill your deficiency, and bring back his own. If he sold to you with a false weight by a stone and a stone, and you wish to sell him back with deceitful scales, know that a stone and a stone are an abomination to the Lord, and making restitution with deceitful scales is also not good, because the Lord warned the Lord in all ways, and as the saying goes, so above a stone And a stone, wherever it is, is an abomination to the Lord, both of them:
text.19_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: What is the path of a man, I have already explained (above 16:9) because although the choice to choose which path to take is in the hand of the person to the right or to the left, 27 since the movement of the feet is from the Lord and His power, He can hinder him from walking on the path he has chosen (as the saying goes: A man's heart considers his way and the Lord prepares his steps), and so how can a person understand his path, for although it seems to him that his path is good and he agrees with the path of goodness according to his understanding, it is useless, that it depends in vain on the hand of the Lord who completes the action, and this will often be ignored by the person, who will sometimes see a delay in his path that will seem to him to be for the worse, and in truth, what is the Lord's path, and what will a person understand whose understanding is short to achieve:
text.19_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: A man's snare for a holy vow, among the snare traps that a man can be trapped in, is a transgression of the lips, and as the saying goes, a transgression of the lips is a bad snare, and a man must guard his lips from setting a snare for him, and one of the snare traps is if he hastily dedicates without considering carefully, and likewise a man who is hasty in his vows and frequently vows, will easily stumble, whether in a dedication he will transgress, or in a vow he will delay it:
text.19_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: (22-27) The wicked are scattered etc. The lamp of Hashem, flesh and blood, even the wisest if he wants to stand on the truth, and find out whether the wicked have committed any sin or not, he uses 10 tricks, by scattering the wicked and separating them and placing each in a special prison, and there he imposes upon them the manner which was a kind of torture in which they would torture the sinner to confess for his deeds, in which they would roll a mat over his body and due to the greatness of the pain he would be forced to confess, and since it could be that out of the torment he would confess to something false, he would scatter the suspected wicked 21 in a special prison, and torture them by the manner he responded to them 25 until he stands on the truth, but Hashem is against these tricks, because the soul of man is the lamp of Hashem that will shine upon him. To know by what means the secrets of darkness, with this lamp all the chambers of the belly are free to know all the hidden things, as the saying goes: "Who will testify against me? The soul of a man will testify against him."
text.19_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: "Mercy and truth have established a king, and his throne is established by mercy - His words are based on the words of his father (Psalms 66:8): Mercy and truth shall sustain him:
text.19_Chapter, 27_Verse, 1_Comment: * The truth is what will be done according to the law,
text.19_Chapter, 27_Verse, 2_Comment: * And kindness is what will be done from kindness,
text.19_Chapter, 27_Verse, 4_Comment: * When the king acts only in accordance with the measure of truth, he is not properly guarded, lest he be harmed by the bitterness of his soul, upon whom the wrath of justice has poured out; but if he sometimes yields to kindness, the people will love him.
text.19_Chapter, 27_Verse, 5_Comment: * And so, if he acts only with kindness, the fear of judgment will not fall upon them, and even in this he will not be safe,
text.19_Chapter, 27_Verse, 6_Comment: But kindness and truth - if he practices both, they will create a king, to the point where he does not need any other guardian over him besides them.
text.19_Chapter, 27_Verse, 7_Comment: And also in leadership, which is attributed to the chair, although the essence of the chair is to establish the trial, in any case you will not stand trial alone, and you must also sometimes behave with kindness, and this will help the chair to survive.
text.19_Chapter, 27_Verse, 8_Comment: And as an example, the word of Isaiah, (Isaiah 9:6): to prepare it and for a feast, in justice and righteousness, Isa.
text.19_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: (29-30) The glory of young men is their strength, etc. Friendship of wounds, etc. It will be said, "Here is the strength of the body, and whoever preserves this strength and does not waste it only at the right time and with the right person as is appropriate, will preserve his strength in his youth, and old age will not come upon him before the time. But the one who is eager for fornication will lose his strength in his youth, and old age will come upon him, and if he exposes himself to more than is appropriate, external wounds and internal pains will come upon him. And here is the strength of young men that is preserved in them, and also the splendor of old men is the return, for old age that comes before time is not elegant, only if it is accompanied by gray hair, which is the old age that comes from the return and a long life, but on the contrary, "beautify with evil," who beautifies and melts the strength of his body through evil, which is fornication and the shedding of blood. The seed, which is called bad, as in the verse, "And when the firstborn of Judah was evil in the sight of the Lord, a band of wounds will come upon him from outside, for the bands and wounds together are dangerous, as in the verse of Isaiah 1. And also strikings of the abdominal cavity will come upon him, so that the intestines and the food and digestive organs will be spoiled:
text.20_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: The king's heart is channels of water in the hand of Hashem. Although the heart of an individual is under his own control and the choice is in his hands, this is not so with the heart of a king. Since the welfare of the community depends upon his choice, and if he chooses an evil path he will destroy many and mighty people, his communal heart is therefore in the hand of Hashem, and in matters concerning the community he is deprived of free choice.
text.20_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: He compares it to channels of water. Water descending from lofty mountains and many springs gathers into a rushing stream. People therefore endeavor to dig a channel for it, divert it to places where it is needed, direct it, and turn it away from places where it is unnecessary—and certainly from places where it would cause harm or flooding—since this is a public necessity.
text.20_Chapter, 0_Verse, 2_Comment: So too is the king's heart. Since the affairs of the community branch out from his actions—whether toward punishment or kindness, war or peace—they are in the hand of Hashem, and He inclines them according to His will in governing the community. If the people merit it, He inclines the king toward good, and conversely if they do not. He does not wait to alter the completed act according to His will; rather, He inclines the heart's initial tendency according to His will, just as channels of water are diverted where they first branch off.
text.20_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Every way of a man is upright in his own eyes, but Hashem weighs hearts. Above (16:2) it says, All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, but Hashem weighs spirits. “Pure” is the opposite of containing dross, while “upright” is the opposite of crooked. Uprightness pertains to understanding, and the straight path is the shortest route between two given points. For example, the path of humility, generosity, and mercy is the straight path, though at times one must act oppositely—with pride or cruelty toward the enemies of Hashem. A person may err in this because of the inclination of his heart and imagine that his conduct is upright because his heart and choice incline toward it. But Hashem weighs hearts: He knows the heart's disposition and weighs its circuits. There is also one who does not err and proceeds uprightly, yet is not pure—that is, he acts for ulterior motives. This depends upon the spirit that raises its images upon the heart, for the spirit is deeper than the heart. Therefore it says there, “but Hashem weighs spirits.”
text.20_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: To practice righteousness and justice is more desirable to Hashem than a sacrifice. People thought that bringing sacrifices was in itself a service pleasing to Hashem, and they therefore exerted themselves and multiplied their offerings. The prophets repeatedly rebuked this view and demonstrated that sacrifices are not ends in themselves but means. Through them a person displays submission, showing that he is prepared to sacrifice himself, surrender his life for the sanctity of Hashem, and obey His words and commandments concerning justice and righteousness, which encompass the commandments between man and his fellow and between man and God. That is the purpose. Therefore, practicing righteousness and justice is more desirable than a sacrifice, since the sacrifice is merely a means toward them, and the end is preferable to the means.
text.20_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: This also explains the preceding statement, Every way of a man is upright in his own eyes... A man who brings many sacrifices imagines that he has fulfilled the commandments of Hashem, but in truth this is not the straight path, which is the shortest path. It is a long route to the city that is justice and righteousness. The shorter path is to practice justice and righteousness themselves, without the circuitous route of sacrifices, for the act itself is not what is desired, but the heart, thought, and intention. Concerning this it says, but Hashem weighs hearts.
text.20_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Haughty eyes and a broad heart. “Haughty eyes” refers to pride in theoretical intellect: a person imagines that he comprehends everything and renders decisive judgment on matters beyond human intelligence and on metaphysical matters, thereby arriving at heresy and denial of God. “A broad heart” means that his heart desires without limit and his appetites have no end. These two are the tillage of the wicked—sin. Tillage means plowing a field to uproot thorns and remove everything that obstructs the seed's growth. The wicked sow sin in the furrows of their hearts, but the seed might fail to grow if restrained either by theoretical or practical intellect. Haughty eyes are the tillage that prevents theoretical intellect from restraining him through fear of Hashem and true understanding of Him; a broad heart is the tillage that prevents practical intellect from restraining him, because the heart's appetite drives him toward sin.
text.20_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: The plans of the diligent surely lead to abundance. The diligent person is swift in his actions, yet a condition of true diligence is thought and consultation: he must not act hastily, but first consider every possibility and determine the best means and the one most likely to yield profit. Although this delays his action, he will always gain abundance from it, for he thereby chooses the best means to the end. But everyone who hastens—who presses the moment and the matter, acting immediately without reflection or thought—surely comes to want. Swiftness, though good in action, is not good in deliberation, which first requires delay and patience.
text.20_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: One who acquires treasures through a lying tongue—by false testimony, forged documents, counterfeit coins, and the like—even though he thereby acquires treasures, they are vanity in themselves, having no substance. They are driven away and do not endure, for the wind will scatter them; and those treasures are seekers of death, because when his forgery becomes known he will incur death.
text.20_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: The robbery of the wicked terrifies them. It has already said, “What the wicked fears will come upon him.” Here it explains that the devastation and ruin destined to befall them frighten them, for their heart foretells what is coming upon them because they refuse to practice justice, practicing only robbery and murder. This may refer back to the statement that acquiring treasures through a lying tongue is a driven vapor seeking death: through this, devastation will terrify them and they will stumble into it. “Robbery” may also mean their own robbing; because they rob others, they become afraid, for transgression casts fear upon the one who commits it.
text.20_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Twisted is the way of a man who is alien. This refers back to the preceding verse and explains why the robbery of the wicked terrifies them: they refuse to practice justice, and the way of man is twisted and alien to them. Man was naturally founded to follow the way of justice, not to rob or commit violence, and to love truth and righteousness, through which society can endure. But to these wicked people—and likewise to the liars just mentioned—the way of man implanted in his nature is twisted and alien. They follow the reverse of man's natural path, moving from justice toward robbery and from truth toward falsehood; the straight path is alien to them. Therefore devastation terrifies them, for all human society opposes those wicked people whose way is reversed and alien. But the pure person's conduct is upright. “Pure” means free of dross and refers to cleanliness from appetites in practical intellect; “upright” pertains to theoretical intellect. Purity belongs to wisdom and uprightness to understanding. One who is not pure in his traits and violates the laws of wisdom cannot be upright, for appetite diverts him from the straight road to its opposite. Because his way is alien through appetite, it becomes twisted; but if he is pure, he will proceed uprightly, because understanding naturally accords with uprightness.
text.20_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: It is better to dwell... Although it is good to dwell in a house of companionship—that is, a house containing a group of friends and companions—and not good to dwell alone, one who has a contentious wife is better off not dwelling in a house of companionship. She will quarrel with his friends until they become his enemies, stir up disputes among them, or disgrace him before them. Therefore it is better to dwell on a corner of the roof, separated from his companions. Verse 19 says that it is better to dwell in a desert land than with a contentious and angry woman. If she is also prone to anger, even dwelling on a corner of the roof in the city is not good, and he must flee from her to the desert. This verse is repeated below (25:24) and will be explained there.
text.20_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: The soul of the wicked desires evil; his fellow finds no favor in his eyes. Although the philosopher explained that love is found among equals, so that love should seemingly be found among the wicked, the Sage explains that the wicked man's fellow finds no favor in his eyes because the soul of the wicked desires evil. This is so for two reasons. First, every wicked person has a tendency toward a different evil—one commits adultery, another steals, and so forth—so they are not equal in their desires. Second, even the evil he shares with his fellow is not truly willed by him, for he knows that it is rejected by rational will and choice; he merely desires the evil, and his appetite compels him toward it. He knows that it is evil and disgraceful, and therefore his wicked companion is contemptible in his eyes, since he knows him to be ruled by appetite and evil.
text.20_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: When the scoffer is punished, the simple person becomes wise; and when the wise person gains insight, he acquires knowledge. Above (19:25) it says, “Strike a scoffer and the simple person will become shrewd; reprove one who understands and he will understand knowledge.” There is a difference between shrewdness and wisdom. Through wisdom one accepts the laws of wisdom in order to conduct himself by them, whereas shrewdness is a human faculty. If the scoffer is struck, the simple person becomes shrewd and learns stratagems to protect himself. But when the scoffer is punished—through judicial or Heavenly punishment, when it is evident that the punishment comes because of the sin—then the simple person becomes wise, accepting the laws of wisdom because he understands that reward and punishment exist and that the laws of wisdom come from God. The wise person, meanwhile, has accepted the laws of wisdom, but those laws are not known with the clarity of sensory perception, which is called knowledge. When the wise person applies insight to the scoffer's punishments and sees how Hashem punished measure for measure one who mocked the laws of wisdom—something grasped through the intellect, which can apprehend matters of wisdom—then he acquires knowledge and knows the ways of wisdom with the clarity of sensory knowledge.
text.20_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: The righteous person considers the house of the wicked. Even when the house of the wicked is firmly established in tranquility—as implied by calling it a “house” of the wicked—the righteous person applies insight and contemplates the reason: this prosperity is in order to overturn the wicked toward evil, for through it they increase their wrongdoing. Had they been punished immediately, they would have feared to do evil. It also means that their tranquility hastens their punishment, as it is written, He repays those who hate Him to their face, to destroy them (Deuteronomy 7:10). Their prosperity thus brings evil upon them, in accordance with the many explanations given for the success of the wicked, all of which serve to hasten their calamity and complete their punishment.
text.20_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: One who seals his ear against the cry of the poor. There is a difference between the dal and the rash. The dal has been reduced from his possessions, generally through oppression and violence, and he cries out to the judges to rescue the oppressed from his oppressors. A judge who seals his ear and does not save him though it is within his power will be punished by himself being oppressed: he too will call and not be answered. This will occur either through Heavenly judgment, measure for measure, or through earthly judgment: just as he did not administer justice, he will be crushed at the gate with no one to save him.
text.20_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: A gift in secret subdues anger, but a bribe in the bosom arouses fierce wrath. Money given in secret is sometimes for good and sometimes for evil. If it is a gift in secret—for “gift” denotes something given without receiving anything in return, such as money given to a poor person or a gift given to officials and wealthy people—it subdues anger: a charitable gift subdues anger Above, while a gift to a judge or official subdues anger below. But money secretly given to bring about perversion of law and distortion of justice is called a bribe, placed in the bosom of the judge. This arouses fierce wrath, whether Above or below, when the matter becomes known to the king of the land.
text.20_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Practicing justice is joy to the righteous, but ruin to workers of iniquity. A righteous person is one who conducts himself according to the laws of righteousness, while workers of iniquity use force to oppress and rob, the opposite of righteousness. When Hashem extends the line of justice and judges according to deeds, or when earthly judges administer justice below, the righteous person rejoices because he desires justice and knows that he will be vindicated when judged, whereas judgment will be ruin to the workers of iniquity.
text.20_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: A man who strays from the path of intellect will rest in the congregation of the shades. Intellect differs from wisdom, understanding, and the other faculties of the soul. It is the acute power found in man by which he apprehends Divinity, spiritual matters, and wonders—things that understanding cannot grasp through syllogisms and proofs, nor knowledge through recognition by the senses. Through this power he apprehends Providence and all beliefs concerning Divinity. The holy spirit generally accompanies it, and it is then called “good intellect,” as it says, “You gave Your good spirit to give them understanding.” A man who strays from the path of intellect errs concerning Divine beliefs, denying Providence, Hashem's knowledge, His governance, and His wonders. These are the heretics who have no share in the World to Come and no remedy; he will rest in the congregation of the shades, for he will descend to Gehinnom.
text.20_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: A man of want. One who loves merriment and wishes always to rejoice is a man of want, because joy does not last. Anything that gladdens him when he first attains it will no longer gladden him after he has seen or possessed it for several days. He will then wish to see another new thing to gladden him and will always feel lacking. But one who loves wine and oil, drinking and anointing his body with luxuries, will not become wealthy, because he will consume his money. Beyond being a man of want, he will also exhaust his wealth, whereas it is possible for one who merely loves merriment not to consume his money.
text.20_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: The wicked is a ransom for the righteous. A substitute is of the same kind as the liability, as in life for life, whereas a ransom need not be of the same kind and may even be monetary and provide atonement. When Hashem judges the world, He judges between the righteous and the wicked, and the one who emerges wicked in the judgment atones through his death for the righteous. “Righteous” and “wicked” are relative designations in that particular case; even if the righteous person might otherwise have been found guilty, he is vindicated relative to the wicked, who becomes his ransom. The traitor is in place of the upright. Uprightness is not relative: the upright person is inherently upright and requires no ransom or atonement. Yet in worldly affairs it can happen that the traitor seeks to kill the upright, but he himself dies in their place—life for life—and they are saved, as it says, “The righteousness of the upright will save them, while traitors will be trapped in their own destruction.”
text.20_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: It is better to dwell in a desert land than with a contentious and angry woman. It already said above that it is better to dwell on a corner of the roof than with a contentious woman. If she is not prone to anger but merely stirs up disputes with her neighbors and household members, he must distance himself from company and live with her on a corner of the roof, where she will find no one with whom to quarrel. But if she is also prone to anger, she will anger him even there, and he must flee from her to the desert.
text.20_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: A precious treasure and oil are in the dwelling of the wise. According to the parable, the wise person does not lose his store and treasure but guards it, so that a precious treasure, such as gold and spices, and fine oil, which is also kept in a treasury—as it says, “He showed them the gold and the fine oil in his treasuries”—remain in his dwelling. But a foolish man swallows it up and destroys the treasure. In the application, regarding physical treasure and oil, the wise person devises means for the treasure always to remain in his dwelling: he gives it in charity to the poor and practices lovingkindness with it, and thus it remains his forever. As the Sages said, “My ancestors stored below, but I stored Above; my ancestors stored where a hand can reach it...” The foolish person who keeps it for himself swallows it up, for in the end strangers inherit his wealth and nothing remains in his hand after death. The verse is also a metaphor for precious spiritual treasure and oil: the soul's virtues and the sacred anointing oil, symbolizing the holy spirit and intellectual attainment, remain in the dwelling of the wise person, who follows the laws of wisdom. But the fool, who departs from those laws because of his appetite, swallows up and destroys the treasure. The next verse explains what the treasure and oil are.
text.20_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: One who pursues righteousness and kindness. The wise person pursues righteousness, meaning commandments between man and God, and kindness, meaning acts of lovingkindness between man and his fellow. Through kindness, his precious physical treasure and oil remain his; through righteousness, his precious spiritual treasure and oil remain his. Consequently, after he enters the world of recompense, there he will find life—eternal life—righteousness from Above, which I define as the boundless good Hashem performs according to His great righteousness, and honor, the soul's eternal happiness, which Scripture calls honor: the true future reward, when the righteous sit with their crowns upon their heads.
text.20_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: A wise man ascended a city of warriors... One who guards his mouth and tongue... According to the parable, it depicts one wise man conquering a city of warriors and the fortress in which they trusted, as it says, Wisdom strengthens the wise man more than ten rulers who were in the city (Ecclesiastes 7:19).
text.20_Chapter, 21_Verse, 2_Comment: * Although it was a city filled with people, a single wise man conquered it;
text.20_Chapter, 21_Verse, 4_Comment: * although the city was situated on a mountain and therefore difficult to conquer, as indicated by a wise man ascended;
text.20_Chapter, 21_Verse, 5_Comment: * and although they possessed a mighty tower in which they trusted, as indicated by and brought down the strength of its confidence.
text.20_Chapter, 21_Verse, 6_Comment: In the application, it speaks of the soul's battle.
text.20_Chapter, 21_Verse, 7_Comment: He already used this parable in Ecclesiastes: There was a small city with few men in it (Ecclesiastes 9:14), where he spoke of the battle waged by the evil inclination and appetite against the soul:
text.20_Chapter, 21_Verse, 8_Comment: * He depicts the soul as dwelling in a city, and it is a small city with few men in it, because the soul's powers are few;
text.20_Chapter, 21_Verse, 9_Comment: * the attacker who comes from outside to conquer it is a great king, and he builds great siegeworks, because the powers of the flesh are many and all of nature and the senses assist them;
text.20_Chapter, 21_Verse, 10_Comment: * only a poor wise man saved the city through his wisdom (Ecclesiastes 9:15). This means that wisdom saves the soul so that the foolish old king does not conquer it.
text.20_Chapter, 21_Verse, 11_Comment: Here, however, he presents the foolish prince and his warriors as being inside, while the wise man comes and conquers the city.
text.20_Chapter, 21_Verse, 12_Comment: This battle is perpetual, and each side has a fortified city. In truth, however, the first is a small city and the second a city of warriors. The powers of the soul and intellect are few; they are strangers in this world and have few helpers. The powers of matter, by contrast, are mighty and are inhabitants of this world, dwelling on a fortified mountain. Nevertheless, one who conducts himself according to the laws of wisdom will conquer the city, compel the children of the flesh and the powers of appetite to obey him, and dispossess them with the sword of wisdom and the shield of understanding, knowledge, and fear of Hashem. The surging forces of appetite will not stand before him.
text.20_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: There is, however, a condition: he must then guard against the conquered forces returning to conquer the city. He does this by guarding his mouth and tongue, which are the fortress of wisdom—the speaking soul—for through them the enemies enter to besiege the soul. This refers both to guarding speech in its literal sense and to the fact that the mouth alludes to the speech of wisdom, while the tongue alludes to the speech of understanding; he must guard them so that they do not depart from the paths of wisdom and understanding. In this way he guards his spiritual soul from troubles, preventing her constantly warring enemies from besieging her when her wall is torn down and her protection exposed.
text.20_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: Presumptuous, arrogant scoffer is his name. The presumptuous person knowingly disputes the laws of wisdom, argues against the laws of wisdom and faith, denies Providence and reward and punishment, and commits sins defiantly. As long as he is not arrogant, however, he is not yet a scoffer, for he argues with claims and proofs rather than mockery, and if refuted he will be silent. But if he is arrogant, he pays no attention to reasons or proofs at all and merely mocks the wise and the faithful. He then acts with overflowing presumption. “Overflowing” means crossing a boundary: he performs evil deeds for which he has no need and which oppose the nature of the soul, solely because his presumption overflows. His willfulness crosses the human boundary, leading him to acts contrary to human nature in general.
text.20_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: The desire of the lazy man kills him... All day long he desires desire. A person is lazy about doing something that he considers unimportant and unnecessary. Do not think that the lazy man neglects work because he has no desires and considers worldly things trivial, and therefore will not labor to obtain them. The opposite is true: his desire is greater than that of one who is not lazy, for one who has bread in his basket is not like one who does not. Rather, he lacks dominion over his hands and the bodily instruments of action, which refuse to obey the ruling power of the soul. Therefore his desire kills him, because his hands, which could save him from death by working so that he may obtain what he desires, refuse to obey him. It adds that all day long he desires desire: while the diligent person works all day and desires only at night when free from his occupation, the lazy man desires all day and does nothing. The verse then praises the righteous person, who gives charity to the lazy man and does not withhold. No one has compassion on this lazy man; even if he dies of hunger, people do not pity him, saying that he could work. But the righteous person has mercy on him, for he is like a sick man unable to work, since his hands are slack and do not obey him. He therefore gives him charity and has mercy upon his affliction.
text.20_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination; how much more when he brings it with an evil scheme. A sacrifice brought by the wicked is an abomination even if he brings it wholeheartedly, so long as he remains wicked—that is, he has not repented of his earlier wickedness. It resembles an enemy of the king bringing him a gift: the gift is abominable in the king's eyes even though the enemy brings it wholeheartedly, because the giver is hated by him.
text.20_Chapter, 26_Verse, 1_Comment: All the more is this so if he brings it with an evil scheme. An evil scheme means the mind's deep absorption in thoughts of sin. Even while bringing the sacrifice, his intention is toward immorality and sinful counsel. Beyond not being accepted because of the person who brings it, it is not accepted because of the offering itself, whose purpose is evil.
text.20_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: A false witness will perish... A wicked man hardens his face. It has already said several times, “One who breathes lies will not escape” and “One who breathes lies will perish,” which we explained in each place according to its context. Here it speaks of the tradition transmitted from generation to generation back to the first foundation of Israel regarding commandments, beliefs, and opinions. If a person testifies to true matters that his ear heard and that were received from the ancient mountains, they will endure forever. Sometimes, however, a man testifies about something he did not hear and seeks to bequeath a false tradition, whether concerning commandments, beliefs, or opinions. Therefore it says, A false witness will perish, for it is part of Hashem's Providence that truth endures while falsehood vanishes like smoke. But a man who listens—whose statement is something he heard through tradition—will speak forever, and his tradition will endure eternally. At times a wicked man hardens his face to deny the received tradition, for in every generation deniers have arisen to reject tradition because it is not apprehended independently but received from the fathers. The upright man, however, understands his way. As explained, the upright person is one who is naturally straight. The term is used regarding the path of understanding: he derives one thing from another with sound intellect, and his character traits are also upright. Through the breadth of his understanding he comprehends the path of truth and can prevail over the deniers by the power of his upright understanding.
text.20_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: There is no wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel against Hashem. A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory belongs to Hashem. Although choice was given to man, and in private matters he succeeds through preparation and diligence, this is not so in matters decreed by Hashem and fixed by Providence, such as general matters affecting an entire people, nation, or state. There a person must indeed do his part and make natural preparations—as in warfare, a public matter, where he must prepare military tactics, horses, and chariots—yet the counsel of Hashem will stand and human effort will not avail. Naturally, a person succeeds either through wisdom, by receiving from his teachers the proper modes of conduct; through understanding, by contemplating independently, deriving one thing from another, and examining matters to which truth and falsehood apply; or through counsel, which comes from perfection of the imaginative and estimating faculty, through which future developments become known to him—how an event will occur and how he should act wisely. Nevertheless, none of these avail against Hashem, meaning in matters decreed and determined by Him. The verse proves this: although a horse is prepared for the day of battle—the natural means by which one succeeds in war—nevertheless victory belongs to Hashem. Since war is a public matter through which a people either falls or rises, victory comes through Providence, and natural means do not determine it.
text.21_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: A good name is preferable to great wealth. Possessions of wealth are imagined acquisitions; they do not adhere to a person or become part of him, and suddenly wealth is lost and vanishes through misfortune. But the name he acquires through his good deeds becomes part of his soul and never separates from him. The purpose of wealth beyond one's needs is to attain honor and have one's words obeyed, and a man of good name attains this more effectively. Great wealth also requires guarding and robs its owner of sleep. Not so a good name. Good favor is better than silver and gold. Silver and gold possess no intrinsic superiority; their value is conventional, assigned to them by agreement above other metals. Good favor is analogous: a person finds favor in the eyes of others by their agreement, yet this is better for him than silver and gold, because the favor is found in him personally rather than in something external. Moreover, what he could obtain from a ruler or official by giving silver and gold he can obtain more effectively by finding favor. A name depends upon deeds, while favor depends upon graciousness, as it says, “I know you by name, and you have also found favor in My eyes.” Correspondingly, wealth is his external possession, and a name—which is his own intrinsic acquisition—is preferable to it; favor, which is not a possession but is found in the eyes of another, is better than silver and gold received from others.
text.21_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: The rich and the poor meet; Hashem is the Maker of them all. This gives the reason that a good name is preferable to great wealth, for wealth is not a permanent possession. The rich and the poor meet. It depicts the rich and poor as not remaining in fixed positions, one standing on the side of wealth and the other on the side of poverty so that they never meet. Rather, they constantly ascend and descend a ladder, until the rich and the poor meet one another. At first, when the rich man ascended to the top of the ladder, the poor man descended from it and they met on the way. Later, when the poor man rises, the rich man has reached the top and begins to descend, for fortune is a wheel that turns in the world; the poor man, having reached the bottom, begins to rise, and they meet again. As the Sages said, the Holy One, blessed is He, makes ladders in heaven, impoverishing one and enriching another. Therefore it says, Hashem is the Maker of them all: Hashem continually makes people rich and poor, for so He established the governance of the world. The rich man will therefore ultimately descend and lose his wealth, while a good name, which never ends, is better than wealth.
text.21_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: The shrewd man sees evil and hides. The shrewd person is not necessarily wise in the laws of wisdom, but shrewdness has taught him to understand the path on which he travels and determine whether it contains any loss, as it says, “The wisdom of the shrewd is to understand his way.” He weighs and assesses whether evil may befall him in the future. Thus he sees evil—he perceives impending evil—and also hides, refusing to follow a path whose end is evil, as it says, “There is a way that seems upright before a man...” But the simple, the opposite of the shrewd, not only fail to look ahead and beware of future evil; they even pass through present evil. Therefore they are punished: beyond suffering the evil itself, they receive punishment for failing to take precautions when they should have done so.
text.21_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: The consequence of humility is fear of Hashem, wealth, honor, and life. The root of humility branches from comprehending the greatness of the Creator of the beginning, His immense power, and the existence He created, until a person realizes that he is as nothing before even some of His creatures. Even if he attains kingship, wisdom, might, and every virtue in this world, he knows that he is like a tiny ant before the great king who stands over him, and as nothing before the least of His angels. This thought ultimately brings fear of Hashem into his heart, so that he fears acting against His will. As the Rema writes: “I have set Hashem before me always... A person's conduct when sitting... is not the same... all the more so when he takes to heart that the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed is He, stands over him and sees his deeds...” One who inherits humility will inherit wealth and honor, for Hashem will elevate him measure for measure; and he will inherit life—both eternal life, because he guards against evil, and life in this world through Hashem's Providence. This is the opposite of the arrogant person, who removes fear of Hashem from before him and whose ways are ways of death.
text.21_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked. The straight path in the soul's conduct is the middle way. A path that deviates from the mean toward either the extreme of excess or the extreme of deficiency is a crooked path, turned away from the straight. He takes a parable from nature: temperate air is balanced and healthy for the body, but air tending to the extreme of heat burns the blood as redness, dryness, and fire prevail; this he calls snares, meaning burning coals. Air tending toward the extreme of deficiency allows cold to prevail and congeal the blood; this he calls thorns, an illness caused by excessive cold. Both kill the body. So too in the soul's conduct: at the extreme of excess a burning fire inflames him, while at the extreme of deficiency cold and weakness freeze him. Therefore one who guards his soul distances himself from the extremes and follows the straight, intermediate path.
text.21_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Train a child according to his way. The verse commands two things. First, train the child: accustom him from youth to perfection in beliefs, deeds, and character traits. A habit acquired in youth produces a powerful imprint and a lasting impression on the soul that will not depart even in old age. By contrast, education begun in adulthood does not produce a fixed impression on the soul and may leave him in old age. Second, it commands that the training be according to his way, because every person is naturally suited to a different matter. In intellectual matters, some have sharp minds while others have straight but less acute intellects, and each must be taught according to his existing aptitude. In practical matters, some are suited to a particular craft or trait and will acquire it easily. This can be recognized in a child by his desire and by what he independently strives to do. He must be trained according to his way and according to the indications of what he is prepared for; then even when he grows old, he will not depart from it. This is not so if he is trained in something contrary to his nature.
text.21_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: The rich rules over the poor... One who sows injustice... One with a good eye... It is known from the histories of the nations that in ancient times the rich lent money to the poor at interest. The law was that if a borrower could not repay, the lender was entitled to take him, his wife, and his children as slaves and rule him with the rod as he wished. The rich lent to the needy, and through interest the borrowers collapsed completely and became destitute—the rash being worse off than the dal, for the dal has been reduced from his possessions, while the rash has nothing—and then became the lenders' slaves. But this repeatedly provoked rebellion among the borrowing populace; they killed the rich and took terrible vengeance upon them. As a result, rulers were repeatedly forced to enact laws canceling debts or paying them from the state treasury to quiet the revolt. At such times, the wealthy who had not lent at interest but had graciously supported the poor with charity were saved and remained honored and blessed among the people. Thus, the rich rules over the poor because the borrower is servant to the lender. Yet in the end, one who sows injustice by lending at interest to perpetrate wrongdoing will reap iniquity, for then the rod of his wrath will end—the rod with which he rules the poor—because they will rise against him and kill him. Then one with a good eye will be blessed, for he gave of his bread to the poor: not one who lent at interest and reduced the poor man to destitution, but one who gave him bread and assisted him with his money without profit; he will be blessed by the people.
text.21_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Drive out the scoffer and contention will depart. Contention is the matter or claim over which a person has a legal dispute with his fellow. I have already explained that contention is aroused by several causes: by hatred, as it says, “Hatred arouses contentions,” and by an angry or wrathful man, as it says, “A wrathful man provokes contention,” because without some cause people would not take offense over trivial matters and litigate or quarrel about them. Here it says that a scoffer also arouses contention, for the scoffer mocks everything and through his mockery unleashes strife. It therefore advises every person to drive the scoffer from his home and not associate with him; with him contention will depart. When there is no contention, they will not need to go to court and suffer the humiliation of litigation. Therefore it says, and judgment and disgrace will cease, for judgment comes from the court's examination of the contentious matter.
text.21_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: One who loves purity of heart, whose lips are gracious—the king is his friend. Having commanded that the scoffer, whose way is to unleash contention, be driven away and not befriended, it now describes the opposite: a man who loves everyone, is pure of heart, and has grace upon his lips. This is the opposite extreme from the scoffer, whose heart is full of dross, whose lips are full of quarrel, and who hates everyone. But the faithful friend whose heart and mouth agree and who speaks not mockery but gracious words is worthy that even the king should be his friend and companion.
text.21_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: The eyes of Hashem preserve knowledge. The laws of wisdom have no demonstrative proof but are received by tradition, and fools despise these laws and cast doubts upon them. Understanding and intellect, though they operate through rational investigation, are not exercised by many people; nor can they be exercised without established foundations upon which their investigations rest. Through Hashem's Providence, however, He implanted knowledge in the human heart: the first principles and the inference from effects to causes through the senses, by which man attains clear knowledge. He can then use the power of understanding to derive one thing from another and arrive at truths. This is through Providence: the eyes of Hashem preserve knowledge, and thereby He overturns the words of the traitor who comes to deny the truths.
text.21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: The lazy man says, “There is a lion outside; I will be murdered in the streets.” There is a difference between “outside” and “street”:
text.21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: * “Outside” is the area behind the houses, which is not public property and is used only by the residents of the courtyard;
text.21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 2_Comment: * while a “street” is the marketplace, where the people of the city gather.
text.21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 3_Comment: The normal situation is that wild animals are found in forests far from habitation, and robbers on the roads. In a city, however—even in its outer courtyards, and certainly in its streets—there are no robbers, much less wild animals.
text.21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 4_Comment: But because the lazy man is too indolent to leave his house, his imaginative faculty makes it seem to him as though:
text.21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 5_Comment: * outside, where crowds are not commonly found, there are wild animals;
text.21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 6_Comment: * and in the street there are murderers, though no wild animals are present there because they fear the multitude. In this way he finds an excuse for his laziness and refuses to move from his house.
text.21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 7_Comment: This is also a parable for one too lazy to engage in Torah and wisdom:
text.21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 8_Comment: * If told to study “outside”—to engage in investigation and wisdom outside the Torah—he says that a lion is there, as the next verse explains: The mouth of strange teachings is a deep pit. He fears that he may fall into heresy;
text.21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 9_Comment: * and if told to go into the “street”—to study matters commonly examined by the many—he fears being “murdered” by people, meaning that he will not understand or attain what he studies.
text.21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 10_Comment: All of this comes from his laziness.
text.21_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: The mouth of strange teachings is a deep pit; one abhorred by Hashem will fall there. “The mouth of strange teachings” means the paths of the wisdom and philosophy of idolaters—and I have explained that the term “mouth” is used of wisdom. It resembles a deep pit. A pit is an excavation made to trap people, and when it is deep, one who falls into it cannot escape. So too their teachings ensnare souls in heresy and denial, and one can no longer emerge from there into the light of life. Nor can he hope that Hashem will help him emerge from the pit, for one abhorred by Hashem will fall there: whoever falls there is under Hashem's indignation; Hashem's curse and wrath rest upon him, for he has been trapped in heresy and destruction. As the Sages said, one who separates himself from heresy dies immediately, and as it says, “None who enter her return.”
text.21_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Foolishness is bound to the heart of a child. Foolishness consists of doubts about the ways of wisdom and opposition to them. When foolishness exists in an adult, it takes root in the depths of his heart and cannot be separated from him, as it says, “A fool rejects his father's discipline,” and “Even if you pound the fool...” But in a child's heart foolishness has not yet taken root deep within; it is merely bound to his heart, like one thing tied to another with a cord. If the connecting cord is severed, the bond is removed. So too foolishness is still external to him and merely attached to him; through the rod of discipline one can distance it from him.
text.21_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: One who oppresses the poor in order to increase for him. This refers to one who oppresses a poor man, though his intention is not to rob him but to treat the money as a loan and have the poor man pay interest so that he can later give him a large sum at one time. Even if he does not keep the money himself but gives it to a rich man to hold at interest, it is nevertheless only for loss. Alternatively, it means one who oppresses the poor man by withholding his wages so that a large amount will accumulate for him at one time and thereby raise him from poverty to wealth. He oppresses the poor man and withholds his wages while increasing it for him, investing the money for the poor man's benefit so that it grows, and afterward gives it to a rich man—for when he returns the large accumulated sum, the recipient thereby becomes rich. Although he imagines that he has done him a great favor, it is nevertheless only for loss. He oppressed a poor man and gave to a rich man: though he now gives him the money and makes him rich, at the time of the oppression the victim was poor and suffered the disgrace of hunger and distress. What benefit is there in giving it later when he is rich, and how can that atone for the pressure and hardship the man suffered through him? The philosopher has already explained in his book of ethics that a condition of the discerning person is that, whenever he arranges his actions to bring about a good end, he must intend to reach it by a good and proper path. Otherwise he is like one who derives a true conclusion from a false syllogism whose middle term is false.
text.21_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge. The words of the wise concerning wisdom are words of tradition, for they received the laws of wisdom from Hashem. Wisdom has no demonstrations and must be received from mouth to ear. Yet King Solomon said in Proverbs that its purpose is “to know wisdom and discipline,” for through his parables he explained the laws of wisdom with analogies until knowledge could be attained from them—“knowledge” meaning clear comprehension of a matter. Therefore you must first incline your ear and hear the words of the wise by tradition. After accepting them through tradition and fixing them in your heart because you trust Hashem, Who gave the laws of wisdom and knows their truth, then apply your heart to my knowledge, according to how I have explained those laws through demonstrations of knowledge. If you do not first accept them by tradition, my knowledge will not help you, because you will deny their foundations.
text.21_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: For it is pleasant if you guard them in your belly; they will be established together upon your lips. After you have accepted the words of the wise, my knowledge is beneficial to you—that is, the way I have used parables and taught you to know wisdom through knowledge—for by this means you can express them with your lips. I have already explained that the lips signify knowledge: a matter that one knows clearly can be spoken and its truth declared with his lips. This is a great advantage. If you guard them in your belly, they are moving and wandering as long as you cannot bring them forth upon your lips—meaning that you do not know them as knowledge—but merely preserve them in your belly through the tradition you received. They move and wander and are not fixed within you like immovable nails. But they will be established together when they are upon your lips. If they emerge from your belly to your lips and are expressed with lips of knowledge, they become established; they no longer move but find a firm base from which they will not depart.
text.21_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: So that your trust may be in Hashem, I have made it known to you today—even to you. This returns to the preceding statement, Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise, which serves so that your trust may be in Hashem. That is, hear the laws of wisdom from the wise men who received them from Hashem, and trust Hashem, Who gave the laws of wisdom and knows their secrets and truth; do not doubt them at all. Afterward, apply your heart to my knowledge, for I have made known to you today the reasons of wisdom and explained them through demonstrations of knowledge, so that even you may know. Beyond trusting Hashem, Who knows their reasons and secrets, even you will know what you are capable of attaining from them.
text.21_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Have I not written for you threefold matters of counsels and knowledge? As it says, “He spoke three thousand proverbs,” the Book of Proverbs is divided into three sections. Therefore it says, Have I not written for you threefold matters of counsels, all filled with counsel for yourself concerning how to conduct yourself, and knowledge, so that you will possess clear knowledge with which to teach others. Corresponding to “counsels” it says in the next verse, “to make known to you,” and corresponding to “knowledge” it says, “to return words...”
text.21_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: To make known to you the certainty of words of truth, so that you may return words of truth to those who sent you. There is a difference between certainty and truth. A thing is true when it is inherently true even if a person does not know its reason; it is certain when its truth is revealed and clear to everyone. That is, the parables I composed will make known to you the certainty and truth of words of truth, so that you understand the truth in its true nature—the reasons and knowledge underlying the truth you received by tradition. You will also be able to return words of truth to those who sent you, for once you attain them through demonstrations of knowledge and they are established upon your lips, you can answer others and clearly make known the reasons and knowledge of wisdom.
text.21_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not rob the poor because he is poor. Although you are warned not to rob a wealthy person either, there the prohibition is because robbery is forbidden. When robbing a poor person, however, besides being warned against robbery, you are specifically warned not to rob him because he is poor. Likewise, do not crush the afflicted at the gate of judgment, where he has no one among the judges to hear him against you.
text.21_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: For Hashem will plead their cause. When a wealthy person is robbed or his judgment is perverted, he has power of his own, and the matter concerns only monetary law.
text.21_Chapter, 22_Verse, 1_Comment: This is not so with the poor and afflicted, who have no one to plead on their behalf. Then Hashem will plead their cause, for Hashem pleads the cause of the weak who possess no power.
text.21_Chapter, 22_Verse, 2_Comment: It is then no longer a matter of monetary law; rather, He will rob the life of those who rob them.
text.21_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not befriend a man of anger. There is a difference between a man of anger and a man of wrath. A man of anger takes revenge openly and does not retain wrath in his heart; concerning him, the verse commands that one not befriend him. A man of wrath keeps anger in his heart and does not take revenge immediately. This is worse, and the verse commands that one not associate with him at all, even outside a relationship of friendship and companionship.
text.21_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: Lest you learn his ways. By becoming accustomed to his ways, you will act likewise, and take a snare for your soul, in which you will later be trapped.
text.21_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not be among those who strike hands. This refers to one who assumes direct liability as a guarantor; it adds that you should not even be among those who guarantee debts without assuming direct liability.
text.21_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: If you have nothing with which to pay, why should he take your bed from beneath you? If the borrower himself has nothing with which to pay, the creditor is forbidden to enter his house to take a pledge. But he may enter a guarantor's house to take collateral, as the Sages expound: “You shall not enter his house”—but you may enter the house of the guarantor. Thus you are in a worse position than the borrower himself.
text.21_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not move an ancient boundary that your fathers established. This warning was already stated in the Torah: You shall not move your fellow's boundary, which the earlier generations established in your inheritance (Deuteronomy 19:14). There it refers to one who encroaches upon his fellow's boundary. Solomon learned from it that one must likewise not remove any boundary established by the earlier generations, such as customs instituted by the ancestors to endure forever; therefore it says, an ancient boundary. The Yalkut likewise states in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: If you see a custom practiced by our ancestors, do not change it—for example, Abraham instituted the morning prayer—thus it says, which your fathers established. The Sifrei (§188) similarly asks: From where do we know that one may not substitute the words of Rabbi Eliezer for those of Rabbi Yehoshua? From Do not move an ancient boundary. See below (23:10).
text.21_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: Have you seen a man skilled in his work? According to the parable, a man may be such a great craftsman that he stands before kings to perform the work of kings. Although he is quick and skilled in his work and is capable of working for common people as well, he will no longer stand before obscure men. Once chosen for the king's work, he will not lower his stature to perform the labor of obscure men. It also means that he cannot stand before obscure men, because they do not understand refined crafts and wondrous artistry, but only coarse work; his craft is not valued in their eyes. This is a metaphor and moral lesson for man. His work in this world is the work of the great King: to keep His charge, commandments, and teachings, and to comprehend His truth. One who is skilled in his work and fit to stand before the King will no longer lower himself to serve matter and the obscure animal soul or neglect the King's service—especially since the spiritual work he performs for his King will not be accepted or appreciated by these obscure beings, who dwell in the dark gloom of matter.
text.22_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: When you sit to dine with a ruler. When you sit to eat bread with a ruler: first, understand who is before you, and do not forget that you are sitting with a ruler, for during a meal a person may forget the ruler's awe and honor and thereby forfeit his life.
text.22_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And put... Second, it commands him not to eat excessively. If you are a man of appetite and desire, then put a knife to your throat to restrain yourself from eating too much.
text.22_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not... Regarding the delicacies themselves, do not desire his delicacies. It explains the reason: they are deceptive food. The ruler does not give them for your sake—to benefit or sustain you, or to honor you—but for his own benefit. They are not true food, but preparation for what he will impose upon you and request from you. All this is a parable for the ruler within man: his desiring inclination and aroused faculty, which rules the body and which Ecclesiastes calls “an old and foolish king.” It invites the true man—his intellectual powers—to eat its bread. He must know who sits before him and guard against its enticement: he must neither broaden his appetitive soul so that it breaches its boundary nor desire abundant delicacies beyond the necessary food, for it is deceptive bread. It is not the food appointed for the soul and for man as man, but for his animal aspect.
text.22_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not weary yourself to become rich. After commanding him not to be drawn after the appetitive faculty in eating and indulgence, it commands him not to be drawn after accumulating wealth, through which he will abandon contemplation of Torah. Thus, do not weary yourself to become rich, for thereby you will cease from your understanding. Not everyone who increases commerce becomes wise, and the Torah is not across the sea, as the Sages said. The next verse explains.
text.22_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Will you cause your eyes to fly toward it, and it is gone? Regarding your understanding, you must not avert your eyes from it even for a moment. It resembles a winged bird in a person's hand: the moment he turns away, it flies upward. So too human intellect and understanding: if a person neglects them for a moment, they fly away, for they are not aroused by themselves but only through great diligence and effort. Thus, if you cause your eyes to fly—closing the eyelid over the eye—your understanding is gone, for it makes wings for itself and flies away from you. The Sages likewise interpreted: “A bird means only Torah, as it says, ‘Will you cause your eyes to fly toward it, and it is gone?’”
text.22_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not eat... This too is presented as a parable: do not eat the bread of one with an evil eye, and do not desire his delicacies.
text.22_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: For as corruption is in his soul, so is he. Natural philosophers have explained that harmful sparks issue from an evil eye, rooted in the degraded soul of the person who looks with an evil eye, and they are like sparks of death upon the object observed. They also related that a person with an evil eye gazed steadily at a loaf of bread, and death and destruction were found within it. Thus it says that the corruption—the defective and repulsive quality within his inner soul—enters the bread as well; the bread receives that corruption and becomes spoiled bread. He says to you, “Eat and drink,” making it appear that he has not placed an evil eye upon it, but his heart is not with you. The food will harm you until you vomit even the morsel you ate. By concluding, and you will have wasted your pleasant words, the verse reveals that it speaks metaphorically of spiritual bread—the study of intellectual truths. One must take care not to eat the bread of the intellect from one with an evil eye. A good or evil “eye” applies to all judgments of the intellect that judge favorably or unfavorably: one with a good eye judges for good, while one with an evil eye judges for evil. Vision corresponds to the faculty of intellect, through which one apprehends matters beyond the power of understanding, including the laws of wisdom—which cannot be understood by the faculty of understanding—and all higher apprehensions concerning the hidden secret of Hashem, concealed from every creature and exalted beyond the path of their understanding. Scripture does not use “understanding” for these, but “intellect,” as in “to comprehend Your truth.” In matters of understanding, all people agree: everyone who understands grasps them in the same way, and one who disagrees does not understand and imagines vanity and falsehood. But matters beyond human understanding, such as the ways and practices of wisdom and higher knowledge, are apprehensions of intellect and may be approached by many paths. Each person apprehends according to what he is: the wise person by the path of wisdom and the fool by the path of folly. One with a good eye judges according to wisdom, which is inherently good, while one with an evil eye judges according to folly—for example, that one should not give his bread to the poor. The verse therefore commands not to eat the bread of one with an evil eye, for the study of wisdom is compared to eating bread and drinking water, as it says, “Ho, everyone who thirsts, go to the water.” The corruption in his soul—his heart being filled with evil images and sinful schemes—enters his bread. Although he says, “Eat and drink,” and appears to teach you words of wisdom, his heart, the ruling faculty, is not with you, for he does not rule his spirit and subdue his appetites. Ultimately you will even vomit the morsel you had already eaten—the words of wisdom you previously received—and you will ruin your pleasant words.
text.22_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not speak in the ears of a fool, for he will despise the intellect of your words. It has already been explained that a fool differs from an ignoramus. The ignoramus doubts the laws of wisdom, whereas the fool may know them but depart from them because of his appetite. If the laws of wisdom could be demonstrated to the ignoramus by proof, he would return from his ignorance. Not so the fool: he flees wisdom despite knowing its value, because it restrains his appetite. The laws of wisdom cannot be demonstrated by proofs of understanding, but they can be apprehended through intellect, an acute faculty that extends even to matters of wisdom. One who possesses intellect can speak in the ears of the ignoramus, for if he can bring him to apprehension, he will return from his ignorance. But this does not help the fool, as it says, “Go away from a foolish man, for you will not know lips of knowledge,” as I explained there.
