Therefore, do not speak in the ears of a fool, for he will even despise the intellect of your words, since he does not desire wisdom or intellectual apprehension.
text.22_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not move an ancient boundary. It already said above (22:28), “Do not move an ancient boundary,” and we explained it there. From the context here we learn that it speaks of the boundary belonging to the poor. The Sifra on Kedoshim likewise explains that it refers to one who steals the gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and corner of the field. We explained there that the concept of a boundary seems opposed to that of the world: a boundary belongs to each individual and is not a single boundary for the entire world. Yet there is a boundary designated for the whole world—the portion set aside universally for the poor to gather their gifts. It commands that this boundary not be moved, and likewise that one not enter the fields of orphans. Do not say that their power is too weak to contend with you in court, for the next verse says:
text.22_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: For their Redeemer is strong. Their fields have a Redeemer—the term denoting the close relative who possesses the right of redemption—and this Redeemer is strong. Moreover, He will plead their cause against you, and you will certainly be punished.
text.22_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Bring your heart to discipline and your ears to words of knowledge. Even if a person has heard and accepted the laws of wisdom from his teachers, it is not certain that he will follow them. Images of appetite contradict and battle the laws of wisdom, and the heart—the ruling faculty in the body—wages an internal war: at times images of wisdom rule it, and at times images of appetite, especially because the reasons for the laws of wisdom are unknown. The Sage therefore advises him to bring his ears to words of knowledge: he should also receive words that knowledgeable people acquired through first principles and the senses—how they saw Hashem's Providence in His world, how He ordered the world with wisdom and repays the wicked according to his wickedness, that the body ultimately dies, and the like. Through this he brings his heart to discipline, fearing punishment and the awe and exaltedness of Hashem. This assists the heart in ruling according to the laws of wisdom and subduing appetite, as explained throughout.
text.22_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not withhold discipline from a child. Although a child cannot receive words of knowledge and cannot bring his heart to discipline through such words by fearing Hashem's punishment and exaltedness, nevertheless do not withhold from him the discipline appropriate for a child—discipline with the rod.
text.22_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: For if you strike him with the rod, he will not die. There is no danger in striking him; thus the act is unlikely to cause loss and likely to bring benefit, for:
text.22_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: You will strike him with the rod and save his soul from the grave. In this way you will save his soul from the grave, whereas otherwise he would suffer the death of the soul.
text.22_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: My son. It presents discipline that a father speaks to his son. If your heart is wise: it has already been explained that one “wise of heart” is a person in whose heart—the ruling faculty—the laws of wisdom are firmly fixed and rule all his powers, so that the images of appetite and the inclination no longer rise in rebellion, and the war within his spirit has quieted. If you reach this level and become wise of heart, then my heart too will rejoice. It already said that a wise son gladdens his father, but this is not yet rejoicing of the heart, which is complete inner joy, for the son might still fall away from the laws of wisdom. But if his heart itself is wise, so that his heart rejoices in his labor because he no longer has an internal war, his father's heart will likewise rejoice.
text.22_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: My kidneys will exult when your lips speak upright things. If you reach the still higher level of uprightness—knowing through understanding the laws of what is straight—you will no longer need the heart's battle at all, for uprightness will have become an acquisition within your heart. As we explained, an upright person is one whose nature inclines toward uprightness and who comprehends its laws through understanding until he knows them clearly and can speak them with his lips to others. As explained, the lips signify knowledge: because he knows uprightness with clear knowledge, he can speak and teach it to others. Then my kidneys will exult, a higher level than the heart's rejoicing. First, exultation is dancing from great joy, the outward expression of joy in action, just as the laws of uprightness have been revealed to our son in action so that he can teach others. Second, the kidneys are closer to action than the heart, as the Sages said: the heart thinks and the kidneys advise, and counsel follows thought.
text.22_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Let your heart not envy sinners. When the verb “envy” is followed by the preposition bet, it means envying another's advantage and desiring to be like him. He tells his son that even if he sees sinners prospering in this world, his heart should not envy them. Rather, envy the fear of Hashem: when he sees fear of Hashem, he should desire the deeds of those who fear Hashem, and this envy should dwell in his heart all day. The trait of envy is thus evil when directed toward sinners and good when directed toward fear of Hashem. One who is wise of heart does not suppress envy entirely, but rules it so that it operates only on its good side.
text.22_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: For surely there is a future. It explains why he should not envy the prosperity of sinners: they have no ultimate future, as it says, “The future of the wicked is cut off.” “Future” means the final purpose and eternal happiness, which comes only through fear of Hashem, whereby a person inherits eternal life. Sinners do not possess this. Moreover, your hope for matters of this world will not be cut off. This is the difference between hope and confident expectation: hope applies to something uncertain and not guaranteed, for success in this world is not promised to them.
text.22_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: Listen, you, my son. Corresponding to “If your heart is wise, my heart will rejoice,” he says: But you, my son, whose heart is not yet wise and remains distant from wisdom—even when wisdom enters your heart, it will still battle appetite and the inclination, the opposite of being wise of heart—you must listen and accept the words of wisdom, and become wise by acquiring wisdom. You must direct your heart on the way. Since two roads lie before you, the road of wisdom and the road of folly, direct your ruling faculty along the road of lasting happiness. This distinguishes one who directs toward happiness from one who merely guides: the former travels on the road of eternal happiness.
text.22_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not be... Even if you have not yet reached the level of wisdom, guard yourself against the appetite for gluttonous eating of meat and drunken drinking of wine. The word “for themselves” may also be understood metaphorically: they consume their own flesh, as it says, “You will groan at your end, when your flesh and body are consumed.”
text.22_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: For the drunkard and glutton will become impoverished. At least act according to benefit and harm, for the drunkard and glutton will lose his possessions, while one who dozes and does no work will be clothed by slumber in torn garments. In the metaphor as well, he will lose the wealth of wisdom and be naked of the garments of noble character traits and the clothing of intellect.
text.22_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: Listen to your father who begot you. It commands him to hear and accept the laws of wisdom from his father and not doubt that tradition as though his father might bequeath him falsehood, since he begot you, and a father does not bequeath falsehood to his children. Likewise, when receiving modes of conduct from your mother, do not despise her because your mother has aged, imagining that these customs were good for the first generation but not the new one, or good for the old but not for youths in whom the heat of appetite burns.
text.22_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: Acquire truth. Even if you must pay a great price for truth—your desires, youthful pleasures, and the longing of your soul—give all of these as its price. Do not sell it: do not acquire it like a merchant who buys in order to sell at another price. That is, do not study in order to obtain wealth or honor, which would constitute buying and selling—receiving another price in exchange for what you acquired. Therefore it says, “Acquire truth,” for truth by definition is pursued for its own sake. It explains what you should acquire and what truth is: wisdom, discipline, and understanding. We have explained that wisdom encompasses the laws of character and conduct by which one must live according to the Torah. All its matters are received by tradition rather than discovered by human understanding, and they oppose man's nature, for appetite disputes the laws of wisdom. The soul can accept them only through discipline, whose root is fear of Hashem: one fears Hashem, Who watches him and punishes, and Who commanded these laws, and binds his soul with the restraints of awe so that he does not transgress His word. He will then also acquire understanding, which distinguishes truth from falsehood in matters of theoretical intellect. If he accepts the laws of wisdom together with discipline until they become firmly established as truth in his heart through faith in Hashem, Who legislated them and knows their reasons, he can then understand one thing from another and derive conclusions from them. This comes through acquiring truth—believing that the laws of wisdom are true.
text.22_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: The father of a righteous person will surely rejoice, and one who begets a wise son will be glad in him. The righteous person differs from the wise person. The wise person has received the laws of wisdom and follows them. The righteous person is not necessarily wise; he has merely accustomed himself to act righteously, though he did not receive the laws of wisdom through study. Rejoicing differs from gladness: gladness is continuous, while rejoicing comes over something newly occurring, such as a discovery or good news. A “father” can include one who raises or teaches him, whereas “one who begets” means specifically his biological father. Righteous conduct does not depend upon birth but upon free choice, as the Sages said: an angel brings the drop before the Holy One, blessed is He, and asks what will become of it—wise or foolish and so forth—but does not ask whether it will be righteous or wicked. Therefore the begetter does not rejoice over a righteous son merely because he begot him. Rather, the father of a righteous person—the one who raised, taught, and trained him in righteous deeds—rejoices. Nor is his gladness necessarily constant, because the son may fall from his righteousness, having not received the laws of wisdom; instead the father rejoices anew each time he sees that the son still holds to righteousness. But one who begets a wise son will be glad in him. The formation of a wise person depends partly on birth, since he is naturally prepared for wisdom, and therefore the begetter is glad. It says “will be glad,” not “will rejoice,” because he is glad over the son's disposition and fine intellect, a constant gladness rather than one renewed each time.
text.22_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: Your father and mother will be glad, and she who bore you will rejoice. He advises the son to conduct himself so that both those who raised him will be glad and those who begot him will rejoice. This occurs if he rules his spirit through wisdom and discipline until he becomes wise of heart—wisdom rules his heart and becomes second nature, so that neither images of appetite that turn him from wisdom nor the doubts and ignorance that question the laws of wisdom rule him. This is achieved by hearing discipline and consistently conducting himself according to wisdom. Then the father and mother who raised him will be glad, since through their guidance they accustomed him to this. His mother who bore him will also experience a new rejoicing beyond her initial gladness over his natural disposition: she will rejoice over the persistence of his free choice and ruling faculty, which is the meaning of rejoicing.
text.22_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, give me your heart. It explains how this is achieved: give me your heart, meaning that the laws of wisdom should rule within it and doubts of heresy and denial should not rule there. The laws of wisdom should remain engraved and written upon his heart so that no contrary matter is found within it. Let your eyes guard my ways. The eyes signify appetites and evil images rooted in the senses, as the Sages explained: “Do not stray after your heart”—this is heresy—“and after your eyes”—this is immorality. The eyes should guard the ways of Hashem and not be moved by the desires of this world or the inclination's enticements.
text.22_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: For a deep pit... Corresponding to “Let your eyes guard my ways,” it says that the harlot, representing the appetitive inclination, resembles a deep pit from which one who is trapped has difficulty escaping. Corresponding to “My son, give me your heart,” it says that the foreign woman, representing heresy, resembles a narrow well: one who falls there immediately drowns in the raging waters and dies. So too one submerged in heresy dies the death of the soul and will not return to see the light of life.
text.22_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: She too... The harlot lies in wait like a robber, for she suddenly snatches one whose spirit of desire rises in his heart and captures him in her net. Had he paid attention, he would have guarded against her, but she seizes him suddenly. The foreign woman, representing heresy, increases traitors among men, for she presents arguments of heresy and denial to ensnare many into betraying Hashem.
text.22_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: Who has woe? Who has longing? If you ask, “Who has woe?” I answer: the one who has longing—desire and craving. Whoever has craving has woe. If you ask, “Who has contentions?”—legal disputes and arguments—I answer: one who has babbling. “Babbling” means speech without intellect, merely blurting out one's imaginings; one who multiplies babbling multiplies contentions and quarrels. If you ask, “Who has wounds without cause?” I answer: one who has redness of eyes. If you ask who has red eyes, I answer in the next verse.
text.22_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: Those who linger over wine. After lingering all night drinking wine, they then come again to investigate mixed wine, seeking the vintner who knows how to blend the wine well, and they begin drinking anew.
text.22_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not look upon wine when it is red, when it gives its eye in the cup and goes down smoothly. Do not desire wine because you see its red color, which indicates that it is good wine and beneficial to the blood, the vital soul. At first it gives its eye—its color—in the cup into which it is poured, and then goes down smoothly as though it contains no evil. The metaphor is that the drinker, who is the cup into which the wine is placed, becomes red like the wine. At first the drinking is smooth and pleasant, but:
text.22_Chapter, 31_Verse, 0_Comment: In the end it bites like a serpent and secretes venom like a viper. The viper is a species of snake whose excrement is also poisonous and harmful. It says that at first the wine injects venom into him like a snake; afterward it “secretes,” meaning that it makes his own excrement like that of a viper, transforming it into burning poison.
text.22_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: Your eyes will see strange women. Corresponding to “My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes guard my ways,” it says that through wine the reverse will occur. His eyes will stray after immorality and see strange women with whom to sin, while his heart will stray after heresy and speak perversities—words of heresy that are the opposite of the words of wisdom.
text.22_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: You will be like one lying in the heart of the sea. At first he will be like one lying in the heart of the sea, floating on its waters and battling its waves. Afterward he will seem like one lying at the top of a mast, from which he will fall into the depths—from a high roof into a deep pit—and drown. So too he falls from his stature into the depths of the pit and drowns in the abyss of destruction.
text.22_Chapter, 34_Verse, 0_Comment: They struck me, but I was not sick. At first he says that they struck him, and although he felt it, he did not become ill. He adds, they beat me, which is more severe than striking, yet not only did he not become sick, I did not even know it. He adds that he remains in perpetual sleep, yet desires to awaken—not in order to abstain from wine, but so that he can seek it again.
text.23_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not envy evil men. First, do not envy their success and wish to act as they do. Second, do not desire to be with them in love and brotherhood—even if you will not imitate their deeds—in order to gain some benefit from them.
text.23_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: For their heart meditates violence, and their lips speak mischief. Corresponding to “Do not envy evil men,” it says that their heart meditates devastation and ruin. It also means that their success is not true success, for they constantly fear the devastation and ruin destined to befall them. Corresponding to “Do not desire to be with them,” it explains that their lips speak mischief, and you will learn from their conduct to practice wrongdoing and iniquity.
text.23_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Through wisdom a house is built... every precious and pleasant treasure. Wisdom is received by tradition: a person gathers the laws of wisdom from outside himself and brings their principles and teachings into his heart one by one. He resembles one who gathers wood, stones, lime, and all the materials needed for a house and builds stone upon stone. Understanding, however, means deriving one thing from another after receiving and gathering the laws of wisdom and accepting them faithfully. It resembles establishing the house by placing its roof and ceiling upon it. If he afterward reaches the level of knowledge, knowing everything clearly as something perceived by the senses or grasped as a first principle, this resembles filling the house with precious and pleasant vessels. The chambers of the house of wisdom are then filled with light, and he produces blossoms and flowers for the Torah. In the same manner Scripture attributes the building of the world—which was built through wisdom—to Hashem: “Through wisdom Hashem founded the earth; He established the heavens through understanding; through His knowledge the depths were split,” as explained there.
text.23_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: A wise man is mighty in strength. One who has received the laws of wisdom and conducts himself by them—the definition of a wise person—is a man mighty in strength. He already possesses strength with which to overcome the soul's enemies, the appetites and inclinations of the heart, for he subdues them through the power of the wisdom he received. Nevertheless, he does not thereby make his power permanently firm. Firmness means remaining strong continually without change, and wisdom alone cannot accomplish this, because the inclination constantly wars with the heart. Since the laws of wisdom are not understood as clearly as sensory facts, the inclination may sometimes prevail and blind the heart's eyes. But a man of knowledge, who has reached the level of knowing the laws of wisdom like things established by demonstration or sense, makes his strength firm continually, and the soul's enemies will never prevail.
text.23_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: For through strategies you shall wage war for yourself, and victory comes through many counselors. I have already mentioned above (12:14) that one counsel alone does not suffice for war, because the enemy also has a plan. One needs strategy—the linking of many plans one after another—so that for every plan the enemy devises, one has another plan against it. War therefore requires many counselors, each proposing a different plan, because every kind of counsel is needed. This is a parable for the soul's war against its enemies. It cannot prevail through wisdom alone, which is one particular counselor, because the enemy too comes with plans opposing wisdom's counsel. All the soul's counselors—wisdom, understanding, and knowledge—must gather together. Through the power of knowledge, which has attained everything clearly, it devises strategies and linked counsels against the plans of appetite and the inclination; then its strength becomes firm.
text.23_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Wisdom is lofty to the ignoramus. The ignoramus is the opposite of the man of knowledge. Not only does he lack clear knowledge through demonstrations; he even doubts the laws of wisdom. To him the forms of wisdom seem lofty, like something descending from the heights that the intellect cannot grasp. Therefore at the gate of battle he does not open his mouth. People commonly fought at the gate, as it says, “They will speak with enemies at the gate,” because the enemy seeks to enter the fortress through the gate and the defenders prevent him. This battle is waged through speech of the mouth—the mouth alluding to wisdom—for through wisdom they defeat the enemy at the gate. But the ignoramus does not open his mouth, so the enemy enters through the gate and conquers the city.
text.23_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: One who plots to do evil. I explained above (12:2) that the verb zamam denotes deep plans in which one delves into how to accomplish something, and when used of secular matters it generally refers to evil. The verb chashav, when used actively, denotes improper thoughts, such as a disqualifying intention regarding a sacred offering or evil against one's fellow. One who plots to do evil will be called a master of schemes as a disgrace: his thoughts delve deeply into evil, as it says, “A man of schemes will act wickedly.”
text.23_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: The scheme of ignorance is sin. Sin comes through the scheme of ignorance. A scheme means immersing oneself deeply in thoughts of immorality; metaphorically, it refers to immersing oneself in the seduction of ignorance—continually doubting the laws of wisdom—from which one comes to sin, meaning violation of the laws of wisdom. If he is also a scoffer, this will transform into abomination—deeds performed repulsively in public—for he will mock and do everything openly.
text.23_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: If you become lax on the day of trouble... if you refrain from rescuing those taken to death. Even when they are being led to slaughter, your punishment will be measure for measure. When the day of trouble comes upon you, you will become lax and your strength will be narrow: your hands will weaken from doing anything to save you, and your power will be so restricted that you cannot accomplish anything through your own strength, just as you did nothing to rescue others.
text.23_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: If you say, “Behold, we did not know this.” If you offer the excuse that you did not know they were being taken to death, or did not know that you had the ability to save them, you may justify yourself before people. But Hashem, Who weighs hearts, understands the heart's thoughts. More than this, because He guards your soul, He knows. Knowledge applies to something perceived by the senses, and your deeds are inscribed and depicted upon the tablet of your soul. He will repay a man according to his deed, measure for measure.
text.23_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, eat honey because it is good. You eat honey because it is good food for the body, and the honeycomb is sweet when it comes upon your palate.
text.23_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: So know wisdom for your soul. Wisdom is likewise good food for the soul. Whereas the honeycomb is sweet only while it is upon your palate, through wisdom there is a future that remains sweet to the soul forever, even when the body ceases; and your hope in this world will not be cut off, as explained above (23:18).
text.23_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not lie in wait, wicked man, against the dwelling of the righteous; do not plunder his resting place. You, wicked man, do not lie in wait against the dwelling of the righteous. That is:
text.23_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: * Some lie in wait from desire for money, wishing to plunder his dwelling;
text.23_Chapter, 14_Verse, 2_Comment: * while others lie in wait from revenge or jealousy, wishing to destroy his resting place so that he will have no repose or rest.
text.23_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: For a righteous person falls seven times and rises. Although the righteous person falls seven times, he rises through Hashem's help. But the wicked, even if they are many, will stumble through the evil they prepared against the righteous; through that very evil they will fall and not rise.
text.23_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: When your enemy falls, do not be glad. There is a difference between gladness and rejoicing:
text.23_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: * Gladness is continual, concerning something enduring;
text.23_Chapter, 16_Verse, 2_Comment: * while rejoicing is momentary, concerning something newly occurring, such as good news.
text.23_Chapter, 16_Verse, 4_Comment: * Do not be glad continually because your enemy has fallen from his position;
text.23_Chapter, 16_Verse, 5_Comment: * and even when he stumbles, at the beginning of his fall, let your heart not rejoice momentarily over the news that his downfall has begun.
text.23_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Lest Hashem see and it be evil in His eyes. When He sees your cruelty and vindictiveness, He will compare your deed with your enemy's deeds. Your conduct will be evil in His eyes until your enemy appears righteous relative to you, and He will turn His anger from him toward you.
text.23_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not become angry over evildoers; do not envy the wicked. When a person sees the wicked prospering, then:
text.23_Chapter, 18_Verse, 1_Comment: * Their deeds may be evil in his eyes and he may not envy them or desire to be like them, yet he becomes angry over their success and complains that Hashem does not punish them. Concerning this it says, Do not become angry—do not be incensed over evildoers and their success;
text.23_Chapter, 18_Verse, 2_Comment: * Or he may envy them and desire to be like them. Concerning this it says, Do not envy the wicked.
text.23_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: For there will be no future for the evil person. It explains:
text.23_Chapter, 19_Verse, 1_Comment: * Do not become angry or feel distressed over their success, for evildoers will have no future. They will receive their punishment in the end, and their future will be cut off;
text.23_Chapter, 19_Verse, 2_Comment: * And do not envy their present success, for the lamp of the wicked that shines for them—their prosperity—will be extinguished. It is not a steadily shining lamp, but one that flickers, sputters, and is liable to go out at every moment. Their prosperity is not genuine, for they constantly fear punishment and calamities and are never tranquil or secure.
text.23_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: My son, fear Hashem and the king, and do not mingle with those who seek change. It commands him to fear Hashem in matters of religion and the king, who establishes the land through justice in governing civil society. Do not mingle with people who wish to alter the political order—that is, to rebel against their king and establish in his place a second regime different from the first—for thereby you also violate fear of Hashem, Who commanded that the king's awe be upon you.
text.23_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: For their calamity will suddenly arise. First, the calamity of these rebels will arise suddenly if the rebellion and conspiracy are discovered. Beyond this, even if the rebellion succeeds and they change the government, who knows the ruin of both? This means the disaster that may arise through their alteration and through the second regime they establish. It may bring evil, ruin, and destruction, for they may establish a government according to their desires in order to oppress, rob, and crush the people.
text.23_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: These too are sayings of the wise. Until this point are the proverbs of Solomon; from here until the end of the chapter the material is collected from the words of other wise men.
text.23_Chapter, 22_Verse, 1_Comment: It says, Showing partiality in judgment is also not good. Even if the judge does not flatter the wicked by calling him righteous, but merely recognizes the face of the righteous—because he knows that this person is ordinarily righteous and therefore favors him as righteous in the present case—
text.23_Chapter, 22_Verse, 2_Comment: although it would normally be appropriate to maintain the righteous person's established status, it is not good in judgment. A judge must regard both litigants as potentially wicked until he investigates the case.
text.23_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: All the more so one who says to the wicked, “You are righteous.” Peoples will curse such a man, for he destroys the foundations of justice and righteousness.
text.23_Chapter, 23_Verse, 1_Comment: There is a difference between peoples and nations:
text.23_Chapter, 23_Verse, 2_Comment: * Nations possess a distinct religion and are united by faith;
text.23_Chapter, 23_Verse, 3_Comment: * while peoples possess a king and a distinct civil law.
text.23_Chapter, 23_Verse, 4_Comment: Peoples will curse him because he destroys civil law, while nations will denounce him because he destroys religion. Denunciation refers to punishment resulting from a curse, as though the nations have already specified his punishment.
text.23_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: But it will be pleasant for those who rebuke. This refers to those who rebuke the wicked, do not flatter them, but correct them with reproof.
text.23_Chapter, 24_Verse, 1_Comment: It will be pleasant in itself, for the good path is pleasant to the soul. Beyond this, a blessing will come upon them, rather than the curse that comes upon flatterers; it depicts goodness as being multiplied for them.
text.23_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: Lips are kissed by one who gives a forthright answer. One who is wise in reproof can answer the person arguing with him and seeking to refute his words; he is trained to answer and overturn the other's claims, which is the definition of a response, with forthright words that decisively establish his position. Such lips receive kisses, for everyone loves them.
text.23_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: Prepare your work outside. If you wish to build a house—meaning to marry a wife and have children—first prepare the means by which you can support them: prepare your occupation outside the home so that you have a livelihood, and make ready in the field for the future, possessing a field of grain sown and prepared to provide bread for your household. Then build your house. Otherwise you will depend upon others, resort to theft, or neglect Torah study. This is a general proverb: for every goal, first prepare the necessary means. The Sages expounded it to mean that before studying Gemara one should prepare through Scripture and Mishnah, which precede and lead to Gemara; and before performing good deeds, one should prepare through the study that precedes action, and similarly in other matters.
text.23_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not be a witness without cause against your fellow. Do not testify against your fellow to make him liable for something he did not do, which would be testimony without cause:
text.23_Chapter, 27_Verse, 1_Comment: * Whether you do so for payment, concerning which it says, and would you entice—meaning, would you earn a piece of bread through your lips?
text.23_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: * Or whether you do so to repay him for evil he did to you, concerning which it says, Do not say, “As he did to me, so will I do to him”;
text.23_Chapter, 28_Verse, 1_Comment: * Or whether you do so because he habitually hires himself out as a false witness, and you say, I will repay the man according to his deed.
text.23_Chapter, 28_Verse, 2_Comment: Do not do so under any circumstances.
text.23_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: I passed by the field of a lazy man and by the vineyard of a man lacking heart. A field requires much active labor—plowing, sowing, and the like—and a lazy man will not perform the work of his field because of his laziness. A vineyard, already planted, requires less labor and needs primarily to be guarded from damage. A lazy man might do this, but a man lacking heart does not understand the loss that will befall the vineyard if he fails to guard it, and therefore neglects even the vineyard.
text.23_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: Behold, it was entirely overgrown with thorns; nettles covered its surface... The pronoun “entirely” refers to the field, which is grammatically masculine; the vineyard's surface was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was also destroyed.
text.23_Chapter, 31_Verse, 0_Comment: I beheld; I applied my heart; I saw and took discipline. Beholding differs from seeing: beholding indicates a vision of the heart and spirit, while seeing refers to the sight of the eyes. Because the matter contains both a parable visible to the eyes and an application perceived by the heart, it says that he beheld and applied his heart to the vision, and also saw with his eyes and took discipline. The application concerns the field and vineyard of the soul. The soul has the potential to produce the fruit of wisdom and worthy conduct if its depths are plowed, its thorns and weeds removed, and the seed of Hashem sown in it, as I explained on Isaiah 28. The field represents the positive commandments that must be actively performed, as well as the labor required in the field of study—to gather and bring in knowledge—which resembles every kind of fieldwork. The lazy person does not perform positive commandments or plow deeply in study because of his laziness. The vineyard represents one who has already planted vines of wisdom and now must guard the negative commandments, and also preserve his learning from being forgotten, which is lighter work. One who neglects this does so not from laziness but from lacking heart, meaning that he lacks the faculty that rules his spirit; appetite breaks through him, leading him to violate negative commandments and abandon his Torah. His field and vineyard therefore become overgrown with thorns, the portion of his soul is ruined by the weeds of the inclination, and it produces no fruit. From this I took discipline, restraining the soul with the bonds of moral discipline so that it would not leave its boundary.
text.23_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: A little sleep, a little slumber. Sleep is settled and deep, while slumber is lighter. When slumber comes after sleep it is unnecessary indulgence: after awakening from his sleep, he still dozes, neither fully asleep nor awake; and after awakening even from that slumber, he folds his hands to lie down longer upon his bed and is too lazy to dress himself. Then:
text.23_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: Your poverty will come walking, and your want like an armed man. Poverty comes without force, merely like a traveler, and you do not sense it at all. But the wants that follow poverty come with sword, spear, and a strong hand, like an armed man. You will fight against the want that oppresses you, but it will wear armor, so that you can no longer defeat it.
text.24_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: It is the glory of God to conceal a matter. In Divine matters, glory consists of concealment and hiddenness, because the intellect can apprehend only things subject to time and place and accessible to the senses, not matters beyond the laws of human comprehension. Whatever is said about them is only by way of parable and outward garment, while the inner content remains hidden. Therefore the Account of Creation and the Chariot are not expounded publicly; the sages clothe and conceal these matters in riddles and allusions, flashing and disappearing like lightning. But the glory of kings in matters of government is to investigate a matter rather than conceal it. Since their governance is civil and can be understood through observation and experience, it is good to publicize its virtues. Concealment here would indicate that their governance is not upright and that they therefore hide their ways; investigation is their glory.
text.24_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: The heavens for height and the earth for depth. The heavens cannot be investigated because of their height: they extend endlessly through the heights of the universe, and the expanses of heaven contain worlds without number. Their multitude and elevation make them beyond investigation. Although the earth is like a tiny point by comparison, it cannot be investigated because of its depth, which is covered by the vast abyss; no one knows what lies in its depths. Likewise, the heart of kings cannot be investigated. Royal government extends over innumerable nations, people, and endless particulars, and it contains profound affairs, royal mysteries, and secrets that cannot be investigated to their full nature.
text.24_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Remove the dross from the silver; remove the wicked man from before the king. The king's throne was established to practice justice, as it says, “Behold, a king will reign for righteousness.” But the throne requires ministers and counselors through whom judgment is brought to light. If his servants are righteous, the throne is like refined silver cleansed of dross; if a wicked counselor is among them, he perverts justice and judgment does not come to light. Just as a silversmith who wishes to make a vessel of pure silver must remove its dross, so, if the throne is to be established in righteousness, one must remove the wicked man who stands before the king; then his throne will be established in righteousness.
text.24_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not glorify yourself before a king. Display no magnificence before a king, for your honor is null before the king's immeasurable honor. If you display splendor, as though your honor too had significance, you diminish the king's honor. Thus David said, “I will make merry before Hashem,” dancing and whirling like a commoner before Hashem. The Jerusalem Talmud explains “Awake, my glory” as: let my honor awaken before the honor of my Creator, for my honor is nothing before His. Likewise, do not stand in the place of the great; stand in a place lower than your rank, not one higher than it.
text.24_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: For it is better that they say to you, “Come up here.” If you stand in a low place, they will tell you to ascend, which brings honor. If you stand among the great, they will lower you before the nobleman whom your eyes have seen and whose rank you imagined you shared, bringing you disgrace. It also means that humbling yourself before this nobleman will itself cause them to say, “Come up,” because they will recognize that your eyes—your intellectual vision—perceive proper conduct and courtesy. As the Sages said, your humility is your elevation.
text.24_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not go out hastily to quarrel. Every action should be directed toward its intended result; one should not act when the consequence will be the opposite of the desired end. When someone disgraces you, do not hastily go out to quarrel, imagining that you will thereby restore your humiliated honor. Through the quarrel, not only will you fail to restore it, but what will you do in the end? The outcome will be that he humiliates you a second time. Instead of restoring your honor, you will gain shame and contempt.
text.24_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Contend your own contention with your fellow. Even if you must quarrel, contend only over your own dispute, which concerns you, and do not reveal another's secret.
text.24_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Lest one who hears disgrace you. Beyond your fellow's humiliation through the quarrel, everyone who hears will subject you to further disgrace, saying that you spread an evil report, gossip, and reveal secrets. Later, when you wish to retract your slander, you will be unable to do so, and you will thereby acquire unbroken shame and lasting disgrace.
text.24_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Apples of gold in settings of silver is a word spoken in its proper manner. Because apples of gold are precious, they are covered with settings of silver, which are less valuable but still important. From the silver settings one understands that gold lies beneath, since silver would not be placed over iron or copper. Likewise, speech is the setting of what is hidden within: the heart's secrets and a person's thoughts are revealed through his words. When the inner content is precious and the soul and its secrets are filled with honor, the speech too is precious, elevated, and free of dross. But if he speaks slander and gossip, it becomes known that iron and earthenware lie beneath his speech and that his soul is base. Thus the word is speech upon its wheels: speech turns and emerges according to the thought and meditation of the soul. If it proceeds according to its proper movement and does not exceed what is fitting, it resembles apples of gold in settings of silver.
text.24_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: A golden earring and an ornament of fine gold. An earring and ornament both adorn the ears. Just as they beautify the outer ear, so a wise reprover, who rebukes according to words of wisdom, adorns a listening ear. Its adornment is that the reproof comes from a possessor of wisdom, like gold and fine gold of Ophir.
text.24_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Like the coolness of snow on a harvest day. On a harvest day, when the sun burns like an oven and beats upon the reaper's head until he faints, the coolness of snow restores his soul. So too a faithful messenger is to those who send him. If the anger of a king and officials burns against his master and his life is endangered by their blazing wrath, he sends a faithful messenger to advocate for him; the messenger cools the fiery anger and restores his master's soul. A messenger, by definition, goes and returns with an answer, restoring the fainting soul. The verse also contains a metaphor: every person is a messenger sent into this world and must be faithful to those who sent him, fulfilling the purpose for which he was sent. He then restores his Master's soul—his own soul, a portion of God, returns to its abode. He will not fear the heat of the coming day that burns like an oven, for “snow falls in Tzalmon” and Gehinnom is cooled for him, as the Sages expounded.
text.24_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Clouds and wind, but no rain. Clouds appear to carry the gift of rain, but a wind comes, scatters them, and no rain falls. So too one who boasts and promises to give charity, but a wind passes over him, he does not give, and his word proves false. The Sages said that he is repaid measure for measure, and rain is withheld.
text.24_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Through patience an officer is persuaded, and a gentle tongue breaks bone. If an officer is angry with you, do not attempt to have your offense completely dismissed, for one who grasps too much grasps nothing. Seek only that he delay his anger and not punish immediately; in this he may be persuaded to be patient. Afterward, a gentle tongue breaks bone, even the hardest bone. The parable comes from flesh-eating animals said to break bones with their tongues. So afterward, through supplications, one breaks the harsh attribute of judgment. The verse also alludes to Hashem, Who is persuaded through prayer to delay anger, after which the power of judgment is softened through a gentle tongue and supplication.
text.24_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: If you find honey, eat what is sufficient for you. Although it is honey and good food, and although you found it without effort, nevertheless do not eat much—only what is sufficient for you—lest you become satiated with it and vomit it. From this, learn the following lesson.
text.24_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Make your foot scarce from your fellow's house. Do not let him become excessively satiated with you even if you are as dear to him as honey, lest he become satiated with you and hate you. The Sages interpreted this metaphorically: do not continually bring sacrifices to the House of Hashem for your sins. Sacrifices are described as food; take care not to “eat” excessively.
text.24_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: A maul, a sword, and a sharpened arrow. These are three destructive weapons. A maul is a great hammer that shatters stones and bones; a sword cuts at close range; and an arrow kills from afar. So one who testifies falsely against his fellow is sometimes like a maul, scattering people and sending contention among brothers; sometimes like a sword that kills at close range; and sometimes like an arrow that kills from afar through secret slander. It also alludes to the Sages' statement that a threefold tongue kills three people—the speaker, the listener, and the subject. To the speaker himself it is a maul, to the listener a sword, and to the one spoken about an arrow.
text.24_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: A broken tooth and a slipping foot. A person trusts a tooth to chew his food, but if it breaks it betrays him; he trusts a foot to bring him to his destination, but if it slips it betrays him. So too is confidence that betrays on a day of trouble: he trusted something but does not find support when he needs it. It also alludes to the Sages' saying, “Examine the teeth and you will find it in the feet.” When the tooth is broken the foot also slips; likewise, when one source of confidence betrays him, it draws the rest after it and all betray him.
text.24_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: One who removes a garment on a cold day. Singing songs, which are intended to gladden the soul, to a sorrowful heart resembles wearing ornamental garments on a cold day. Though beautiful on a clear day, in cold weather they are not only unbeautiful but fail to warm the body, which chills; warm clothing is needed then. Likewise, these songs will not gladden him or brighten his face, but will increase his sadness. It also resembles pouring vinegar upon natron. Although strong vinegar can strengthen a vessel prepared for it, soft natron dissolves, the vessel is ruined, and the vinegar spills. So songs will not strengthen his soul, but will break his heart and fail to penetrate the inward person and deep heart. This is a parable for applying anything to something unprepared to receive it. The Sages interpreted it of one who teaches Torah to an unworthy student: the student's exterior has not been beautified by good deeds, and he cannot contain the waters of wisdom; he dissolves and goes wandering.
text.24_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: If your enemy is hungry, feed him bread. One who wishes to take a great revenge upon his enemy should not take revenge by withholding bread and water. On the contrary, he should do him every good: if he is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him water to drink, for you will gain two things.
text.24_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: * First, you heap coals upon his head. When you do good to him, he feels as though you heap burning coals upon his head, for he remembers how he sinned against you and harmed you, and is ashamed and humiliated that he must now receive bread and water from you in return for his evil. Second, Hashem will repay you: you will receive reward from Hashem for the charity you performed. If you take revenge by refusing to give him, you will receive no reward.
text.24_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: The north wind brings forth rain. The north wind generates rain. Vapors rising from the earth are filled with light airy spirit and are thereby carried upward. When the north wind leaves the vapors, the drops of water, made heavy when the wind departs, fall downward as rain. Although the north wind itself is invisible, when rain appears we know its cause, for the wind produced it. Likewise, a secret tongue brings forth angry faces. Although the stormy wind born from slander is hidden deep in the heart, it becomes recognizable through the angry expression visible on the offended person's face.
text.24_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: It is better to dwell on a corner of the roof than with a contentious wife in a shared house. This was already stated above and is repeated here in light of what is said below: “A constant dripping on a rainy day and a contentious wife are alike; one who would hide her would hide the wind.” It compares a contentious wife to constant dripping. Rain is generated by the north wind emerging from its enclosure; if one attempts to contain this north wind that produces the rain, he has hidden wind, yet the oil in his right hand still calls attention to itself. Thus, after saying that the north wind brings forth rain, it says that the hidden spirit of a contentious wife likewise gives birth to quarrels. It is better to dwell on a corner of a roof with no shelter from rain falling above than to dwell with the constant dripping that drives everyone from a shared house, for there is no shelter from it.
text.24_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: Cold water upon a weary soul. Just as cold water is brought to a weary person thirsting in a place without water, carried from elsewhere, so one whose soul is weary to hear what has happened to his family or household in a distant land, from whom he has no news, receives good tidings from there concerning their welfare. It restores his weary soul within him and revives him.
text.24_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: A muddied spring and a ruined source is a righteous person who falters before the wicked. A source lies deep in the earth, from which water flows into a spring. When a righteous person falters, even if the spring is spoiled—meaning his abundance, wealth, and livelihood—the source is not ruined, for it is his trust in Hashem, from which abundance flows to the spring. But if he falters before a wicked person, then beyond the spring becoming muddied, the source—trust in Hashem—is also ruined, for people will cast doubts upon Providence: “Why are You silent when a wicked man swallows one more righteous than he?” and the like.
text.24_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: Eating much honey is not good, and investigating their honor is honor. It answers that just as excessive eating of honey is not good, so excessive investigation of their honor is not honor. One who extensively investigates the honor of the righteous will not attain it, because the phenomenon of a righteous person faltering before the wicked belongs to the secrets of Providence, concerning which “It is the glory of God to conceal a matter.” Just as too much honey causes harm, one should not investigate excessively. Although you see the honor of the righteous profaned by the wicked, honor in this world is not true honor. Essential honor is in the eternal world, where true honor exists, as it says, “You will guide me with Your counsel, and afterward take me to honor.” Since eternal spiritual honor is among God's secrets—the intellect, while imprisoned in matter, cannot comprehend the honor of a spiritual soul separated from matter—one should not investigate excessively. Rather, the righteous person lives by his faith and does not doubt it.
text.24_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: A breached city without a wall is a man who has no restraint over his spirit. Man has already been compared to a small city besieged by a great king: the inclination, imagination, and appetitive faculty seek to conquer the soul's powers, while the good inclination fights for the city and prevents the soul's enemies from taking it. The lofty wall that restrains the attacker is the restraint placed upon the spirit, for the spirit raises images to the heart, and most human inclinations are evil—images of pride, envy, revenge, and the like. When the spirit rises and brings evil images into the heart, the enemy reaches the city and battle is joined within it; one can then easily be drawn after those images and act according to their tumult. But man possesses a ruling faculty that can restrain the spirit and still its noise, as it says, “A fool releases all his spirit, but a wise man quiets it from behind.” This is the wall that prevents the enemy from entering the city. But one who has no restraint over his spirit allows evil images to rise in his heart; the inclination prevails and the soul's enemies conquer the city, for no wall restrains them.
text.25_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Like snow in summer and rain at harvest. Snow and rain both benefit seed and grain: snow makes the earth fruitful, and rain causes it to sprout, as stated in Isaiah 55. Nevertheless, they are not good in summer and harvest, when there is no seed. Rain harms the harvest, which precedes summer, by rotting the ripened grain; snow harms in summer, when the sun's heat is needed to dry the figs. If snow comes early in summer, though its proper time follows the rain after summer, or rain comes at harvest, though its time follows summer, their untimely arrival causes loss and destruction. So honor is not fitting for a fool. Honor given to a wise person, who has plowed and sown the Divine seed of wisdom in the portion of his soul, benefits him like rain and snow: it arouses his spiritual powers to bring all his potential into actuality. But honor given to a fool who has sown nothing causes destruction and corruption, for it strengthens him in his folly. It is out of place and destructive. See verse 8 below.
text.25_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Like a bird wandering, like a swallow flying. The bird nests even in a house, yet naturally wanders from place to place and does not remain permanently. The free swallow accepts no authority and is not found in a house at all, only in a nest, as it says, “Even the bird has found a house, and the swallow a nest for herself”; it flies far outside the house. Likewise, an undeserved curse will not come. According to the written form, not only will it fail to remain permanently and will wander like a bird, it will not enter the house even temporarily, like a swallow flying away. According to the reading with vav, it will come to him—it returns to the one who curses, like the bird and swallow that return to their own nests after wandering and flying.
text.25_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools. Unreasoning animals, lacking intelligence to guide themselves, require a whip or bridle. A horse needs a whip; a donkey, still more foolish and not understanding even through a whip, needs a bridle to restrain it from leaving the road. Man possesses intelligence and choice and should follow the good path independently. But a fool, who departs from wisdom because of appetite, resembles an animal guided by nature rather than intellect and likewise requires a rod; through punishment and suffering he is compelled to follow the paved road.
text.25_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you too become like him. A fool does not observe the laws of wisdom because he follows appetite, which opposes them. To mask his conduct and pacify his soul when those laws stand against the flood of his desire, he pursues ignorance—that is, he casts doubts upon the laws of wisdom and faith. Arguing with him to refute those doubts accomplishes nothing, for he too knows the laws of wisdom but forcefully casts them aside because of his appetitive inclination, as it says, “The folly of fools is deceit” and “The folly of fools is folly.” Even if his opponent presents sensory facts, he stops his ears, as explained in “Go away from a foolish man, for you will not know lips of knowledge.” It is therefore better not to answer his folly and doubts, lest you become like him, as though you too were uncertain and needed to resolve the doubts. Alternatively: do not answer the fool merely from fear that, if you remain silent, people will think you are like him; do not argue simply to display your wisdom. Nevertheless:
text.25_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes. Answer him in a manner that prevents him from imagining himself wise because you found no response. Answer with simple words whose main purpose is to show that he is a fool, not with sharp arguments designed to display your own wisdom. The following verses explain what to answer him.
text.25_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: He cuts off feet and drinks violence who sends messages by the hand of a fool. The legs of a lame man hang down, and so does a proverb in the mouth of fools. Answer him with this response: the violence he drinks, which cuts off the feet, sends messages by the hand of the fool.
text.25_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: What message does it send? It says, “The legs of a lame man hang down.” The metaphor compares the banquet of appetite that the fool drinks—his being drawn after desire like one drunk with wine—except that he drinks violence instead of wine. The violence he drinks cuts off feet. Just as wine disables the drunkard's feet so that he cannot stand, violence cuts off the feet of the fool who drinks it.
text.25_Chapter, 5_Verse, 2_Comment: It depicts the violence that he drank, which cut off his feet and made him lame through intoxication, as sending a message concerning the lame man: let them also remove his legs. The leg is above the foot and supports the body; the body rests on the legs, and the legs are carried by the feet. But to a lame man who cannot walk on his feet, the legs are a burden and superfluous, and they too must be lifted, removed, and cut off.
text.25_Chapter, 5_Verse, 3_Comment: These words sent by the violence he drank—through the fool—to remove the legs of the lame man whose feet were cut off are the proverb in the mouth of fools. After becoming drunk with the wine of appetite, the fool cannot stand upon his feet—that is, he cannot conduct himself in practice according to the ways of wisdom, but reels and staggers like one drunk with desire. He therefore wishes to remove and cut off the legs as well—the foundations and bases of wisdom—by casting ignorance and doubts upon them. Since appetite has made him lame and unable to stand firmly against desire, the legs upon which man stands, the laws of wisdom, seem to him superfluous and burdensome; he wishes to cut them off just as legs are superfluous to one whose feet have already been severed.
text.25_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Like binding a stone in a sling is one who gives honor to a fool. It explains why you should not answer him at length and respectfully, but contemptuously. One who binds a stone into a sling appears to honor the stone by wrapping and securing it, but does so only to hurl it at people, stone them, and kill them. Likewise, the honor you give the fool by answering him with wisdom will be cast from his sling to kill upright people, for he will transform your answers into sling-stones of heresy.
text.25_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: A thorn rises into the hand of a drunkard, and a proverb into the mouth of fools. This fool, drunk with the wine of appetite and with his feet and legs cut off as described above, lies down and moves upon his hands until a thorn pierces the hands upon which he walks. Nevertheless, a proverb remains in the mouth of fools with which he seeks to cut off the legs—the pillars of wisdom. The next verse explains the proverb in his mouth.
text.25_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: The Great One brings forth all, and hires the fool and hires transgressors. He says that Hashem creates and produces all people—the righteous and wicked, those who walk in wisdom and those drawn after appetite. Everything comes from Hashem, and man possesses no free choice. Hashem “hires” the fool, giving wages even to the fool drawn after appetite, and gives wages to those who transgress His commandments and to every passerby in the world. Righteous and wicked alike are His hired workers, acting according to how He created them and the power He implanted within them, whether for wisdom or appetite. There is therefore no deed, knowledge, reckoning, or punishment, because man has no choice and is compelled in his actions; a hired worker merely comes for his wages.
text.25_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Like a dog returning to its vomit, a fool repeats his folly. After explaining that one should answer the fool with simple words of contempt, it explains why he should not answer him through wise argument. The fool repeats his folly like a dog returning to swallow food it vomited—bad food it could not tolerate, yet swallows again. So the fool returns to repeat the ignorance he vomited, although he himself knows it is repulsive. We have explained that the fool knows his folly and doubts have no substance, as it says, “The folly of fools is deceit” and “The folly of fools is folly”; nevertheless he repeats them. What benefit can argument provide?
text.25_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Have you seen a man wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him. It now explains why one must answer the fool in a way that prevents him from becoming wise in his own eyes, and what is lost if he does. A fool has more hope than one wise in his own eyes. The fool is drawn after his appetites and breaches the boundaries of wisdom because of their flood, though he knows wisdom's value. There is therefore hope that when his appetite eventually subsides, he will repent and accept discipline. But one wise in his own eyes imagines that his actions accord with wisdom. He knowingly disputes true wisdom, not because appetite compels him, but because he imagines that his corrupt way is wisdom. He has no remedy. You must therefore answer him so that he at least knows that his path is not the path of wisdom; then hope remains.
text.25_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: The lazy man says, “There is a lion on the road.” The lazy person, who does not seek wisdom because of laziness, will ultimately reach the still worse trait of being wise in his own eyes, which is worse than being a fool. Wisdom requires diligence and much labor. The lazy person who relaxes his hands from it comes to imagine himself wise, thinking that all his deeds accord with wisdom and that he need not seek its laws from the wise. He imagines that a great lion is on the road and a smaller lion in the city streets. That is:
text.25_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: * If he goes out to seek lofty forms of wisdom that are not commonly available, such as the Account of Creation and the Chariot, he says the great lion will devour him—meaning that he will fall into heresy;
text.25_Chapter, 12_Verse, 2_Comment: * And even if he studies commonly available matters of wisdom, he fears that a smaller lion will devour him, as was also stated above.
text.25_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: As the door turns on its hinge, so the lazy man turns upon his bed from side to side without leaving his couch.
text.25_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: The lazy man buries his hand in the dish. Even when food is given to him, he extends his hand into the vessel containing it but is too weary to return it to his mouth and put food into it. The application is that even when essential food for the soul is given to him, he buries his hand in its vessel but does not take the food itself. For example, when given the Torah's narratives, which one must know, he consumes only the external garment and story of events, without taking the inner content, discipline, and wisdom beneath the vessel and garment.
text.25_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: The lazy man is wise in his own eyes, wiser in his estimation than seven great sages who answer him with reason and explain the reasons and inner meaning of things. He imagines himself wiser than they; this is the man for whom there is less hope than for a fool.
text.25_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Like one who grasps a passing dog by the ears. A passing dog was going on its way and had not barked at him, but when he grasps its ears it barks at and bites him. So is one who becomes enraged over a quarrel not his own. The quarrel that barks and sharpens its tongue like a dog had not barked at him; by grasping the barker's ears, he causes it now to bark at him, speak insults and contempt against him, and even bite him.
text.25_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Like a madman... Like one who mocks his fellow: first he shoots sparks of fire that burn garments, then arrows that inflict wounds, and afterward arrows smeared with the drug of death that kill.
text.25_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: So is a man who deceives his fellow. One who deceives his fellow first harms his possessions, then his body, and afterward his soul—yet to him it is all like play.
text.25_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Without wood, fire goes out; without a complainer, contention grows silent. Contention consists of matters aroused for which people go to judgment before a judge. It has been explained that hatred arouses contentions, because without hatred people would not object to minor harms from neighbors but would yield to one another. A complainer continually claims that others harm him and thereby arouses disputes. Without a complainer to protest, contention becomes silent, just as fire goes out without wood.
text.25_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: Coal for embers and wood for fire. To kindle embers, a coal—a spark of fire—is sufficient; to kindle a great fire, however, wood is needed and a coal does not suffice. Likewise, to kindle a quarrel, a contentious man who arouses disputes is sufficient, like a spark and coal that starts the quarrel. But to ignite a great fire requires the words of a complainer, which are like blows, as though others struck him severely. In truth, they are not blows from outside, but descend into the chambers of his belly—he only imagines them so. This is also a parable for one who complains about the attributes of the Holy One, blessed is He. There is an ordinary contentious person, and worse than him a chronic complainer who thinks Hashem created man for evil and that evils outnumber benefits, as explained above (18:3).
text.25_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: Drossy silver plated upon earthenware. Worse still than the complainer is one who speaks one thing with his mouth and another in his heart: burning lips, aflame with apparent love, while the heart is evil. This resembles drossy silver plated upon earthenware, deceptively appearing to be silver while truly being clay.
text.25_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: An enemy disguises himself with his lips. The enemy makes himself foreign and unrecognizable with his lips, disguising his hatred in outward speech as though he were a friend, while within himself he sets plans to deceive and cast the other into destruction. Metaphorically, this refers to a hypocrite who flatters with his lips while his heart is distant: with his lips he disguises himself as a believer and servant of Hashem, while he deceives in his heart.
text.25_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: When he makes his voice gracious, do not believe him. Do not believe the apparent supplication in his voice, for many abominations are in his heart. In the application, do not believe him merely because he multiplies prayer, for his heart is filled with abomination.
text.25_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: Hatred is covered by deception. Hatred covers its plans in darkness—that is, he conceals in his heart what he intends to do through hatred. Afterward his evil will be revealed in the assembly, until ultimately:
text.25_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: One who digs a pit will fall into it. He himself will fall into the pit he dug, and one who rolls a stone to harm his fellow will have the stone return upon the one who rolled it. The next verse explains the reason.
text.25_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: A lying tongue hates those crushed by it. It depicts metaphorically that the lying tongue itself hates those humbled before it. The habitual receiver of slander loves bold speakers, not crushed and timid ones. Those who speak slander quietly and secretly because they fear to speak openly are hated by the lying tongue, for their fear testifies that their words have no substance. A smooth mouth brings about a downfall. The smooth mouth itself—which speaks flattering words and says one thing with the mouth while another is in the heart—creates a slippery place that casts down the person who uses it; he himself will slip and fall into the pit.
text.26_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not boast about tomorrow—Since the events of time renew themselves at every moment, you cannot boast about what you will do tomorrow, for even what the present day will bring is unknown to you, and tomorrow is not yours.
text.26_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Let a stranger praise you, and not your own mouth; a foreigner, and not your lips—A person’s praise of himself is no praise. It is better that you perform deeds worthy of praise, so that a stranger will praise you. There is a difference between a stranger and a foreigner: a foreigner is from another land. He says that after a stranger praises you, even the foreigner who does not know you will praise you, for he will hear it from the stranger, who will publicize your praise. Moreover, the “not” of your lips—the very fact that you do not praise yourself with your lips—will itself praise you, for it demonstrates humility and virtue. The lip is external in relation to the mouth; that is, others will not hear you praising yourself even from your lips. Alternatively, they will hear “not” from your lips, meaning that you minimize yourself and say that you do not possess this praise—as the Sages said, “In three matters scholars deviate from the truth,” etc.—and this too will bring you praise.
text.26_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: A stone is heavy, and sand is a burden—A stone is heavy in itself, even a single stone, whereas sand is heavy only when much of it is lifted upon one’s shoulders; its weight comes through its accumulation into a load and burden. But a fool’s anger is heavier than both, for each separate outburst of anger has its own weight, like a burdensome stone, while the accumulation of all his continual angry outbursts has the weight of sand. Thus the Midrash applies this verse to “Come to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart”: Pharaoh’s sin in saying, “Who is the Lord? I do not know the Lord,” was heavy like a stone, and by continuing to harden his heart time after time, he acquired the heaviness of sand. His burden was therefore compounded of both stone and sand.
text.26_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Wrath is cruel, and anger is a flood, but who can stand before jealousy? Wrath is the inward anger that preserves hatred in the heart, while anger is its outward expression. There can be anger without inward wrath, and it has the quality of a flood, for in his anger a person sweeps forward and chastises, but without cruelty. There can also be wrath without outward anger: his fury burns in his heart and contains the cruelty of hatred and wrath, but not the flood, for he does not punish at once. Jealousy for one’s violated honor, however, contains both cruelty and flood, for the jealous person takes revenge immediately in a flood of anger and acts with the cruelty of wrath.
text.26_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Open rebuke is better than hidden love—If a person rebukes his fellow for his evil way, and the rebuke proceeds from hidden love, like a father rebuking his son out of his great love for him—as it says, “For the Lord rebukes the one He loves”—then even though this rebuke is given openly, it is very good.
text.26_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Faithful are the wounds of a friend—Even if a loving friend strikes him to discipline him and return him to the good path, the love remains faithful, for all this proceeds from great love, as it says, “As a man disciplines his son, the Lord your God disciplines you.” But the kisses of an enemy are profuse: the enemy multiplies kisses and neither disciplines nor rebukes, because in his hatred, when he sees the other acting badly, he kisses him so that he will continue doing so.
text.26_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: A satisfied soul tramples honeycomb, but to a hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet—What is pleasant or unpleasant does not depend upon the nature of the food, but upon the condition of the person. One accustomed to delicacies comes to despise them, while one who lacks them finds pleasure in everything. This rebukes those who seek delicacies and pursue them, for the more abundantly they obtain them, the more their pleasure ceases; conversely, they would enjoy everything if it had been withheld from them. The poor person finds more pleasure than the rich. It is therefore clear that such pleasures are not the sought-after purpose: they are attained when they are not attained, and not attained when they are attained.
text.26_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Like a bird wandering from its nest, so is a man wandering from his place—Human beings share their natural constitution with other living creatures, and it is embedded in animal nature not to change their place. Even a bird, whose way is to wander—as it says, “Like a bird that wanders”—nevertheless seeks to return when it has wandered from its nest. Likewise, it is human nature to return to one’s place. The allegory is that the human soul also longs to return to its place, to God who gave it. While it is in this world it is like a bird wandering from its nest, yearning to return to its place and be bound in the bond of life.
text.26_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Oil and incense gladden the heart—The heart, which is the dwelling place of the vital soul, rejoices through fragrant oil and incense. Although God has already arranged that it draw in pure air and that the lungs wave life-giving air over the heart, the spirituality of the soul is awakened by fragrance coming from outside, which adds strength to its inward power. So too, although the power of counsel is implanted in the soul, it is strengthened through the sweetness of one’s friend: by sweetly consulting with his friend, so that when his friend’s counsel comes from outside and joins the counsel of the soul, the counsel becomes complete.
text.26_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not forsake your friend or your father’s friend—If you have a companion whose love has long been proven to you, so that he was always your friend and your father’s friend, do not forsake him. Although nature implants love between brothers, a brother’s love may exist only while things go well for you and you do not need him. But on the day of your calamity his love may cease, either because “all the brothers of a poor man hate him,” or because he will not wish to help you. Then a neighbor who is near—one close to you because he constantly dwells beside you—is better than one who is far away, even if he is a brother.
text.26_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Be wise, my son, and gladden my heart, so that I may answer the one who taunts me—That is, even if until now you have not accepted the laws of wisdom, be wise now and gladden my heart, for until now people taunted me because of you, as the Sages said, “Cursed is the one who bore him; cursed is the one who raised him.” Now I will be able to answer the one who taunts me.
text.26_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: A prudent man sees evil and hides—This was already explained above (22:3). There it referred to the evil of circumstances; here, in the allegory, it refers to evil affecting the soul. The prudent person foresees the punishment destined for one who abandons wisdom. This relates to “Be wise, my son”: see the end of a matter from its beginning, and do not be like the simple.
text.26_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Take his garment, for he has guaranteed a stranger—This was already explained above (20:16). There it was stated according to the literal illustration, and here it is repeated according to the allegorical meaning explained there.
text.26_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: One who blesses his friend in a loud voice, rising early in the morning—it will be considered a curse to him—A blessing should be given discreetly, not loudly, lest the evil eye take hold of it, and it should be given at a favorable time after prayer, not early in the morning, since one should not greet another before praying; otherwise, it is considered a curse. This may also continue the preceding verse, “Take his garment, for he has guaranteed a stranger.” One may not take security from the borrower himself, but may take it from the guarantor. One must return a garment needed at night, and Scripture says, “He shall lie down in his garment and bless you”; the Sifrei says it is a mitzvah for him to bless the lender, though even if he does not, “it shall be righteousness for you.” But one is not required to return the guarantor’s pledge. Thus, if the guarantor comes in the morning and loudly blesses him as if the pledge had been returned, that blessing is considered a curse, since there was no obligation to return the guarantor’s pledge and he is not owed a blessing.
text.26_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: A constant dripping on a rainy day—Dripping is troublesome only on a rainy day, when the clouds are closed together by the wind that God brings forth, as it says, “He brings forth the wind from His storehouses.” But a contentious wife is comparable to it at all times, for she constantly troubles him even on a clear day.
text.26_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: One who conceals her conceals the wind, and the oil on his right hand calls out—It has already been explained that the north wind brings forth rain: as it emerges laden with vapors it generates rain, while so long as it remains hidden within the vapors there is no rain. But if one wishes to hide the wind of this woman and restrain the rain, he is trying to hide the wind even as it roars and storms to emerge. Moreover, the oil found on his right hand, applied to the blows he received from her—for blows are customarily softened with oil, as it says, “They have not been bound up or softened with oil”—will call out, publicize the matter, and expose what was hidden.
text.26_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Iron sharpens iron—The defining form of a sword or knife is its sharpness. When one wishes to restore its form, one sharpens the iron against another piece of iron and removes the rust. So a man sharpens the face of his friend—his defining form—because when they occupy themselves with wisdom and each helps the other understand, as the Sages said, “I learned much from my teachers, and more from my colleagues,” their faces, which represent their form, are sharpened; for the form of a human being is his intellect, wisdom, and powers of the soul.
