text.26_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: One who guards a fig tree will eat its fruit, and one who attends his master will be honored—One who wishes to eat the fruit of the fig tree must guard it carefully—for this term denotes more than ordinary guarding—because its fruits ripen one by one and must be gathered every morning before sunrise; otherwise the ripe fruits become wormy, as stated in the Midrash and Jerusalem Talmud. Likewise, one who attends his master must be present every morning to gather the fruits—that is, the fruits of his master’s wisdom—as Scripture says of Joshua, “He did not depart from within the tent.” Through this, he will be honored: Joshua merited the honor of Moses laying his hands upon him, as the Sages taught.
text.26_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: As water reflects face to face, so the heart of man reflects man—The heart sends the flow of blood to all the limbs and gives them life, while all the limbs return the choicest blood to the heart. Thus the heart gives back to a person what it received from him. It resembles water, in which an observer sees his face: the face that the water presents to his eye is the same face it received from the form of the person standing before it. So too, the heart returns what it receives. The heart tells a person his inner speech, for the form of all his powers appears in the heart; it therefore sees all his powers and foretells good or evil to him, just as the form of a person’s face appears in water. This also serves as an allegory for the general “heart” of a collective body: the king is the heart of the state, and the Torah scholar the heart of the community. What the people give the king in taxes and the like returns to them, just as the limbs receive from the heart after supplying it; likewise, what they give to support a Torah scholar returns to them as blessing through his merit. God is the heart of creation: according to how people prepare their deeds, they give strength, as it were, to the power above to bestow abundant blessing upon them. Zion was the heart of the Land of Israel, and the abundance brought to Zion and the Temple returned to the people, as it says, “For there the Lord commanded the blessing,” and similarly in other cases.
text.26_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Sheol and destruction are never satisfied, and the eyes of man are never satisfied—A person’s eyes and desires are never satisfied, for whatever temporal delight he attains causes him to seek still more. The matter from which man was created is prime matter, constantly casting off one form and clothing itself in another without interruption. Sheol and destruction are never satisfied, because matter does not remain for even a moment without continual loss and destruction. Human nature is likewise to seek novelties at every moment: every desired thing that reaches his hand is immediately lost to him as an object of desire, and he seeks another in its place. His eyes are also never satisfied with wealth, because this belongs to the nature of his prime matter, with Sheol and destruction bound to its heel.
text.26_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: A refining pot is for silver and a furnace for gold, and a man is tested according to his praise—Silver is refined in a refining pot, while gold, which is more precious and better than silver, requires a furnace whose fire is greater, because it does not melt and release its impurities as easily as silver; and because of its greater value, greater care is taken that it be entirely free of dross. So too, a man is refined according to the measure of his praise: the more highly praised he is, the more particular people are about even the slightest impurity. Thus the inadvertent sins of Torah scholars are regarded as deliberate ones, and they are refined by fire and sufferings more severe than those of ordinary people.
text.26_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: Though you pound a fool in a mortar among crushed grain with a pestle, his folly will not depart from him—The fool will not be refined, nor will his impurities be removed even by the greatest sufferings. The fool is one who doubts the laws of wisdom and does not believe in them; therefore suffering does not help him. This differs from the dullard, who does not doubt the laws of wisdom but is blinded by desire, and from the simple person, who has no doubts of his own but is seduced by the counsel of others, as it says, “The simple inherit folly.” These can be disciplined, unlike the fool, who attributes everything to chance. We explained at Isaiah 28 that some grains have chaff attached only as a neighbor and it is easily removed, whereas the husk of wheat or barley, when one wishes to make groats from it, must be pounded in a mortar because it is intrinsically attached. Yet even if the fool is pounded in a mortar, his husk will not be removed, for it has become mingled with his inward being: the root of folly lies in his intellect, unlike the dullard, whose defect is rooted in desire. Even when the fool is pounded, he doubts both the pounding and its purpose. Though he is pounded among the crushed grain and sees that all the groats have lost their husks, recognizes that this is the purpose of the pounding, and identifies the pestle as the instrument made for that purpose, he nevertheless remains in doubt and persists in his folly. That is, even when he sees general sufferings and many wicked people repenting, he remains with his doubts and folly.
text.26_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: Know well the condition of your flocks—This teaches you not to leave your affairs in the hands of others, but to supervise them yourself until you know your sheep face to face; and endeavor that they be fruitful and multiply until they become flocks upon flocks.
text.26_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: For wealth is not forever—Even if you possess strength and vast wealth, do not rely upon it, for it does not last forever and you may become impoverished. Even if you possess a crown that endures throughout your lifetime, it does not endure from generation to generation, and your children may not inherit it.
text.26_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: The hay is removed—When summer arrives and the hay appears, which is food for cattle kept at home, as it says, “Who causes grass to grow for the cattle,” and the fresh grass is seen clothing the ground for pasture in the field, then the vegetation of the mountains, to which the sheep cannot climb, is gathered into the house and prepared for a time of need. Then:
text.26_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: Lambs will provide your clothing—The lambs, whose wool is suitable for clothing—as the Sages explained regarding why they are called kevasim—will supply your clothing; the goats you will sell, and with their price purchase a field.
text.26_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: And there will be enough goats’ milk for your food—The goats, whose milk is beneficial to health, will provide food for you and your household. Even the maidservants, though they do not consume the milk regularly as their staple food, will derive life and health from it.
text.27_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: The wicked flee when no one pursues—The wicked person is always afraid, to the point that he flees when no one pursues. Moreover, when even one wicked person is found among the people, fear falls upon them all and they all flee. But the righteous are like a young lion that is confident even when pursuers come against it, as it says, “As the lion and the young lion growl over their prey,” etc.
text.27_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Because of a land’s rebellion, its rulers are many—Sometimes, when a land rebels against its king, the people think they are casting off the yoke of one man; as a result, many tyrannical rulers rise over it, all governing and oppressing the land.
text.27_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: Only if there is then an understanding man who knows what is right—that is, one who knows the principles of justice and can halt the flood of rebellion—will he prolong it, meaning that he will bring healing and a cure to this illness.
text.27_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: A poor man who oppresses the needy—That is, sometimes the rulers do not prevail; rather, the poor prevail through their rebellion, and all the people rule over one another. Those poor people who have nothing oppress the needy, whose property was depleted through the rebellion.
text.27_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: This resembles a sweeping rain: when rain comes through the bursting of clouds, a torrent of water breaks forth and sweeps everything away, until there is no bread. Instead of bringing bread, the rain carries everything away, and no bread comes because of it. So too, the flood of impoverished oppressors sweeps everything away like mighty rushing waters.
text.27_Chapter, 2_Verse, 2_Comment: The same metaphor appears in Job 13.
text.27_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Those who forsake the Torah praise the wicked—Those who forsake the Torah envy the wicked person’s success and praise his deeds. But those who keep the Torah understand that his deeds are evil and that he will ultimately be punished, and they contend with those who praise the wicked.
text.27_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: It may also refer back to what was stated above: in a time of transgression and rebellion, a wicked man rises to rule the people. Those who forsake the Torah praise his conduct of violence and plunder, while those who keep the Torah enter into contention and war with the wicked ruler and the faction that supports him.
text.27_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Evil men do not understand justice—According to the first interpretation, evil men praise the wicked because they do not understand the Lord’s justice, by which He repays the wicked according to his wickedness. Those who keep the Torah, being seekers of the Lord, understand all the Lord’s ways as righteous and just, and therefore contend with them. According to the second interpretation, evil men praise a wicked ruler who robs justice and governs by murder because they do not understand justice: since they persist in evil, the opposite of the ways of justice, they do not recognize the value of justice at all. But seekers of the Lord understand and teach everyone the ways of justice and the evil of the wicked ruler’s conduct.
text.27_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than one who is crooked in his ways, though he is rich—This depicts two roads. One begins with thorns and ends in level ground; the poor man travels it, and it is the straight road to the desired destination. Though he is poor now, he walks in integrity and its end is level. The rich man twists his ways and travels a road whose beginning is level but which is crooked because it ends in thorns; in the end, he will become poor.
text.27_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: One who keeps the Torah is an understanding son—The understanding son does not pursue gluttony and desire, because he keeps the Torah, which restrains his desires. But the son who turns rebelliously from the ways of the Torah associates with gluttons and shames his father who begot him, for it would have been better had he not come into the world. The Torah has testified to his end: ultimately he will rob people.
text.27_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: One who increases his wealth—All these verses explain “Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity.” He first explained that if the beginning is thorny because one restrains desire, the end is level, whereas the opposite course ends in thorns. Now he explains this regarding the accumulation of wealth: one who follows a crooked road whose beginning is level, increasing wealth through interest and usury, will ultimately lose it and see his money vanish. The one who is gracious to the poor by lending to them without charge, whose beginning is thorny, will receive the wealth accumulated through interest; his end will be level and he will become rich.
text.27_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: One who turns his ear away from hearing Torah—If a person turns away his ear and refuses to hear Torah study, even if he does so because the time for prayer has arrived, his prayer too is an abomination. Thus the Sages related in Shabbat 10a that Rabbi Yirmeyah was sitting before Rabbi Zeira when the time for prayer arrived and Rabbi Yirmeyah began to hurry; Rabbi Zeira applied to him the verse, “One who turns his ear away,” etc., because Torah is eternal life, while prayer concerns temporal life.
text.27_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: One who leads the upright astray onto an evil path—In the literal illustration, if a person sees upright people and leads them from the straight road onto an evil road so as to cast them into the pit he prepared, he himself will fall into his own pit: one who digs a pit will fall into it. But the wholehearted, who do not deceive, will inherit good, for one who had the opportunity to sin but refrained is rewarded. In the allegory, the verse speaks of the path of reasoning, for uprightness belongs to understanding. Although upright people follow a straight path, they may suffer an intellectual error—this is the meaning of “to err”—through someone who misleads their understanding. His punishment will be to fall into his own pit, for the corruption is attributed to the one who incites and leads astray, not to the person misled by him. The wholehearted, however, cannot be led into error in this way, for they do not rely upon their own understanding at all; they walk in wholehearted faith and live through faith. They inherit good like an inheritance that cannot be taken from them and that does not result from their own labor, for they rely not on the understanding of their hearts but on the inheritance of their faith.
text.27_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: (11–12) A rich man is wise in his own eyes; when the righteous rejoice, glory is great—It has already been explained that one who is wise in his own eyes is worse than a dullard. The dullard deviates from the ways of wisdom because of desire but knows that his ways deviate from wisdom; one who is wise in his own eyes thinks that his evil ways are the ways of wisdom and mocks the laws and concerns of wisdom. This can occur in many ways, one of them through great wealth: seeing his ways prosper and God not punishing his evil deeds, he thinks his deeds are desirable and conform to wisdom. But a poor man who has understanding, through which he can explain matters and uncover hidden truths, will examine him and understand that this is not so. Although the rich man prospers, his success is not true success, for wealth and the pleasures of this world are successes only for the animal body, which is not the true human being but a man disguised and clothed in animal form, like other creatures that readily find all their needs—indeed, none is richer than the pig. Such success is not glory for the true human being. But when the righteous rejoice—the verb “rejoice” always denotes the soul’s joy in spiritual matters—the righteous rejoice before God with spiritual joy through their righteousness, and in this glory is great, for their happiness is human happiness and brings glory to humanity. But when the wicked rise, a man disguises himself: the essential human being disguises and changes himself in his clothing, for the wicked person’s success belongs to the animal body, and the man disguises himself in animal garb; such people leave the category of man and become animals in human form.
text.27_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: One who conceals his transgressions will not prosper—A person who busies himself concealing his transgressions will not succeed in hiding them, for his evil will be revealed publicly; then people will not have mercy on him, having seen that he does not regret his evil but seeks to hide it from human beings even though it is known to God. But one who confesses his transgressions and undertakes to abandon his way thereby shows that he regrets and repents, and will be shown mercy.
text.27_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Fortunate is the man who makes himself fearful always—
text.27_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: There is a difference between one who fears, expressed in the simple verbal form, and one who makes himself fearful, expressed in the intensive form. The latter acts fearfully even where no actual cause for fear is present.
text.27_Chapter, 13_Verse, 2_Comment: One who is actually afraid thereby shows that he has sinned, as it says, “Sinners in Zion were afraid” (Isaiah 33:14), and as the Sages said in Berakhot 60a: when one Sage saw another afraid, he told him, “You are a sinner.”
text.27_Chapter, 13_Verse, 3_Comment: But fortunate is the person who makes himself fearful: although his heart is sound because he has not sinned, he makes himself fear lest he sin in the future, and thereby guards himself from sin and weighs his ways. One who hardens his heart is the opposite: he sees himself afflicted with suffering and has reason to fear, yet hardens his heart, like Pharaoh, who hardened his heart and did not fear the Lord. Such a person hardens his heart and will have no recovery.
text.27_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: A roaring lion and a ravenous bear—A lion roars when it has prey, but it growls when it has no prey and groans from distress; then it is very dangerous, for it will tear apart whatever it finds to satisfy its hunger. Likewise, a ravenous bear thirsts for blood. Such is a wicked ruler over a poor people. If he rules over the rich, from whom he has something to rob, he resembles a lion roaring over its prey and is not so dangerous; but over a poor people he continually growls for flesh, thirsts for blood, and destroys everyone he encounters.
text.27_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: A ruler lacking understanding and great in oppression—If a wicked ruler is not greatly oppressive, some people under his government will still earn money and survive. Even if he is greatly oppressive, if he possesses understanding, he will leave merchants who make profits in place, so that he can take taxes and gifts from them while they accumulate wealth for him. But if he also lacks understanding, then as soon as he sees a person who has gained profit and money, he kills him to take his wealth. He does not plan to preserve wealthy people and merchants in his realm, for he lacks the understanding to consider future days. Then only one who hates gain will prolong his days: only one who neither profits nor earns, and therefore appears poor, is not in danger of death; but one who profits and earns will not live long. The next verse explains this.
text.27_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: A man oppressed through the blood of a life—The person oppressed by this foolish ruler is oppressed unto bloodshed: the ruler not only seizes his money but spills his lifeblood. Even if the victim wishes to flee from the wicked ruler, he will flee until the pit, and no one will support him, for all are afraid to help him after the ruler has sentenced him to death because of his wealth, like Naboth the Jezreelite, who was killed so that Ahab could inherit his property.
text.27_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: One who walks wholeheartedly will be saved, but one crooked in two ways will fall in one—In every matter there are two paths, a path to the right and a path to the left. For example, among the paths of character traits:
text.27_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment: The paths of pride and humility;
text.27_Chapter, 17_Verse, 4_Comment: A person must conduct himself on every path according to wisdom—for example, being humble toward the righteous and proud against the wicked—and similarly with all the other traits.
text.27_Chapter, 17_Verse, 5_Comment: These two paths are called “two ways,” using the dual form, because they are paired, one corresponding to the other.
text.27_Chapter, 17_Verse, 6_Comment: One must walk each path wholeheartedly, and then he will be saved.
text.27_Chapter, 17_Verse, 7_Comment: But one who is crooked in both ways is crooked in each of the paired paths. For example:
text.27_Chapter, 17_Verse, 8_Comment: He is humble before the wicked but exalts himself over the righteous;
text.27_Chapter, 17_Verse, 9_Comment: He is generous for a sinful purpose but stingy for a mitzvah.
text.27_Chapter, 17_Verse, 10_Comment: Then he will fall in one—that is, in each one of the two paths he will fall into a snare.
text.27_Chapter, 17_Verse, 11_Comment: He will now explain an example of this.
text.27_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: (19–20) One who works his land will be satisfied with bread; a faithful man abounds in blessings—The illustration contrasts diligence and idleness, and in each there is wholeheartedness and crookedness. On the path of diligence there is wholeheartedness when a person works his land and enjoys the labor of his hands; he will be satisfied with bread, and this is the good aspect of diligence. Conversely, one who pursues empty things and does nothing will be satisfied with poverty, the evil path of idleness. Yet there is also a good aspect of idleness: a person should not be excessively diligent and rush to become rich through robbery and murder, for such diligence is evil and crooked. Here idleness is good: after working his land, he should adopt the path of restraint, become a faithful man, and trust that God will send blessing upon the seed he planted and the produce of his vineyard. Then he will abound in blessings, for God will send him His blessing. But one who hastens to become rich will not go unpunished; this is the crookedness within the path of diligence. Thus one road begins with thorns and ends in level ground: one who works his land first toils and labors, but its end is level, for he then rests and trusts, and afterward is satisfied with bread from God’s blessing and the fruit of his hands. The other road begins level and ends in thorns: one pursues empty things, then hastens to become rich through violence; therefore he will not go unpunished, and in the end will be satisfied with poverty.
text.27_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: Showing favoritism is not good—Even if you recognize someone as trustworthy, you cannot always rely upon your recognition of his face, because sometimes, under pressure and lacking bread, even a strong man who ordinarily masters his impulse may transgress for a piece of bread because of poverty. Following this introduction, Scripture now addresses the miserly.
text.27_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: A miserly man hastens after wealth—The miserly person, unwilling to give to others, hastens after wealth; therefore poverty will come upon him, for wicked people will rise and plunder his money. If even a faithful man may fail under the pressure of hunger, all the more so the masses. This is also the meaning of the sequence above (22:6–7): “The borrower is servant,” “One who sows injustice,” “One with a good eye will be blessed,” etc. Alternatively, the deprivation he caused will come upon him: through his miserly hoarding of grain to accumulate wealth, he deprived the poor of bread; that very deprivation will come upon him and his wealth will be plundered. On the allegorical level, this may also mean, “The salt that preserves money is diminution”: wealth comes to a person specifically through giving some away, not through hoarding.
text.27_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: One who rebukes a person will afterward find more favor than one who flatters with his tongue—Ordinarily, people favor one who does not rebuke their sins, especially one who smooths his tongue to praise and flatter their deeds. Thus the Sages said of a Torah scholar beloved by his townspeople that this may be because he does not rebuke them regarding heavenly matters. It would therefore seem that the flatterer finds more favor than the rebuker. But this is true only at first. Later, if punishment comes for their evil deeds, they will realize that the rebuker admonished them for their own good while the flatterer harmed them. Then, afterward—after matters have reached their conclusion and the end of the affair—the rebuker will find more favor than the flatterer.
text.27_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: One who robs his father and mother and says, “There is no transgression”—This illustrates the flatterer. A person robs his father and mother, an especially evil act: robbery is intrinsically evil, and robbing one’s parents is worse still, for instead of guarding his father’s property and honoring his father with his own money, he robs him. Nevertheless, the flatterer says, “There is no transgression,” smoothing his tongue and flattering until he declares even the gravest sin no offense. Such a flatterer is a companion to a destroyer: he is a companion of the robber who corrupted his way, and also a companion of the destroyer who comes to destroy the sinner and exact his punishment, for the flatterer caused the punishment. How, then, could he find favor?
text.27_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: A broad-souled person stirs up strife—One whose soul’s appetite is exceedingly broad and who finds no limit to his desire stirs up quarrels and complaints against God’s governance, because he does not obtain all he desires. He thinks the whole world was created to harm him and constantly protests God’s attributes. But one who trusts in the Lord, who does not crave excessively but is satisfied with what he has and trusts that God will provide what is necessary for his livelihood, will be made prosperous, for he will find his needs, as Maimonides explains regarding the verse, “God made man upright, but they sought many calculations”; see there.
text.27_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: One who trusts in his own heart is a dullard—It has already been explained that the impulse of the human heart is evil from youth, for the heart’s images incline toward desire and oppose the laws of wisdom. A person must follow the laws of wisdom, through which he escapes being trapped by the images of his heart. But one who trusts in his heart and follows wherever it inclines, according to its evil images, is a dullard, for the dullard deviates from the laws of wisdom because of his desires, as it says, “A dullard does not desire understanding, but only the revelation of his heart.” But one who walks in wisdom will escape the evil images of the heart’s impulse, for wisdom will guide him beside still waters in the struggle against those impulses.
text.27_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: One who gives to the poor—One who gives charity to the poor will suffer no lack, for because of this deed the Lord will bless him; moreover, his wealth will not diminish, for the “salt” that preserves money is giving some of it away. Conversely, one who hides his eyes from charity will not merely forfeit blessing; many curses will also be sent upon him.
text.27_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: When the wicked rise—When the wicked rise to rule, then one who is truly a man hides himself, for people deny Providence, abandon the way of the Lord, and become like beasts; the righteous man must hide from those who mock and persecute him. But when they perish, everyone afterward recognizes the Lord’s Providence and punishment, and thereby the righteous increase.
text.28_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: A man of rebukes—A person may return from sin either through rebuke or through suffering. That is, he may be shown by rational argument that his path is not good, and return through the awakening of his intellect. But if he is a man of rebukes—one who argues against and refutes the rational proofs brought to him, opposing them with disputation—then suffering may help him return from fear of punishment. If, however, he also hardens his neck, so that even when suffering comes upon him he does not turn from his wickedness, then he will suddenly be broken, beyond healing. Because he is a man of disputes he will suddenly be broken; yet if he does not harden his neck, this breaking can heal his soul, just as the body is healed by bitter medicines. If he hardens his neck, however, there is no healing.
text.28_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, because:
text.28_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: They conduct themselves with righteousness and justice;
text.28_Chapter, 1_Verse, 3_Comment: There is tranquility in their palaces;
text.28_Chapter, 1_Verse, 4_Comment: And the Lord’s blessing rests upon them.
text.28_Chapter, 1_Verse, 5_Comment: But when a wicked man rules, the people groan, because:
text.28_Chapter, 1_Verse, 7_Comment: There is neither justice nor righteousness in the country;
text.28_Chapter, 1_Verse, 8_Comment: And the Lord’s curse is upon their homes.
text.28_Chapter, 1_Verse, 9_Comment: It says, “When the righteous increase,” but “when a wicked man rules,” because:
text.28_Chapter, 1_Verse, 11_Comment: Does not rule by domination, for domination is exercised with a strong hand;
text.28_Chapter, 1_Verse, 12_Comment: Nor does he lead alone; rather, he takes counsel, and together they guide the people beside still waters. The righteous then increase, whether numerically or in abundance and greatness.
text.28_Chapter, 1_Verse, 15_Comment: And he rules alone, for he shows favor to no one.
text.28_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: A man who loves wisdom gladdens his father—If the faculty of love implanted in the soul is used properly, it will be directed toward love of wisdom, goodness, and righteousness. A man who uses love to love wisdom gladdens his father, as it says, “A wise son gladdens a father,” for afterward wisdom will enter his heart and he will become a wise son. But one who uses love to love prostitutes squanders his father’s wealth. Allegorically, if he loves external systems of wisdom—the strange, foreign, and licentious woman mentioned in this book—he will lose the soul’s wealth accumulated from the laws of wisdom. The Sages interpreted “one who associates with prostitutes” as one who says, “This teaching is pleasing and this one is not”; he loses the wealth of Torah. Such a person loves foreign women—external philosophies—and does not accept the laws of wisdom faithfully, but investigates them by his own intellect and decides which are pleasing in his eyes and which are not; he will lose his wealth.
text.28_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: A king establishes a land through justice, but a man of contributions destroys it—The king and the High Priest established the foundations of justice and righteousness. The king was appointed to establish justice in the land between one person and another, while the High Priest was charged with guarding the House of God, the service of the Lord, and instruction in Torah and mitzvot, thereby establishing righteousness in matters between man and God. When both followed the way of the Lord, they established the land. Yet sometimes the king establishes the land through justice, while the man of contributions destroys it: if the High Priest and the priests under him do not occupy themselves with guiding the people uprightly but only with receiving terumah and becoming wealthy, they destroy what the king builds. Without service of the Lord, faith, and righteousness, justice too cannot stand. Thus it says, “Remove the wicked from before the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness.”
text.28_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: A man who flatters his fellow—The Hebrew word translated “his fellow” may be read as “the injustice of his fellow.” If he smooths over his fellow’s injustice with a flattering tongue and tells him it is not an injustice, he spreads a net for his steps, wishing him to continue committing injustice until he is caught in the net. He resembles one who smooths the path along which an animal walks so that it will be caught in his trap. So too, he smooths the rough places of his fellow’s evil spiritual paths so that the man will be trapped in sin and cut off.
text.28_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: In the transgression of an evil man lies a snare—The transgression itself is the snare in which the evil man is caught. Then the righteous man sings and rejoices, because the Lord’s judgments become visible, as it says: “The nations sank into the pit they made… The Lord is known by the judgment He executes; the wicked is snared by the work of his own hands—Higgaion” (Psalms 9:16–17). Then people learn the moral lesson not to do evil.
text.28_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: A righteous man knows the cause of the poor—The righteous person is one who performs deeds of righteousness, and he knows the cause of the poor. There is a difference between a cause and a judgment: a judgment concerns a matter whose legal ruling is clear, whereas a cause consists of the arguments in a matter whose ruling is not clear. Nevertheless, the righteous person knows the proper ruling with certainty, because his engagement in righteous action enables him to recognize which side is right. The wicked person not only fails to know the disputed cause; he does not even understand knowledge. Even a clarified matter, which is called knowledge—the clear judgment—he does not understand, because in his wickedness his path is the reverse of righteousness and justice. Therefore he does not understand even a known judgment.
text.28_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Men of mockery inflame a city—Through their mockery, scoffers blow up a hot and stormy wind; they spread falsehood, slander, and heartbreak in the city. But the wise, who conduct themselves according to the laws of wisdom, know how to turn away anger. It may also mean that scoffers bring a trap, a snare, and severe judgment upon the city, whereas through the wise the Lord’s anger turns away: they awaken the people to repentance and pray to turn aside the Lord’s wrath and indignation.
text.28_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: When a wise man enters judgment with a fool—The fool is one who casts doubts upon the laws of wisdom and does not believe in them. When a wise man argues with a dullard—one who knows the laws of wisdom but deviates from them because of desire—he becomes angry with him for deliberately sinning against those laws. When he argues with a simple person, who turns from wisdom because he does not understand it, he smiles and shows him a pleasant face until he teaches him the laws of wisdom. But when he argues with a fool, on one side he becomes angry, because even after the fool understands the laws of wisdom he will not accept them, but will continue raising doubts. On the other side he laughs, because the fool does not act deliberately but from doubt, and his doubts cannot be conclusively resolved, since the laws of wisdom do not rest upon demonstrative proofs. Either way, there is no rest: the wise man cannot comfortably settle him upon the path of wisdom. Allegorically, when God seeks to return the fool through repentance, neither punishment nor added goodness will help him, because he remains in doubt and does not believe in reward and punishment at all.
text.28_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Bloodthirsty men hate the wholehearted, and the upright seek his life—Throughout Scripture, the phrase “seek his life” means seeking to kill him and nowhere denotes love, except apparently here. It is therefore better to explain that bloodthirsty men hate the wholehearted and the upright, and seek his life to kill him. Alternatively, “the upright hate those who seek his life”: bloodthirsty men hate the wholehearted person and seek pretexts to kill him, while the upright hate those who seek his life and take up the cause of the wholehearted.
text.28_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: A dullard releases all his spirit—The spirit is the faculty that raises images upon the heart, and most human images are evil, such as images of pride, jealousy, vengeance, and the like. When the spirit expands, raises these images from the soul’s depths, and storms over the surface of the heart, the activating faculty is aroused to act according to them. The dullard, who deviates from wisdom because of desire, releases all his spirit outward: he places no restraint upon it, but raises its images upon the heart and the surface of the soul and conducts himself according to them—with desire, pride, and every evil trait. The wise man, however, who follows the laws of wisdom, rules his spirit and does not allow it to rise from the depths of the soul to the surface of the heart. Rather, he quiets it behind him: he lowers the spirit that storms upward toward the surface of the soul and the eye of the heart, leaving it behind and below, unseen before him. Through the laws of wisdom, he learns to suppress evil images so that they do not rise upon the heart but remain concealed in the lower abyss of the soul.
text.28_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his servants are wicked—This statement has both an illustration and an allegory. Literally, if a ruler listens to lies, his servants strive to speak lies and slander before him and to destroy many people; they all become wicked. Allegorically, when the ruling heart follows the laws of wisdom, its servants are also righteous: the images of the soul that rise before the heart, man’s ruler, conform to the path of wisdom, and wicked impulses do not stand before it, for he quiets them behind him. But if the ruling heart listens to falsehood, the wicked servants—the evil images—rise up and stand ready to serve it by bringing before it images of desire, hatred, and an evil spirit. This continues the preceding verse, “A dullard releases all his spirit.”
text.28_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: The poor man and the man of deceptions meet; the Lord enlightens the eyes of them both—This contains both an illustration and an allegory, as stated in Midrash Shocher Tov on Psalm 7. Poverty wished to enter Noah’s ark, but Noah did not allow it because it had no mate. On the way it met Falsehood, which was going to the ark, and they married so that each would have a mate. They stipulated that whatever Falsehood produced, Poverty would take. According to this allegory, the poor man, meaning poverty, and the man of intrigues and deceit, meaning falsehood, met and married one another. The essence of the allegory is that neither deserves to endure alone, but together they endure: deception remains so that poverty and destitution may take whatever it gains through deceit. People thereby see and learn that acts of falsehood and deception do not succeed. Thus the poor man and the man of deceptions meet, and through this the Lord enlightens the eyes of them both: their eyes are opened, they cease practicing deceit, and poverty and destitution come to an end. This is the purpose of their meeting, union, and marriage.
text.28_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: A king who judges the poor in truth—The king’s throne is founded upon justice, as it says, “Behold, a king will reign in righteousness.” Sometimes a case is fraudulent and the king must investigate the truth. Then his throne will be established forever, just as truth is among the things that endure eternally.
text.28_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: The rod and rebuke give wisdom—If one strikes a youth with the rod and admonishes him with rational rebuke, this teaches him to accept the laws of wisdom. Rebuke alone does not affect the heart of a youth whose images are evil, as explained above. But a youth left unrestrained, whom no one disciplines, casts off the laws of wisdom and ultimately shames his mother for failing to educate him properly.
text.28_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: When the wicked increase, transgression increases—When wicked people increase, whether in number or in the quality of their greatness and success, transgression likewise increases, for the more numerous and powerful they become, the more they add to their offenses. Yet wickedness has a boundary and darkness an end. When transgression increases until the measure is full, they perish. The righteous will see their downfall: as soon as transgression increases, the righteous already perceive with the eye of their intellect the downfall soon to come, and afterward they see it with their physical eyes.
text.28_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Discipline your son, and he will give you rest—A father who does not discipline his son will ultimately be hated by him and have no rest from him; the Sages said how grievous it is to have an ill-bred person within one’s home, and the son certainly will not support his father in old age. But if he disciplines him, the son will not only give him rest but also give delights to his soul, for he will follow the laws of wisdom and afterward increase in love and honor toward his parents.
text.28_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Without vision, a people casts off restraint—When the last of the prophets concluded his prophecy, he said, “Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet,” and, “Remember the Torah of Moses My servant.” So long as prophecy existed in Israel, prophets came on the Lord’s missions to guide the people. But when vision was sealed, they needed to remember the Torah. Thus without vision, a people casts off restraint; then fortunate is one who keeps the Torah, for he attains happiness by observing the Torah, which takes the place of vision and prophecy.
text.28_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: A servant will not be disciplined by words, for though he understands, there is no response—A servant does not accept discipline through words. A free person has a human nature and can be disciplined by moral instruction that teaches him fear of the Lord and His punishment. But the servant’s nature is animal-like: “a whip for the horse and a bridle for the donkey,” not words. Although he is superior to an animal because he understands the matter, nevertheless there is no response: speech does not subdue him, only whip and rod. Allegorically, a person who is like a servant, serving only from fear of punishment, will not submit until punishment actually comes upon him.
text.28_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Have you seen a man hasty in his words? There is more hope for a dullard than for him—The dullard knows the laws of wisdom, but desire leads him astray from them. Nevertheless, there is hope for him: if his desire departs, he may return and recognize what he distorted, for his ideas are fundamentally ordered and he knows the truth. But one who is hasty in his words, decisively speaking error about the Lord and His Providence and disparaging wisdom, has no hope at all.
text.28_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: One who pampers his servant from youth—If a person pampers his servant and does not make him work from youth, because he is still young and lacks strength, in the end he will bring grief: the master will be defrauded by him, for the servant will always remain idle. On the contrary, he must accustom him to labor and service from youth, so that he will be worth the money paid for him. Allegorically, one who pampers the body, which is the soul’s servant, and does not make it labor in Torah and mitzvot from youth will find his hands weakened even when he grows older, for a person must accustom himself to toil from his youth.
text.28_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: An angry man stirs up strife—There is a difference between outward anger and inward wrath: wrath is the inward heat, while anger is its external expression.
text.28_Chapter, 21_Verse, 1_Comment: One who is outwardly angry but lacks inward wrath, and wishes to harm his fellow, stirs up strife: he seeks legal claims and arguments against his fellow so that he will have a justification for harming him.
text.28_Chapter, 21_Verse, 2_Comment: But one who possesses inward wrath seeks no pretense of justification at all; rather, he abounds in transgression and commits evil without any legal claim or justice.
text.28_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: A man’s pride will bring him low—One who is proud shows that he does not understand his own worth: he is a fading flower and is accounted as nothing. This very pride brings him low. But one of lowly spirit, who stands at the opposite extreme from pride, will uphold honor. This also operates as reward and punishment, as it says, “Pride precedes destruction,” etc.
text.28_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: One who shares with a thief hates his own soul; he hears the oath and does not report—Although he did not steal personally, but only shared with the thief, because he knows of the theft and does not disclose it, he too hates his own soul. When he hears the oath by which anyone knowing of the theft is adjured and placed under a curse, the oath obligates him to testify; when he does not report it, the curse falls upon him.
text.28_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: The trembling of man sets a snare—Although it said above (Proverbs 28:14), “Fortunate is the man who makes himself fearful always,” trembling denotes sudden panic, and this sets a snare, for it shows that the person does not trust in the Lord.
text.28_Chapter, 24_Verse, 1_Comment: But one who trusts in the Lord will be raised beyond danger and will not panic, as Hillel said (Berakhot 60a), “I am confident that this cry does not come from my household,” for it says, “He will not fear bad news; his heart is steadfast, trusting in the Lord” (Psalms 112:7).
text.28_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: Many seek the face of a ruler, but a man’s judgment comes from the Lord—When people face a capital judgment before a ruler, they seek his favor so that he will have mercy upon them. They would do better to seek the Lord’s favor, because a man’s judgment comes from the Lord; everything is under His Providence, and He inclines the ruler’s heart as He desires.
text.28_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous—Good hates evil and evil hates good, until the opposite path becomes an abomination to each of them.
text.29_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: The words of Agur—In this section, the men of Hezekiah copied the words of a wise man named Agur son of Jakeh, who was appointed over song; therefore his discourse is called “the burden.” Agur answered matters posed to him by sages. On one occasion he answered a sage named Ithiel, and on another he answered Ithiel and Ucal, when the two sages Ithiel and Ucal questioned him and he responded.
text.29_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: (2–3) For I am more brutish than any man—Agur’s response concerned questions these sages asked him about the world’s creation and formation and the secrets of Creation. His answer indicates that they investigated these subjects philosophically, seeking to expound what is above and below, what came before and what comes after, and advancing intellectual theories, as philosophers in every generation have done, only to come away empty-handed. Agur replied: How can they seek from him “knowledge of holy things”—those sublime truths that cannot be known through human investigation but only through Divine illumination granted to holy people? Knowledge received from God’s secret counsel to those who fear Him concerning these profound matters is called “knowledge of holy things.” How could he know such things when “I am brutish rather than a man,” etc.? We have explained that the order and levels of cognition are wisdom, understanding, and knowledge. First comes wisdom, which is not known through demonstrative proof but from God alone, who revealed the laws of wisdom in His Torah and taught them to humanity. Next comes understanding: after receiving the laws of wisdom from God, one who understands one matter from another can contemplate them, understand their reasons, and derive one matter from another. After understanding comes knowledge, meaning clear certainty like one’s knowledge of sensory facts and first principles. When a person reaches this level, the spirit of God illuminates him with knowledge of holy things—the truths concerning Divine mysteries, Creation and the Chariot, the secret of creation and governance, the connections among the worlds, and the like. Therefore, since I am brutish rather than a man—“brutish” being the opposite of knowing, as in “A brutish man does not know”—and beyond this I do not possess human understanding, which precedes knowledge, as the Sages said, “If there is no understanding, there is no knowledge,” and beyond this I have not learned wisdom, which is the beginning of them all, how could I know knowledge of holy things, the final and highest level? With each phrase he further humbled himself. There is a form of knowledge lower than all these: the simple knowledge possessed by every person of things perceived by the senses or the first principles implanted in every human intellect. One who does not know even these is called brutish, like an animal, having left the category of humanity; therefore he says, “I am brutish rather than a man.” Understanding also has a level lower than wisdom: the ordinary understanding found among many people who use their reason; therefore he adds, “I do not possess even human understanding.” He has also not learned wisdom—he has not even begun to study it. How, then, could he know knowledge of holy things, truths reserved for holy people upon whose intellect the Divine light has shone?
text.29_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Who has ascended?—That is: How could I possess knowledge of holy things so as to know who ascended to heaven and descended? His question about Creation investigated how the two first forms of prime matter from which heaven and earth were created came into being, and who set their places above and below—the places of heaven and earth. Who ascended to heaven to set the boundary of the highest height, and who descended to set the boundary of the deepest depth? He also asked, Who gathered the wind in His fists? The element of air naturally spreads wherever empty space exists; who gathered and confined it so that it remains around the globe of the earth up to the sphere of respiration, where air surrounds the earth, while above it our breathable air is no longer found, having become thinner and more refined? Who gathered it in this fashion within His fists? He further asked, Who bound the waters in a garment? Water naturally would surround and cover the entire globe; who bound it so that all the waters gather into the ocean and placed sand as the sea’s boundary so that it cannot spread, as though tied in a garment from which it cannot escape? He further asked, Who established all the ends of the earth? Who fixed the earth’s nature so that it stands upon its center, suspended upon nothing, with all its surrounding extremities drawn toward the gravity and attractive force found at its center? Clearly he arranged questions about all four elements: heaven was regarded by the ancients as the place of the element of fire, followed by air, water, and earth, the element of dust. What is His name, and what is His son’s name? The questioner philosophized according to the philosophers’ view that from the First Cause emanated a first effect, the emanated intellect, which they called the “son” of the supreme emanator.
text.29_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: If you know—That is, you wish to know and comprehend all this; or, you boast that you know it through your own intellect and investigation. But it is impossible to comprehend through human investigation, and can be known only as follows.
text.29_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Every word of God is refined—In all these investigations one must rely upon the Torah’s testimony that everything was created from nothing through the Lord’s utterance. God’s word—the Torah’s account of Creation—is refined of every impurity, while everything the ancient philosophers said about it is dross-covered silver over earthenware. The Lord is a shield to all who take refuge in Him, and they do not go astray after empty vanities and delusions.
text.29_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not add to His words by asserting ideas derived from your own intellect, lest He rebuke you by showing that you do not even know yourself—how you were created, the details of your limbs and their connections, or how the soul is joined to the body. How much less may you dare ascend the heights to speak about the structure and creation of the universe? Then you will be found false, and it will be revealed that you made falsehood your shelter and invented lies and fabrications without substance.
text.29_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Two things—Accordingly, Agur said to the Lord: I have asked two things of You; do not withhold them from me before I die the death of the soul by straying from the path of faith and following philosophers who weave spiderwebs and envision false and misleading visions.
text.29_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Remove vanity and falsehood from me—Let me not be poor in understanding, unable to comprehend anything, so that I come to believe a vain faith—things with no substance at all, like the idolaters who believed every form of foolishness and simplicity. Nor let me be so rich in intellect that I break forth into excessive investigation and produce false assertions, as investigators multiplied falsehoods to deny that the world was created from nothing. They claimed that the world is eternal like God and necessarily proceeds from Him like a shadow from the sun or the object of thought from the thinker; similarly, they denied and invented falsehoods concerning all foundations of faith. For this he gives the illustration: Give me neither poverty nor wealth. The first is intellectually poor, the second excessively rich, and both depart from faith. Rather, feed me the bread allotted to me. Allegorically, let him become wise through the wisdom of the Torah, which is the soul’s bread appointed for its perfection and life.
text.29_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Lest I become satisfied and deny because of excessive good. Allegorically, one who delves too deeply with his intellect into metaphysics may come to deny God’s existence and claim that the world is eternal and God did not create all things. And lest I become poor and steal, and seize the name of my God by swearing falsely. Allegorically, one who is intellectually poor will steal natural powers or the powers of the stars, apply the name of divinity to them, and worship idols. Therefore the middle path is best: the intellect should not breach the fixed faith of the Torah, but should believe everything taught by the Torah given from God.
text.29_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not slander—This too is Agur’s answer to the sages Ithiel and Ucal. Because these matters are extraordinary, I will explain them both literally and conceptually.
text.29_Chapter, 9_Verse, 2_Comment: (10–15) The discussion of these sages concerned political affairs and a certain king of their time and his evil government. The answer indicates that in Agur’s day there was an insolent king who denied God and led his generation in the same way. He had two wives, daughters of one mother named Alukah. These wives corrupted the people, and upon their counsel he killed and destroyed many. There was also drought and a withholding of rain, and fire consumed all the cities of the country, so that the people suffered many grave troubles. When this king took power, he removed his father from the throne, rebelled against his father and mother, and ruled in his place upon his wives’ advice. He had a maidservant named Shemamit, a woman of cunning and schemes, with whom he committed adultery. She spread her net over him until her husband—a servant of the king named Alkum—rebelled against the king, removed him from his throne, killed him, and gave his flesh to the birds of heaven. The maidservant then inherited her mistress’s place. Ithiel and Ucal learned of the rebellion and considered warning the king, so they consulted Agur son of Jakeh. He answered, “Do not slander a servant to his master”—do not inform against him—“lest he curse you and you be found guilty.” Since the servant was trusted within the royal household, the curse might rebound upon the informer: the servant could vindicate himself at trial, they might be unable to prove the charge, and they would be found guilty of falsely informing against him. Beyond this, Agur told them that the king and his generation deserved destruction, for it was (11, 13–14) a generation that curses its father. Just as the king despised his parents and removed them from their thrones, the people followed him in despising their parents. It was also a generation pure in its own eyes although unwashed from its filth and committing every abomination; a generation whose eyes were raised in pride, arrogance, and an evil path; and a generation whose teeth were swords for devouring the poor of the earth. Thus they were evil and sinful toward both God and other people, in deeds and in character. Therefore the Lord punished them: Alukah has two daughters, the king’s two wives, daughters of Alukah, who say, “Give, give!” robbing, extorting, and destroying the people. Alternatively, perhaps the women were named Hav and Hav. These two daughters—three things are never satisfied—were not satisfied with the blood of the slain while destroying the first three evil groups listed: the generation that curses its father, the generation pure in its own eyes, and the generation whose eyes are raised. The fourth group, the generation whose teeth are swords, never said, “Enough,” for the women consumed them completely—measure for measure, just as they had consumed the poor from the earth.
text.29_Chapter, 9_Verse, 4_Comment: These men, Ithiel and Ucal, who philosophized before Agur, believed in the eternity of the world or in eternal matter. They said the world sustains itself through continual generation and decay and through the four elements, which continually exchange forms, transform into one another, and mingle together. Consequently, they adopted the Epicurean view that the world follows its course without a supervisor or ruler, and mocked the service of God, saying: What profit is there in serving Him when no one supervises or accepts human service? To this Agur replied:
text.29_Chapter, 9_Verse, 5_Comment: (10–11) Do not slander a servant to his master—Do not speak slanderously about a servant who serves God, lest his Master, who exercises Providence and hears your words, curse you on this account, and you be found guilty; for the guilt of the heresy produced by your system will be rolled upon you. A generation then arises that curses its father, denying its Father in heaven and claiming that the world came into being by itself without a father who generated it—that is, without a Creator. It does not bless its mother either: even the matter from which, in its view, the world developed, it does not bless, for it calls matter a source of corruption that devours its children, destroys its offspring, and replaces them with others, in which evil overcomes good, as is known concerning the view of these heretics. According to their corrupt view they also denied the obligation to honor father and mother, saying it would have been better for a person not to have been born and that existence in this world harms him; therefore they curse the father who caused their existence.
text.29_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: A generation—They are also a generation pure in its own eyes although unwashed from its filth. They claim there is no need for deeds commanded by the Torah, nor to sanctify oneself and wash away desires and every evil trait, because in their view no Divine Torah or religion exists. They practice every abomination conceived by their desires, saying that people should conduct themselves according to the disposition of matter, its traits and properties, whatever enters their minds, and the wishes of their animal souls.
text.29_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: A generation—They are also a generation whose eyes are exceedingly raised, for they raise the eyes of their speculation to investigate matters too great and wondrous for them, expounding Divinity and metaphysics as though their intellect could comprehend everything. Even their eyelids, which close the eyes, are lifted up: they do not close their eyes or hide their faces from gazing toward God, but send their eyes into the place where darkness is His concealment and thick cloud His covering.
text.29_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: A generation—They are also a generation whose teeth are swords. Because they do not believe in a Divine Torah, Providence, reward, or punishment, they possess no civil law either. They become like the fish of the sea, where the great swallow the small, and with their teeth they consume the poor and needy.
text.29_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: (15–16) Alukah—He now explains how they deny their Father in heaven: they say the world came into being by itself through eternal matter. This prime matter, they said, has two daughters. “Alukah” may be the name of a philosopher whose system is meant, or Agur may call prime matter “Alukah,” meaning a bloodsucking creature, because matter continually sucks blood and commits slaughter by wearing away everything generated from it. It has two daughters that say, “Give, give,” three that are never satisfied, and four that never say, “Enough.” He explains: Sheol and the barren womb are the two daughters that say, “Give, give”—decay and generation implanted in matter. Sheol represents decay, while the womb’s dominion is generation, giving birth to everything. Through these two daughters everything that comes into existence is produced, because generation occurs only through decay. The three that are never satisfied are “the earth not satisfied with water”—the three elements earth, water, and air, which continually mingle and transform into one another. Air and water are known to be intermingled, for water is composed of two airy elements and contains seventy-nine parts oxygen and eleven parts nitrogen; air too is composed of them, but in a different proportion, containing less oxygen, as is known in chemistry, and they continually transform. He teaches that even dust, the third element—“earth not satisfied with water”—absorbs water together with the air contained in it, and they too transform into one another. The fourth is fire, which never says, “Enough,” the element that melts them all and is the great agent in the world’s generation and decay. According to Alukah’s system, these are the foundations of creation, together with the two daughters that say, “Give, give,” generating and destroying everything.
text.29_Chapter, 15_Verse, 1_Comment: Sheol and the barren womb—They were therefore punished through “Sheol” arising from the womb’s dominion—that is, the government of the king’s wives, whose appetite expanded like Sheol to swallow and destroy. Other providential punishments also came upon them: earth not satisfied with water refers to the withholding of rain, and fire that never says, “Enough” to the fire that consumed all their cities.
text.29_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: The eye—The king’s end will be that the eye that mocks a father—for he rebelled against and despised his father and his royal mother—will be picked out by ravens of the valley, measure for measure, because ravens likewise do not recognize their mothers. The young eagles will eat it; their traits are the opposite of the raven’s, for they recognize their young and their parents, as the Sages explained.
text.29_Chapter, 16_Verse, 3_Comment: The eye—He answers him: “An eye mocks a father”—the eye of this philosopher mocks the Father of all creation, the Lord who formed everything, and despises obedience to the mother, meaning matter created from nothing, through which God produces all later existence after the completion of the first creation from nothing, like a father who generates through a mother. They claim everything occurs by chance. Ravens of the valley will pick out that eye, measure for measure, as the Sages explained and as stated in the literal interpretation.
text.29_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment: (18–20) Three things—After relating this response, Scripture presents the discourse of parables and allegories then spoken about the new king, King Alkum, a servant who rebelled against his master and reigned in his place, and about his wife, the maidservant named Shemamit who reigned in her mistress’s place. Four parables and allegories were spoken about them. The first concerned the new queen, who had originally been a maidservant, committed adultery with the king her master, concealed her adulteries, and betrayed the king who was her companion and lover. The poets said of her that three things are too wondrous, meaning they leave no trace of their path, as though they never passed there: the way of an eagle in the air, a serpent upon the dust, and a ship in the water. In the fourth element, fire, there is likewise a phenomenon that leaves no trace: the love of an adulteress, whose flames are flames of fire. Therefore he says, “The fourth I do not know,” because its trace too is erased: “the way of a man with a maiden.” He explains that this is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats and wipes her mouth as though no fire of love had ever existed.
text.29_Chapter, 17_Verse, 3_Comment: (18–20) Three things—He shows them their error. Who implanted the power of reproduction in all living creatures, so that through mating they reproduce in their image and form, preserving all species throughout creation? The intellect cannot comprehend how this results from mating, which seemingly should leave no trace. He explains that just as each element contains actions leaving no trace—the eagle’s flight through air, the serpent’s movement upon the rock of earth, and the ship’s passage through water—so the way of a man with a maiden, operating through the heat of the element of fire, seemingly should produce no lasting trace. Indeed, we see that this is true of an adulterous woman, who eats and wipes her mouth, leaving neither union nor offspring, so that she can deny the act itself and say, “I have done no wrong.” It is therefore evident that reproduction is a work of God, who established it throughout creation. It does not arise naturally from prime matter and the mingling of the elements, but from the will of the Creator of all, who commanded and they were created and established them forever, thereby preserving the species in existence.
text.29_Chapter, 20_Verse, 1_Comment: (21–23) Under—The second parable was spoken jointly about the king and queen: under three things the earth trembles. Under a servant when he becomes king, for he had been a servant and reigned in his master’s place; and he was previously a base man who now became satisfied with bread. When a generous person has abundant bread, he shares his good with the poor, but a base person retains his baseness and increases his evil. Of the king’s wife they said, under a hated woman when she is married: she was hated because of her adultery and evil deeds, yet was possessed by the king and became his lover through an adulterous union. Worst of all is a maidservant who inherits her mistress, for she now inherits the kingdom.
text.29_Chapter, 20_Verse, 3_Comment: (21–22) Accordingly, he explained another parable: under three things the earth trembles and the pillars of the soul’s house shudder, while the fourth is worst of all. The first is under a servant when he becomes king, referring to the imagination ruling the chambers of the soul in place of the intellect. Imagination was created to serve the intellect and submit to its discipline. When it prevails in the chambers and secret places of the soul, the earth trembles, for it leads truth astray and invents falsehoods and nonexistent things. It continually casts doubt upon every faithful and established truth, or seduces hearts into believing every foolish thing. This is the level of the fool or the simple person explained in this book. The second is a base man when he becomes satisfied with bread: one who is base and has not gathered the laws of wisdom into his noble soul, but has collected base and foolish ideas and imagines himself satisfied with the bread of wisdom. This is the level of one wise in his own eyes, repeatedly discussed above, who imagines that all his deeds are wise.
text.29_Chapter, 22_Verse, 1_Comment: Under—The third is under a hated woman when she is married: a person whose soul is dominated by evil images and traits opposed to the laws of wisdom, such as anger, desire, pride, and jealousy, and who takes them as his wife in place of the beloved doe—wisdom, the woman of valor whose praises are spoken, meaning the soul’s powers governed according to the laws of wisdom. The powers of the soul corrected by wisdom are all beloved, meaning they agree with one another and with the intellect. Powers opposing wisdom are marked by hatred and mutual conflict, and therefore are called “a hated woman.” This is the level of the dullard described above: though he knows the laws of wisdom, his evil wife rules him. He has married the hated woman—desire and evil traits—and because of them deviates from wisdom. The fourth, which cannot be borne, is a maidservant who inherits her mistress: when a person abandons the Lord’s Torah and wisdom received from God, the true mistress, and chooses false philosophical opinions produced by the human intellect—the maidservant given to the mistress as a perfumer, cook, and baker. He chooses misleading syllogisms and methods with which to dispute the Torah’s laws; the maidservant inherits her mistress and drives her from her house of delights. This is worst of all: the insolent person who deliberately disputes the Torah and brings misleading arguments and syllogisms against it—“The arrogant, presumptuous man, scoffer is his name; he acts in presumptuous wrath.”
text.29_Chapter, 23_Verse, 1_Comment: (24–28) Four things—The third parable concerned Queen Shemamit. Though she was among the smallest of the earth, she prevailed through her schemes and achieved power until she sat in royal palaces. Because her name was Shemamit, they took the allegory from the spider, which seizes with its hands, weaves nets and traps to catch flies, and sits in the royal palaces it has woven for itself. So too, her heart was traps and snares; she wove nets through schemes produced from her own mind, as the spider produces its thread from its body. She sat in royal palaces—first when she caught the former king in the nets of her love, and now when she rules the land.
text.29_Chapter, 23_Verse, 2_Comment: The poet joined three other small creatures of the earth to the spider, each accomplishing great things through its strategies: ants through diligence; rock badgers through lofty construction, making rocky fortresses their stronghold; locusts through the unity of their force, marching out in companies as the whole host goes forth armed; and the spider through weaving hunting nets.
text.29_Chapter, 23_Verse, 3_Comment: The poet joined three other small creatures of the earth to the spider, each accomplishing great things through its strategies:
text.29_Chapter, 23_Verse, 5_Comment: The rock badgers, through lofty construction, making rocky fortresses their stronghold;
text.29_Chapter, 23_Verse, 6_Comment: The locusts, through the unity of their force, for they march out in companies and the whole host goes forth armed;
text.29_Chapter, 23_Verse, 8_Comment: It may also mean that she brought under her rule three nations then renowned for their strength. One nation was diligent like ants in gathering wealth, riches, and every kind of food; one built fortified cities with walls, gates, and bars; and one was a free people without king or ruler whose assembly acted by unanimous agreement, thereby displaying great strength. Shemamit caught them all in her fine nets, though they were only like spiderwebs, and sat in royal palaces ruling over them all.
text.29_Chapter, 23_Verse, 10_Comment: Four things—Corresponding to the four matters above, he says there are four living creatures that are small upon the earth, yet exceedingly wise, from which lessons of wisdom may be learned, the opposite of the four evil conditions he listed. God implanted in these four creatures traits that are superfluous to their own survival and nourishment, solely so that human beings would learn wisdom from them. Therefore the Hebrew calls them “made wise,” using the causative form.
text.29_Chapter, 24_Verse, 1_Comment: The ants are not a strong people, and an ant’s food for its entire life amounts to only a grain and a half. Yet God implanted in their nature that they prepare their food in summer, gathering and storing grain they do not need at all. This teaches human beings to gather wisdom continually, never resting throughout their lives from collecting and storing the laws of wisdom and never saying, “Enough.” This is the opposite of “a base man when he becomes satisfied with bread”—one wise in his own eyes who imagines that he has already gathered more than enough laws of wisdom into his soul.
text.29_Chapter, 25_Verse, 1_Comment: The rock badgers, though not a mighty people and capable of finding protection from enemies in earthen burrows and hollows, were given by God the nature to build their homes in strong rocks and crags. From them we learn to build the soul’s house in rocky fortresses—the intellect and its powers—not upon imagination, which lacks substance and is full of folly and doubt. “Wisdom has built her house” upon strong rocks, and the fortified house of intellect is her stronghold. This is the opposite of “a servant when he becomes king.”
text.29_Chapter, 26_Verse, 1_Comment: The locusts have no king, yet God implanted in their nature that they all march out armed and unite as one company without separating from one another. This even harms them, because it makes it easy for anyone to eradicate and destroy them. God placed this nature within them solely so that human beings would learn wisdom: all the soul’s powers should likewise march out together, bound as one, through conducting themselves according to the laws of wisdom. This is the opposite of “under a hated woman when she is married,” for powers opposed to wisdom are scattered and conflict with one another.
text.29_Chapter, 27_Verse, 1_Comment: The spider grasps with its hands and weaves weak and repulsive cobwebs drawn from its own body, though it is in beautiful and splendid royal palaces and although this will cause people to remove and kill it.
text.29_Chapter, 27_Verse, 2_Comment: God implanted this in its nature so that a person would see that corrupt opinions and cobwebs woven by his intellect through syllogisms produced from his own mind resemble a spider’s webs, though he imagines that he is weaving a lofty fortress with them. Although he is in royal palaces and possesses a strong tower in which to find refuge—the Divine Torah—people nevertheless set their own images and investigations within the King’s palaces, investigating Divinity and His palaces, the worlds He created. This brings them harm, just as the spider’s behavior causes its death; it likewise causes the soul’s death and expulsion from the palace of the King of the universe, while its paths descend to the shades. This is the opposite of “a maidservant who inherits her mistress.”
text.29_Chapter, 28_Verse, 1_Comment: (29–31) Three things—The fourth parable concerned the servant who became king, whose name was King Alkum. He was neither mighty nor a skilled schemer who knew how to ensnare the people through cunning. He merely resembled a he-goat walking at the head of the flock because he is male and his sheep are females. So too, Alkum gained power through his wife and because he was her husband. The poets said: Three things stride well. The lion rules the animals because of its might, being mighty among beasts. The greyhound rules through its swift running and skill in hunting, and rules through its loins. The he-goat is the third, and it too strides well at the head. King Alkum joins it, striding together with the he-goat, for he is like a he-goat that walks at the head of the flock not because of his virtues, but merely because he is a male with women through whom he reached the leading position.
text.29_Chapter, 28_Verse, 3_Comment: Three things stride well upon the path of the commandments, while the fourth walks well in the course of speculation and attainment of truth.
text.29_Chapter, 29_Verse, 1_Comment: (30) The lion represents the soul’s power of courage, by which it prevails like a lion over its animal nature, matter, and desires. It retreats before nothing, allowing no power of its material nature to restrain it. This is the courage required never to violate any negative commandment.
text.29_Chapter, 30_Verse, 1_Comment: (31) The creature girded in its loins is one who runs like a gazelle, swiftly and diligently fulfilling positive commandments and overcoming laziness; therefore the Sages said, “Be mighty as a lion and run like a gazelle.” Alternatively, the he-goat represents form prevailing over matter. Form is designated male in relation to the flock of ewes, the receptive material powers, and the male must walk at their head. This is the trait of boldness referred to in “Be bold as a leopard”: inward strength and the assertion of form over the other powers. King Alkum is with it: together with form goes the king—the intellect and its powers—which rules the soul’s kingdom, so that no bodily power rises against it to dispute or rebel against its rule. This is alluded to in “light as an eagle,” flying upon the lofty wings of intellect. Then a person walks well on the path of speculation and attainment of truth.
text.29_Chapter, 31_Verse, 1_Comment: If you have acted basely—He says to King Alkum, the servant who became king and the base man satisfied with bread: Did you become base through exalting yourself? You were base from the beginning. And if you schemed to rebel against your master and placed your hand upon your mouth while plotting evil in secret—know what follows.
text.29_Chapter, 31_Verse, 3_Comment: (32) If you have acted basely—Agur said to Ithiel and Ucal: If you find yourself becoming base and turning from the good path, it comes through self-exaltation, by raising yourself to investigate matters too great and wondrous for you, as you did in your questions and investigations concerning Creation and the world’s existence. And if you have devised—if you have delved into profound thoughts about these subjects—put your hand to your mouth and do not bring your thoughts outward through your lips.
text.29_Chapter, 32_Verse, 1_Comment: For the pressing of milk produces what is extracted from the milk and floats above it—butter, the milk’s best and choicest part. But what is pressed from the nose is mucus, a repulsive substance, and produces blood if pressed further, an even more repulsive substance. The pressing of anger likewise produces strife, rebellion, and contention throughout the land.
text.29_Chapter, 32_Verse, 3_Comment: (33) For the pressing of milk produces butter—What is gathered from true wisdom, of which it says, “Honey and milk are under your tongue,” produces butter—a clear and intelligible matter. But the pressing of the nose produces blood: if you extract speculative and investigative ideas from a corrupted source and misleading demonstrations, they produce corrupt syllogisms and conclusions. And the pressing of wrath—if you become angry over the Lord’s governance, as in the question of the prosperity of the wicked and the suffering of the righteous—produces contention against the Lord, as it says, “Anger kills the fool.”
text.30_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: The words of Lemuel—The book of moral instruction with which his mother admonished Lemuel, king of Massa.
